<page-type>preface</page-type>

<image-desc>A circular purple ink stamp from the "CHRISTIAN BROTHERS ST. HELEN'S" library or archive. The center of the seal contains a religious icon or figure, likely a monk or saint.</image-desc>

->*The place, time, person, and cause of the making of this book.*<-
->*The Latin title <note>original: "Silva Gadelica"</note> which is at its head has the same meaning*<-
->*as the phrase "The Treasury of the Gaels."*<-

The **PLACE** was great London of the Saxons. The **TIME** was when the age of the Lord was one thousand eight hundred and ninety-two years [1892]. The **PERSON** was Standish, son of Hayes, son of Dermot the younger O'Grady, of the Limerick tribe; though he was born in the territory of MacBrien of Ara <note>Mac Bhriain ua gCuanach</note>, specifically at the very foot of the beautiful hill of Knockgreine. The O'Gradys, moreover, who are also called the *Cinel Dungaile*, are a branch of the descendants of Aodh <note>Síl Aodha</note>, to whom belong MacNamara and many others. The descendants of Aodh themselves are a division of the *Dál gCais* of Thomond: namely, O'Grady (Ainéislis), son of Murtough, son of Edruth, son of Maelmaith, son of Grada (from whom the O'Gradys are named), son of Tresach, son of Art, son of Conn, son of Follachtan, son of Cormac, son of Sechnasach, son of Flaithri, son of Ruadghus, son of Fodalbach, son of Dúnghal (from whom the kindred is named), son of Tiopraid, son of Forannán, son of Fionán, son of Brendan, son of Eochaidh, son of Caisín, son of Cas (where all the *Dál gCais* meet), son of Conall of the Swift Horses, son of Lughaidh the Swift, son of Aonghus the Lawgiver, son of Ferchorb, son of Cormac Cas, son of Oilill Olum, son of Eoghan Mór, who was called Mogh Nuadhat.

The **CAUSE OF ITS MAKING** is the necessity of the benefit that exists at this present time for every one of the Gaels, however weak, to join together and apply themselves diligently to their day of battle <note>meaning: to make a collective effort</note>, to see if they might be able to rescue some fragment or small piece of the art and scholarship of the ancients from this point forward, without it being drowned or permanently lost; for now the day is drawing to a close, and the sweet mother tongue is almost exhausted.

Alas, after all that, there is no group on the land of Ireland, nor among the descendants of Gaedhal Glas <note>the mythical ancestor of the Gaels</note>, son of Niul, son of Fenius Farsaid, who today would be more likely to be a prominent people with even a small spark of desire for the sweet stories or the sweet history of their country. So it is, if what David O'Bruadair <note>a famous 17th-century Irish poet</note> sang two hundred years ago regarding the children of Connacht was true:

<summary>Standish Hayes O'Grady introduces his work "Silva Gadelica," providing his own lineage back to the mythical ancestors of the Irish and explaining that the book was compiled in London in 1892 to preserve the dying Irish language and its ancient literature.</summary>
<keywords>Standish Hayes O'Grady, Silva Gadelica, O'Grady genealogy, Dál gCais, Irish language preservation, London, 1892, David O'Bruadair</keywords>

->SILVA GADELICA.<-

### The Life of Ciarán of Saighir

*Beatisimus episcopus Ciaranus sanctorum Hibernie primogenitus* <note>The most blessed bishop Ciarán, firstborn of the saints of Ireland</note>; that is, Bishop Ciarán of Saighir was the first saint born in Ireland. He was from the western part of the province of Leinster, which is called Ossory. The Irish were all non-Christians and pagans at that time. Laighne was his father's name, and he was of the nobles of the Ossory people. Liadain was his mother's name, and she was from the southern part of Munster, of the Corca Laoighde <note>A tribal group in southwest Cork</note> by race. His mother saw a vision before she conceived Ciarán in her womb: as if a star had fallen into her mouth. She told the vision to the druids and the learned men of that time, and they said to her: "You will bear a miraculous son, and his fame and virtues will be great until the end of the world." After that, that holy son, Ciarán, was born. He was born and raised in Corca Laoighde on the island called Cape Clear <note>original: "Cléire"</note>. Truly, God chose him while in his mother's womb. When his name was heard throughout Ireland at that time, the spirit of Christian devotion began in Ciarán. His parents and everyone else who saw him marveled greatly at how virtuous his deeds were. He was gentle by nature, his speech was sweet, his traits were fortunate, and his counsel was instructional; and so it was with everything else that pertained to a holy person.

One day when he was on the island we mentioned—Cape Clear—he performed the first of his miracles, and he was a young child at that time. A kite <note>original: "priochaigh"</note> came above him in the air and landed in his presence; it snatched a small bird that was lying in its nest in front of Ciarán and carried it away, wounding it. Ciarán felt pity for the small bird, and he was displeased that it was in the state it was in. The kite turned back and left the small bird in front of Ciarán, half-dead and wounded; and he said

<summary>This page introduces Saint Ciarán of Saighir, the first saint born in Ireland, detailing his noble parentage, his mother's prophetic vision of a falling star, and his first miracle as a child involving a wounded bird.</summary>
<keywords>Saint Ciarán of Saighir, Ossory, Liadain, Corca Laoighde, Cape Clear, hagiography, miracles, early Irish Christianity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Life of Ciarán of Saighir," picking up immediately after Ciarán witnessed a kite snatch a smaller bird from its nest.</meta>

Ciarán [told it] to rise and be whole. The bird rose and went safely to its nest by the grace of God.

Moreover, Ciarán spent thirty years in Ireland in holiness and integrity of body and soul before he was baptized, for the Irish were pagans as we said. However, because the Holy Spirit inhabited His own servant in Ciarán, he lived in devotion and perfect manners during all that time.

He heard at that time a report of Christian devotion being in Rome <column-break/> and he left Ireland and went to Rome. He was baptized in Rome and was taught in the Catholic faith. He was there for twenty years reading the divine scripture, collecting his books, and learning the rule of the Church. And when the Roman people saw the wisdom, cleverness, devotion, and faith of Ciarán, he was ordained in the Church. After that, he reached Ireland, and on the way in Italy he met Patrick, the archbishop of Ireland. When they saw each other—that is, the people of God—they shared great joy and happiness. And Patrick was not a bishop at that time, though he was afterwards.

*Celestinus* <note>Pope Celestine I</note> made him a bishop and then sent him to preach to the Irish. For although there were other saints in Ireland before Patrick, God reserved the mastery and the archbishopric for him until he arrived. And their kings and lords did not believe through anyone else until his coming.

Patrick said to Ciarán: "Go before me to Ireland, and you will find a well at the boundary of the northern part and the southern part of it, in its center, and build a monastery for yourself at that well. Its name is Uarán <note>A cold spring or fountain</note>. It is there your honor and your resurrection shall be forever." Ciarán answered and said: "Describe for me the place where that well is." Patrick said to him: "The Lord will be with you; move straight ahead and take my little bell with you. It will remain silent until you reach the well we mentioned. And when you reach it, the bell will speak with a clear, sweet voice, and you will recognize the well in that way. And at the end of twenty-nine years, I will follow you to that place."

They blessed and kissed each other, and Ciarán went on his own way toward Ireland, while Patrick remained in Italy. Ciarán's bell remained silent until he came to the place where the well was that Patrick spoke of, namely Uarán. For upon his coming...

<keywords>Ciarán of Saighir, Saint Patrick, Rome, Uarán, Irish Christianity, Pope Celestine, miracles, bell of Ciarán</keywords>

<page-num>514], 3</page-num>
# Betha Chiaráin tSaighre.

God directed Ciarán in Ireland to that well, and upon reaching it, the little bell spoke quickly with a bright, clear voice. It is called Ciarán’s *barcán* <note>a small bell</note>. It remains now as a sign in the parish and city of Ciarán, and it is carried throughout the surrounding lands to be used for swearing oaths between kings to ensure the truth is kept. It is also brought to fulfill the needs and benefits of the successors of Ciarán’s monastery for the general public. It was made by Bishop Germanus, the master of Patrick, and it was he who gave it to Patrick.

That well we mentioned is located on the boundary of two divisions of Ireland: Munster, the southern division, and <unclear>....</unclear> the northern division. However, the land called Eile is in Munster. Ciarán began to live as a hermit in this place, for it was surrounded by great woods at that time. He began at first by making a small cell of humble workmanship; then, by the grace of God, he began a monastery and finally a city which is commonly called Saighir Chiaráin <note>Seir Kieran</note> by everyone. When Ciarán first arrived there, he sat in the shade of a tree, and a very fierce wild boar rose up from the other side of the tree. When she saw Ciarán, she fled, but she returned again as a gentle servant to Ciarán, having been made tame by God. That same boar was Ciarán’s first disciple and first monk in that place. She went, indeed, to the wood and cut wands and thatch between her teeth to help with the cell. There was no person with Ciarán at that time, for he came alone from his disciples to that hermitage. Afterward, irrational animals came to Ciarán from every direction of the wilderness: a fox, a badger, a wolf, and a doe. They were gentle toward Ciarán and obeyed his teaching like monks, and they did everything he told them.

One day, the fox, who was greedy, crafty, and malicious, came for Ciarán’s shoes; he stole them and left the community, going ahead to his own cave where he intended to eat the shoes. When this was revealed to Ciarán, he sent another monk of his community—the badger—to find the fox and bring him back to the same place. The badger came to the fox’s cave and found him eating the shoes, for he had already eaten their "ears" <note>the flaps or loops</note> and their laces. The badger compelled him to come with him to the monastery, and they came...

# The Life of Ciarán of Saighir

In the evening, they came to Ciarán and brought the shoes with them. Ciarán said to the fox: "O brother, why did you commit that theft, which was not becoming of a monk to do? And you had no need to do that, for we have pure water in common and we have food likewise. If, however, your nature drove you so that you thought it better to eat meat, God would have made it for you from the bark of these trees around you." The fox then asked Ciarán for forgiveness for his sin and to impose a penance upon him. It was done so, and the fox did not eat food until he received permission from Ciarán; and from then on, he was righteous like the others.

It was after this that Ciarán’s own disciples came to him along with many others. He then began to build a splendid monastery, and those animals remained in their service from then on with Ciarán, for they were pleasing to him. After that, the Christian faith grew in Ireland. There were three most holy bishops in Ireland before Patrick’s arrival there: namely, <term>Ailbe</term> of Emly, Bishop <term>Ibar</term>, and <term>Declan</term> in his own land and territory in the <term>Déise</term> of Munster. And the holy Ciarán converted many people of his own territory, the <term>Osraighe</term> <note>Ossory</note>, to the Catholic faith.

It was after this that the glorious archbishop Patrick came to Ireland from Pope <term>Celestinus</term>. Through him, all of Ireland was full of the faith and Christian baptism. Then a maiden came to Ciarán, and he made a Christian of her and a true servant of God. Ciarán built a small, honorable cell for her near the monastery, and he gathered other holy virgins around her. Among them was the most choice virgin named <term>Bruinnech</term>, who was the daughter of a noble lord of Munster. She was dearly and fervently loved by Ciarán’s mother, and she was a foster-child to <term>Liadain</term>, and she was noble in her manners.

When, however, the chieftain of the <term>Uí Fhiachrach</term> heard the report of the beauty of the maiden we mentioned, he came with large bands of kerns <note>Irish light infantry</note> and took her away by force. His name was <term>Díoma</term>. She was with him in his castle for a long time; he slept with her and loved her greatly. Ciarán came to Díoma to ask for the maiden, but Díoma did not consent to let her go. He said, moreover, that he would not let her go at all unless it were the voice of a crane that should waken him from his sleep the following morning. And it was a season...

# The Life of Ciarán of Saighir
<meta>515]</meta>

It was winter at that time, and a great snow fell there; yet in the place where Ciarán was with his disciples, not a single bit of snow fell. On the following morning, even though it was against nature, <column-break/> a heron spoke on the top of every single house that was in the fortress. When Díoma heard that, he came quickly to where Ciarán was. He fell on his knees before him and released the girl. She was pregnant at that time, and Ciarán did not like it. He placed the sign of the cross on the girl's womb, and the pregnancy vanished; then he took her with him to her own cell, which is called <term>Ceall Liadain</term>.

However, Díoma was greatly bound by love for the girl, and he regretted letting her go, so he came again to take her back with him. Nevertheless, God acted according to the will of three people—namely Ciarán, his holy mother, and the girl herself—so that as he was coming to the town, Bruinnech died. Díoma thought this was an evil thing, and he said to Ciarán: "Why did you kill my wedded wife?" he said. "For she knew no man before me, and I bound her to me as a wedded wife. For that reason, your dwelling shall not be in this place, for I will drive you out." Ciarán said: "Those powers by which you would do that, or anything else, do not come from yourself; rather, God gives power to you like an earthly shadow for as long as He pleases. Therefore, I will not leave my place for you, but I will stay here whether you like it or not." 

When Díoma heard that, he departed with great anger and made a threat against Ciarán. Then a misfortune from God came upon Díoma in revenge for his lawlessness. For when he came to his castle, he found it on fire, along with the houses that were around it. He had a beloved son, and he had forgotten him in the house while he was sleeping in Díoma’s bed. When his nurse saw that it was not within any person's power to rescue him from the fires, she said in a loud voice: "I bestow you, my dear son, to Ciarán of Saighir, and I place you under his protection." Nevertheless, after the fires fell and the places were destroyed, the child was found completely healthy, as if he were still asleep. 

When Díoma saw that, he went to where Ciarán was, and the bishop named <term>Edus</term> went with him. He took a spark of repentance from Ciarán and gave his two sons to him—namely <term>Donnchad</term>, the son who was himself saved from the fires, and another son—along with their seed and their offspring after them, including the monastery, its rents, and burial rights. And Díoma returned to his own place with joy and with...

# The Life of Ciarán of Saighir
<page-num>6</page-num>
<meta>[515 b</meta>

Ciarán's blessing. Ciarán, however, was displeased that his pupil should depart from the world so soon; and he knew that Díoma would not commit any further violence against him from then on. He went to where the girl’s body was and <column-break/> prayed to God for her sake, so that she rose from death and lived for a long time afterward.

Another day, the steward he had for the work of the monastery came to Ciarán and said, "We are in need of pigs," he said. Ciarán said, "Just as God gives us every other thing, He will give pigs." On the next day, a very large sow with twelve pigs came to the craftsmen, and many pigs descended from them after that.

Another day, the same man asked Ciarán for sheep. Ciarán said, "He who gave us pigs will give sheep." And upon the steward going out, he saw twenty-eight white sheep on the lawn eating grass. He brought them with him, and many sheep descended from them.

There was a powerful man named Fionntan in that land, and he brought his dead son to Ciarán to be restored to life. Laogaire was the son's name. After Ciarán performed prayers to his Lord, the boy rose from death and lived for a long time afterward. In gratitude for that, that man gave the land named Ráth Feráin to Ciarán and to his successors forever.

After that, Patrick, the preacher of the Irish, came to the King of Munster, Aonghus son of Nadfraoch; and he believed in God and in Patrick, and Patrick baptized him.

At that time, a person of the <term>Síl Duach</term> from the territory of Ossory came and intentionally killed Patrick's horse. He was seized by the king's people and placed in bonds without delay to be put to death. His friends pleaded with Ciarán on his behalf, and he came to the king and gave a wealth of gold and silver for him. The man was released to his own country, and after he had departed, the treasure turned to nothing. The king was filled with anger because of this; he summoned Ciarán to him and asked why he had given him a "useless benefit"—that is, false things—on behalf of the guilty man he held. Ciarán said, "All wealth comes from nothing and to nothing it shall go." The king became angry and made a threat against Ciarán. ...in the presence of everyone. Carthach, a pupil of Ciarán, was present at that time, and he was related to the king. He pleaded with Ciarán on the king's behalf. It came to pass through the prayers of Carthach and many others that Ciarán enlightened <column-break/> the king's eyes and he was restored to health. Indeed, it appeared to many people that the king had been dead, and that Ciarán had performed a resurrection from the dead. Upon the king's recovery, he gave many alms to Ciarán and gave thanks to God.

Aonghus had excellent harpers at that time, and they were very musical, performing poetry and playing their harps. One day they were traveling through <term>Múscraighe Tíre</term> in the province of <term>Muman</term> <note>Munster</note>, and they were killed there by their enemies. Their bodies were hidden in a lake near the plain where they were killed, and their harps were hung in a tree on the bank of the lake. Aonghus was saddened by this, and he was troubled that he did not know what had happened to them. He knew that Ciarán was full of the grace of the Holy Spirit, and he came to obtain knowledge from him as to what had happened to the harpers; for he did not wish to ask his druid because he had accepted the faith of Christ.

Ciarán said to him: "Your harpers were killed secretly," he said, "and their bodies were hidden in a lake near the place where they were killed, and their harps were hung in a tree on the bank of the lake." The king asked Ciarán to go with him to the lake so that they might find the bodies and retrieve them. They went to the lake, and Ciarán performed a <term>tréidhenas</term> <note>a three-day fast</note> so that the bodies might be recovered. Upon finishing the three-day fast, the water of the lake receded so much that there was no covering left over them. They were retrieved and brought before Ciarán, and he offered prayers to God so that the dead rose in the presence of everyone, just as if they had only been sleeping. There were eight of them in number, and they had been in the lake for a full month. They took their harps from the tree as Ciarán instructed them and performed pleasant music in the presence of the king, Ciarán, and everyone gathered there. There was such sweetness in that music that a great number of the host fell asleep from it, and glory and praise were given to God and to Ciarán. As for the lake in which they were drowned, the water never rose in it again, except that it is called "The Lake of the Harpers" to commemorate that miracle. After receiving the blessings of the king and the harpers, Ciarán returned to his own city.

The king turned back from that stream and departed to his own land once he saw that the stream, which had been easily crossed by his armies before that, had risen up against them. Another time, large bands of robbers from other lands came to the borders of Munster to plunder and kill people. A nobleman of Munster named <term>Lonán</term> caught up with them, and the outlaws took to flight. When they saw that it was impossible for them to escape in any way, they prayed to Ciarán to save them from that peril. And when Lonán and his people intended to capture and kill them, a thunderbolt fell between them and the robbers. Great fear seized Lonán and his people, and they did not pursue them any further but returned to their own home. The robbers recognized that it was Ciarán’s miracles that had saved them. They came to him and told him their story, and they decided to put on religious habits and serve God and Ciarán from then on. That resolution was fulfilled by them, and they remained under Ciarán’s direction in good works and piety until they died.

Another day, a thief came from the province of Leinster and stole a very fine cow that belonged to Ciarán’s monks. His name was <term>Cairbre</term>. As he was going toward <term>Slieve Bloom</term>, a mist and darkness fell so that the path was not visible to him; he fell into a river and was drowned. The cow returned to Ciarán and the monks again.

His company was very cold, for it was snowy weather. Old Ciarán went out and stretched his hand toward God with fervent prayers. Another day, a brother of Ciarán’s named Báithín came and accidentally extinguished the fire again through negligence. He performed penance and received absolution. That day, Ruadhán of Lorrha came to the settlement to visit Ciarán. There was no fire in the monastery while the guests were there. Ciarán went to a stone that was near him and blessed it. When Ruadhán and his disciples saw that, they gave glory and praise to God and to Ciarán.

The brother we mentioned, that is, Báithín: he spilled a vessel of milk that he was carrying, and Ciarán placed the sign of the Holy Cross upon the vessel, and it was full. The brother who had spilled the milk and a group of the other brothers were filled with awe of their master, Ciarán; and they were strengthened in faith and in good works afterward.

One day Ciarán was praying to his Lord, and an angel came and revealed to him that the time of his death was very near. He asked for three petitions from God in the presence of the angel, and he received what he asked for from the angel, as they were promised to him by God: the first petition of these was that every person who should be buried in his city and in his own graveyard would not have the gates of hell closed upon them after the Day of Judgment. The second petition was that whoever should give honor to his own day <note>his feast day</note> would not lack worldly wealth and would have heaven hereafter. The

# Betha Chiaráin tSaighre.
<meta>[520 b</meta>

The third petition: that the people to whom he himself belonged, namely the people of **Osraige** <note>Ossory</note> of whom he was the patron, should never be defeated in battle by a foreign people who might come unlawfully to seize their own territory from them; and that they themselves should not go to make an unjust conquest in another land.

This holy person of whom we spoke, namely **Ciarán of Saighir**, was very humble in every place, and he loved to hear, read, and learn the divine scripture until the time of his death. It is told that he was with the saints of Ireland in his own time at the school of <term>Finnian of Clonard</term>, and that he reached a mature age and great holiness in that school. He was called a pupil of Finnian, as was said of other saints of Ireland. Even when he was of an advanced age and great wisdom, and had been perfectly instructed (as we said) and was an honorable bishop, he still thought it fitting to continue learning while teaching others, out of love for humility and wisdom.

Furthermore, from his youth until the time of his death, Ciarán never drank any beverage that would intoxicate him, nor did he wear downy or soft clothing. He never indulged in feasts, never slept his fill, and never participated in revelry or worldly drinking in any place. He converted his own people, the **Osraige**, to the faith, along with many others. He was frequently visited by angels and ordained a great number of bishops, priests, and other orders of the church. An angel revealed a sacred well to him, and many diseases and illnesses are healed by that well; its name is <term>Tobar Ciaráin</term> <note>Ciarán's Well</note>.

Ciarán spent thirty years diligently serving God before his baptism. Eventually, as he was weakened by old age and illness, the days of his death drew near. He summoned his people and parishioners from every direction and blessed them. He commanded them to keep the commandments of God, and then, amidst choirs of saints on the third *nonas* <note>the 5th</note> of the month of March, he received the sacraments of the Church. In the peace of Christ, he bid his people farewell. By God’s permission, thirty bishops whom he himself had ordained went with him on that same night to the kingdom of Heaven.

The end of the Life of Ciarán, written by Muiris O'Connor, a shipwright in Cork.

Specifically, his kindred are witnesses; for it is clearly signify by those two pure genealogies that, through his customary descent, he was nobly ordained throughout all Ireland as the subject of a high saint from the two high hearths of the sovereignty of Ireland: namely, from Cashel and from fair Tara, as the poet said in testimony:

> Noble Molaise of the miracles, son of Nadfráich, was a leader of hosts;
> half of him from Cashel of the hundreds, half (it is no lie) from Tara.

Furthermore, Patrick, the eminent and sweet-praying, prophesied the good, red-flaming light of Western Europe: that is, miraculous Molaise son of Nadfráich, thirty years before his birth, when the chief prophet came to Beinn Osnadh. The poet spoke this testimony, confirming the prophecy of the <term>Táilgenn</term> <note>The "Adze-head," a traditional nickname for St. Patrick</note>:

> Welcome, guest of many virtues, constant sun, chaste and pure-bright;
> devout, pious, and merciful, a gentle and truthful guardian. ||
> At the end of sixty great years, miraculous Molaise shall be born;
> in the oak-wood of many blessings, the true cleric shall be full of miracles.
> The saints of Ireland without dispute, they shall be very joyful at this;
> because of the fervor of his deep devotion, and for the strength of his fighting faith.
> Little trouble in this world, great is his importance as a lord;
> he will be a faithful heir, I say to him: Welcome.

Molaise’s mother, moreover, saw a vision in the night: that she found seven fragrant apples, and of the apples she took in her hand, the last one was so large her palm could not enclose it. It seemed to her that gold was not more beautiful than that apple. She tells this vision to her husband. "I understand that," said the man, "and you will bear a wonderful and eminent child, of whom the mouths of the men of Ireland will be full, and he will surpass his contemporaries."

Nevertheless, the time of birth for Molaise’s mother arrived, and the pangs of labor seized her. The druid said to her: "If you can delay your child from being born until the sun rises tomorrow, he will be famous, and he will be a great, miraculous, righteous, and truly noble dignitary; and the good child you shall bear, O woman, will be a birth of profit and healing for the western world." And he said:

> Tomorrow if you bear a son, O Monoa <note>The mother of Molaise</note>, he will be a saint with power;
> he will be a man of great deeds thereafter, he will be famous over the ridge of the world.
> He will be a shield of protection for every group against the immense pains of hell;
> a man without accusation or fault, his rule will not be too soft.
> He will go to Rome, the grace of the divisions, for the good of the men of Ireland;
> he will bring, as is heard from the east, holy soil and treasures remarkably. ||
> He will be the "white one" of lawful judgments; how good are his tributes and his fines:
> because of the greatness of his wisdom that was known, his fear will be in every kind of knowledge.
> Happy are you, O fair woman, and understand what is in your destiny:
> if you struggle in that battle [of labor], and do not bear the son until tomorrow comes.

The true God delayed the birth in Monoa’s womb until he was brought forth in a high pasture <note>The word *airidh* refers to a shieling or mountain pasture</note> under a stone slab at sunrise the next morning. He was brought to Bishop Eocho to be baptized and blessed, and it was he who later conferred the first holy orders upon him, as it was said:

> Angelic Bishop Eocho baptized miraculous Molaise;
> from him he truly received holy orders; the King of Kings was eternally grateful for it.

The grace of the Holy Spirit was clearly evident in Molaise’s company, for he spoke and praised the Lord just a month after his birth, fulfilling the words of the psalmist, as was said:

> As the psalm says *ex ore infantium* <note>Latin: "out of the mouths of babes" (Psalm 8:2)</note> without fear:
> one month after Molaise's birth, he praised the King of the fair rain of grace.

He would not swallow rich food, nor unholy food, nor any kind of food obtained by theft. If he were fed such things against his will, he would vomit them up immediately. Furthermore, every increase in Molaise’s physical growth was matched by the growth of his humility, nobility, diligence, and integrity, as Christ said:

> He who exalts himself and does not obey,
> his dwelling shall be lowly, and he shall be locked in pain.

Molaise pursued his studies until he became a highly learned sage and a miraculous chief monk. He kept nothing for himself; instead, whatever he received, he gave to the poor and to || God’s helpless ones for the love of his Maker and Creator, following the example of the psalmist, who said *dispersit, dedit pauperibus* <note>Latin: "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor" (Psalm 112:9)</note>:

> For God’s sake, he gave fervent charity to the poor at all times;
> guidance to the ignorant from his dwellings, and clothing to the naked constantly.

Another miracle of Molaise’s occurred when one of his monks mixed meal with water and prepared a loaf of bread, but he had no fire and complained of this to Molaise. Molaise said to the monk, "Bring two firebrands to me." The firebrands were then brought to Molaise, and he breathed upon them until they blazed like torches. This was a wonder to the monks, and though they were amazed, they were pleased. "O dear sons," said Molaise, "that which is difficult for men is easy for God," as it was said:

> If every person believes faithfully and rightly in the God of the elements,
> every path shall be easy for them, and they shall reach the mysteries of the King of Heaven.

Miraculous Molaise, moreover, spent the forty days of Lent with his monks without consuming a morsel, a drink, or any food in the world.

# The Life of Molaise of Devenish

...except for the fruits of trees and the plants and herbs of the earth. He observed another Lent, however: forty days with his monks without any kind of food at all, except for a palm-full of the steward’s barley grain for each monk from one midday to the next, as was said:

> Lent for Molaise and his monks was on the fruits of the earth and trees;
> without food that any person on earth tasted, for fear of the Lord of the elements.
> He and his monks had another Lent, for the love of the Lord who departed;
> for every man of them there was a portion || of food: a palm-full of pure grain.
> Their anxiety in the world was small, and they did not fulfill the desires of the weak;
> great was the power of their prayer-hours in their oratory, for the love of the Lord who departed.

Once, two lepers came as guests to Molaise at a time when he had no specific food. He called his steward to him and said: "Give them their fill of drink and food." The steward replied: "I have neither little nor much food." "Go into the pantry," Molaise said to the steward, "and you will find in it two loaves with their accompaniment of butter, two portions of fish, and two vessels full of milk." The steward went and found the pantry just as the saint had said, and then gave the poor men their fill, as was said:

> Once for Molaise, who did not desire death—a man who lived without boastfulness until death—
> he saw two lepers coming to him; they asked there for good sustenance.
> He called the steward without fault and said to him: "Give them food;
> do not let the two poor ones go from you until their needs are met tonight."
> "It is not their needs that I would be reluctant to meet," said the steward inside,
> "but I myself am without food to eat, as my King in heaven knows."
> "Go into the pantry, steward," said Molaise, who deserves his prayer-hours;
> "you will find in it, according to your honor, your fill of food and drink."
> Two loaves that were not small in estimation, with their accompaniment truly;
> two bare cups and two portions of fish he found on a dish from the King of kings.
> The two poor men were fed by him with the food of paradise, as was || proper;
> they were satisfied, cheerful, and grateful; for them the journey was not difficult.

Another time, the men of Ireland were under the sorrow of death and mortality in their distress from the Yellow Plague <note>The *buide Conaill* or Yellow Plague was a major epidemic in 7th-century Ireland</note>, after it brought a massive slaughter upon the nobles of Ireland. During this time, Diarmaid and Blathmac, the two kings of Ireland, died, along with Feichín of Fore, Oilerán the Wise, and many of the nobles of Ireland. Those who died there exceeded number and comparison, reason and memory. According to some, one out of every three men in Ireland died; others say that two-thirds of the men of Ireland died there. The men of Ireland took counsel as to how that plague might be warded off from them, and they all agreed to perform a fast of a day and a night with Molaise and with God for their help and relief, as the poet said:

...a three-day fast of diligent service. The tribes made a complete decision; the diseases of the people remained. The nobles of Ireland prayed to him; they beseeched the high, ordained saints. Welcome, Molaise of the miraculous deeds! From him comes your strong help. Seek a fixed tribute for the sake of your protection. The Yellow Plague will be weakened by the holy, powerful, and pious man. God, the good helper, has removed the affliction from Ireland through his bright and pure saints. He performs many miracles for the people diligently; they reckon a three-day fast.

In short, the men of Ireland fasted with Molaise, and Molaise fasted with his God until they found relief and help from 그 plague. Consequently, the men of Ireland gave a <term>screball</term> <note>A silver coin or scruple</note> from every household to Molaise, provided there were at least three people in the household. They also gave an ox of three hand-spans from every king of a <term>trícha cét</term> <note>A territorial unit or "thirty-hundred" district</note>, and the riding horse of every provincial king, as well as the horse of the King of Ireland and his battle-dress. These were to be fulfilled every Lammas to Molaise, his relics, and his people honorably after him forever. As the poet said:

> A dangerous plague of hideous disease brought great loss to the men of Ireland:
> the Yellow Plague of hard wounds was a great distress to men and to women.
> Two-thirds of the men of Ireland perished; it was a cause of great fear;
> those who remained alive were trembling and out of their minds.
> They fasted with the son of miraculous Nadfráich, with Molaise of pure intention;
> Molaise fasted with the Son of Mary to turn back the Yellow Plague.
> Then the men of Ireland found help through Molaise of the relics;
> they gave to Molaise afterward a tribute without dispute for his sake.
> A silver coin from every single household throughout Ireland as a regular fulfillment;
> a cow or a horse from the king of every district—misfortune upon him if he should refuse it forever.
> A riding horse from the king of every province, the gear of the horse of the King of Ireland himself;
> every year fulfilling the duty to them on account of the powerful plague.

After that, the sons of Declán came to visit Molaise, and he asked them to write the gospels for him. They wrote all the gospels in two days and a night, and the light did not fail them during that night, but rather it was just like every day. Molaise’s fame was greatly magnified through that miracle <gloss>miracle</gloss> indeed. He went to hell with a cloak of badger skins around him, and from that, he is named the <term>Brocainech</term> <note>Badger-faced or Badger-mantled</note>, which is one of the good relics of Molaise. He also held a small leather strip in his hand to summon the druid, namely Manann the leper, so that God brought him out of hell with his three times fifty namesakes along with him. As the poet said:

> Molaise brought three times fifty Mananns from hell without false boasting;
> summoning dear Manann the druid on the edge of the terrible hell.
> He did not leave any of the Mananns behind until the judgmental Day of Doom;
> they shall be without conflict or sin, and the devil shall have no power over them.
> Great was the honor that the God of the right hand gave to Molaise without deceit or trickery;
> good was the result in every place, as every fifty sang.

# The Life of Molaise of Devenish
<page-num>22</page-num>

One day Molaise was naked, bathing in water, and even if there were ice upon it, it did not stop him. No one, however, dared to look at him in that state, for his skin was merely clinging to his bones, because he ate no food at all for a week, and even then, only as much as another might eat in a single night. A monk among his monks came upon him. Molaise did not like this and said to him: "Do not do that again, and do penance for the deed you have done." "I will do as you command," said the monk. "Come into this water then," said Molaise. "I will go," said the monk. But the monk had not been there long when he said to Molaise: "I cannot endure the water because of its great intensity and its coldness." "If that is what you say," said Molaise, "come into this other water." Then the monk went into that water. He was there only a short time when it felt too hot to him, and he said: "Lord, help me, for I cannot endure these hardships. It is clear to me that God’s grace is in your company, and we will do nothing that you might forbid." Molaise blessed the water so that it was temperate, between cold and heat. It is certain that the elements were tempered for Molaise according to his will and were humble according to their nature, as the poet said:

---

> God’s elements, oh God’s elements, served Molaise of the pure appearance:
> fire, earth, air, and water, obeyed the man of understanding.
> Gentle light, oh gentle light, he could make darkness like the sun:
> he made darkness of the bright day; his path was toward the King of Wonders.
> Ice on water in the summer, boiling upon it in the winter as he commanded:
> he does not let his friend suffer pain, and every element was subject to him.

---

One night, while Molaise and his monks were eating their dinner, they saw the roof of the house on fire, with its flames boasting of their height. The monks intended to leave the house for fear of being burned. "Be still," said Molaise. "Bow your heads and bend your knees and be ready for death; leave it between me and the fire, and let none of you look up." The monks did so, and they were there only a short time afterwards when the ridge-pole of the house fell to the ground in front of them, and yet the fire did no harm to them except for that. "Understand, my dear brothers," said Molaise, "that your patience is clear to God, and you are God’s chosen children. Rise up, for God has saved us from the fire." As the poet said:

---

> When Molaise and his monks were dining yonder in the house:
> they saw there, as it twisted, a fire blazing up in the house.

# The Life of Molaise of Devenish
<page-num>23</page-num>

The monks of the son of Nadfráich of the miracles attempted to flee through every door, but Molaise said to them: "Stay; do not dare to go beyond my rule. Bow your heads to the gracious King; let your knees touch the ground. I will save you, on behalf of the King of the Sun, from the trials of pain and plague." They all believed what he said—a chaste company that spoke little. He told them no lie, and without fault, the ridge-pole of the house fell to the ground. The blaze of the fire was suppressed; Molaise diminished its power. The monks believed greatly that they had received help from the King. God’s name was magnified on that occasion; Molaise was miraculous in his time. He never ate a portion nor gave a gift that the Lord did not understand as it truly was.

Another time, Molaise was in the house of a good king among the kings of Ireland when fire broke out in the house so that it could not be saved. Molaise blessed the house and stretched out his hands in a cross-vigil, and the fire burned only three rafters inside. The name of that place today is Druim Cleathchóir. The king offered that place to God and to Molaise from then on forever. One day, Molaise happened upon a synod of clerics who had a fine book of laws with them. He wished to copy something from it, but he had no pen, and neither did anyone in the <note>ms. gun (without)</note> company. Molaise saw a flock of birds flying above them and he stretched out his hand toward them. A feather fell from them to him, and he used it to copy the book afterward, as it was said:

->The bird gave its feather to Molaise of the firm faith; when God saw that what he asked for His honor was just.<-

Once, while Molaise was traveling through the territory of Cairbre with a group of his clerics, he saw a woman milking and asked her for a drink of fresh milk for his servant. The woman said: "I will not give the milk to the servant alone, but to all of you." "That is better," said Molaise. "If that is so, my lord," said the woman, "I have been a barren woman until now; help me and pray for me so that I might conceive a child." "Call your husband to us then," said Molaise, "and let him take my cup to the well and bring it back to us full of water." Then the water was brought to Molaise’s hand; he blessed and consecrated the water and gave it to the woman to drink. "Be certain, woman," said Molaise, "that you will be pregnant from this moment on, and you will bear a good, miraculous, saint-like, and righteous son. God the Creator and all the saints of Ireland will grant him immense honor and full respect. His first name will be Mac na Creatra <note>literally "Son of the Consecrated Vessel"</note>, after the vessel and the consecration I performed upon the water; and his name hereafter shall be the truly noble Bishop Finnachadh."

...forever. "I welcome him and rejoice at his coming," and he spoke these words:—

I welcome a true vision: a sun shall rise above the constant stars; a great and victorious sage shall come here, the son of the powerful holy one. His first name is the yoke of the hard-devout: Bishop Finnchad of the true miracles—the proper name of that good saint. His true dwelling shall be an illustrious church at the head of the mountain of the old paths. Warriors shall not dare to harm him, nor shall hosts of many seekers attempt to outrage him. I leave to them and to those who truly attack him that they shall not live for a single year after returning from their malice.

Molaise then blessed Bishop Finnchad while he was in his mother's womb and said: the saints of Ireland and the Creator of the elements would grant him great honor, reverence, and protection. He himself would be the fifth high saint in his place, protecting them and fulfilling every request asked of him, avenging any outrage against him and repaying every evil and injustice done to him <column-break/> against him. Short life and hell to his attackers; heaven to his successor, provided he does not violate his honor or diminish his dues. As he said:—

> A victorious child is in your womb, O woman; welcome the son of the chaste holy one. You shall bear a noble bishop with success; your pregnancy will not be a cause of shame for you.
> At the head of the great red mountain of games, there shall be a path for a great host. Though the bed on which his side rests be hard, he will serve God humbly.
> All the saints of Ireland from every place will come under the fame of a just cause. They will obtain their will without fail from Bishop Finnchad of the miracles.
> They will all be around the cool yew tree on the north side after their prayers. The pure, clear-voiced company comes to recite their lessons as was customary.
> The berries of the clear-topped tree will fall down into the laps of the saints. Each one takes his blood-red berry—a company that was not prone to anger or hardship.
> I ask of you, Bishop Finnchad, a gift that is not difficult for you: that the berries be placed in my cemetery, so that they may be a single secret place without separation.
> We will give you what you ask, a fitting gift, not a false sight. We will put the round berries for you without anger, so that they might become a yew tree.
> "The Yew of the Saints" is its original name, a name given by the miracle-worker of <term>Leath Cuinn</term> <note>The northern half of Ireland</note>. This dwelling shall not be sought after; its like is not on land or sea.
> Decay to the land of the one who cuts the wood of the Yew of the Saints with force. I proclaim strongly according to the rule, that his grave shall be ready by the end of a year.
> Five are the founders of that place, true saints without reproach from God. A long time awaits their enemy, though he who came there was no more.
> Beoith, Molaise, and Moedhóg, Bishop Finnchad, and the priest Fraoch: miraculous ones watching over the place, whose duty is to guard it against every trial. <column-break/>
> The saint will be under the stone, flaming in the center of the place where he is taken. He will not be challenged by many; blessed is the place where he was born.

In short, Molaise was made famous for the perfection of his age and for the renown of his faith, his piety, his wisdom, and his knowledge.

He went to Finnian of Clonard, as did all the other apostles, so that he might read the Gospel there. After that, the apostles said to Finnian that he should go with each of them to their own monastery to consecrate it. Finnian did not wish to do this, for he was an old man, and Finnian said: "I will go with the holy one whose dun-colored cow <note>The *odhar* refers to a specific cow, often used as a guide in Irish hagiography.</note> I follow, whichever of you it may be." The saints then scattered, and the dun-colored cow followed Molaise and Ninnidh. Finnian, with his twelve apostles, followed them to Devenish, and they stayed there with Molaise for a year.

Twelve saints were ordained there, along with Molaise at the fair mound:
According to the number of the dear apostles, who served the Creator.
Colum, Féichín, and Cainnech; Maedhóc of the full-radiant light;
The priest of holy Clonard who excelled, and Bishop Mac Cairthinn.
Mochta and strong Tigernach; Bishop Ibar and Beccán;
Beloved Arnain of purity, and angelic Enna.
Molaise and noble Arnain; Bishop Ibar and Beccán.
The abbots were fed without theft; fifty saints of the covenant.
Molaise loved the way of Christ; they followed the way of the apostles.
Without falsehood they completed every journey; twelve saints he had chosen.

The king over that land at that time was Conall Red, son of Daimín. His druid said to him: "Unless you attack Molaise at Devenish and unless you quench his fire tonight, he will be the lord over this territory and over the lake upon which it sits. His successor after him will be greater in voice, strength, and reverence." Because of this, his horses were caught for Conall Red, and he came forward toward Devenish. He whipped them vigorously until he reached the place called *Omhna Gabtha* <note>The "Oak of Capture."</note>, for the feet of the horses were held there so that they could not take a single step; they remained there to the astonishment of the king and his people. They were surprised and troubled by this, and a young warrior of his people said to the king: "Let the heads of the horses be turned to the east, and if they move without delay, then Molaise is a man of God." The heads of the horses were turned to the east, and they moved immediately. As for Conall Red, however, he left the horses alone and went forward on foot to Molaise. He brought a blackthorn boat that he had upon the bull's pool, and a boiled bull in its center, until the bull leapt into the lake and the boat was submerged. Furthermore, the king had two white horses with purple manes and tails; they died instantly. Then fear seized Conall Red, and a messenger was sent from him to Molaise so that he might raise the horses from death. Molaise came and brought the horses back to life again, and the king was pleased by that. "Let us make a bargain now," said Molaise: "I will give the kingship of this territory to you yourself on behalf of my Lord..."

# The Life of Molaise of Devenish.
<meta>9 b. 10]</meta>

Molaise turned his back sharply toward Conall Red, who was of good appearance; he left the king meager afterward, so that he was blind on the spot.

Because great reproach was felt by the king, though the conflict had been rough, he thought three times, without hesitation there, of making peace with Molaise without deceit.

He made a feast there in his house and brought it to the cleric; he prostrated to the worthy saint there and bestowed the land upon him.

He truly gave his monastic service <note>Mainchine refers to the duties, service, or tithes owed by a layman or a tenant to a church or monastery.</note> to Molaise and to the King of Kings; the heart of the cleric became guileless, so that his great anger was appeased.

The king’s eyes were healed, and help was truly given to him: the kingship for himself as long as he lived, but without it continuing to his descendants.

Against Molaise of the relics, no man rose, I believe; every claim was his by day, and every dispute that occurred.

Once, the apostles came to the island of protection <note>Referring to Devenish, *Inis Coimhéta*.</note> and they were one night without fire there, so they sent a small boy they had to fetch fire from Edardhruim. He took two embers with him, but he was drowned, along with his two embers. The little boy was then sought, and he was lifted up with the black embers in his hand. Molaise, through the power of his Lord, called him to life, and his soul entered him at that moment. He blew his breath under the wet, black embers so that they blazed like torches. God’s name and Molaise’s were magnified by this, and he spoke the poem:—

The apostles of Ireland came, together with Molaise without envy,
To sing their hours without fail at the famous island of protection.

They were in hardship without fire; that was a great difficulty to them;
They sent a small boy, without blame, to seek it where there was life.

At Edardhruim of the guests, he found fire for the benefit of the herds;
He took two embers from there as quickly as he could.

Because of the haste with which he came, he was drowned in a small boat;
For a day and a night he was missing, and not found until it was God’s will.

Then Molaise came without weariness to seek the little boy in the lake;
He found him immediately, as I say, and restored his life early.

A black ember was in each hand of the drowned youth, who was not boastful;
Molaise let out his clear breath under them until they shone and blazed.

The man of those miracles every day is of the people of the son of great Mary;
Woe to him who opposes the person who is His faithful servant.

Another time Molaise was in Devenish without food, and many guests came to him, for it was a path for travelers, guests, and strangers. It was also a path for the poor, the naked, the weak, and the helpless. Anyone who did not find help elsewhere in Ireland, and who could not manage work, service, or herding, came at last to Molaise, so that Molaise would help him against cold, famine, thirst, and hunger. Indeed, this is what Molaise did for guests and for the poor:

Once when Molaise went to Magh Carna, where King Aodh was holding a great feast, Molaise sent his servant with his vessel <note>The Irish term is *ballán*, a wooden cup or vessel.</note> to request ale and food. He was refused, and he came back to where Molaise was and told him. "Therefore," said the saint, "let the feast come to nothing, both ale and food." As for the king, his ale was turned into bitter water and his food into foul dung. The king came and said: "What has spoiled the feast?" "It is not difficult," said the steward: "Molaise’s servant came here and I refused him regarding ale and food." "That is an evil deed you have done," said the king, "and let this place be his because of the refusal you gave him, and let it serve him forever." Molaise was brought to them, and the king prostrated to him and offered him the land. Molaise blessed the land, the feast, and the food, and he restored them so that it was a worthy feast for the king and for Molaise himself afterward. As the poet said:—

# Betha Molaise Daiminse. [12. 12 b

After that, Molaise went across the sea toward Rome to Tours of Martin; <column-break/> he found the sacred church of Martin closed, and there was a single guardian from God and from Martin watching over it. Molaise asked for it to be opened before him. “It shall not be opened at all,” said the guardian, “unless God and Martin open it before you, if they permit it.” After that, the seven locks that were on the door opened by themselves for Molaise, and the door-leaf moved back until the door was open. Molaise performed Mass there then for God and for Martin, and he took the way toward Rome after that. While they were there a certain night, when Molaise was dining, they saw a serpent coming toward him. Great fear and horror seized everyone before it. Molaise called it to him and crumbled some bread for it; it ate it and licked his palm afterward, and it did no harm to him. On another day, as Molaise was traveling through the world in the east, he happened upon craftsmen doing their work. Molaise set about rebuking them, for he was not pleased with how the work was going. The craftsmen rose up to attack Molaise and laid hands violently on him. That was displeasing to God, and He turned the craftsmen back and seized their hands and their feet; their feet stuck to the ground and their tongues left them, until Molaise had mercy on them and restored their sense and their faculties for the sake of faith. And they believed fervently afterward in God and in Molaise, and the grace of God came upon them, as he said:—<note>The poem is missing</note>.

Nevertheless, Molaise reached Rome in the evening at the hour of nones, and the city was completely shut before him. He asked for it to be opened, but the gatekeeper did not open it for him. <column-break/> And Molaise struck the knocker three times upon the gate of the city. A great earthquake and a thunderous noise then came into the city, so that an enormous fear seized the people of Rome because of it, and they said that it was the Day of Judgment. Moreover, the great gate of Rome opened, and everything that had a lock or a fastening in the town opened by themselves, both in the center and on the outskirts. Molaise entered Rome after the door was opened before him in that way. He stayed there that night. Furthermore, all the people of Rome assembled in one place the next day where the Pope of Rome was, and the Pope asked them all together: “Do you know what that great earthquake was that came into Rome, from which everyone was generally terrified?” The gatekeeper came and said this: “A great, pale-faced cleric of the Gaels came to the gate of Rome yesterday evening when the doors were shut, and he asked for them to be opened.”

# The Life of Molaise of Devenish

...and it was not opened before him; and although it was not opened by human hands, God opened it before him. “Bring that Gaelic cleric to us,” said the Abbot <note>The Pope</note> of Rome. After that, Molaise was brought to him, and he was welcomed, and he was commanded to say Mass in the presence of the Pope and all the people of Rome. “If you are a man of God,” they said, “you will accept this task.” They did not fail to disparage Molaise, seeking to deceive and test him. Molaise went with them to the great altar of Peter in Rome. The altar was prepared for Molaise then, but no missal was given to him at all, nor was a cruet or a bell provided. <column-break/> Molaise, however, vested himself then and said that the altar was not fit for Mass in the absence of those three things. The Romans said, “Let the God who gives everything to you give you the three things you ask of us.” “Let that be a test for me,” said Molaise, “and my Lord in heaven hears it.”

As he was saying this, he raised his two hands up toward his Lord and prayed to the King of Heaven for help at that time. When the Creator of the elements heard that, He placed a missal that was not large upon the altar; He placed a cruet and a bell along with it. Molaise was pleased with that, and he performed Mass and offered a pure sacrifice there in the presence of the Pope and the rest of the Romans. He delivered a sermon afterward, which cleansed every heart in which there was evil, injustice, and malice in everyone who heard it. And the Pope and his twelve cardinals and all who were there gave a blessing also; they all gave him their soul's love at once after the Mass and the sermon he delivered.

And Molaise said then, “What shall be done with these three things God placed on the altar?” “Take your choice of them,” said the Pope, “for yours is the greatest labor among us today.” “I will take that little gospel-book,” said Molaise. The Pope said, “Its name shall be ‘little’ forever.” Therefore, it is called the *Soscéla Beg* <note>Little Gospel</note> of Molaise. 

Molaise stayed for a time in Rome then, in the triumph of joy, honor, faith, devotion, wisdom, and knowledge, until he wrote there whatever he needed of law, rule, and every knowledge that was not in Ireland before. By the Pope’s permission, he then came to Ireland as a distinguished High Legate. And when <column-break/> he reached his home, he found the bell that had been given on the altar in Rome hanging on a birch branch, and he found the cruet in another place. And though they were returned to Rome three times, they escaped back after Molaise every time; therefore, the name *téloidhech* <note>The Escaper or Fugitive</note> was given to the bell. He also brought with him...

# The Life of Molaise of Devenish

...a load of the soil of Rome and the relics of Paul, Peter, Lawrence, Clement, and Stephen; some of Mary's hair; Martin’s reliquary <note>lit. "fist-shrine"</note>; and many other relics of noble saints, along with some of the relics of the holy successors who were buried in Rome. After that, Molaise came to Ireland. This was revealed to Maodhóg, and he spoke these words:

“Welcome, miraculous Molaise, who has reached angelic Ireland; profitable was the journey of the promised one, who reached Rome without opposition. Victory forever to this Ireland <note>Banba</note>, an angelic, noble practice; no cause was found to rebuke him, for the purity of his body and his fine customs. A wise, ready, and faithful man; chaste, sweet-voiced, and habitually honorable. Radiant, holy, and strongly pious; strictly devout without pride. A pilgrimage without regret; our noble champion; welcome is Molaise.”

Maodhóg had not been there long after that when Molaise came to Ferns. Maodhóg rose to meet him and welcomed him. Maodhóg asked Molaise about all his travels from the day he left Ireland until he returned again. Molaise told him everything, how he had fared in Rome and in every other place. “Leave me my share of the gifts you brought with you from Rome,” said Maodhóg. “I will indeed,” said Molaise, “and open the fold <column-break/> of your cloak so that I may give them to you.” Then Maodhóg opened the fold of his cloak, and Molaise bestowed them: some of Mary’s hair, Martin’s reliquary, some of the relics of Paul and Peter, some of the relics of Lawrence and Clement, and some of the relics of Stephen the martyr. Maodhóg was pleased to see those holy relics in his cloak, and he said to Molaise: “You have speckled <note>or 'marked'</note> me well now.”

“The *Breac Maodhóic* <note>The Speckled One of Maodhóg</note> shall be its name forever,” said Molaise, “and its honor shall be complete and its miracles many. No one shall dare to violate it. It shall be a red wind of death to the seed of Fergna, and it shall be a heavenly fire to all the children of Brian, both west and east. It shall bring loss and destruction to the children of Niall or the people of Oirgialla if they do not satisfy its demands when it encounters them. Let it be enshrined well, and it is not proper for anyone but an ordained man to carry it, or someone who is entirely without corruption.” And he spoke the poem then:

“The stories of Molaise are told by us, from the day he left Ireland...” <note>And so on; we do not follow the poem any further because it contains nothing except what has already been said, and it is better as it is than as a poor poem.</note>

While coming from Rome, Molaise met another holy man, his namesake, Molaise the Hebrew, on a single flat stone in the middle of the sea. There Molaise and that man exchanged places, so that...

For it was on that stone that Molaise came to Ireland; and that stone still remains in Devenish to prove those miracles and to commemorate that story. However, Molaise reached Devenish after coming from Rome, and he interred the relics of Paul, Peter, Lawrence the martyr, Saint Clement, Stephen the martyr, Mary, and the other saints of Rome. The reason he brought those relics and that soil there was so that it would not be necessary for the Irish to go to Rome, unless they went <column-break/> for some grave reason, or unless a saint whose life was being written went there.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Good was the land we found, a broad lake on a mountain field;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;a common Rome for the Irish, the proper home of God the Father.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Great is the virtue of the Little Cemetery for whoever reaches it through habit;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;with its soil, every face—provided it is purified—is not tormented after the meeting of death.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The relics of Peter and Paul, Molaise brought from Rome in the east;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;it was he who also brought to Ireland the relics of Clement, who is in heaven.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Two martyrs of the weightiest judgment are in noble heaven with the King of Stars:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Lawrence and Stephen without boasting; he brought their relics with him, I believe.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Every holy relic he found in the east, he brought without fault—true is the cause;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;they are in the Little Cemetery securely; welcome is he who makes the circuit at the canonical hours.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Everyone who chooses them as their companions, and the Little Cemetery of Molaise truly;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;their soul will be promptly in Paradise, as I declare according to the King.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Rome of Ireland it is in every way; it is not right to neglect the salvation of the hosts;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;its honor shall not fade; it is the King of Kings who magnified it.

After Molaise interred those holy relics in the Little Cemetery, as we have said, he was not long in Devenish when the apostles <note>the twelve apostles of Ireland, a group of prominent saints</note> sent messengers for him from Tara. For that was the hour and time of the great war and conflict between Diarmaid mac Cerbhaill, King of Ireland, and Ruadán of Lorrha and the other apostles, because the King had violated the protection of the saints regarding Aedh Guaire, king of Connacht. For King Diarmaid had taken Aedh Guaire from Ruadán and from the saints of Ireland by force while he was under their protection. This was because Aedh Guaire, king of Connacht, had killed Aodh Baclámh—a servant of Diarmaid mac Cerbhaill—shortly before, because he found him troublesome.

Molaise arrived at the place where the apostles were in their tents on the green of Tara. They all rose to meet him <column-break/> and they bowed their heads to him, and Molaise’s tent was then pitched among the tents of all the other saints. This was the battle they waged against the King of Ireland: the saints, on the strength of their holiness, their prayers, and their miracles, fasted one night; the King of Ireland, however, on the strength of his truth, his royal law, and his sovereign right, fasted the other night against them. There were eleven saints fasting until Molaise came; he made twelve when he arrived. And they were...

# The Life of Molaise of Devenish

Those high saints of Ireland were those apostles: namely, Ruadhán of Lorrha, Maodhóc of Ferns, Féichín of Fore, Colum Cille, Cainneach the pious, Tigernach of Clones, Enán the angelic, and the priest Fraoch. Also Becán son of Culu, Bishop Mac Cairthinn, old Mochta of Louth, Mochuda the pious, and Molaise of Devenish. At the evening hour, Molaise came to Tara while the snow was falling heavily. It was those saints who were fasting that night, and Molaise fasted with them. The King of Ireland was not allowed any comfort or rest that night, and he did not sleep or nap. It appeared to him as a heavy burden from the people of God, who stayed every night on the green fasting against him. The time seemed long to Diarmaid until day came. And when it came, it required great strength to open the doors because of the depth of the snow. The King of Ireland rose and looked out at the tents from where he was, and it was so that they were all completely white with snow except for Molaise's tent alone. No snow adhered to it at all, and the ground did not take any snow for seven feet on every side of it. "Who is in that tent that the snow has not touched at all?" asked the king. "Molaise of Devenish, who arrived at evening yesterday," everyone replied. <column-break/> "That is for my overthrow," said Diarmaid, "and the bright one of Lough Erne dealt heavily with me last night. He is a living fire ablaze. And it seems to me he had no right to lie against me, for my burden was already vast before him. I place myself under his protection and the protection of the King of heaven and earth, whom we both believe in." This was revealed to Molaise, and he felt pity for him. 

The King of Ireland met to speak with the saints that day, and Molaise attempted to make peace between them and Ruadhán, but he could not. And since he could not, Molaise gave the King of Ireland his choice: either to have his life shortened, his body tormented, and heaven for his soul, with kingship and leadership for his descendants <note>his seed</note> forever after him; or else a long life and hell for himself, and no one of his descendants to take the kingship or sovereignty after him until the end of the world. This is the choice the king took: his body to be tormented and his life shortened, heaven for his soul, and leadership for his descendants after him. God fulfilled it well in that way, and for that reason, the Clan Colmáin and the descendants of Aodh Sláine <note>the two primary branches of the Southern Uí Néill</note> owe a yearly tribute to Molaise every winter habitually. As it was said:

> The twelve apostles of Ireland, great was the dread of them when a host gazed upon them: 
> it was they who were strongest in the end, it was they who brought every victory.
> Ruadhán of Lorrha, beautiful Maodhóc, Tigernach whose strength was not weak: 
> the priest Fraoch, Cainneach without sorrow—they did great good of their own will.
> Féichín of Fore, holy Colum—great was their affection, good was their manner: 
> Angelic Enna with beauty, Bishop Mac Cairthinn far from sin.

Pious Mochuta of the crosses, for protection without turning back: a holy pair without stinginess between them, Mochta and Becán son of Cúla.
They send messengers for Molaise to put him on the same path as themselves: against the king until he believes, so that he might take him with sharp conflict.
Molaise approaches without fatigue until he reached Tara of the battles: the apostles rise to meet him, for they were certain of his help for their distress.
The prelate’s tent is arranged, a short distance from the tents of the saints: it stood against the snow until there were white messengers on every side.
The king rose early in the morning; no dream was allowed to him: the tents of the saints were harshly whitened, completely full of snow by day.
Though the snow was falling for a long time, it did not take Molaise’s tent: the king understood that it was a miracle, for every plain was strongly whitened.
Fear seized the high king of Ireland before Molaise who came to meet him: Diarmaid knelt to him certainly; do not hide it from the men of Ireland.
"Make peace between me, O high king, and Ruadhán of the great law: you will not incline toward partiality; settle between us as is proper."
Molaise made an offer willingly; they refused everything he said: for the cleric, its condition was not proper; great is its depth for the men of Ireland.
The primate was almost angered by Ruadhán of the hard grip: but unity did not shatter without ignition, though Ireland was inclined without victory.
"Take your choice: eternal life," said Molaise on behalf of the King of the stars <note>God</note>: "with no one of your seed taking Ireland, and you truly in the middle of pain yonder <note>in the afterlife</note>.
Or a premature and ready death, and heaven for you and kingship for your descendants: thus, Diarmaid, I say, and I do not hide it from any right."
"There is no delay for me at all; my choice is the heaven of the saints: with you I shall have no quarrel, though we may both be separated."
Tara was destroyed by that event; the king of Ireland passed away: the churches of red Ruadhán remain in his wrath without happiness for a time.
The seed of Aodh Sláine and the clan of Colmán owe service to Molaise for all time: he left it, as I have heard, for them food and virtues as they are.

As for Molaise, however, after that he did not remain at all at the contention of Tara with the saints, for he was sorrowful for Tara to be forfeited and for the royal city of Ireland to be turned from its course. For he knew that the saints would be stronger than the king of Ireland in the end. It was from that undertaking that the saints of Ireland and the men of Ireland gave the leadership of miracles and the precedence of the holy relics of all Ireland's saints to Molaise. For he did not stop performing miracles and destroying "sons of curses" <note>the wicked</note> and raising up the righteous and blessing the tribes and the districts generally throughout all Ireland.

He came to Devenish after that, and he met a group of the students of the church who were clearing brambles and thorns; and they were complaining about their hands and feet to him, because thorns had pierced them. He gave his cloak to them immediately so that precious gloves were made of

# Betha Molaise Daiminse. [17. 17 b]

...one part of it was like the softened leather of a skin-worker, and thick 
bark-tanned shoes like a tanner's leather were on the other part of it.

At that time the Dartraighe were at the end of the 
great and hateful expulsion which the Munstermen had inflicted on them because of the wickedness of their lordship to Cashel, and 
because of the number of the Uí Chonaill Gabra they had killed, and for 
how much they had helped the foreigners and heathens 
against the Gaels, acting as guides for every path and every road for 
their enemies and for their other injustices besides. For that reason the 
Dartraighe were expelled from their native land and from their own proper 
inheritance, namely || a cantred and a half of their ancient patrimony in Leth Mogha: 
from the assembly-place of the Uí Cairpre in the south to the Cave of the Giant 
westward on the coast of Cechtraighe; and from the River of the Horses 
from the west in the territory of the Uí Chonaill Gabra to Loch Leithit westward in 
the territory of Torad. They were in exile throughout Ireland 
extensively for forty years, and five hundred armed men 
was their number. They did not stay for more than three years 
on any one land during that time, but they were under the contract and 
protection of the provincial kings for a time and a season until their own crimes 
turned against them, or until the weariness of the provincial king came upon them 
because of the amount of land they consumed, and because of their vehemence and 
their fierceness, and the frequency of their fights and conflicts in meetings and 
assemblies and in every other gathering. They themselves, moreover, committed 
sieges and violence against the sub-kings of Ireland while defending their land by 
force against them, so that it was necessary for those kings to complain to their 
friends and neighbors. It was in Connacht that they stayed longest during 
that time, until they themselves ruined Connacht because of the killing 
of the king of Umhall by them and the king of Partraige on the same day 
while besieging Western Connacht, until they were driven 
eastward across Athlone into Meath. They settled there 
in the middle of Delbhna. The Delbhna and Western Meath rose up 
against them and plundered them. Scarcely had they reached any 
single place when the Dartraighe overtook them in the middle 
of Durrow. They fought a firm and brave battle there, and the Delbhna <note>sic</note> and 
Western Meath were defeated, and a great slaughter was inflicted on them there. 
They then settled || back toward Connacht and held Delbhna 
by force for three half-years. From there they reached the Fir Ceall; they 
contested the land with them for a time and a season. After that, 
the Fir Ceall, the Delbhna, and the men of Meath gathered against the Dartraighe 
until they had plundered them of almost everything. The Dartraighe overtook them 
while pursuing their cattle and fought a battle there on the Slope of the Horses, 
which is called the Slope of the Gríbach today. The Delbhna and the Fir Ceall were defeated.

## This is the Life of Maignenn of Kilmainham.

Maignenn, Toa, Cobthach, and Libréan were the four sons of Aodh, son of Colgan <gloss>so written</gloss>, son of Tuathal, son of Fedlimid, son of Fiachra, son of Colla Fochríth. That bishop was a pillar of piety from the Shannon to Benn Edair, and a chosen vessel of wisdom in his time. He was a man who never told a lie from the age of seven years onward, and he never looked a woman in the face for fear of seeing the accompanying devil.

Once, Bishop Maignenn went on a visit to the house of his companion and friend, namely the place where Lommán of Loch Uair was in Meath. He had a friend in that place who was his confessor. This is how he saw him: with two large cataracts upon his eyes. The holy cleric started at the sight of his friend and said: *Deo gracias*, he said, that is, "Thanks be to God." "And it is a pity, my friend, how your eyes are mocking the world and the world is mocking them. It has been thirty years until this moment since I last saw you; if you had followed my advice until today, you would have secured your share of the inheritance of the heavenly city. For even the bird with the smallest and harshest voice in the heavenly city is more delightful and sweeter than all the wealth of the earth," said Maignenn. "I place myself under your protection, friend," he said, "and I will follow your advice from now on." Maignenn took him under his protection before God and said to him: "That which you would hate to have done to yourself, do not do it to anyone else, and God will come to you even though you are in your final days." Bishop Maignenn and Lommán of Loch Uair took their leave of each other, formed a union, and each of them blessed the other.
