# Betha Maignenn.

And at that time, Maignenn preached a sermon to Diarmaid mac Fergusa Cerrbeoil, the King of Ireland. When Lommán of Loch Uair heard the signs of the Day of Judgment and the harsh judgments of the chosen Trinity, he cried out with a loud lament in the presence of the king and his people. When the king's people heard the responses, the harsh judgments, and the stern discourse of the holy cleric, thirty of them abandoned the deceitful world in the presence of the king. Diarmaid mac Fergusa also did what was best for his own soul before God from then on; he made confessions and gave great alms to Maignenn: a <term>screball</term> (silver coin) for every nose, and an ounce of gold from every chief’s daughter who would take a husband—or if their stewards preferred, the set of clothing that was on them. And the king gave material for a staff and material for a crozier from the gold he had received as a gift from the foreigners. Maignenn's sermon at Loch Uair was famous at that time, as was his alliance with the King of Ireland. He gave a blessing to Diarmaid and his descendants after him and said to him: 

> *misericordia domini super uos et super filios uestros*

that is: may the mercy of God come upon you and upon your sons.

Once, Bishop Maignenn went to the house of Finnian of Moville. They greeted each other and went out for Sunday Vespers. Upon hearing the bell for Vespers, <column-break/> they bared their hearts to God; and while they were there, they saw an altar cloth descending from above, floating out of the firmament. "Take that, O Finnian," said Bishop Maignenn. "Do not say so, O holy bishop," said Finnian, "for such a thing is more fitting for you than for me. Let it be <note>ms. bith</note> yours." "By the angels," said Bishop Maignenn, "unless I receive its like from God, I will not take it." They looked toward God a second time and saw a second altar cloth between them. God’s name was magnified through that miracle, and they offered great prayers there in the great triumph of their piety; and those altar cloths remain there still.

Another time, a steward of the King of Ireland came to demand tax from Maignenn’s foster-mother <note>ms. mbuime</note> while Maignenn <gloss>so written</gloss> was at the end of his three years, sitting in his foster-mother’s lap. The steward did not take what was rightfully owed, but instead demanded what was not owed. Maignenn's foster-mother wept a great cry while he was in her lap. Immediately after that, the steward lost the use of half his leg, half his hand, and half his eye. The steward cried out and said: "I have seen a vision," he said, "as if I were guilty against a lamb of mercy, and I believe that the child you have is that lamb of mercy. If I could obtain help from God in the name of the child, I would never collect tax from you from this day forward." His foster-mother looked upon the boy and said:

# Betha Maignenn.

"O dear son, poverty would need to find relief," she said. When the child heard his foster-mother’s words, he raised his eyes and his two hands toward God on high, and the steward was immediately and quickly helped. A shout was raised in the house, and it was told that he was the child-saint Maignenn. Thus, those were the first miracles of Maignenn.

Once, a ram used to accompany Maignenn, and whenever they walked, the ram would carry Maignenn’s prayer book. A certain evil man came to Maignenn and stole the ram. Maignenn went with his twenty-seven <note>literally "three nines"</note> clerics on his trail to the thief’s house. The thief swore on relics and on Maignenn’s hand that he was not guilty concerning the ram. The ram was in a pit in the ground in the thief’s house, slaughtered, and what was in its belly had been eaten. God performed a manifest miracle for the holy cleric so that the ram spoke even from the pit where it was. Maignenn and his twenty-seven holy clerics looked up to God and gave thanks to Him for how He had increased His own miracles. As for the thief, the sight was taken from his eyes, the strength went out of his legs and his hands, and a great suffering was inflicted upon his whole body. He said with a loud voice: "Woe is me, a sinner! For God's sake, Maignenn, do not take heaven from me now." When Maignenn heard the sinner repenting, he felt affection and mercy and made a fervent prayer to God. Through the grace of prayer, he obtained from God that the blind man’s eyes returned and were put in their own place again. God’s name and Maignenn’s were magnified through that miracle, etc. ||

Another time, Maignenn went on a religious visit to the house of Molaise of Leighlin <note>Lethglenn</note>, that is, the son of Cairill, son of Muiredach Muinderg. Molaise was in this state: thirty diseases were in his body while he was in a narrow cell of devotion. He was prostrate in the shape of a cross with his face to the floor, weeping fervently, and the ground beneath him was wet from his tears of repentance. "For God's sake," said Maignenn, "tell me why you asked God for thirty diseases to be in your body?" "I will tell you, O holy bishop," said Molaise. "It is because it is revealed to me that my sin is like a flame through my body. And this is why I am so: I would like to have my purgatory here so that I may have eternal life yonder. And do you know, Maignenn, how the grain of wheat—before <note>ms. cr. ria sul</note> it is put in the soil—must be threshed and beaten? It is in that manner that I wish my body to be threshed by diseases before I am put into the grave." And Molaise said: "Thanks be to God," he said, "that you have arrived..."

# Betha Maignenn.
<meta>[49 b : 2]</meta>

"...to me before death, as death is now very near to me," he said. "And prepare me well for God’s sake; perform the last rites and the burial for me." Maignenn performed those burial rites, and that is one of the three noblest burials that was ever performed in Ireland: namely, Patrick in Downpatrick <note>Dún dá lethghlas</note>, Mochuda in Rahen <note>Ráithín uí Shuanaigh</note>, and Molaise after being buried by Bishop Maignenn.

Once, Bishop Maignenn went to the place where Finnchú of Brigown <gloss>ms. gobo</gloss> was, and he asked him to go on a visit to Aran, the place where the ridge of Aran is, and where the holy people of Ireland and all the saints of Europe visited, and where there was a great pope. After that, Maignenn went to Aran and made his covenant with the saints of Aran. And he came out of there after the victory of penance and pilgrimage, with his twenty-seven <note>literally "three nines"</note> holy clerics who were in his company from Aran. One night they were near Garmna without food. "It is a pity for us, O holy cleric," his people said to Maignenn, "that we are not in Tallaght <note>Tamhlachta</note> tonight, where we would find satisfaction for the night, for we are hungry." "Do not say that, O youths," said Maignenn, "for God helps the wretched and the strong, and He can no more fail to help us here than in any other place." They had not been there long when they heard a cry and the voice of a hound, with a deer before it. And when it came near the holy clerics, it gave a wild, startled leap so that it broke its neck in their presence. "*Deo gratias*," said Maignenn, "eat moderately and give thanks to your Creator for how well you are being treated." Maignenn’s people did so, and they took the remains of the meat with them, and thus they traveled until the time of the fast came. "For God’s sake," said one of his people to Maignenn, "tell us the instruction and sermon of the fast." "I tell you," he said, "that the fast is of no use when food is kept from you || because you cannot find food; or a fast for pride and arrogance, where you avoid food yourself; or a fast out of greed to save your food or your wealth. For a person is no more bound to observe the fasting from food than to observe the fasting of the mouth and the avoidance of sins. And I say to you, O wretched ones," said Maignenn, "that God does not prosecute the evils one does any more than He prosecutes a person who could do good and refuses to do it. And woe," he said, "to him who sees evils being done and does not fear the Lord forever."

Another time, Maignenn went on a visit to the place where Maelruain of Tallaght <gloss>ms. tablachta</gloss> was, and this is how he found him: he was coming from a well of water after reciting the one hundred and fifty psalms of the Psalter <gloss>ms. dé</gloss>. And Maelruain, through humility, blessed the holy bishop.

Once, Bishop Maignenn went on a visit to the place where Moling lived. A meal and provisions were brought to them <note>ms. qk</note>, and the meal was blessed according to the teachings. "We saw," said one of his people, "a cross and a new grave today, and we do not know what was buried there." "Where did you see that?" asked Bishop Maignenn. "On a height beside the Windy Gap," he replied. "I never saw a cross to which I would not make three prostrations," said Bishop Maignenn. He then left his meal, even after it had been blessed, and set out with his company of twenty-seven <note>three times nine</note> holy clerics. He reached the Windy Gap and stood for a long time gazing at the cross and the grave, but he did not speak to anyone and did not prostrate before the cross. 

His people asked him what was the reason for his silence, but he did not answer them. He remained like that for three hours, and then said with a soft, gentle voice: "I adjure you," he said, "to tell <note>ms. co ninnisedh</note> who was placed in that grave, and why I did not see the cross when I approached it." "I will tell you that, O holy bishop," said the soul, answering him, "though I find no protection from my suffering. I was a heathen," he said, "and there was no evil I could do that I did not perform. I used to plunder the weak, and I was a well-rewarded servant to the strong. I used to persecute the vulnerable churches, and I received the ringing of bells, the lighting of candles, and the curse of the righteous, and I died without repentance. And all the philosophers of the world could not describe even half of my pain, unless Almighty God Himself told it. That is why, O holy bishop, the guardian angel you had would not allow you to see me. For God’s sake, holy bishop, pray for me and let <note>sic</note> your mercy come upon me." 

He then looked up toward God. His guardian angel said to him: "Do not provoke God's anger, and do not spend your time in vain any longer." They made their union and covenant after that, and Bishop Maignenn and his three groups of nine <note>twenty-seven followers</note> departed. It happened that they went astray that night, and he began to pray fervently to be delivered from the wandering. He happened to come upon a household in which there were many violent and lawless people. <column-break/> "Alas," he said, "though the wandering was bad, the horror of this company and their lustful words are worse." He asked if there was a quiet place nearby. He was told of a poor, wretched widow who lived close by, and he went to the place where the widow was. The widow was joyful at the holy company she saw approaching her. The clerics blessed her and settled down in that place, and Maignenn greatly praised the modesty and the silence. "Welcome is the poor life in which you are," he said, "provided it is not wretchedness born of unwillingness; if it were, it is not praised in the church, for its companion is sin and despair."

Maignenn rose the following morning, and he and his three groups of nine were traveling throughout Saturday. When the end of Sunday came, the holy bishop happened to be on a level plain, and they settled there for the night. Much rain and hard, contrary winds came upon them throughout the cold, wet night. Bishop Maignenn stuck his four-edged staff <note>trosdán</note> above them, and each man of his people stuck their crooked sticks around his staff. The holy bishop then raised his four-cornered hood over his company of clerics and clearly performed miracles for that group. Though the storm and tempest of the night were great, and though every pool and site was full, not a drop of the storm fell upon the saints. They rose early on Monday morning, and the miracles performed for the saints were evident, and the news of those miracles spread throughout all Ireland.

The character of Bishop Maignenn was such as he was destined: he never accepted gold, silver, or the metal called money. A <term>Céile Dé</term> <note>a Culdee or "servant of God"</note> who was in Kilmainham <note>Cill Maignenn</note> gave this great testimony about him, saying: "Maignenn the miracle-worker, never guilty with women; Maignenn the prophetic, a man whose habit was to be weeping." Furthermore, he never said the same word twice during a sermon, and he never delivered a sermon that did not bring someone to the faith. And

# Betha Maignenn.

He never sat at the side of a king or a prince for fear that he would be seized by pride. He used to rebuke the honor of kings and powerful lords greatly, and he said that woe to anyone who finds satisfaction in the honor of the powerful after leaving this world. After that, a thief came from Howth <note>Beinn Edair</note> to steal the cow of a leper woman of Maignenn's church. This leper woman had a perpetually milking cow that sustained the poor, those in need, and those suffering from palsy <note>crithgallraig</note>. She discovered the thief's actions and went, crying out, to the place where Bishop Maignenn was with his assembly of saints and clerics. She told them bitterly how she had been robbed of her only cow and that she herself was falling into decline and misery because of it. The holy bishop and his company of clerics were greatly angered by this news. The bells and handbells <note>ceolána</note> in the settlement were struck, and they raised a clamor of bells and pronounced excommunications and curses upon the thief. After that, <column-break/> the holy bishop did not speak; he remained in silence, without moving a foot, a hand, or any of his limbs. He then spoke composedly and said that he had almost given his blessing to the thief, such was the extent of his resentment toward him, yet no saint or righteous person could obtain a prayer or a sigh of repentance from the thief.

"Tell us, O righteous man," they said, "why do you do this?"

"I will tell you," he said: "it is because of the greatness of my anger and the weight of my indignation; I wished to rouse the wrath of God to increase the eternal punishment in the next world—that place where no help is found from a friend, and where no saint or righteous person finds their prayer answered once the soul reaches the grasp of Máilmanntas in the depths of the abyss of hell.

From this time forward, I pronounce three heavy cries for those who violate me or my monks: first, the closing of their eyes to the world they loved; second, the closing of the heavenly city against them, so that they have no power to enter it; and third, I leave to those who violate me a death by the sword's point, and a scarcity of produce for their successors after them, as David said in the Psalter: *semen impiorum peripit* <note>the seed of the ungodly shall perish</note>. That is, I petition God that on the day when the twelve royal thrones shall be on Mount Sion, and the day when the four rivers of fire shall surround the mountain, and the day when the three hosts are present—the hosts of heaven <note>uime/nime</note>, of earth, and of hell—that those who violate me shall be condemned to death in hell. As for those who honor and protect me, I myself shall be their judge at the Last Judgment, by the permission of Christ and the authority of Patrick."

He also used to say that there are three things for which God is grateful in this world: namely, love for Himself, performing great charity, and the fulfillment of peace. It is this: when someone separates their heart, their mind, and their goodwill from the vices of the world, they find God directly in that manner. When someone goes on pilgrimage but their mind remains on their children, or their wife, or their land, and they choose them over God, their pilgrimage is useless. For there is little benefit for someone to leave their native home unless they truly perform the pilgrimage <note>The MS. is abbreviated here; likely "ailithre"</note> afterward. 

When the faithful *Abraham* went out from his native land, the Lord gave him counsel, and this was the counsel He gave: 'Withdraw your mind henceforth from your country and your land, and let your thoughts never return to it again.' Let that be the advice of the angel, clear to every person who undertakes a pilgrimage: not to practice the habits of the country where they lived ever again throughout their pilgrimage, whether by the movement of feet, hands, or body. It is through the practice of virtues and noble deeds that God judges every member of the human race.

Another time, a person performs a pilgrimage even while staying in their home among their own people—that is, when their heart is set upon pilgrimage, but hardship, poverty, or family obligations prevent them from going, despite having the desire in their heart. To such a person, it is the same as if they had traveled to the shrines of Peter and Paul or to the burial place of Christ. If it were only the physical body that hindered them, the soul would take the merit of the pilgrimage upon itself. Every Christian ought to live under the rule of the Church, for the Lord of just judgment accepts contrition of heart as an act of devotion. And that is the answer to the question about conversation and fellowship that you asked of me." ||

### *This is the Life of Cellach of Killala.*

A king took power over the Connachta, namely, Eogan Bél, son of Cellach, son of Ailill Molt, son of Nath Í, son of Fiachra, son of Eochaid Mugmedon. He plundered every province in Ireland and returned with victory and his spoils with him. No spoils were ever taken from him out of his province because victory was always before him. And when he did not overtake his own plunder, a raid was made by him that very day upon the land where his spoils had been taken. Indeed, the people of Munster and Leinster were obedient to him, and they used to give him thanks even after he frequently took their cattle against their will.

But one thing happened: a great conflict arose between Eogan and the Clanna Néill, so that the two provinces were against the one province—that is, the Connachta and the Ulaid. Yet their encounter was not equal, for Eogan Bél was never defeated in battle, and nothing was ever taken from him. There is no counting the frequency of his raids and his battle-careers against the Cenél Conaill, the Cenél Eogain, and the Airgialla. For not a day of peace was made while he lived, but he plundered them every month and every quarter, putting them to the edge of the sword. It was difficult and grievous for the Clanna Néill to endure the oppression of Eogan Bél and the Clann Fiachrach, and the rest of the Connachta upon them. Therefore, the counsel they took was for all the Ulaid to assemble, to organize a great plundering expedition, and to invade the territory of Connacht.

Two kings ruled over them at that time, namely, Fergus and Domnall, the two sons of Muirchertach mac Erca. They made great raids upon the Connachta so that they plundered before them as far as the River Moy, completely and thoroughly, and there were five battalions of troops engaged in making those raids. Then a pursuit was attempted against them by the warriors of the Clann Fiachrach and the rest of the Connachta. Nevertheless, not a single cow was taken from them, nor were they defeated, until Eogan’s household troops and his followers caught up with them at Drochet Martra. And they waged a fierce battle against them until Eogan himself also overtook them at Sceichín na Gáithe. When he saw the great host...

# The Life of Cellach

He sent messengers from among the people of poetry and art to Fergus, to Domnall, and to the rest of the nobles of the province to tell them to leave the plunder in its entirety and then depart unharmed. And if they did not do that, battle was to be declared upon them immediately. They went to the place where Fergus and Domnall were with the rest of the nobles of the Ulaid, and they delivered Eogan Bél's message. They did not consent to the restoration of the spoils at all, for they were high-spirited and eloquent about fighting the battle and keeping their plunder before them. There were five battalions of the Clanna Néill, the Ulaid, and the Airgialla there; and there was one immense battalion of the Clann Fiachrach and many bands of the warriors of the province besides, under Eogan Bél, son of Cellach.

Eogan dismounted there while listening to the responses of his poets from the Clanna Néill at that time. They told him that battle would be the payment for that journey, and that he would not get a single cow except by giving battle. However, the Connachtmen armed themselves and they attacked the Clanna Néill suddenly, swiftly, and relentlessly. When the Ulaid saw Eogan’s standard and the banners that had often taken their spoils, they turned, and they were filled with horror and trembling toward one another until the Battle of Sligo was fought between them there. The North of Ireland was defeated in that battle, and Fergus and Domnall were killed there; furthermore, their plunder was taken from them, and an uncountable slaughter was inflicted upon them. And Eogan Bél was heavily wounded there, so that he was carried upon the shafts of spears. He lived for three days according to some, and a week according to others. The nobles of the province came to him and went from him; great was the extent of their mourning for him.

After that, hands were laid upon the king, Eogan, so that he was certain to face death. And the Clann Fiachrach were consulting with him as to whom they should make king in his place. "Your situation is difficult," said Eogan Bél. "I have two sons: Cellach the cleric, a foster-son of Ciarán of Clonmacnoise, and Muiredach, the young son who is not yet fit for kingship because of his youth. And this is my advice to you: go to Clonmacnoise, to where Ciarán is. Ask him and let him permit Cellach to come with you to be made king, since you have no other royal candidate among you. And entreat him greatly regarding that matter." After that, Eogan ordered his burial with his red spear in his hand in the field: "And let my face be toward the north, on the side of the <term>Airgead</term> <note>Possibly a reference to the river or a specific territory of the Uí Fiachrach</note>, that is, the Uí Fiachrach there. And as long as I remain with my face toward them, they shall not prevail in battle against the Connachtmen while the face of my grave is toward them." [Let defeat be] upon the host of the Clanna Néill and upon the North there. The plan that the Clanna Néill and the North of Ireland made was to come with a great army to the fort of the Uí Fiachrach, to take Eogan and carry him with them north across the Sligo river. He was buried over there in the assembly-place of Lough Gill, with his face toward the ground . . .

However, the Clanna Fiachrach, as Eogan Bél had instructed them, went to Clonmacnoise to the place where Ciarán was praying. When they arrived, Ciarán welcomed them and put them in a guest house. They were well served that night. They told Ciarán their mission, but Ciarán would not grant his foster-son to them at all. Even though he did not grant it, they stayed a second night in Clonmacnoise until Cellach came on a visit to them. They spoke with him and begged him to come with them, and he then agreed to go with them. He departed the next morning without taking leave of his tutor at all. This was told to Ciarán: that his foster-son had fled from him without consulting him. "If he has gone," said Ciarán, "may the choice he has made not be prosperous for him, and let him carry a curse with the decision he made. May it be an evil fate that takes him in the end, and may it be death by a spear-point that takes him. I also leave it as a charge from my Lord—the King of Heaven and Earth—that whoever leaves his studies forever, may it be death by a spear-point that takes him, without help and without doubt." As for Cellach, the Clanna Fiachrach took him with them and gave him the kingship of the Uí Fiachrach—that is, from the River Robe to the River Codnach. He was there for a time in that manner, but his life was not pleasing to him since he heard of his tutor's curse.

This is how Guaire mac Colmáin was then, his reputation and hospitality having risen throughout Ireland, and all the Uí Fiachrach Aidne were with him on his land. Things were not good between them at first regarding their territory, and it was known that they felt hatred for each other. Nevertheless, they held a meeting and a conference and made peace with each other. But there was treachery on Guaire's part in that peace, for he betrayed Cellach and killed every single one of his people he could capture there. Cellach and twenty-seven <note>literally "three times nine"</note> of his people escaped out of the camp.

As for Cellach, he was a full year in the woods <note>as a fugitive</note> after that, until sorrow and repentance filled him for leaving his studies and for the curse Ciarán had placed upon him. He was reproaching himself, for the decision he had made was heavy upon him. "Woe to me," he said, "that the decision happened by which I abandoned my studies and my holy tutor for the worldliness of this miserable, fleeting life." As he said:—

> Woe to him who abandons the clerical life for a trade,
> Of the trades of the red world:
> Woe to him who abandons the great love of dear God
> For the kingship of the transient world.

Woe to him who takes up arms in this world, unless he performs penance:
> better for a man are white books, by which the hours of the psalms are sung.

Though the craft of weaponry be good, it earns little and involves great wandering:
> a life of eternal hardship results from it, and hell is obtained because of it.

The worst of crafts is the craft of theft, wandering, swearing, and swift plundering:
> but though the person who does it is good, he will be an evil man afterward.

Cellach, son of Eogan, found much of every such evil:
> let him avoid the strife from troop to troop, traveling with a wicked band.

Woe to him who forsakes holy, saintly heaven for black, dark, enslaved hell:
> O Christ, O Lord of the hosts, woe to him who forsakes the Great Lord.

And after that great repentance which Cellach felt, the plan he made—along with the three groups of nine who were with him in the war—was to go to the place where his foster-father was, namely, Ciarán of Clonmacnoise. He was timid about facing Ciarán because of his previous disobedience. He waited outside the monastery until he found a group of his fellow-students and clerics outside Clonmacnoise. They welcomed him and then kissed him. He came into the settlement with them and stayed that night there without Ciarán knowing. The next day, the elders of the community went with him to where Ciarán was to seek peace and mercy for him, and he prostrated himself before his foster-father there. Although Ciarán's anger against him had been great before, he granted him peace then, and he regretted the curse he had made against him. "My son," he said, "if I were able, I would take back your curse. Since I cannot, may it not be the worse for you before God, and may your place in heaven be no less because of my doing it."

Then the grace of the Holy Spirit and the love of the Trinity entered Cellach, and he told his followers to go back to where his brother Muiredach was. That young lad was then in the house of his foster-father, the King of Luighne. "Stay with him," said Cellach, "and follow him always." They departed as Cellach instructed them and were Muiredach's followers afterward.

As for Cellach, he bowed his head to his studies diligently and pursued them with eagerness and care. Whatever progress he made in his studies, his piety, charity, chastity, and good habits in general were three times as great. The fame of his piety spread throughout Ireland. Everyone gave him equal love, and his foster-father Ciarán was pleased with him because he was obedient to his counsel. Afterward, the orders of the priesthood were conferred on him, and he remained in those orders for a long time. After that, the clerics of his own district came to him and elected him to the bishopric. The rank of bishop was conferred on him, and <term>Killala</term> was given to him as his episcopal city. He visited the bishopric greatly and frequently, though he used to be in Clonmacnoise more often than in his own <term>diocese</term>. But there was not...

# The Life of Cellach.
<meta>273 : 2]</meta>

In all Ireland, there was no single person of greater fame for hospitality, piety, and clerical standing than he, nor any whom the men of art loved more; and every group of them used to follow him.

Once, he came with a mounted troop of clerics on a visitation of the bishopric to Cill Mhór Muaidhe. It happened that Guaire son of Colmán was in Dúrlus that day with many of his officers along with him. Nár son of Guaire, his son, was with him there, as was Nemed son of Firchoga, a troublesome foster-son to Guaire. Nemed said to Guaire: "It is unfriendly and spiteful that Cellach the bishop passed us by." "It matters not," said Guaire, "I will send messengers after him to tell him to come and speak with me." And he sent one of his officers to the place where Cellach was; it was precisely Saturday evening then. That man said: "Guaire is displeased with you," he said, "for passing him by. But come now to speak with him." "I will not go," said Cellach, "for it is the time of Vespers, and I do not violate the Sabbath. But I will perform my canonical hours and my mass tomorrow; and if he wishes, let him come to hear it and to converse with me, for it is but a short distance from him. And if he does not wish that, I will go on Monday to the place where he may be, if he so desires."

the messenger went to where Guaire was and related to Guaire all the words that Cellach had spoken; and he said further that Cellach refused to come with him, and he reported that Cellach had no love for Guaire at all. A great anger came upon Guaire because of that, and he said to the messenger: "Go to Cellach and command him to leave my land tonight; and if he does not do so, the church in which he stays shall be burned over his head—it and all its people." After that, the same messenger went to Cellach and did not hide Guaire’s message from him. "God judge between me and the unrighteous one," said Cellach. And nevertheless, he did not leave the place until Monday morning, and he went from there until he reached the shore of Loch Con. He spent a night there; then he came to the lake which is called Claenloch today. He was looking at the lake until he saw an island out from him, named Oilén Etgair; and a great service of angels appeared to him above that island. He went there afterward and asked if a saint’s blessing was upon it. They said that no saint had ever blessed it. "It is true," said Cellach, "it is there that I am to live as a hermit." His followers, however, were mocking him and at other times discouraging him for thinking of staying on the island. "It is certain that I shall stay here," said Cellach. "And you, depart," said Cellach, "for there are many places for you in my bishopric." That, indeed, is what they did, though they were reluctant; they left Cellach.

# Betha Chellaigh. [274 : 1]

He was there alone except for four young clerics who were in his company: Maelcróin, Maeldálua, Maelsenaig, and Macdeoraid, who were also Cellach’s foster-brothers. From Shrovetide until Easter, they spent their time performing their daily prayers and their devotion to God. It was proclaimed throughout all Ireland that Cellach, son of Eogain Bél, the holy bishop, was living in a wilderness after having abandoned his bishopric. At that time, Easter arrived, and Muiredach, son of Eogain Bél, his brother, visited him frequently and did nothing except according to Cellach's advice.

When Guaire heard this news, he was filled with madness and hatred for Cellach; and though things had been bad between them before, it was far worse afterwards. For he was afraid that Muiredach might seize the kingship through the instruction of his brother Cellach, and because of Muiredach's own excellence and his greatness, it was understood that he was a fit candidate for the kingship himself. Then Nar, son of Guaire, and Nemed, son of Firchoga, were constantly urging Guaire to kill the holy bishop Cellach, and they were framing malicious reports about Cellach to Guaire both day and night. They then devised a plot among themselves: to invite Cellach to come to them and to prepare poison for him. For although Guaire hated him, he did not wish to use weapons against him in his own presence. This is how they did it: they prepared poison for Cellach and messengers were sent for him to the island in the lake where he was. They were instructed that if Cellach refused to come, they should ask his foster-brothers to come to Guaire so that they might act as faithful messengers between Guaire and the cleric Cellach. 

In any case, those messengers arrived at the place where Cellach was on his island, and they greeted him while he was performing his daily prayers there. Cellach greeted them. They told him that they had come for him from Guaire to a great feast that he had prepared for him, and to speak with him privately. "I will not go there now," said Cellach, "for I will not abandon my prayers for the sake of feasting or the idle mirth of this fleeting world." "If that is the decision," said the foster-brothers who were with Cellach, "it is difficult for Guaire to believe that you are not ill-disposed <note>Literally "in a bad state of mind/intention"</note> because of this." "Therefore," said the messengers, "let your foster-brothers come with us, and Guaire will be grateful to you, and they will bring to you every conversation and every secret counsel he has for you." "I will not prevent them, nor will I command them," said Cellach. Upon hearing this, Maelcróin and the other three immediately went, all four of them, with the messengers to the place where Guaire was in Dúrlus. Guaire welcomed them, and their coming to him was good. <column-break/> They were served diligently with food and drink.

The best drink in the fortress was brought to them. Two of them were seated on each side of Guaire. They were bound to these terms, and they were also given a sufficient supply of weapons. They stayed there that night and unanimously agreed to kill Cellach before breaking their fast. From there, they set out for Lough Conn. They found the boat in the place where they had left it and traveled in it to the place where Cellach was.

He was there with his psalter before him, reciting his psalms, but he did not speak to them until he had finished his recitation. He looked at them then and saw their eyes trembling in their heads and the hue of <term>fingal</term> (kin-slaying) upon them. "Your appearance is evil, young men," said Cellach. "Your nature has changed since you left me, and I recognize that you have agreed with Guaire to kill me." They did not deny this to him at all. "We will not take your advice at all, Cellach," they said, "for we would find no protection in all of Ireland from Guaire if we did." While they were saying this, they thrust their spears into Cellach all at once. They then dragged him toward the boat, and he placed his psalter and his cowl between them. He was laid in the middle of the boat, with two of them in the bow, until they reached the port; then they took him into the dark recesses of the great wood and the forest.

"Indeed, young men," said Cellach, "it seems to me that the plan you wish to complete is truly evil. You would find protection in Clonmacnoise forever against Guaire, or if you preferred to go to Bláthmac and Diarmait, the two sons of Aed Sláine, who hold the kingship of Ireland." *As Cellach said:*

> O young men who have terrified me, evil is the pride against the King of Heaven;
> though the look in your eyes is deceptive, the intent of your heart is worse.
> You have consented against me to a harsh decision that cannot be undone;
> your infamy will last long, and you will repent of this treachery and kin-slaying.
> Though it is you—no, I do not believe it is you—who kill me with a captive's blow;
> the consequences will be a greater burning, save for the groan of Ciarán, my foster-father.
> Though the curse is bad for me, I do not avoid martyrdom;
> the plague for you shall be its sudden onset, for laying a red hand upon me.
> I have a certainty, there is none like it:
> my cause is close to Christ; the heaven of the angels shall be my dwelling.
> A decision you made was treachery against me, an unjust course;
> death by the point of your weapons, and hell is ready for you, O young men.

"It is useless for us to take advice from you henceforth," they said regarding that matter, "for we will not act upon it." "If it must be so," said Cellach, "grant me the respite of the night tonight for God’s sake." "We will grant it then, although we are reluctant to give it." They drew the swords that were hidden under their clothes. Great fear seized Cellach upon seeing that. They then searched the wood until they found a hollow oak tree in it with a single narrow entrance, and Cellach was put inside it. They sat by the entrance, watching Cellach until morning. Thus they remained until the time of the end of the night. Then a desire for sleep came upon them, so that a heavy slumber fell on them there. Cellach did not sleep at all due to the anxiety of his death, and it was in his power then to escape if he wished. But he said in his mind that it would be a lack of faith to avoid the destiny of the living God. He also thought that they would overtake him if he attempted to escape, for he was slender, wretched, and weak after his Lenten fast.

However, the morning was then shining upon them. He closed the door then for fear of seeing the morning, because of the dread of death. "It is bad faith for me," he said, "to avoid the judgment of God, when Ciarán my foster-father promised that this death would come for me." He spoke these words even as he opened the door of the tree. The raven, the scald-crow, the wren, and the other birds called out then. Then came the kite of the yew of <term>Cluain Eó</term> and the fox <note>literally "red dog"</note> of <term>Druim Meic Dáir</term>—that is, the deceiver who used to be constantly around the port of the island. "My dream of Wednesday night has indeed come true," said Cellach, "namely, four wild dogs tearing me and carrying me through the ferns, and my falling into a great ravine without ever rising out of it." Muiredach quickly recognized, when he heard that the young clerics had gone to Guaire's house, that it was Cellach who was betrayed by them and killed there. The path he took led to where the pass was between Loch Con and Loch Cuilinn. A fierce beast <note>Literally a "poisonous leopard" or "water-hound," likely a legendary otter</note> rose up at the pass against them, so that it killed nine of his people in his presence there. His foster-brother, Conall mac Eochaidh, rebuked him for that, saying it was a cowardly king's son who allowed his people to be killed by the beast in his presence. Muiredach then went in pursuit of the beast. He searched under the lake, but did not find it the first time. He went a second time, and on the third time he found the track of the beast || and followed it up from the lake until he found it sleeping and satisfied. He thrust the sword through it to the ground. It leaped into the lake with the sword still in it. Muiredach followed its track until he encountered it. Muiredach was greatly wounded in that fight, and he killed the beast afterward. Then he brought its head onto land to where Conall his foster-brother and his people were. Conall said then: "That is a brave combat you have fought, O son; namely, killing the hound of the pass, and Cúchoingelt <note>meaning "Hound of the Pass"</note> shall be your name from this." Thus the name stuck to him, so that he was called Cúchoingelt.

They went out then and followed the track of the five <note>the murderers</note> throughout the desert wood. They followed it diligently until they found their staves where they had left them. "That is true," said Muiredach, "it is a wonder these staves were given to kill Cellach by Guaire. Leave these staves," he said, "and let us follow the track of the party." After that they followed the track until they found the tree and Cellach's body there, after it had been eaten by wild beasts. That death weighed heavily upon Muiredach, as he said:

> Dear is everyone and this body; I liken this death to my own death:
> but it seems to me the little body of Cellach, son of Eoghan, is full of blood.
> Alas, I have no sister in the land of Ireland or Scotland:
> my father and my mother are dead; God has left me without a brother.
> Unless it be with pure Gelghéis or with Conall mac Eochaidh:
> I do not know if anyone holds my honor or my love.
> O Loch Claoin, O Loch Claoin, henceforth you have no value:
> since you did not protect the little body of Cellach, son of Eoghan, from his wounding.
> You abandoned troops of soldiers for bright psalm-singing:
> you abandoned deeds of valor for books of full purity.
> You abandoned drinking houses for frequenting the altar:
> you gave up tributes, O man; you gave love to dear Jesus.
> Macdeoraid shall fall by me in revenge for the son of high Eoghan:
> Macdeoraid shall be full of blood, for he mangled the son of dear Eoghan.
> Good was his pious clerkship in his beautiful church of yews:
> dear was the white hair and the beloved little body.

> Maeldálua shall fall by my hand, in vengeance for fair-skinned Cellach;
> and Maelsenaig shall fall, if there was a great treachery;
> against Maelchróin, fiercely to wound him, I would give gold, however dear.

After that, they lifted Cellach's body with them to the great ridge which is called Turlach; but the people of Turlach did not allow his burial there for fear of Guaire. They went from there to Lis Calláin, and the people of the church of Callán also refused his burial, still for fear of Guaire. That was a grievance to Cúchoingeilt, and he said that he would take vengeance on them for their refusal. They had not gone far from the church, carrying Cellach with them, when they saw the church in a high flame—that is, being burned from heaven because they did not permit Cellach's body within it; and there has been no inhabitant in it from then until eternity.

While they were there, they saw two wild stags coming toward them with a strong cart between them, until they came alongside the body. They lowered the cart to the ground in the middle of the troop. Everyone wondered at what was seen, and they were joyful at the great miracle God performed for Cellach, the holy bishop. They then put the body in the litter that was on those wild stags. They carried him until they reached the ridges from the west. They saw a church there and an oratory within it. The stags left the body at the door of the oratory. The bells of the church rang by themselves then. The clerics came to the body and asked who it was. When they knew, they sang the psalms fervently for his soul over his grave and his burial place. A circle of angels also descended from heaven, honoring his soul and his burial on earth. Those stags used to come every day and plow like other oxen; they came after their plowing every evening and lay by Cellach's grave. Cúchoingeilt came after that and stood over his brother's grave and said:

> Sad and weary am I here, after my brother who was in my company;
> henceforth I shall not go to his house, since the son of Eoghan no longer lives.
> It will be bad for the one who betrayed you; his high-fort shall be empty after him;
> the one who butchered you in the east shall be upon the dark flagstones of the devil.
> Woe to him who puts trust in them, in the family of Colmán son of Cobthach;
> the deed Guaire has done brings me under the sorrow of eternal misery.

After that, the supporters and kinsmen of Cellach gathered to Cúchoingeilt from every part of Connacht, until their total number was three hundred armed men in one place. Since he found no path of war against Guaire, his plan was to go to Marcán where he was—namely, the king of Uí Maine and Medraige; for he had a year's protection from the men of Ireland. Cúchoingeilt then placed his hand in his hand <note>an act of formal alliance or submission</note>, and Marcán gave a year's quartering to his people, and he himself stayed in Marcán's house.

They were welcomed then. Afterward, Cúchoingelt's followers were billeted upon the tribes of Brega and Meath, and he himself was in the company of Bláthmac, along with a group of his high officers, with great honor. 

Bláthmac had a proud, unmarried daughter named Aife. Courtship began between her and Cúchoingelt son of Eogan Bél. They both gave intense love to one another, and few people knew of their courtship then. One day, when Cúchoingelt was playing <term>fidchell</term> <note>an ancient Irish board game</note> and Aife daughter of Bláthmac stood over him as the game was being won against Cúchoingelt, she taught him a winning move against her father there. 

Bláthmac looked sharply at her and said, "Your instruction against me was intense, daughter," said he, "for you have taken the game from me. Truly, there is courtship between you and Cúchoingelt."

"I do not hide it," she said. 

"If you admit it," said Bláthmac, "why did you not ask my permission?" 

"We have committed no sin yet," said Cúchoingelt, "and we will not do so except with your permission." 

"If so," said Bláthmac, "I will not come between you and your love. I will give her to you, though many men seek her, for I consider you a worthy son-in-law." 

They slept together that night after having their wedding, and things were well between them for a length of time, until one night a conversation happened between Aife and Cúchoingelt, and she said to him: "Though your appearance and your honor are good, it is a great fault in you how poor your prowess and your spirit are."

"Why do you say that, maiden?" asked Cúchoingelt. 

"Because," she said, "of how poorly you avenge your brother against those who killed him." 

"What you say is true, maiden," said Cúchoingelt. He was ashamed then of what the woman said to him.

The four men who killed Cellach son of Eogain were captured there immediately: namely, Maelcróin, Maeldálua, Maelsenaig, and Macdeoraid. All their officers were killed around them then, and the assembly was ordered to remain in their places of drinking and pleasure, for they were all friends of Cúchoingelt. Cúchoingelt and his followers sat and mingled with everyone, and they remained drinking and enjoying themselves until morning after the destruction of their enemies. They rose early the next morning and brought those four men, bound, westward through the length of the country until they reached Dúrlas of Guaire. Past the rock of Lic Turscair, near the roaring Moy <note>the river Muaid</note> and not far from it, four long, thick posts were brought to them. The captives were placed upon these, and all their limbs were hacked off while they were still alive; afterwards, their bodies were hanged and executed. Therefore, the name of that place ever since is Ard na Riag <note>Hill of the Executions</note>, as it was said:—

After those four were hanged by them, Cúchoingelt went forward into Tír Fhiachrach and took hostages and power over them after the destruction of many of their people. His reputation for hospitality and prowess was great after that, and though Guaire’s fame was great, Cúchoingelt was more beloved by the people of every art in Ireland. So it was that Cúchoingelt took the kingship of Uí Amalgaid and all of northern Uí Fiachrach, while Guaire ruled over Uí Fiachrach Aidhne in the south. <column-break/> A conflict of war arose immediately between Guaire and Cúchoingelt; it is impossible to describe the extent of the evil and violence Cúchoingelt inflicted upon Guaire. Indeed, the two assemblies and the rest of the province were nearly destroyed between them.

Now Gelghéis, Guaire's daughter, was the devoted lover of Cúchoingelt, for she never consented to sleep with any man because of her love for him. When both sides grew weary of the war—namely Guaire and Cúchoingelt—Cúchoingelt asked Guaire for his daughter, but Guaire did not wish to give her to him at all. Nevertheless, he consented because of the petitions and to end the war. He agreed to host their wedding feast himself and for Cúchoingelt to come to his house. Cúchoingelt did not agree to this at all, and so they remained at war with one another for a long time until, at last, Guaire was forced to make Dúrlas [available] for all his people...

Beside himself, and after she had been exhausted in that way, Gelgéis was delivered to Cúchoingelt, so that there was love between them. The fame of Cúchoingelt's hospitality was great throughout all Ireland at that time; however, although he was forgiving toward Guaire’s people, he turned the churches of the entire country into a wilderness, and Guaire thought that was an evil thing. This is the trick that Guaire then performed: he went to the place where Ciarán of Clonmacnoise <note><term>Ciarán cluana mac Nóis</term></note> was with his clergy and urged Ciarán to go to Cúchoingelt and bring him to a state of peace and friendship. The kingship was even promised to him in Ciarán’s presence, provided he would come into Guaire’s house. After that, Ciarán reached the place where Cúchoingelt was and was urging him not to let the kingship of Connacht go by trusting in Guaire. Gelgéis was also urging him, for she knew that Ciarán had no deceit in him, and she also hoped that Guaire would not practice a trick against Ciarán. Cúchoingelt agreed to go against his own nature with Ciarán, for there were many people entreating him to do so. *As he said* <note><term>ut dixit</term></note>:—

After that poem, Ciarán, the clergy, and Cúchoingelt arrived at Dúrlas Guaire. They were served and ministered to there for the length of three nights, and a bond and friendship were made between Guaire and Cúchoingelt in the presence of Ciarán. Ciarán left the place after that, and the counsel that Guaire quickly and readily decided upon afterward was to commit a treacherous kin-slaying upon his kinsman and his brother-in-law, in defiance of the chief saint of Ireland. Nevertheless, that plan was completed by Guaire son of Colmán son of Eochaid in Dúrlas Guaire, so that Cúchoingelt son of Eogain Bél was killed by him at that time . . . . . . *as he said*:—

> Empty tonight is the dwelling of Eogan, for it is God who willed it:

> He was the head of noble women and exiles, the heroic warrior without blemish:

> He was good at protecting his friends; he did not promise harm to his enemies:

&emsp;generosity and battle-spirit are not the same for you as for the children of Colmán."
**"I**f I am killed tomorrow," said the sociable Cúchoingelt:
&emsp;"I will go against you, since you wish it, to the house of the son of Colmán of the poets."

**C**úchoingelt and the clerics quickly prepared themselves:
&emsp;until they reached us truly, even to Dúrlas under Cúchoingelt.
**T**hough Ciarán of the Meadow was angry, though Brénainn of the victories was miraculous:
&emsp;the son of Colmán of the raids did not look upon the perfect company of clerics.

**A**fter that, they performed the slaughter, both in the hollow and on the heights:
&emsp;until he died as was fated, by the children of narrow-backed Colmán.
**T**hose saints excommunicate him without delay, that wounding Guaire:
&emsp;they destroyed his life and his death, so that his place is empty and desolate. [. *Finished* .]

### The Story of Aed Baclám.

Aed Baclám, the spear-bearer of Diarmait mac Cerbaill, was seized by a heavy fit of sickness and lay in a wasting illness for a year. After he recovered his health, he went to speak with Diarmait and said to him: "How has the arrangement of your discipline and your peace been during this year that I have been lying down?" "I do not perceive any disturbance upon it," said Diarmait. "I have a way to find that out," said Aed Baclám. "I will go," he said, "across Ireland to the southwest, carrying your spear crosswise in the crooks of my arms until I reach the door of every fort in Ireland, and I will carry the spear crosswise through them. Thus, the discipline and peace of Ireland will be tested through this."

Aed Baclám then set out from Tara to the province of Connacht, accompanied by the King of Ireland's herald to proclaim the peace of Ireland. He reached the house of Aed Guaire of Cenél Féichín in the territory of Hy Many. It was like this: Guaire had a red oak palisade around his fort and a new house he had built for his wife's wedding feast. He had heard a week before Aed Baclám arrived that he was coming, and he ordered the palisade to be opened before him.

Aed Baclám arrived then, and Aed Guaire welcomed him. Aed Baclám demanded that the house be cut open before him <note>because the spear held crosswise would not fit through the door</note>. "Order it yourself," said Aed Guaire, "as you wish it to be cut." And as he said this, he struck Aed Baclám with a sword and cut off his head.

This was the law of Ireland at that time: whoever killed an innocent person was to be killed himself, and no cattle or compensation was to be accepted in his stead, unless the King of Ireland ordered or permitted cattle to be taken for it.

Upon hearing of the killing, Diarmait sent his young recruits and his officers to raid and plunder Aed Guaire. Aed Guaire fled to Bishop Senán, for they had the same mother. Then Bishop Senán went with him to Ruadhán of Lorrha, because two of Ruadhán’s sisters had raised Bishop Senán—Cael and Ruadhnait were their names. But Aed Guaire did not find sanctuary with Ruadhán || <column-break/> until he was exiled to Britain, where he remained for a year. Diarmait's people went to search for him in Britain.

<summary>Aed Baclám, King Diarmait's spear-bearer, tests the king's peace by carrying a spear crosswise through the doors of Irish forts, but is killed by Aed Guaire for demanding his house be breached. Aed Guaire flees Diarmait's vengeance and seeks sanctuary with Bishop Senán and Saint Ruadhán before being exiled to Britain.</summary>

...that he was sent again to Ruadhán. Diarmait himself went to Ruadhán to seek him, and Ruadhán had him placed in a hole in the ground which is called Ruadhán’s Pit today. Diarmait sent his servant to search Ruadhán’s cell to see if Aedh Guaire were in it. After the servant went into the cell, his eyes were immediately blinded. When Diarmait saw this, he went into the cell himself but did not find Aedh in it. He asked Ruadhán where Aedh Guaire was, for he was certain that Ruadhán would not tell a lie. "I do not know," said Ruadhán, "unless he is under that thatch."

Diarmait went home after that, but he remembered the cleric's words and turned back again and came into the church. He saw a candle being carried to the place where Aedh Guaire was, and he sent a favorite servant of his to fetch Aedh. Donnán Donn was the servant's name. They dug up the hiding place <gloss>the concealment</gloss>, and the hand that he stretched out to take Aedh withered up as far as the shoulder. He prostrated himself before Ruadhán after that, and the two of them stayed with him, and they have been in Ruadhán's Pit <gloss>tent</gloss> from then on. Afterwards, Diarmait took Aedh Guaire with him to Tara.

Ruadhán went to old Brendan of Birr and to the Twelve Apostles of Ireland, and they all went together after Diarmait to Tara. That night, they fasted against Diarmait, and Diarmait fasted against them by the power <gloss>strength</gloss> of his sovereignty and his truth. Furthermore, that night the sons of the twelve pillars of Tara, who belonged to the King of Ireland's steward, died. Ruadhán resurrected them in the morning after the steward entreated him in the name of God.

They remained like that for <insert>a year</insert> at the gate of Tara, under Ruadhán’s tent, exposed to the weather and the wet. Every other night they went without food, as Diarmait and the clerics fasted against each other.

It was then that Brendan son of Findlug was searching the sea, seeking the Promised Land, until the angel revealed to him that the Twelve Apostles of Ireland were at the gate of Tara, struggling against the King of Ireland because he had violated Ruadhán's sanctuary. Brendan came from the sea until he reached port at Dún Rosarach and stayed there that night || and he blessed the fort afterwards. However, when Diarmait heard the news that Brendan had come to help the saints and the clerics, great fear seized him, and he said to the saints: "If you would give me," he said, "fifty blue-eyed horses with golden bridles, I would give Aedh Guaire to you." This message reached Brendan. Brendan summoned fifty seals and turned them into

Those who were around the sacred tree were the twelve swift men;

Concerning Diarmait mac Cerbaill: after that vision, he rose at early morning until he heard the clerics singing psalms, and he went into the house where they were. "It is a pity indeed," said Diarmait, "the unlawful struggle you have waged against me; for I seek the good of Ireland, and to preserve her discipline and the law of kingship. But you seek war, strife, and the manslaughter of Ireland. For God himself gives the ranks of lordship, and of the righteous and the true judge to a person—namely, so that he may have the preservation of His truth, his lordship, and his sovereignty. For this is what is required of a king: to have mercy combined with the binding of the law, peace for the tribes, hostages in shackles, help for the wretched, the drowning of enemies, and the banishing of falsehood. For unless one does the will of the King of Heaven here, satisfaction will not be accepted from him there. And you, Ruadhán," said Diarmait, "the destruction and wounding of my kingship and my truth before God has come heavily from you; and I pray to God that your parish shall be the first parish rejected in Ireland, and that it be the first sanctuary to be attacked." Ruadhán said: "May it be sooner that your kingdom goes to nothing, and that neither son nor grandson of yours shall ever hold Tara." Diarmait said: "May your church be forever a wasteland." Ruadhán said that Tara would be a wasteland forever and ever. Diarmait said: "May you lack one of your limbs before you go under the earth; and may you lack one of your eyes also. May you have a visible, ugly face before death," said [Diarmait].

Once, when Diarmaid mac Cerbhaill’s praisers were praising the king, his peace, and his good virtues, Aedh Dubh mac Araidhe was in the presence of Bec mac Dé. Diarmaid, however, had killed Araidhe of the Ulstermen and had taken his son, namely Aedh Dubh, into fosterage. Bec said: "I see the dog-like hound who will destroy the excellent peace." "O Bec," said Aedh Dubh, "which hound?" "Perhaps it is you," said Bec. "How so?" said Diarmaid. "It is not difficult," said Bec: "This hand of Aedh Dubh is the one that will give a drink of death to your lips in the house of Banbán and Bainbhshige, when you have a shirt of a single flax-seed <note>aonroisne: flax grown from a single seed</note> around you, and a cloak of a single sheep, and ale of a single grain in your horn, and the fat of a pig that was never farrowed on your dish." "He shall not be in Ireland," said Diarmaid, "as long as I am alive." "Kill him!" everyone said. "No," said Diarmaid, "but he shall be banished from Ireland." After that, Aedh Dubh was banished to the land of Scotland.

One day, Diarmaid saw the warrior in the house. "Where have you come from?" asked Diarmaid. "From nowhere far," he said. "Come with me to spend a night of hospitality with me." "Good," said Diarmaid. "Tell Mughain." "I will not go on an invitation as long as I live," she said. Nevertheless, they went with Banbán to the fort of Bec. When they had sat down, they saw a beautiful, shapely young woman with fine attire passing through the middle of the house. "Where is the woman from?" asked Diarmaid. "She is my daughter," said Banbán. "Good woman," said Banbán to his daughter, "do you have clothing for Diarmaid?" "Indeed I do," said the woman. She brought a shirt out of a casket and a cloak and put them on him. "The shirt is good," everyone said. "It is good," said Banbán, "the shirt of a single flax-seed. That daughter of ours is a very diligent girl; it was she who planted a single flax-seed and tended it until she made a crop of it, and it became a ridge of flax." "The cloak is good," everyone said. "It is good," said Banbán: "It was made from the wool of a single sheep." After that, food and drink were brought to them. "The bacon is good," everyone said. "It is good," said Banbán: "from the fat of a pig that was never farrowed." "How is that?" they asked. "It is not difficult," he said: "There were pregnant sows; knives were taken to them so that their young were taken out while they were alive and then fed." "The ale is good," everyone said.

"Good," said Banbán, "if it is ale from a single grain. One day I went out to inspect the plowing, and I killed a wood-pigeon. A grain was found in its crop. It was not known what kind of grain it was. It was sown at the head of a ridge until a sickle-measure was harvested from it in the end, so that is its grain and its ale here."

After that, Diarmaid looked up: "The lower part of the house is new," he said, "but its upper part is not young." "Once," said Banbán, "we went in curachs to catch fish until we saw the ridge-beam of a house coming towards us upon the sea. A house was built by me under that ridge-beam." "It is true," said Diarmaid; "that is the ridge-beam of my own house which was cast by me into the sea. "Come out before us," said Diarmaid. "I will not," said Aodh Dubh mac Suibhne, having come from Scotland after being exiled by Diarmaid and after being dishonored by him at the fair of Tailltenn.

> O Aedh Dubh mac Suibhne of the ranks, who was a respected king of Ulster:
> It is he, without dark mystery, who killed Diarmaid mac Cerbhaill.

### This is the Death of Diarmaid son of Fergus Cerrbeoil, as the Book of Sligo says.

When Diarmaid mac Fergusa Cerrbeoill was in exile from Tuathal Maelgarbh on Lough Ree and on the Shannon, at that time <gloss>ms. time</gloss> Ciarán, son of the carpenter, came to establish his monastery at Druimm Tibrat, the place where Clonmacnoise is today. Ciarán went on the lake with eight men (others say he went with twelve hundred) on land. A fire was kindled by the clerics.

Diarmaid was there in his fleet, swimming after two birds on the Shannon.

...namely, two birds that Nár son of Finnchad, son of Conall Cernach, killed on the shoulder of Estine the female warrior <gloss>ms. female warrior</gloss> there, so that from this it is called *Snám dá Én* (The Swim of the Two Birds). The cleric was then busy staking out a church. "What work is he doing?" asked Diarmaid. "Building a little church," said Ciarán. "Let that be its name then," said Diarmaid: "*Eclais Bec* (The Little Church)." "Help me drive the stake," Ciarán said to Diarmaid, "and let my hand be over your hand; and your hand and your sovereignty shall be over the men of Ireland before this time tomorrow." "How shall that be done?" asked Diarmaid, "for Tuathal is in the kingship of Ireland and I am in exile." "God is capable of that," said Ciarán. Mael Mór grandson of Argata, Diarmaid's foster-brother, went to the place where Tuathal was at Grellach Eilti, towards Ross Ech in the northeast, and he drove || a spear into Tuathal's breast so that he left him without life. Mael Mór himself was killed immediately after that, so that it is called "The Adventure of Mael Mór." Mael Mór was of the Conaille Muirtheimne; he was the third foster-brother of Diarmaid, the other two foster-brothers being Luchta of Áth Ferna and Enna mac ú Laigsi. The men of Ireland then made Diarmaid king before a week had passed.

The Great Assembly of Uisneach was held by Diarmaid and the men of Ireland at Beltaine; for those were the three high assemblies of Ireland at that time: the Assembly of Uisneach at Beltaine, the Fair of Taillten at Lughnasadh, and the Feast of Tara at Samhain. And whoever violated those among the men of Ireland, the one who broke that law was a criminal deserving of death. Word came from Diarmaid to Ciarán to come to the assembly, and Diarmaid himself came to Cnoc Bracáin to meet him and stayed there; so it is from that that it is called the Hill of the Residence. Ciarán then went to join him. "What is the matter then?" asked Diarmaid; "for it is here that we first met after I took the kingship through your blessing. This plain, as it is, with its herds and its cattle, is yours as an offering for the altar." Now, the king had an enemy on the plain: Flann the Fair, son of Díma, from whom *Telach Díma* or *Telach Fhloinn* is named. His house was burned by the king and he was wounded inside. The young warrior went into a bathing tub that was in the house, and he died in it. "You have quickly gone against your testament," Ciarán said to Diarmaid, "for you have violated the land you gave to us. However," he said, "though I will not take || heaven or earth from you or your children, the death that man received at your hands shall be the death you yourself will receive: namely, wounding and..." <gloss>ms. death</gloss>

### The Birth of Aed Sláine here below.

Tara of the kings was the proper residence for every king who would take Ireland; for it was common for the laws, penalties, and rents of the men of Ireland to be brought there. It was also common for the men of Ireland to come from every direction to Tara to partake in the Feast of Tara every Samhain; for there were two great assemblies held by the men of Ireland: the Feast of Tara every Samhain—for that was the Easter of the pagans—and the Fair of Tailtiu every Lughnasadh. Every rule, moreover, and every law that was ordained by the men of Ireland in either of those places, no one dared to violate until the period <note>facsimile: thísed</note> of that year arrived.

Now, there was once a great assembly at Tailtiu held by the Gaels. He who was king over Ireland at that time was Diarmait mac Fergusa Cerrbeoil. The men of Ireland were arranged upon the assembly platforms; that is, everyone according to their ranks, crafts, and duties, as was the custom until then. There was also a separate platform for the women around the king’s two wives. These were the queens who were with Diarmait at that time: Mairenn the Bald and Mugain, daughter of Conchrad mac Duach Duinn of the men of Munster. Mugain felt great envy toward Mairenn, and she said

# The Birth of Aed Sláine. [53 : 1]

...queens and the blessing of the seed that would be born from her. He put water into his cup and gave it to the queen; she drank from it and bathed with it. The queen became pregnant from that and bore a son, and he was Aed Sláine. Truly, the child conceived there—namely Aed Sláine—was excellent. His descendants, the men of Brega, are also excellent: in generosity, in fame, in dignity, in hardiness, in laws, in leadership, in uprightness, in skill, and in destiny. They excel in order, in hospitality, in gentleness, in custom, in wisdom, and in pride; in renown, in battle, and in kind-heartedness; in form, in sense, and in intellect; in nobility, in goodness, and in serenity. For the race of Aed Sláine across the Plain of Brega was like a golden beam across a board of white bronze; for every good thing and every great, well-ordered household—whatever is considered the greatest good—is compared to Aed Sláine. So that this deed might be remembered and stored in the memory of all, the historian Flann Mainistrech sang this:

Mugain, daughter of fair Conchrad,
Son of Duach from West Munster:
She earned noble generosity without fail,
The wife of Diarmait, son of Cerball.

Grief seized the queen—
It was a cause of sorrow with true vengeance—
Since her offspring was not yet realized,
So that she was nearly abandoned.

Then came the brilliant, heroic warrior,
The keen descendant of Fiatach, Finnia:
To the grace of the Plain of Brega with strength,
To our noble man, to Diarmait.

He came toward the fierce king,
Without hardship and without failure:
Lest there should be a contest for fame,
He then protected the queen.

He said to him that she had need
Of something that would cure her distress:
For her loss there would be a clever pledge,
For she had been for a time in barrenness.

Keen Finnia blessed her,
So that it might be a bargain for his pleasant will:
From his cup he distributed a drink
To the powerful, bright-white woman.

Afterward Mugain was pregnant,
A healthy, god-like, and joyful pregnancy:
She conceived a lamb that was no distress to her,
Though it was not in the form of a human.

Because of it, darkness spread over her clear cheek,
Mugain the good, the great queen:
She preferred waiting without true children
Rather than a four-legged conception.

"Do not be afraid of it, for God's sake,"
Said the truly wise Finnia:
"The beautiful, bright, great lamb
Has reached the consecration of your womb."

Then the woman was pregnant again,
It was a great and honored pregnancy:
The little boy who was brought forth from it
Was a beautiful, silver-like salmon.

She offered it to pure-hearted Finnia,
For the God whom he faithfully served:
"Whatever the salmon above the hill may be,
A little boy shall come to her after it."

It was performed by Finnbarr of pure sound,
A slow-building and good omen:
It was a blooming deal without sorrow
For the great salmon of Mugain.

Mugain conceived, greater than any offspring,
For the right and fitting son of Cerball:
Then, over the red-pathed span of time,
The noble, host-leading Aed Sláine was born.

They advance upon the strength of Ireland,
Just as Finnia had prophesied for them:
Pure and glorious in clear deeds
Are the great children of Mugain.

This is, without a deceptive reputation for harm,
The opinion of another historian:
That Mugain, with her blameless great fosterings,
Was of the Connachta.

# The Wooing of Becfola.

Once Diarmaid mac Aedha Sláine was in the kingship of Ireland, and Crimhthann mac Aedha, his foster-son, was held as a hostage by him from the people of Leinster. He and Crimhthann his foster-son went one day to Áth Truim <note>Trim</note>, and they had their many weapons with them and a single lad. They saw a lone woman coming across the ford from the west in a chariot, more beautiful than any woman of the women of the world. "From where have you come, girl?" asked Diarmaid. "Not from far," said the girl. "What brings you into solitude?" asked Diarmaid. "Seeking wheat," said the woman. "You shall find it with me," said Diarmaid. "I do not refuse," said the woman. After that, he took the woman with him to Tara <note>Temair</note> so that she was in his fair bed. "Where is the woman from, Diarmaid?" asked everyone. "I will not tell," said Diarmaid. "Small is her substance <note>or bride-price</note>," said everyone. "That shall be her name," said the druids: "Becfola" <note>Small-substance</note>.

After that, the woman gave her love to the king's foster-son, that is, to Crimhthann mac Aedha, instead of Diarmaid, and she began to entreat him for a long time. Then the lad said he would come to meet her at Cluain Dá Chaillech <note>the Meadow of the Two Nuns</note> around the time of tierce <note>mid-morning</note> on Sunday to take her away in elopement. However, his people prevented him from taking the wife of the King of Ireland in flight.

She rose after that in the early morning of Sunday from Diarmaid's side. "Whither is the early rising, woman?" asked Diarmaid. "To Cluain Dá Chaillech," said the girl. "Why so?" asked Diarmaid. The girl answered: "Eight tunics with gold embroidery, and eight pins of full-setting, and three gold diadems I left there for safekeeping." "Do not go on a Sunday to seek them," said Diarmaid, "for a Sunday journey is not good." "It is a necessity for me," said the woman, "for it is certain that I shall go." "It shall not be with my consent," said Diarmaid.

So she and her handmaid went from Tara southward to Duibtir Laigen <note>the Black-land of Leinster</note>. And they happened to go astray there until nightfall, when they saw a pack of wolves coming toward them on the mountain. She went into a tree to escape them, and the hounds <note>wolves</note> devoured her handmaid. She was not long in the tree until she saw a fire in the middle of the wood. She went toward the fire until she saw a young warrior <column-break/> who was of the fairest form in the world, with both weapons and attire by the fire.

## The Wandering of Caenchomrac.

There was a noble bishop in Clonmacnoise named Caenchomrac, and Mochta was his name at first. He was a chaste man <note>literally "son of virginity"</note> and a successor <note>comarba</note> of God, and he had come to Clonmacnoise on a pilgrimage. His honor and dignity were great in Clonmacnoise, for he used to find out from God for every person who died whether they would receive a reward or whether they would receive punishment. And he used to tell everyone who would die within the year their circumstances during the final quarter of the year. His honor in Clonmacnoise then seemed too great to him, and he came to Inis Endaim on Lough Ree to perform his pilgrimage there, for he found it solitary for the office, the mass, and prayer.

There was a prayerful group of monks with him there, and they used to go out onto the land for alms and first-fruits in Teffia, for the men of Teffia were in great submission to him: a hundred young pigs, a hundred calves, a hundred lambs, a loaf from every kneading-trough, and a *screpall* <note>a unit of value or silver coin</note> from every household. And their losses in battle would not exceed nine men, provided they were under tribute to him, as it was said:—

I give thanks to my King; the men of Tethbae have returned to their land. Not one of them was wounded, nor did they wound anyone. I say to you, this boast shall not be a lie: if I am mentioned, your number shall be nine <note>a reference to a protective prayer or company</note>.

And furthermore, he said, "Though there may be many in pursuit of you, and though you are few, as long as you remember me, you shall go safely." To which he said:

> Nine from the land of Tethbae, against a hundred thousand miles:
> If they make mention of Caenchomrac, they shall go safely to their lands.
> The hosts of the world’s armies shall not take their victories from them,
> provided they are in my service, and my service is to God.

He remained in that way for a while between Clonmacnoise and Inis Endaim. Once, while he was in Inis Endaim, the monks went out. Eogan and Ecertach—the two sons of Aedhacán of the Uí Maine and the two beloved foster-sons of the cleric—went until they reached Slieve Leitrim in Uí Maine. The Uí Fhannáin were there hunting on the mountain; they had killed a number of wild pigs there and gave a piglet from them to the clerics. They brought it home with them and put it on the spit over the fire. 

And as the cleric was chanting his psalms, he saw a large man coming toward him from the base of the waves out of the lake. The man greeted the cleric, and the cleric greeted him. "It is well," the man said, "that the one who is on the spit over the fire should answer you and should chant psalms with you." "How can that be at all?" asked Caenchomrac. "It is not difficult to say," he replied. "We have a monastery beneath this lake; for it is no more difficult for the Lord to have people dwell under the waters than in other places. But the youths of the monastery committed a sin, so they were sent out in the form of wild pigs, and it is they who were killed today on Slieve Leitrim. And one of those is the one on the spit over the fire. I am his fleshly father, and here is his psalter in my hand, which I give to you." 

It was called the "Psalter of the Pig" afterwards, and it remained for a long time in Clonmacnoise. As for the piglet, it was given to Eogan, and that was the "piglet at the boar's mouth." Caenchomrac permitted the man to take the body with him for burial. "Why is it, O cleric," the man said, "that you do not come with me to see the monastery that is down under this lake?" "I will go," said Caenchomrac. 

The two of them went under the lake and entered the monastery. Caenchomrac stayed there from one canonical hour to the next. He returned home the next day, and he was covered in the lake-refuse. He used to visit under the lake often, and from then on it was never hidden from him as long as he lived.

### The Eulogy of Cormac, grandson of Conn, and of Finn son of Cumhall here.

A noble and venerable High King took power over Ireland: Cormac, son of Art, son of Conn of the Hundred Battles. He was then forty years in the kingship of Ireland, besides the two years that the Ulstermen <note>Ulaid</note> took power, namely: Fergus Black-tooth for one year, and Eochaid Gonnat for another year. The Ulstermen deposed Cormac twice. Indeed, that same Cormac was missing for four months at sea, and it was not known where he went until he returned himself and told of his adventure <note>echtra</note>.

There was no king in the world then who was comparable to Cormac except Solomon, son of David, for the brilliance of his wisdom and the wealth of his reign. For Cormac never gave a judgment without having three foundations of judgment with him: the foundation of natural wisdom, the foundation of legal precedent, and the foundation of traditional custom. So it was that according to the wisdom and knowledge of those judgments, a calf would be born at the end of a single season during the time of Cormaс. There was a sack <note>miach</note> of grain for every furrow in his time. Heifers were as large as calving cows in his time. Every river, provided it reached only to the knee, was found...
