# The Eulogy of Cormac

A salmon was in every single mesh of the net during his time. The cow’s udder was full of beestings <note>The first milk after calving</note> during his reign. Honey was gathered by the fingertip in his day, having been showered from heaven through the princely righteousness of Cormac. It was also during his time that enough vessels could not be found for the milk, for the cows were dripping their milk without ceasing.

That king was then compared to Octavian Augustus because of how everyone paid the Roman tax <note>literally "Caesarean tax"</note> from their inheritance. In that same way, everyone paid the royal tax to Cormac from their ancestral lands, for Cormac never took his inheritance from anyone.

There was not a king in the world then who was equal to Cormac. For he was the best in form, appearance, and attire; in stature, proportion, beauty, and symmetry; and even in his eyes. There were seven pupils in each of his two eyes, as Senuath the poet relates, saying:

->A beautiful distinction between them, of the two speckled, noble eyes:<-
->fourteen pupils in the man's eyes.<-

He was one who <insert>never</insert> was weak in wisdom, skill, or speech; in deed or valor; in kingship or leadership; in sense or generosity; in dress, arms, joy, abundance, or dignity; in custom or lineage. He made a Promised Land of Ireland in his time: that is, without theft, without captivity, without violence, without need for watching or herding, and without any person having a concern for food or clothing.

These are but a few of the praises of Cormac, for no man can tell them all unless an angel instructs him. Great indeed was his discipline and his power over the men of Ireland, for he would not allow anyone among the men of Ireland to be idle, unless they were performing military service for Cormac.

He who was the leader of the household and the master of the hounds for Cormac was Finn son of Cumhall. For the best troop a king of Ireland ever has is his master of hounds. A lord's hand never took the hand of a better warrior than Finn; for he was a warrior in his bravery, a landowner in his hospitality, a king in his kingship, and a hero in his heroism. He was a mercenary in his service and a champion in his strength; for every champion from then until today is compared to Finn. Finn was common throughout Ireland, hunting and fowling with the king's troop.

It was in Almhain of Leinster, however, that Finn resided most often. After the weight of maturity and old age fell upon Finn, and after the death of Cormac, he lived habitually in Almhain, except—

...unless he should come to visit her. She was a wife to Finn—Smirgad, daughter of Fatha Canann. She was a prophetess and a seeress. It was she who told Finn that whenever he should drink a drink from her father's horn, it would be the end of his life; therefore, he never drank a drink from a horn from then on, but drank from cups instead.

One day Finn went from Almu until he arrived at Adarca Iuchba in Offaly. He found a spring on the hill and drank a drink from it. He put his thumb under his tooth of wisdom <note>literally "tooth of knowledge"</note> until it was revealed to him through *teinm laegha* <note>a prophetic ritual</note> that the end of his life and his days had come. Then he spoke these verses:

> The prophecy has come for Finn: a sanctuary of a pool of blood for a drink;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;going across the Segda river of the host, to sleep with the great daughter of Mac Lir.
> The venom of the horn—a terrible stream—has changed my form, once perfect and bright;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;it has reddened my heart and my body, and there is more in store for me.
> You drank a drink from the green pool; you drank a poison of fierce shouting;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;it is certain to me that from now on, this shall be the final satisfaction.
> It seems to me it was not the drink given on the day by the bank of Inber Abrat,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;from the cup of white silver, by Aine, daughter of Manannán.
> It was not the sweet drink of hazel-mead given to me by the daughter of Conn's grandson,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;on the early morning that the face of Diarmuid was reddened in Inis Dairbrech.
> It was not the drink for which songs were sung to me on the bank of Sescenn Uairbeoil,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;when the two daughters of Conan of Cualu served me with many hands.
> It was not the drink without cause for sorrow that Sadb, daughter of Bodb, gave me
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;with her men upon Femin, when she left me in darkness.
> It was not the sweet drink of mead on the day by the bank of Inber Bera;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;it is certain my day has come, and the deed that remains is terrible.

Finn departed after that until he reached Druim Breg. There was long-standing ill-will against Finn and the Fianna in that land, for it was by him that Uirgriu of the Luaighne of Tara had fallen. The Luaighne then gathered, along with the three sons of Uirgriu and Aichlech Mór mac Duibrenn (the son of one of the three sons of Uirgriu). A fierce, merciless, powerful, manly, furious, and brave battle was then fought between them, where each of them remembered their old grudges against the other, both from long ago and more recently. That battle was fought at Brea on the Boyne, and they remained in combat for a long time until the losses were great on both sides. However, the battle was turned against Finn, and he fell there. It was Aichlech mac Duibrenn who killed Finn and decapitated him. In order to commemorate that deed and to bring knowledge to those who are uninformed, the historian sang this verse:

> The great battle of Brea of the sharp deeds, fought by the Luaighne and the Fianna of Finn:
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;the destruction of the Fianna in the battle, while the Luaighne were victorious.
> There was mangled the bright royal champion, Finn mac Cumhaill of great spirit;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;had the Fianna been by his side, he would not have fallen by Aichlech's hand.

> Evil was the violent, powerful deed performed by the three sons of Uirgriu:

That then is the death of Finn according to the truth of history as the experts relate it; however, they teach differently about his origins. Some of them say he was of the Corca Oiche of the Uí Fhidhghinte. Others say—and this is true—that he was of the Uí Thairrsigh of the Uí Fhailge, and that they were of the *aithechthuatha* <note>vassal or rent-paying tribes</note>, as Maelmura said in the chronicle: "Six tribes who will not take a place from the sea of Breoghuin: the Garbraide of the Succa, the Uí Thairrsigh, and the Galeóin of Leinster."

However, the Leinstermen say that Finn was a descendant of Nuada Necht, and this is his genealogy: Finn, son of Cumall, son of Sualtach, son of Baiscne, son of Nuada Necht.

So those are the praises of Cormac and the death of Finn.

### The Enumeration of Finn’s Household.

This is the account of Finn’s household: their number was ten and seven score <note>150</note> royal champion-leaders, with three groups of nine warriors accompanying every one of those men. They possessed champion-feats such as Cú Chulainn had in his time. They were bound not to seize livestock or commit robbery; never to refuse any person a gift or food; and that no single man of them should ever flee from nine warriors.

No man of them was accepted into the Fianna—neither at the great assembly of Uisneach, nor at the fair of Tailtiu, nor at the feast of Tara—until his father, his mother, his tribes, and his kindred gave [securities] on his behalf. This was so that if he were killed, they would not demand compensation for him, so that he would have no hope of anyone else avenging him but himself. Likewise, if he himself committed great evils, no vengeance would be taken upon his kinsmen.

No man was accepted among these until he was a master-poet of the twelve books of poetry. Furthermore, no man was accepted until a large pit was dug that reached the fold of his waist; he was placed <gloss>(sic)</gloss> in it with his shield and a hazel-wood staff the length of a forearm. Nine warriors would then come at him with nine spears, and at a distance of ten furrows between them, they would cast at him all at once. If he were wounded despite his defense, he was not accepted into the rank of the Fianna.

No man was accepted, moreover, until his hair was braided and he was sent running through the forests of Ireland, with all of them pursuing him through...

### This is the Colloquy of the Ancients.

After the Battle of Comar, the Battle of Gabra, and the Battle of Ollarbha were fought, and after the destruction of the Fianna, they scattered afterward in groups and bands throughout Ireland. At that time, no one remained alive of their name except for two good warriors of the last of the Fianna: Oisín son of Finn, and Cáilte son of Crunnchu son of Rónán, whose vigor and prowess were now weary. Twice nine warriors were with them, and those eighteen heroes came from the borders of flower-strewn, wooded Slieve Fuait out to the white gardens which are called Louth <note>Lugbadh</note> at this time. They were gloomy and dispirited there at the setting of the evening clouds that night.

Then Cáilte said to Oisín, "Well, my soul, Oisín, what way shall we go before the end of the day to seek hospitality for this night?" 

"I do not know," said Oisín, "since there remain of the elders of the Fianna and the old household of Finn mac Cumhaill only three: myself, you, O Cáilte, and Cámha, the noblewoman and female guardian who was guarding Finn mac Cumhaill from the time he was a youth until the day he died." 

"We are entitled to a night's lodging and food from her," said Cáilte, "for it is impossible to count or recount the amount of treasures and wealth that the prince-warrior Finn bestowed upon her, besides the third best treasure Finn ever obtained, which he gave to her—that is, the *Anghalach*, a drinking-horn that Moriath, daughter of the King of the Greeks, gave to Finn, and Finn gave to Cámha."

And they received a night's lodging that night from Cámha. She asked them their names, and they told her; and then she wept intense showers of tears. They then asked news of one another, and after that they went into the bed-chamber that had been prepared for them. The noblewoman Cámha ordered their maintenance—that is, the newest of every food and the oldest of every drink to be given to them—for she knew how people like them should be fed, and she also knew what would be enough for Oisín and Cáilte, having known it many times before. She rose up, weak and frail, and was reminiscing about the Fianna and Finn mac Cumhaill. She spoke of Oscar son of Oisín, of the son of Lugaid, and of the Battle of Gabra and others, and a great wave of grief <note>tocht</note> broke over them because of that.

Then Cáilte said: "This is no more grievous to us now than the fact that we, the twice nine who remain as the last of that great, good company, must part || and scatter from one another." Oisín answered him: "By my word indeed," he said, "there is neither strength nor power left in me after them." And though the warriors were brave, they wept gloomily, sorrowfully, and dispiritedly along with the noblewoman <gloss>[ms. mbanlaith]</gloss>, namely Cámha. Their fill of drink and food was given to them, and they stayed there for three days and three nights. They bid farewell to Cámha after that, and Oisín said:

->Cámha is sorrowful today; she has reached the end of her journey.<-
->Cámha, without son or grandson, has become a withered old woman.<-

Then they went forward out of the dwelling onto the grassy green. They took counsel there, and the counsel they decided upon was to part from one another; and their parting was like the parting of soul from body. They did so: for Oisín went to the fairy mound of Ucht Cleitig where his mother was, namely Bla daughter of Derg Dianscothach. And Cáilte went forward to Inber Bic Loingsig in Brega, which is called the Monastery of Drogheda <note>Droichead Átha</note> at this time—that is, Bec Loingsech son of Arist fell there, the son of the King of the Romans who came to conquer Ireland until a tidal wave drowned him there—and to Linn Feic on the white-streamed Boyne <note>Bóinn</note>, and across the ancient plain of Brega southward, to Ráth Droma Deirc, the place where Patrick son of Alpin <note>Pátraic mac Alprainn</note> was.

At that time, Patrick was singing the divine office and praising the Creator, and blessing the fort where Finn mac Cumhaill used to be, namely Ráth Droma Deirc. The clerics saw them approaching, and horror and fear seized them before the huge men with their huge hounds, for they were not people of the same era or time as them.

Then rose up the salmon of sovereignty, the pillar of lordship, and the earthly angel, namely Patrick son of Alpin, the Apostle of the Gaels. He took the aspergillum to sprinkle holy water on the huge men, for until that day, a thousand legions of demons had been above their heads. The demons fled into the hills, the rock clefts, and the borders of the territory, driven away from them on every side. After that, the huge men sat down.

"Well, my soul," said Patrick to Cáilte, "<insert>[who]</insert> is your name, O warrior?" "I am Cá<insert>[ilte]</insert> son of Crunnchu, son of <insert>[Rónán]</insert>," he said. <insert>[The clerics]</insert> || were in great wonder watching them for a long time.

"Did you have horses or horse-herds in the Fianna?"
"They did indeed," said Cáilte: "one hundred and fifty foals from a single mare <note>Manuscript: lára</note> and a single horse."
"From where were those obtained?" asked Patrick.
"I will tell you the truth of it, O soul," said Cáilte:—

A young warrior named Artúir, son of Béine <note>Manuscript: benne</note> the Briton, was with Finn, and his following consisted of thrice nine men. A hunt was held at Beinn Edair by Finn, and that hunt was successful and fruitful. They released their hounds, and Finn sat upon the warrior’s cairn between Beinn Edair and the sea. He was well pleased in his mind listening to the belling of the fierce and frantic deer being vigorously killed by the hounds of the Fianna.

It happened then that Artúir, son of Béine the Briton, was guarding the coast between the hunting ground and the sea so that the deer-herd would not swim away from them. While Artúir was out at the head of the bay, he saw three of Finn’s hounds: Bran, Sceolaing, and Adhnuall. Artúir then decided that he and his thrice nine men would depart across the sea and take those hounds with him to his own country. That plan was carried out. Indeed, they went across the surface of the sea with those three hounds, and they took harbor and landing at the estuary of the Gaimiach sea in the territory of Britain. They went ashore and traveled on to the mountain of Lodán, son of Lir, and held a hunt on that mountain.

As for the Fianna, after their hunting and their heroic slaughter was finished, they made camp at Beinn Edair, the peak of Edair, son of Etgaeth the warrior. The hounds of Finn’s house were then counted, as was their custom. Many were their <gloss>kennel-companions</gloss> as the poet said:

> The branch-reckoning of Finn’s hounds, with his beautiful and ever-melodious pack:
> three hundred full-grown hounds, and two hundred beagles.

"There were many people who owned those," said Patrick.
"That is indeed true for you," said Cáilte, "for this was the number that used to be in Finn’s house:"

> One hundred and fifty were in Finn’s house, of truly fine Fianna leaders:
> three hundred high-ranking attendants, and two hundred worthy foster-sons.

Upon the counting of the hounds, a great loss was found among them: Bran, Sceolaing, and Adhnuall. This was told to Finn. "Search among the three battalions of the Fianna," he said. And though they were searched for, the hounds were not found.

Then a washing-basin of white gold was brought to Finn; he washed his royal face and put his thumb under his tooth of knowledge. The truth was revealed to him, and he said: "The son of the King of the Britons has taken your hounds from you. Choose nine men to go in search of them." And it was chosen so, and these were their names: Diarmaid mac Duinn, son of Donnchadh...

# The Colloquy

Aran of the many deer, the sea reaches against its shoulders;
An island where companies are fed, a ridge where blue spears are reddened.
Skittish fawns are on its peaks, soft bogberries on its marshes;
Cold water in its rivers, mast on its brown oaks.
Greyhounds are in it and hunting dogs, blackberries and sloes of the dark blackthorn;
Its dwellings are close to the woods, deer parting around its groves.
Purple lichen is gathered on its rocks, faultless grass on its slopes;
Over its crags, a fair protection, speckled calves are leaping and gambolling.
Smooth is its plain, fat are its pigs, pleasant <gloss>its fields—a story to be believed</gloss> ||
Its nuts on the tips of its hazel-trees, longships sailing past it.
It is delightful for them when fair weather comes, trout under the banks of its rivers;
Seagulls answer around the white cliffs, Aran is delightful at every season.

"Victory and blessing to you, Cáilte, my soul," said Patrick. "Your stories are trustworthy to us, and you yourself are as well from now on."

Then Patrick saw a fortress and a fine dwelling directly away from them. "What settlement is that, Cáilte?" asked Patrick. "A settlement that was the proudest that ever was in Ireland or in Scotland," said Cáilte. "Who lived there?" asked Patrick. "The three sons of Luigdech the Fair, son of Aengus—that is, three sons of the King of Ireland. Ruidhe, Fiacha, and Eochaid were their names." "What gave them that great wealth?" asked Patrick.

"Once upon a time, they came to speak with their father at the Druids' Mound to the northwest of Tara. 'Where have you come from, young men?' he asked. 'From the house of mourning in the south,' <gloss>ms. from the south</gloss> they said, 'from the house of our foster-mother and our foster-father.' 'What has brought you here, young men?' asked the King of Ireland. 'To ask you for territory and land,' they said. The king was silent for a while and then said, 'It was not a father,' he said, 'who gave me territory or land, but my own good fortune and my own brilliance. And I will not give land to you; win land for yourselves.' Then they rose up as one man, quickly and nimbly, and they went forward to the lawn of the Brug and sat there without anyone with them. 'What is your counsel tonight?' asked Ruidhe. 'Our counsel,' said his brothers, 'is to perform a ritual fast against the Tuatha Dé Danann to obtain the luck of territory, an estate, and land, and to receive great and precious wealth from them.' And they were not there long before they saw a pleasant, peaceful young warrior coming toward them. He greeted the sons of the King of Ireland, and they answered him in the same way. 'Where are you from, young warrior,' they asked, 'and where do you come from?' 'From the bright-colored Brug nearby,' said the young warrior. 'What is your name, young warrior?' they asked. 'I am Bodb Derg, son of the <note>The</note> Dagda,' he said. 'And it was revealed <note>to the Tuatha Dé</note> Danann that you had come to fast || here tonight for land and great fortune. And come with me, young men.' They rose up all at once and went into the Brug. Food was brought to them, but they did not eat it."

# The Colloquy

Bodb asked them why they did not eat food. "The King of Ireland," they said, "our own father, has refused us territory and land. There are only two equal assemblies in Ireland: the Sons of Míl and the Tuatha Dé Danann, and we have come to visit the second of those assemblies."

Then the Tuatha Dé Danann went into counsel, and he who was the noblest and most distinguished in that counsel was Midhair the yellow-haired, son of the Dagda. He said: "Give them three wives," he said, "for it is from women that prosperity or fame is obtained." And three daughters of Midhair were given to them: Doirenn, Aiffe, and Aillbe. "Tell us, Bodb," said Midhair, "what shall be given to them?" Bodb said: "We are one hundred and fifty king's sons in this <term>síd</term> <note>fairy mound</note>; let one hundred and fifty ounces of red gold be given to them from each of those king's sons. And one hundred and fifty garments from me to them," said Bodb, "of every various color." "<gloss>A gift</gloss> from me to them," said Aed son of Aed of the Abusachs, from the high peak out in the sea called Rathlin at this time—he was a youth of the Tuatha Dé Danann—"a cup and a vat from me to them," he said. "And the vat, when filled with blue-rimmed water, shall make drinkable and intoxicating mead of it. And bitter-deep brine put into the cup shall make wine of it at once." "A gift from me to them," said Lir of Síd Finnachaid: "one hundred and fifty swords and one hundred and fifty whistling, long-shafted spears." "A gift from me to them," said Aengus Óg son of the Dagda: "a fortress, a stronghold, and a very great royal residence with tall palisades, with bright glass sun-chambers, and with very great houses of far-reaching view, in the place that they desire: between Rath Cobhthaigh and Tara." "A gift from me to them," said Áine daughter of Modarn: "a female cook whom I have, and it is a taboo for her to refuse anyone food, for she will obtain more as she gives it away." "A gift from me to them," said Bodb Derg: "a good <gloss>minstrel</gloss> I have—Fer Tuinne son of Trogan is his name—and men exhausted by slaughter, and women in <gloss>sharp pains of childbirth</gloss>, and warriors <gloss>wounded</gloss> and mangled would fall asleep to the haunting music he makes. And he is no more a minstrel for the fortress in which he is than for the people of the territory." And they remained in the <term>síd</term> for three days and three nights.

And Aengus told them to take three apple trees from Fid Omna with them: an apple tree in bloom, an apple tree shedding its blossoms, and an apple tree with ripe fruit. They went to the fortress after that and were there for one hundred and fifty years until those kings passed away. Then they went back to the Tuatha Dé Danann because of their marriage alliances, and they have remained there from then on. "And that is the fortress you asked me about, Patrick," said Cáilte.

### Cáílte sang:

Three floods, oh three floods, used to come to the high fort of Ruide:
A flood of youths, a flood of horses, a flood of the hounds of Luigdech’s son.
Three musics, oh three musics, were there for noble kings:
The music of harps, the music of the famous timpan, and the deep bass of the Wave of the son of Trogán.
Three shouts, oh three shouts, were there <note>The manuscript says 'bidh'</note> that were never scarce:
The shout of the singer on its lawn, the shout of racing, and the shout of the cattle.
Three shouts, oh three shouts: the shout of the large-handed pigs of Dega,
The shout of the host above the courtyard, the shout of merriment and the shout of mead.
Three harvests, oh three harvests, used to be there upon the branches:
Harvests falling constantly, trees in bloom, and trees ripe.
Three sons did Lugaid leave, though their deeds were far-reaching:
Ruide son of broad Lugaid, Echaid, and manly Fiacha.
I will give a testimony for Echaid: he never retreated a foot in defeat;
He was never without constant music, nor a time without drinking ale.
I will give a testimony for Fiacha, though his raids were far-reaching:
He never spoke a word that was too much, and none was more brave.
I will give a testimony for Ruide, to whom the three floods used to come:
He never refused anyone anything, and he never asked anything of anyone.
Thirty lords, thirty chiefs, thirty heroes were in the king's company;
That was the number of his host of hundreds: thirty times three hundreds.

"Victory and blessing to you, Cáílte," said Patrick, "for that is a cheering of the mind and spirit for us."

And they were not there long [until] they saw a lone young man coming straight from the south toward them, [with a fine] appearance. He wore a purple cloak with a gold brooch in it, and [a shirt] of yellow silk against his skin. He carried a lapful || of round yellow-topped nuts and beautiful gold-yellow apples, and he placed them on the ground in front of Patrick. "Where did you get this harvest, young man?" asked Patrick. "From the beautiful-branched wood of Gaibhle," he said. "What is your name, young man?" asked Patrick. "I am Falartach son of Fergus," he said. "What is your heritage?" asked Patrick. "The kingship of the territories of Brega, Meath, and the Deise of Tara is my heritage," said the young man, "but I am a robber and an outlaw." "Against whom do you commit robbery?" asked Patrick. "Against my own brother, Becan son of Fergus." "Your heritage shall be short for you," said Patrick. "When will it end, O holy cleric?" asked the young man. "In this very year," said Patrick. "Where did you get the harvest? I know well," said Cáílte, "where it was taken from. It is from Ros Meic Treoin in Fid Gaibhle over there. It was a hunting garden belonging to a favorite warrior of Fionn mac Cumhaill, namely Mac Lugach, the strong and great-deeded." "That is good, my soul," said Patrick, "for a favorite man of my own people is there now, namely Oessán son of the King of Scotland, who is my table-priest." "That was a hunting garden for the Fianna," said Cáílte, "and whenever a scarcity of hunting came to the Fianna in either Ireland or Scotland, they would find enough game for three days and three nights in Ros Meic Treoin."

> Cluain Cesáin was heard of far and wide, which the son of Lugaid used to frequent;

"What time of day is it now?" asked Patrick. "It is near evening," said Benén. "Has our meal come to us yet?" [asked Patrick.] "It has not indeed," said Benén. "O soul, holy Patrick," said Fulartach son of Fergus, "I will give you knowledge of the place where you might find a meal and food tonight." "Where is that place?" asked Patrick. "In the house of Becán, my own brother, in the territories of Breg and Meath."

And the clerics went before Patrick to the house of Becán. And it was thus: he had eight score white-milch cows <margin>cattle</margin>, and he refused them food. Benén and the clerics came back and told the news to Patrick. "I permit," said Patrick, "that whatever cattle and people he has, not one shall escape alive tomorrow." And that thing was fulfilled, as Patrick said:

> Becán indeed, and from Becán, let his fasting not be many;
> as long as the sun moves sunwise, let Becán not be a companion to them.

It was then that the earth swallowed all at once: Becán with his people and his wealth, both beast and human. "The entertainment and food of this night from me to you, O holy cleric," said Fulartach son of Fergus, "namely, twenty-nine cows that were feeding my band of warriors who were formerly engaged in raiding and lawlessness." "Kingship from me to you from noon tomorrow," said Patrick, "and to your descendants after you until they should go against the church." And Becán was put into the earth in that way, and Patrick gave the kingship to Fulartach.

Then Patrick asked Cáilte: "How many brothers did Fionn have?" "He had two brothers," said Cáilte, "namely, Fíthal and Dithran."

# The Dialogue. [162 b : 2 ; 163 : 1]

"Whose son is Mac Lugach?" Patrick asked. "I asked you this last night." "That would be a question for anyone else," said Cáilte, "but not for me. He is the son of Daire Derg, son of Fionn," said Cáilte, "and of Lugaid, Fionn’s daughter—a daughter both legitimate and illegitimate whom Fionn had. All the womenfolk took an oath that the girl was Fionn's legitimate daughter. Her own brother lay with her after drinking at a feast with her in Tara Luachra, and he begot that son by her—that is, Mac Lugach. On the night the boy was born, Fionn and three battalions of the Fianna, along with the boy’s father, Daire Derg, came to Tara Luachra, and they were told of this. 'It is a benefit (*gáine*) to me,' said Fionn, 'since a son was born; had it been a daughter, it would have been an evil thing for her to be born to her own brother.'"

"May you have victory and a blessing, O royal leader of the Fianna," everyone said. "The name you have given him is auspicious: Gáine." As the poet said:

> Gáine was the name of the son of fierce Lugach,
> Daire was his father, set above every tribe;
> Cúmaighe was the name of the son of a ram,
> Briun was his father, most certainly.

The boy was then placed in Fionn's lap, and Fionn placed him in the lap of Moingfhionn, daughter of Dubán, Fionn’s wife. It was she who had raised eight hundred shield-armed men for the Fianna, and she reared the boy until he was a full twelve years old. She gave him a full supply of arms and armor, and he went forward to Carraic Conluain at the end of the mountain of Smól, son of Edlecar—which is called Slieve Bloom today—to the place where Fionn and the Fianna were staying. He came into the presence of the prince Fionn, and Fionn gave him a truly warm welcome. The boy then made his covenant and alliance with Fionn and placed his hand in Fionn's hand. He remained with the Fianna for a year, but during that year he treated the Fianna with great <gloss>sluggishness</gloss>. No more than a group of nine men from the Fianna <gloss>managed</gloss> || to strike a pig or a deer because of that lad, as he was also busy beating their dogs and their servants.

Then the Fianna came to the Warrior’s Wood on the shores of Lake Lein in the south. When the three battalions of the Fianna arrived there, they made a complaint against Mac Lugach to Fionn. The three battalions said, "You have a choice: keep us with you, or keep Mac Lugach alone."

Then Mac Lugach was brought to speak with Fionn, who asked him, "Well now, Mac Lugach, my soul, what wrong have you done to the Fianna, seeing that they all hold such a hatred for you?" "I give my word," he replied, "that I do not know the cause, unless they dislike my performing feats || of agility or marksmanship among them."

There was virtue in his counsel, and that counsel remained with Mac Lugach. And Fionn said:

> O son of Lugaid, of many graces, if the warrior's way is your rank:
> Be peaceful to a powerful household; be difficult in a rugged wilderness.
> Do not strike your dog without cause; do not accuse your wife until you know the truth.
> Do not meddle with a fool in battle, however crazed he be, O son of Lugaid.
> Do not shame an honorable man; do not rise up for a dispute.
> Do not let yourself be drawn together with a witch or an evil person.
> Two-thirds of your gentleness should be for women and for the children on the floor,
> and for the poets who compose verses; do not be harsh with the common folk.
> Do not take the best place in bed from your companions and advisors.
> Avoid false oaths and sin; do not let all your hospitality be exhausted.
> Do not speak a boastful word; do not say you will not do what is right.
> For it is shameful to speak boldly if it cannot be fulfilled.
> Do not abandon your lord as long as you live in this world.
> For gold or for any jewel on this earth, do not abandon your protection.
> Do not complain manfully <note>Meaning boldly or persistently</note> about your people to a lord.
> For it is not the work of a good man to complain of his troop to a high prince.
> Do not be a teller of tall tales or a liar; do not be talkative or quick to cause harm.
> Though your shouts be many, do not be an enemy of the assembly.
> Do not be a frequenter of the ale-house; do not be grasping with an elder.
> The judgment you hear in the assembly is the right one; do not meddle with a wretched person.
> Do not be one who refuses food; do not let the ungenerous be your companion.
> Do not force yourself upon a prince; do not let every high prince be complained of.
> Stick to your clothing, stick to your weapons, before the grey-green battle ends.
> Do not be stingy with your fortune; hold fast to gentleness, O son of Lugaid.

"Victory and a blessing to you," said Patrick. "That is a good story you have told us. And where is Brocán the scribe?" "Here, O holy cleric," said Brocán. "Let that story be written down by you." And Brocán did so immediately.

The world’s handiwork was with the woman,

Not long after that, they saw seven large youths approaching them. "From where have you come, O youths?" said Patrick, "and who are you?" Then his tent was spread over Patrick, and the king of Munster came with the nobles of his people and placed his head in Patrick’s lap and knelt to him. And he remained there for a week, raising the dead and healing people of sickness, disease, and every other ailment.

# The Dialogue.

Then Patrick was granted his own judgment. Eogan Red-side went on before the kings to his own fortress, and the nobles of Munster returned to their own fortresses and fine towns after that.

"Well, my soul, O Cáilte," said Patrick, "why was this hill we are on called Fionntulach <note>Fair Hill</note>?" "I will tell you the truth of it," said Cáilte. "It was from here that we, the three battalions of the Fianna, set out to fight the Battle of Ventry. Our spears were brought to us, and rings of withes were placed upon the shafts of our spears. ->Cáilte sang.<-

O this high and lovely hill, to which the fair Fianna used to come;
   a vast encampment used to be upon you, with a band of bright youths.
It was our portion to recount, we who came to the height of the smooth plain:
   beautiful blackberries from the bushes, and nuts from the hazels of Kintyre.
Tender shoots of thorny brambles, sprigs of wild garlic without fault;
   we used to consume every Beltane the blooming tips of watercress.
Birds from dark oak-woods would reach the Fianna’s cooking-pit;
   speckled martens from Berramain, and woodcocks from the mountain peaks.
Swift salmon from Linnmhuine, eels from the noble Shannon;
   woodcocks of the true forest, and otters from the secret places of the Dóil.
Marine fish of the sea from the lands of Bái and Béire;
   the white-bellied fish of truly pure Fáide, and dulse from the harbors of Cape Clear.

I and Oisín of great fame used to go in the prows of currachs;
   I found the perils of the grey sea around the waves and the hills.

"And it was from here that we went to fight the Battle of Ventry. Then we saw a young warrior of Fionn’s people approaching us: Cael the brave, the hundred-slayer, grandson of Nemnann. 'Where have you come from, O Cael?' asked Fionn. 'From the dewy Brugh <note>Newgrange</note> in the north,' said Cael. 'What did you seek there?' asked Fionn. 'To speak with Muirinn, daughter of Derg, my own foster-mother.' 'And what was the reason for that?' asked Fionn. 'Because of a fairy lover, a noble bride, and the fulfillment of a vision: Crédhe, daughter of fair-skinned Cairbre, daughter of the king of Ciarraige Luachra <note>Kerry</note>.' 'Do you know, O Cael,' said Fionn, 'that she is the greatest female deceiver in Ireland? For there is hardly a precious object in Ireland that she has not enticed to her fortress and her fine dwelling. And do you know,' asked Cael, 'what conditions she demands of everyone?' 'I know,' said Fionn. 'Whoever possesses the skill or the poetry must compose a poem for her, describing her bowls, her horns, her cups, her jars, her great vessels, and her massive royal palace.' 'I have it ready,' said Cael, 'given to me by Muirinn, daughter of Derg, my own foster-mother.'"

Just as the girl surpassed the women of the Fianna in the bestowing of jewels and wealth, her husband surpassed others in valor and heroics against three battalions of the Fianna in that battle. A tragic thing was done on the last day of the battle: the drowning of Cael. There were other living creatures who shared the same lifespan as Cael; and the wave brought him back in after he was drowned. The girl and the nobles of the Fianna came to him, and he was carried by them to the southern beach, south of Ventry, so that Cael's Strand has been the name of that beach from then on, as well as Cael's Grave.

The girl came and stretched herself by <insert>his</insert> side, and she made a loud lament and a great sorrow. "Why should I not die of grief for my husband," she said, "when even the soaring wild birds are dying of grief for him?" And Créide said:—

And the maiden stretched herself out beside Cael and died of grief for him. And they were both buried in one grave there. And it is I myself, said Cáilte, who raised the stone that is over their grave, so that it is called the Grave of Cael and Créide.

"May you have victory and a blessing, Cáilte," said Patrick. "It is a good story you have told. And where is Brocán the scribe?" "Here," said Brocán. "Let all that Cáilte has sung be written by you." And it was written.

It was not long for them after that until they saw a troop of a goodly host approaching them, and a shelter of dark-purple shields around them, and a "wooded sanctuary" <note>fidneimhed: a metaphor for a dense thicket of spears</note> of very high, gold-socketed spears at their shoulders. And they came into the pavilion where Patrick was. And their lord put his head into the lap of Saint Patrick and they prostrated to him. "Who are you yourself, young warrior?" asked Patrick. "I am Bran mac Deirg," said the warrior, "the son of the King of Munster." "Why have you come here?" asked Patrick. "I wished to learn <term>fiannaigecht</term> <note>The lore and warrior-skills of the Fianna</note>, holy cleric, for I heard that a warrior of Fionn’s people was with you, and I wished to learn the <term>dórd fiansa</term> <note>The characteristic war-cry or chant of the Fianna</note> from him."

"Do you hear that, my soul, Cáilte?" said Patrick. "I hear it," he said. "Good, Bran," said Cáilte, "how do you yourselves hunt?" "We close around the hill, or the cairn, or the wood of the mountain-plain; and we are there for the duration of the fair day following the hounds, and we kill a deer..."

### In Agallamh
<meta>[165 b : 2]</meta>

One time and another time passed from us. Then Cáilte wept in the presence of Patrick, so tearful and sorrowful that the front of his garment and his chest were wet with his tears.

Then Patrick and Cáilte, with all the hosts they had, went up to the top of Cenn Febrat on Sliab Cáin. The layout of that place where they arrived was such that there were three glens around the mountain and a lake between them; *Loch Bó* [Lake of the Cow] was its name. *Osmetal* was the name of the mountain, *Cnoc na hAeire* [Hill of the Penance] lay to the west of the lake, *Finninis* was the name of the eastern hill, and *Cnoc Maine* was the name of this hill. It was here that the deceptive stag lived, namely the *Liath na dTrí mBeann* <note>The Grey One of the Three Peaks; the manuscript variant is *luath*, meaning "swift"</note>. For twenty-seven years, he used to escape from the <term>Fianna</term>, evading both hound and man. A young warrior of the <term>Fianna</term> killed him, and I am that warrior.

After that, Cáilte rose and stationed his people around the lake—to the east and west, south and north. Patrick sat down, and so <term>Suide Pádraig</term> [Patrick’s Seat] is the name of that place at Cenn Febrat on Sliab Cáin. Then Cáilte raised his hunting-call, his game-call, and his victory-shout on high. He let out three fierce, warlike battle-cries, so that there was no wild game in the vicinity—neither in plain, nor bog, nor mountain-field, nor wood—that did not come in a great, rushing stampede until they went to cool themselves after their journey in the mighty Loch Bó before them. Horror, fear, and dread seized the people at that noise and vast clamor—at the wild stags, the swift red hinds, and the heavy-sided boars. The animals were nearly killed instantly by the length of their run and their exhaustion. <column-break/> The host spread out around the lake, and not a single creature escaped the hunt. They divided the kill, and eight hundred portions were shared among them.

"Give us the tithe of the hunt," said <term>Beneoin</term>. But <term>Bran mac Deirg</term> was not willing to share the portion that belonged to the <term>Fianna</term> with anyone.

A sickness seized the belly <note>The manuscript reads *ana*</note> of <term>Bran mac Deirg</term>, the son of the king of Munster. "Put your hand on this, O holy cleric," said Bran. "By my word," said Cáilte, "the sickness will not leave you until you pay its price." "What is the price?" asked Bran. "Since the sickness is in your belly," Cáilte replied, "the belly-cut of every cow, pig, and sheep shall be given by you to Patrick and the holy church forever." "I will give that," said Bran, "and my son after me shall give it." This became a custom among the men of Ireland from that time forward. Then Patrick placed his hand on the belly of <term>Bran mac Deirg</term>, and he was healed instantly.

"It is time for us to depart now," said Cáilte. "Which way shall we go?" asked Patrick. "I remember, O holy Patrick, that no host or company dared to sit upon these three hills because of a challenge from the <term>Tuatha Dé Danann</term>."

### Cáilte sang:

> I remember three hills that are without age or decay:
> the Grey One of the Three Peaks used to run there, from border to border.
> I remember three churches that were once well-fortified forts:
> no sound of a bell was in them then; more frequent was the druid’s knot around them.
> Cáilte is my true name; I was a leader of the fair <term>Fianna</term>:
> we used to make no haste while traversing the glen.
> The warlike Fionn, when he was alive, would not endure
> a foolish buck bellowing above his wide encampment.
> I and Flann, son of Failbe, reddened many a hero with a spear:
> this is my confession indeed—many a battle I remember.

And the host departed with their hunting-loads upon them.

Cáilte cast a glance to his left toward the mountain and saw a fortress and a fine homestead. "By my conscience indeed," he said, "that fortress was not known to us. Let us go over to the homestead," he said.

After that, they came forward to the fortress, and they were surprised to see no hosts or multitudes there, but only nine female slaves and three male slaves. They entered a secluded sun-room <note>grianán</note> that was in the homestead, and two women were in the sun-room, weeping and grieving. They were welcomed and attended to, and their traveling clothes and gear were removed from them. Cáilte asked them, "Whose fortress is this?"

"It is the fortress of the two sons of the King of Fermoy," they said. "Lochán and Eogan are their names."

"Why are you gloomy and sorrowful?" asked Cáilte.

"We have reason for it," they said. "We are married to two brothers, and we ourselves are two sisters. Our husbands have gone to bring home [new] wives tonight, and there is nothing to keep us in the fortress once our husbands and the new women arrive with them."

Then Cáilte glanced past them into the back of the building and saw the great royal stone pillar that used to belong to a beloved warrior of Fionn’s, namely Senach son of Maeilchró, of the old household of Fionn mac Cumhaill. And this was the nature of that stone: Fionn had given it to him as payment—three times fifty ounces of gold, three times fifty ounces of silver, and three times fifty ounces of <term>fionndruine</term> <note>a white bronze or precious alloy</note>—for enclosing that stone pillar around them.

Then Cáilte said to the women, "What reward would you give me if I were to help and rescue you, and if I brought your own husbands back to you?"

"If we had any reward in the world that you desired," they said, "we would give it to you."

"There is one indeed," said Cáilte: "that royal stone pillar there on the edge of the building."

"It is a pity for you to say that," they said, "for the great multitudes of the country were needed to set it in the place where it is. It was a massive labor to arrange it there, even if you could do anything with it by yourself."

"I myself am deceived by it," said Cáilte, "unless..."

It was there that Muiredach the Great, son of Fínachta and King of Connacht, was waiting for Patrick. His tent was spread over Patrick and his clerics. <meta>This page continues the narrative of the death and burial of Cormac Cas at Dún ar Sléib (Duntryleague), and transitions into a new account of a miracle performed by Saint Patrick for the son of the King of Connacht.</meta>

# In Dialogue. [167 b : 1]

He went forth to the fort on the mountain, to his own father’s fort:
three pillar stones were set up by him to cool his fair, curly head.
Because of the three stones you see, it is called the Fort of the Three Stones:
that has been its name ever since, after Cormac of Cenn Claire.
The son of the King of Munster died after that, from wounds and bloodshed:
he was buried in the clean, pleasant fort, in a cool, delightful bed.

*As for Muiredach son of Finnachta, the King of Connacht, he had a beloved son named Aed son of Muiredach. A hurling match was proclaimed by the youths of the province of Connacht at that time, and Aed son of Muiredach won six matches against the youths without anyone helping him. And he sat down after that, and a thick, lingering cold and a heavy disease seized him, and he died there. This was told to his people and to his mother, namely Aife, daughter of the King of Ulster. A great lamentation was made by the women of the province for the death of that youth, and his mother said to bring him into the lap of the "Adze-head" <note>A nickname for Saint Patrick</note>, namely the one to whom God granted all of Ireland and the power to heal everyone in it. "This is a great disgrace to me on the part of the King of Connacht," she said, "unless it were by his own will."* <note>The manuscript reads *bhudh*</note>

Then they went to fetch Patrick from the tent where the King of Connacht was with his hosts. The dead boy was there, with a fringed cloak over him and a fair purple hood around him. His mother, his three foster-brothers, and his sister said they would die of grief along with him. When Saint Patrick heard that, he felt pity for them, and his heart went out to them.

Then a long basin of white gold was brought to the cleric with its fill of water in it. He blessed the water, and the water was poured into a beautiful cup of white silver. The holy cleric rose and lifted the fair purple hood, and he put three drops of the water into the mouth of Aed son of Muiredach. At the third draught he put into his mouth, the boy rose up perfectly whole, passed his hand over his face, and rose out of the bed. The hosts were joyful and high-spirited because of that; they believed in God and bowed their heads in Patrick's lap, and they gave him authority over them from the smallest to the greatest. They remained there for the duration of that night <note>The manuscript reads *hoighthi*</note> and they left the place the next morning. 

All the hosts came before them into the small plain which is called Magh Finn at this time, and to the Causeway of the Women’s Troop, which is called the Causeway of Finn at this time. They passed on the right-hand side of the Wood of Fratricide, which is called Roscommon at this time (where the nine sons of Uar son of Idas killed each other, so it is called the Wood of Fratricide because of it), and to Ráith Glais, which is called Ráith Brenainn. The King of Connacht’s tent was pitched there, and Patrick and Cáilte arrived.

Muiredach asked Cáilte: "Why was the name Almha <note>The Hill of Allen</note> given to it?" Cumall son of Trénmhór took her, and she died giving birth to a son for Cumall. This green-surfaced hill was heaped over her, so that the hill is named after her; until then, its name was the Hill of Watching. # In Dialogue.

News of that fleet reached us, and that news was brought by Sprédh Aithinne, daughter of Mughna Mucraesach, the female messenger of the King of Ireland. Her messenger was called to Fionn to assemble and muster the Fianna of Ireland and Scotland. Cormac ua Cuinn also assembled the tribes of Tara, the bands of Bregia, and a great host of the men of Ireland. Twenty-five battalions came to this plain, and lots <note>The original text uses "crannchar," meaning the casting of lots.</note> were cast between the Fianna and the husbandmen to see which of them would be the first to give battle to the foreigners. 

It fell to the Fianna to give battle first. The battle was fought every day for a week, and fifteen hundred of the foreigners and the Irish were killed. Then the great battle was fought, and Glas fell by Fionn mac Cumaill, and his seven sons fell by the Fianna. One hundred and fifty warriors of us went with Fionn to fight that battle, and fifty warriors fell by each one of us. 

Three warriors of the Fianna, including myself, went along with Fionn into the tent where Glas son of Dreacan was, and we found nine pillars of gold there. The smallest of those pillars was as large as an outer yoke. We hid them in this red bog on the north side of the fort. Glas son of Dreacan was buried under the earth here, so that from him this fort is called Ráth Glais.

"Success and a blessing to you, Cáilte," said Patrick. "It is a good story you have told us, and let that story be written down by you, Brogán." And Brogán wrote it. They remained there for the rest of that night, and they rose early the next morning and went forward to the chariot-way of Fergus, which is called the ridge of the son of Conrach at this time, and to the Hill of the Kings, which is called the spring of Garad. They took <column-break/> rest and encamped there, and a tent was stretched over Patrick.

"The most difficult thing," said the King of Connacht, "is that there is no water near it." "If it be the will of the Creator," said Patrick, "there will be water here."

"Tell us a story, Cáilte," said Patrick. 

"I will tell you a story," said Cáilte, "about how it almost happened that the Fianna of Ireland, both hounds and men, were killed on this hill where you are—specifically because of Guaire Goll and Flaithes Faebhrach, two attendants who carried Fionn's <term>fidchell</term> <note>A traditional Gaelic board game, often compared to chess.</note> board. A young warrior came to play <term>fidchell</term> against Guaire on this hill: Fionn Bán, son of Bresal, son of the king of Leinster.

"I will play for a wager against you," said Guaire Goll. 

"What is the wager?" asked Fionn Bán. 

"Three ounces of gold from each of us," said Guaire. 

Now, Fionn Bán was the third-best <term>fidchell</term> player in the Fianna—the others being Fionn mac Cumaill, Diarmait ó Duibne, and Flaithes Faebhrach, the attendant of the <term>fidchell</term> board. Those two played for three days, and Guaire did not win a single game during that time, and so he lost his wager. He then insulted and reproached the other young warrior, saying that he was no true servant in his service, no true warrior in his conduct, and no true hero in his valor. 

Fionn Bán raised his hand and struck Guaire with his fist, knocking three front teeth out of his upper jaw, so that Guaire fell lying across the <term>fidchell</term> board. This was reported [to Fionn mac Cumaill], and Fionn ordered that Fionn Bán [and his followers be killed]. 

"By my word," said Oisín, "he shall not be killed, but the matter shall be submitted to the judgment of Cáilte, Diarmait ó Duibne, and Fergus Finnbhéil—the <term>ollamh</term> <note>A high-ranking poet or learned man.</note> of the Fianna—for your sake, Fionn." 

Those three delivered their judgment: "In the place where you and the attendant of Fionn Bán meet, you shall strike him with your fist. Furthermore, a tribute shall be given to you: <column-break/> an ounce of gold from every leader of the Fianna of Ireland." And thus, peace was made between them.

At the end of twenty years, we came to the Wood of Guarding in the territory of the Uí Tairrsigh of Leinster, which is called Druim Criadh at this time. The Fianna went out to hunt, and they left a warrior of the Fianna named Garad mac Mórna to guard the women. Garad was quite elderly then, as most of his life had passed and his brothers had been killed. 

The women said to him, "Well now, Garad, would you like to play <term>fidchell</term> with us?" 

"Indeed I would not," he replied. 

"Why is that?" the women asked. 

"One day we were at the Hill of the Kings and at the Lake of the Bird in the province of Connacht..." and he told them the story, and this is it, O holy Patrick. Then one of the women remarked that Garad had not been left with them to make fires or to play <term>fidchell</term> with them, but rather because his strength and his skill in throwing had left him, and the weight of old age was upon him.

And they stayed there for the duration of that night. They set out the next day past Eas Ruaid meic Mhodhairn <note>Assaroe</note> and to Síd Aeda Esa Ruaid. Upon arriving there, they saw a warrior on the green-surfaced hill before them, wearing a fringed purple cloak. A silver brooch was in the cloak over his chest, and he carried a bright shield with red gold animal designs. His hair was in a knotted coil, and in his hand he held two hunting dogs on twisted chains of ancient silver, along with strong, heavy grey weapons. When Cáilte reached him, the warrior gave him three fond and fervent kisses, and Cáilte sat down on the burial mound beside him.

"Who are you, young warrior?" asked Cáilte. 

"I am Derg Dianscóthach, son of Eoghan, from the territories of Uisnech; I am your own foster-brother."

"How is your life among your mother's people?" asked Cáilte. 

"We lack for nothing in food or clothing," said the warrior. "But there were three men in the Fianna who had the poorest lives: Ligairne Licon, Semenn Sacaire, and Bec, the lad of the colts. I would rather have their life than the life I lead in the fairy mound."

"Though you are few in number hunting today," said Cáilte, "I once saw you with a great company at the meeting of the three waters in the south—where the Suir, the Nore <note>Beoir</note>, and the Barrow <note>Berba</note> meet. There were fifteen hundred warriors, fifteen hundred servants, and fifteen hundred women." And he said:

> This is a lonely hunt, O Derg; you have parted from your war-band and your hunting.
> Do you have the skill to tell clearly of the deaths of the Fianna?
> I am knowledgeable of their many feats and every place where they fell;
> though my faithful hound is in the fairy mound, my mind is still on the Fianna.
> I have never yet been, in the east, north, south, or west,
> in any place that was more joyful to my spirit than among them, even if we were few.

"Well now, Derg," said Cáilte, "which of the Fianna lies in this mound that we are sitting upon?" 

"It was you and I who buried him," said Derg, "so it is right that I should know." And he said:

> Cuinnscleo the lad, son of Ainnscleo, who overcame men in battle;
> nine men under a leafy oak were overcome by that warrior of combat.
> Though Cuinnscleo was impulsive, he was not a man of many words; he was a hero on the day of swift plundering;
> in the place where speckled shields were pierced, he was never a fearful coward.

"Against whom did he run that difficult, swift race, Derg?" asked Cáilte. 

"Against the black horse that belonged to Dil mac Dá Chrec," said Derg:

> Dil mac Dá Chrec had a black horse that won every game they played;
> at the rock above Loch Gair, it took the three full prizes of the assembly.

"It is the end of the day," <gloss>The end of the day is</gloss> here, said Cáilte, "for the beautiful, bright clouds of the day have departed, and the dark gatherings of the night have come to us."

Then Derg Dianscóthach went ahead into the fairy mound to report Cáilte’s words to Ilbrec of Assaroe and to Aed Minbrec son of the Dagda. He told of his conversation with Cáilte from the time he reached him until that very hour. "Bring him into the fairy mound," they said, "for we have heard of his hospitality and his prowess." Derg went out to meet him and brought him and his people, and they were <gloss>seated</gloss> in their proper and worthy places in the fairy mound. 

That was the time when a great war occurred between Lir of Síd Finnachaid and Ilbrec of Assaroe. A bird with an iron beak and a tail of fire would come to a golden window in the fairy mound; it would shake itself there every evening so that it left no sword on a head-rest, no shield on a peg, nor any spear on a rack without knocking them down upon the people of the mound. The people of the mound would throw missiles at it, but it would happen that the strike would hit a son, or a woman, or a foster-child of the people of the mound. 

The drinking hall was prepared for them that night, and the same bird came and did the same destruction. The people of the mound were throwing at it, but they could do nothing to it. "How long has the bird been like that?" asked Cáilte. "For a year now," said Derg, "since we began the war with the people of the other fairy mound."

Then Cáilte put his hand into the hollow of his shield and took a bronze rod that he had, and he made a cast at the bird with it so that he killed it.

Then Ilbrec reached his hand up and took a sharp, blue-edged spear from its rack and placed it in Cáilte’s hand. "Look, dear Cáilte, what spear is this and which of the Fianna of Ireland owned it?" There were thirty rivets of gold from the land of Arabia [on its socket . . . . . . .] the spear of Fiacha son of Congha [. . . that spear . . . and it is through it] that Fionn mac Cumhaill first took the kingship of the Fianna of Ireland. It was given from the green-grassed fairy mound of Finnachaid. 

Aillén mac Midhna, of the Tuatha Dé Danann, used to come from the cairn of Finnachaid in the north to Tara. He used to come with a musical <term>timpán</term> in his hand, and everyone who heard him would fall asleep. Then he would emit a ball of fire from his mouth. He came to Tara on the festival day of Samhain every year and played his <term>timpán</term>, and everyone would sleep to the fairy music he made <note>the manuscript says "he used to make"</note>. He would blow his breath upon the ball of fire and burn Tara with all its furnishings every year in that way for twenty-three years. That was the time when the Battle of Cnucha was fought, and Cumhall son of Trénmór fell there, leaving a pregnant wife behind him—namely, Muirne of the Fair Neck, daughter of Tadg son of Nuada.

After the death of Cumhall, the leadership of the Fianna of Ireland was given to Goll the Great-Deeded, son of Morna, and he held it for ten years. Then a son was born to Cumhall—namely, Fionn—and he was an outlaw and a marauder until the end of his tenth year. The Feast of Tara was held in the tenth year by Conn of the Hundred Battles. As the men of Ireland were drinking and making merry in the great mead-hall, they noticed nothing until a young, handsome youth came to them. He sat before Conn of the Hundred Battles and Goll son of Morna, with the nobles of the Fianna of Ireland around him in the house. It was one of the rules of the Feast of Tara that no one dared to bring a feud or counter-feud for the space of six weeks while they were drinking at the Feast of Tara. The King of Ireland looked at the youth, for he was known neither to him nor to anyone else who was in the hall.

Then all the men of Ireland rose around their king on the green of Tara where Fionn was. The king saw that Fionn had the head of the man who used to burn Tara, along with his pipe, his harp, and his musical pillar of fire. Thus, it seemed to me, Tara and all its furnishings were saved.

Then the place was filled with people and a council was held. The decision they reached was to grant the leadership of the Fianna of Ireland to Fionn. "Well, my soul, Goll son of Morna," said Conn of the Hundred Battles, "what is your choice: to leave Ireland, or to place your hand in Fionn's hand?" "I give my word," said Goll, "that I will place my hand in Fionn's hand."

Then, indeed, power came into that omen and good fortune. The leaders of the Fianna rose and placed their hands in Fionn's hand || and Goll son of Morna went before them, so that others of the Fianna would feel less shame in doing so. Fionn remained in that leadership, according to Caílte, until he met his death and tragic end at the Badger’s Rock in Luachair.

# In Agallamh.

"Her daughter is a match for three hundred, and no one can prevail against them." "Where do they come into the harbor?" asked Cáilte. "By the settlement from the northwest," said Eoghan. They remained there for the duration of that night and were attended and served on every side.

Cáilte rose alone early the next morning and took his shield, his sword, and his two spears. He went forward to the impregnable rock by the side of the harbor. He was there for a time until he saw the <term>curach</term> approaching him. There were three in the <term>curach</term>: a rough-haired, grey-dun dog with a harsh iron chain around its neck; a bald, black monster of a girl who, from a distance, looked like a mountain peak, in the front of the <term>curach</term> with a strong iron spike in her hand; and the giant in the rear of the <term>curach</term>. They reached the harbor and landing place near Cáilte, and horror and fear seized Cáilte at the sight of them. The big man said to his daughter, "Unloose the dog," he said, "and let it at that big lone man so it may eat its fill of him before we set out on our journey." The girl unloosed the dog, and horror and fear seized Cáilte because of it—a fear he had never felt in battle or combat. He said, "My Creator and my <term>táilgenn</term> <note>A common epithet for St. Patrick, meaning "adze-head"</note> be between me and you!" said Cáilte. He had a bronze needle, and he made a casting throw with it at the dog so that one end of the spike went into the upper palate and the other end into the lower palate, so that it closed its maw. It fell out of the <term>curach</term> and died in the depths of the sea, and the wave cast it ashore afterward. 

The other two came ashore toward Cáilte and fought him boldly and hard-heartedly. The girl gave him thirty wounds from the fork of his foot to his forehead. Then Cáilte gave her a sword blow so that her guts and entrails spilled out of her. He grew bold and intensified the fight with the big man. He made three pieces of him, and the third piece was his head. He took their three heads and brought them to the hostel. Eoghan and Cáilte's people rose and recognized those heads and gave thanks for the deed. Cáilte sat down, weak and exhausted, and faints and swoons fell upon him. Healing herbs (<term>lossa ícce</term>) were brought to him, and he was treated for a fortnight until he was made smooth and his wounds were healed.

"We depart tomorrow," said Cáilte, "and we leave a blessing with you." They bid farewell to Eoghan and went forward from there to the Hill of the Hundreds, which is now called the Hill of the Two Horses, and to the <term>Cúillios</term> of the Fenians to the north, and to the marsh

Cáilte greeted the warrior, and the warrior returned the greeting. "Whose people are you?" asked the warrior. "Our lord and master, Fionn mac Cumaill, no longer lives," said Cáilte.

Your father was seeking law and justice from Mac Smaile—that is, whatever was due between a king and a warrior should be given to him."

They went forward to Conall’s house at Dún na mBarc. “Tell us news, Donn,” said Conall mac Néill. Donn told how Cáilte had given the weapons to him and that he was on his way to the king. “He shall receive that,” said Conall, “for he is of the side of Leth Cuinn <note>The northern half of Ireland</note> and because of the good he himself has done.” Donn showed the weapons and the many sharp blades Cáilte had given him. “Those gifts were obtained from a noble man,” said the assembly. “He is a noble man indeed,” said Conall, “for it was never said of any warrior’s son that there was one better than he.” And when Cáilte was seen coming toward the fort, Conall arose with the nobles of his army and his people to welcome Cáilte. Cáilte sat upon the mound at the entrance of the fort, and the host sat around him.

Conall asked Cáilte why this mound was called the Mound of Garb Daire. Cáilte answered that question, for he possessed the knowledge of it: “A beloved warrior of Fionn mac Cumhaill was here,” said Cáilte, “namely Garb Daire, son of Aengus, son of the king of Munster from the south. He was hunting here one [day] and he killed three times fifty stags, three times fifty hinds, and [three times fifty boars]. And the people of the territory and [the land saw him] || and they rushed toward him and took his game and his catch from him, and three hundred warriors fell by his hand. The people of the country surrounded him and made an orchard of spear-points through him and killed him. And we, the three battalions of the Fianna, arrived to avenge him; we laid waste to the territory and the land, and we killed the three kings of the country, while another group of them escaped to the islands:—

->Garb Daire was killed upon the shore, by the whole of Cenél Eogain:<-
->we killed fifty of their warriors, here in revenge for Garb Daire.<-

And it is he who is in this mound with his weapons, and he possessed the chain of Lugh mac Eithlenn, which used to guard the necks of the Sons of Míled and the Tuatha Dé Danann. “We would like to obtain those weapons,” said Conall. “If you wish,” said Cáilte, “let the mound be dug up now.” “Not so,” said Conall, “but let it be dug tomorrow; for there shall be a night of drinking and pleasure held by us tonight.” And they went forward into the great hall, and Cáilte and his people were brought into a private, secluded room and were served well. The wife of Conall was Bébionn, daughter of Muiredach son of Finnachta, the daughter of the king of Connacht. “Well, lady,” said Conall, “however long or short a time Cáilte remains here, let a meal for a thousand men be given to him every day; and let eight score cows be put in a grazing field near him, and let their milk be given to him every night.”

They remained there for the duration of that night and rose the next day to go to the Cairn of Garbh Daire. The cairn was dug up, and the chain of Lugh son of Eithliu was found. The shield was also found whole, just as it had been placed by his side. Goll said, "There is a condition upon which I would give her to you: that you never let her go forever, that she be your third wife, and that you never refuse her anything she asks of you." She was Fionn's beloved wife until her foster-brothers—the sons of Mórna—went on a raid and rebellion against Fionn. Their number was thirty-one hundred warriors, as Cáilte said in the verse:

> Ten hundred and twenty hundred there, the number of the noble clan of Mórna;
> Fifteen hundred besides, the number of their kings and leaders.

The sons of Mórna went to Daire Tarbgha in the province of Connacht, and three battalions of the Fianna overtook them there before they could leave their camp. Fifteen excellent, well-armed men of the sons of Mórna fell in the oakwood. After that, the great and brave warrior Goll mac Mórna arose and provided cover for the retreat; we could do nothing to them once Goll took up his shield to protect them. The sons of Mórna then took counsel and decided not to let anyone who was in friendship with Fionn or the Fianna escape without being killed. It was Conán the Bald, son of Mórna, who gave this advice, for he was <column-break/> a man of strife and an instigator of conflict among hosts and multitudes.

The sons of Mórna went forward to the green lawn and were debating what they should do with Berraig Brec, their own foster-sister. They decided to offer her terms: she could take her jewels, her property, and her wealth with her and leave Fionn, and then she would have no reason to fear them. "That is a pity," she said. "Is it my harm you wish to perform, my dear foster-brothers?" "It is indeed," they replied. The girl said, "I will not abandon my husband, my first-spouse, and my fair lover for you at all."

The sons of Mórna rose in a battle-line toward the stead. They all joined hands around the stead and set fire to it from every direction. The queen and thirty of her women fled out of the stead, and Art mac Mórna saw her from the battlements of the fortress as she was going out onto the bright sandy beach toward her ship. He placed his finger in the thong of his spear and made a cast at her. The queen heard the whirring of the spear and turned her face toward it; it struck her in the chest and breast, breaking her back in two so that she died. And she was carried up afterward...

Muiredach son of Finnachta, King of Connacht, was at his hand; Eochaid Leithderg, King of Leinster, was at his hand; and Eoghan Derg son of Aenghus, King of the two provinces of Munster, was at the King of Ireland’s hand.

Conall son of Niall came after that and placed his head in Patrick’s lap and knelt before him. "Come over here, Conall," said Diarmait. "I shall be in Patrick’s presence," said Conall, "so that it is he who will be over me in heaven and on earth." "Kingship from me to you," said Patrick, "and thirty kings of your seed in kingship; my city and my abbacy to you also, and whatever I shall obtain from the five great provinces of Ireland for your use."

Conall placed the golden vessel in Patrick’s hand. "Your own friend Cáilte son of Rónán gave that gift to you," said Conall. "By my word, he is a friend," said Patrick; and Patrick passed it into the King of Ireland’s hand. The King of Ireland was examining it for a long time and said, "We have never seen a treasure better than this vessel; and look at it, Oisín, to see who owned it." "My own father," said Oisín, "Fionn son of Cumall; and he gave it to his wife, Berrach Brec, daughter of Cas of Cuailgne. It was she whom the sons of Mórna killed. Glenn Rois Eanaigh, it is true for me, sweet was the sound of a bell there at any time; though it might be occupied by red stags, its high virtues were many.

A dark storm has taken hold, not fair weather but changing by turns; the earth has become weary, and a hood has covered the head of the marsh.

The marsh of the Fianna, with spoils and blood, where I moved among the rough dogs; the streams of the flocks of the marsh, following the three days of the autumn's end.

The shell of the Fianna, the phantom of the marsh, over red-tipped leaves; the rushing of the wind and mist over the glens, over long reaches upon the pools.

I see the victorious shore, the dragon’s eye a judgment over the hosts; green-sided, bright and shining, it will be in the possession of Kevin <note>Caimgin, the patron saint of Glendalough</note>.

The fierce shore of Loch Eanaigh, the wave following after it; she <note>the monster</note> used to strike the Fianna, and the youths of the Fianna used to strike her.

Ten years and twenty years, and eight is the rule for the graveyard; and twelve hundred noble years, until the brightness for which he was born.

Loch Eanaigh, a dwelling of swans, is weary without the Fianna beside it; the holy men shall gather around it, and most sweetly shall they sing their chant.

Loch Eanaigh, a dwelling of swans, a place of ... between two boundaries; the marsh of the autumn, a plain that is traversed from one hill to another.

The Glen of the Marsh between two mountains is the most beautiful I have ever seen; a river between two lakes in its center, and the full tide from the western side.

It will be a cold home for pilgrims, it will be a home for the poor and not the strong; it will be a burial place of kings, one after another, when Kevin comes into the glen.

Thirty vats would be appropriate for Oisín. They spent that night cheerfully and high-spiritedly, without any lack of food or drink.

The hosts rose on the following day, and a tent was pitched over the King of Ireland on the hill, and no one was allowed inside the tent except a king or a crown prince. Patrick and his clerics were brought into the other side of the tent, and no one was allowed in the side where Patrick was except a bishop, a priest, or a beloved disciple <note>literally "son of the breast"</note> of the King of Heaven and Earth. Then the King of Ireland asked: "How many of the kings of Ireland gave land to the Fianna?" Cáilte answered that, for he knew the answer: "A king took possession of Ireland, namely Feradach the Righteous, and he had two sons, Tuathal and Fiacha. When Feradach died, his two sons divided Ireland between them; that is, the jewels, the treasures, the wealth, the cattle, the herds, the forts, and the strongholds went to one man. The halls, the estuaries, the forest-mast, the great fruit, the beautiful speckled-sided salmon, the hunting, and the spoils of the Fianna went to the other man." "Where did they make that division?" asked Diarmait. "Around this very hill upon which we are sitting," said Cáilte. "Those two divisions are not equal," said the nobles of the men of Ireland. "Which of those divisions would you prefer?" asked Oisín. "The feasts, the houses, and all the general wealth," they said. "The division they liked least," said Cáilte, "is the one we preferred." The reign of Feradach was good, until the great prince fell by the hand of Mál; it was the report of a king who reddened his valor, the death of the prince Feradach.

Fiacha went to Tara with prosperity after Feradach fell; he seized the power of all Ireland against Mál the Great, son of Rochruide.

After that, Fiacha gave the Fianna to Mórna of the great spirit; four of them, a fierce band of valor, took leadership after him.

Mórna son of Cairbre, with strength, was in supremacy for ten years; ten more for Garad, I believe, until his fair head was parted from him.

Daigre son of Garad, with strength, had five years in the chieftainship; a count of seven years without deceit for Donn son of Mórna, the last of them.

Eochaid son of Marcada from the east, king of the Fianna of Ireland from Ulster; a year and a half was his term over the Fianna in the high-kingship.

Cas son of Cannan, hard was his valor, had one year from Ulster; Dubán his son, a man of pleasant deeds, had two years, I count.

They seized power in Munster, a pride of deceits: Liath Luachra and Labraid Red-Hand; ten years for them—no small feast—of the sons of the serfs of Aran.

Trénmhór, grandson of Báiscne, was strong; he was the grandson of Sétna Sithbac; he was the grandfather of Finn—noble is the lineage—and the father of Cumhall and Crimhall.

Trénmhór, strong in his affection, overtook the Fianna of Ireland in one gathering; they made him king in the north and the south; seventeen years was his reign.

Amhall the hard took his poison <note>meaning his fierce power</note> by means of shield and sword, a reign in which he fought thirty battles—scandalous, contentious, and warlike; seven years for him then, until he fell in the Battle of Cnucha.

After that, the sons of Mórna took command through sorrow and perpetual misery; thirty heroes of great fame, including Daigre, Goll, and Garad.

Great Goll was a soldier in battle, a son of the last Mórna; ten years for him—no small feast—in the high-kingship of the Fianna of Ireland.

After that, the golden hero <note>literally "golden salmon," a metaphor for a prince</note> took it: Fionn son of Cumhall, son of Trénmhór; our generous, noble, host-leading leader, our wonderful, many-victorious sage.

Two hundred years with bloom and thirty without weakness; Fionn’s life was a long span, until he fell while making a leap in his old age.

The seventeen kings, I am certain, who took the kingship of the Fianna of Ireland: Fionn was better than all of them, the high war-soldier of Almhu.

Five druids—a difficult company—were the best who ever visited the western land <note>Ireland</note>; I remember accurately the report of them in their druidry.

They were Baghna of Síd Baghna, and Cathbad the very famous druid, Stocán son of fair Curc of the hundreds, Mogh Ruith, and Fionn of Formaell.

Five physicians—a noble feast—were the best who ever visited the land of Banba <note>Ireland</note>; though I am long after them, I am knowledgeable in their reports.

Miach and Oirbedh of the poetic gatherings, and their father Diancécht; Gabrán the physician from across the sea in the east, and Fionn himself of the bright-haired Báiscne.

Five noble poets—a noble group—were the best who ever visited the land of Ireland; I remember accurately the report of them in their poetry.

Cairbre the poet who was found across the sea, Amairgin of the island of the Gaels, Ferchertne who was with Labraid Lorc, Mogh Ruith, and bare-bladed Fionn.

Five who were wisest in sharp intellect were together in one house in Ireland: Fíthal and Flaithrí his son, Aillmhe and Cairbre and Cormac.

Any question they put forth through their intellect, Fionn himself quickly solved; but any question Fionn of the feasts made, none of those five was able to solve.

And it was done accordingly.

The sons of Morna were no match for Finn’s people, and they themselves fell without a single survivor among them. As for the company of women, they turned their faces to the ground and died from the terror of the battle. Because of that, "the Hill of the Women’s Company" is the name of this hill, said Cáilte.

Then Finn and three battalions of the Fianna arrived at this place and saw the slaughter. As for the two sons of the King of Leinster, they came onto the hill, placed their mouths to the ground, and died from grief for their foster-brothers. Finn saw this, and his weapons fell from his hands; he wept heavy, truly sorrowful showers of tears until his garment and chest were wet, and all the Fianna wept as well. Finn said: "Woe," said he, "to those who would reach the house of Conn of the Hundred Battles, or the Mound of Liamhain of the beautiful mantle. And it is a bad story that will be told to Dubh son of Aengus Tírech, the king of the two provinces of Munster to the south, as far as the city of Sliabh Claire and the borders of Sliabh Cua. And it is a bad story that will reach Bodhb Derg at the Mound of the Fair-Haired Women to the south—namely, the death of his daughter."

Finn rose after that and surveyed the slaughter, but he did not find Sadhbh. The Fianna rose and placed those four hundred of Finn’s people into the hollows of the earth; and it was thus that they were found: every man of Finn’s people had a man of the sons of Morna dead beneath him. Their <term>ogham</term> names were written above them and their funeral games were held. Because of this, "the Hill of the Warriors" is the name of this hill, "the Hill of the Women’s Company" is the name of this other hill, and "the Height of the Youths" is the name of this hill to the north, after the sons of the King of Leinster who were buried there. "And that, O Conall, is the matter you asked me about," said Cáilte.

Cáilte answered that: "A red stag," he said, "used to live in the slopes of the dewy, lush rushes to the south, and three times every year it would escape from the men and the dogs of the Fianna. They followed it [for years] until they reached this place. Four of us from the Fianna caught up to it: Diarmaid ua Duibne, Mac Lugach, and Glas mac Éincherda Beirre."
