"May victory and a blessing be yours, Cáilte," said Colmán. "It is a great thing for such knowledge and true history to survive in a person." "Look, son of the church," said Cáilte, "has the moon risen into its airy pavilion?" "It has risen," replied the cleric, "so that sea and land are equally illuminated by it." Then Cáilte rose in the western corner of the island; he reached his hand down into the bank, brought up the antler, and laid it on the floor of the house where the clerics were.

The King of Ulster at that time was Eochaid Foebardherg <note>Red-blade</note> son of Firghlinne. He was nearby at the Hill of Weapons, which is called Mag Rath. Colmán, Eoghanán, and six other clerics rose early, and they took the antler with them to show it to the King of Ulster and the rest of the Ulstermen. There were two hundred armed men there. The cleric brought the antler before the king, and they all could have fit under it for shelter during a storm or tempest. "Who found the antler?" asked the king, "and where was it found?" "Cáilte found it in the Lake of the Red Stag," they said. "He would be welcome to me," said the king, "if he would come to visit me, for he would leave with us the history of every territory and every meeting-place, and the boundaries of every land."

As for the clerics, they returned to the island and left the antler with the King of Ulster. "Tell me, my soul, Colmán," said Cáilte, "what is the reason for those eight canonical hours for which you all rise, both by day and by night?" "The reason is great," said Colmán. "There are eight vices that follow the body and soul of every person, and those eight canonical hours atone for them." And Colmán said:—

The eight carnal sins, they graze until the sun;
the eight chosen hours, to banish them swiftly:
Prime against gluttony that is not moderate; Terce against the cause of anger;

"May you have victory and a blessing, Cáilte," said Colmán. "You have solved that question well. And why should I not," said Cáilte, "attend those eight hours, since God has delayed me to be contemporary with them?"

Then Colmán asked Cáilte: "Why is this well at the head of the lake called the Well of the Womenfolk?" Cáilte explained that: "Niamh, daughter of Aengus Tírech, the King of Munster, eloped with Oisín, son of Finn, from the Fort of Ships in the province of Munster to this well. Oisín remained with her there for six weeks, hunting and fowling in the province of Ulster. The girl and thirty women used to come every morning to wash their hands and their faces in this blue-green water.

It greatly distressed the King of Munster that his daughter had eloped with Oisín. Two provinces of Munster were gathered by him—five brave and equally great battalions—and they came in pursuit of the Fianna to this place. Niamh and her women were washing at the well at that time, and they saw the five battalions on the hill above them. 'Woe is that,' said the girl; 'happy is she who would find death and destruction before she should see her foster-father, her father, her three brothers, and the nobles of Munster in such a state.' She put her face to the ground and died there, as did the thirty women who were with her. Her heart turned into a clot of black blood and came out through her mouth. Therefore, the Hill of Slaughter has been the name of that hill from then until now." And Cáilte said:—

He then came toward them and dismounted from his chariot. The King of Ulster, along with his armies, gave him a diligent and warm welcome. "Well, my soul, O Cáilte," said the king, "what better thing could we ask of you than the history of this fort—namely, Ráith Áine?" 

"I have the story of its origin," said Cáilte.

"Áine, the daughter of Modhorn, was the daughter of the King of Scotland from over the sea. The men of Scotland used to ask her: 'Why is it, O Queen, that you do not wed a good man in Scotland or in Ireland?' Finn heard of this and told Finn Fer-an-Champa <note>Literally, "Finn of the camp."</note> and Rónán the royal warrior—two of the royal warriors of Scotland—to go and woo her from her father. "'Good, O royal warrior,' they said. 'Let two trusted men of your own regular household come with us, so that the Queen will more readily believe us.' Finn told me and Mac Lugach to go with them, saying: 'And however much you may ask for yourselves, I will grant it to her.'"

"We four noble warriors went forward to Dun Monadh in Scotland and were brought into a private house. Modhorn, the King of Scotland, came into the house with his daughter Áine. 'I will wed him,' said the daughter. "A king ruled over Scotland—Iruath son of Ailpín—and he had three daughters named Muiresc, Aife, and Aillbhe. They gave their love to three warriors of the <term>Fianna</term> of Ireland, namely the three sons of the one-handed smith of Beirre: Gér, Glas, and Gaba. Aine sat at Manannán's right hand and gave him three dear, fervent kisses, and everyone asked news of each other. When Manannán's wife saw Aillén, she fell in love with him. Then Patrick said: 'That storytelling is complicated <note>literally "forked" or "branching"</note>,' namely, that the sister of Aillén son of Eogabail gave her love to Manannán, and Manannán's wife gave her love to Aillén. From that comes the old proverb: *storytelling is a complicated thing*. And Manannán gave his own wife to Aillén son of Eogabail, and he himself took Aine, Aillén's sister. And those, my soul, Aedh," said Cáilte, "are the two questions you asked of me." And they remained in that place for the space of a week. They took their leave of Eogan the great hospitaller, and Patrick gave him heaven for all he had done according to his will.

Then they went forward to the Valley of the Spectre <term>Glenn in Scáil</term> to the east, which is called the place of the people of Diugra at this time. This was the place where Patrick had been in slavery under Milchuin son of Ua Buain, the king of Dál nAraide. And they saw a fruitful church before them, with thirty churchmen in it praising <note>God</note>.

...of bronze. And there were two young lads in the boat wearing mantles <note>The Irish word *tuignech* refers to a cloak or mantle</note> that reached the tops of their shoulders. Ciabhán greeted them || and they answered him. "Who are you, young men?" Ciabhán asked.

"I am Lodán, son of the king of India," one of the men said, "and that other man is Eolus, son of the king of Greece. A wave moved us," he said, "and a wind drove us, and we do not know what land or nation of the world we are in."

"If someone wished to travel the sea with you," said Ciabhán, "would you give him a place in the boat?"

"If you were alone, we would give it to you," they said.

"Well, Ciabhán," his people said, "is it Ireland you wish to leave?"

"It is indeed," he replied, "for I find neither protection nor sanctuary in it." And he went into the boat and bid farewell to his people. And they were gloomy and low-spirited, and parting from him felt like the separation of body from soul. Ciabhán and the warriors who were in the boat then made a pact of friendship.

Then bright, laughing waves rose up for them until every great sea-swell was as high as a mountain. The beautiful, speckled-sided salmon that usually stayed near the sun-drenched sand were now alongside the gunwales of the boat. Horror, fear, and dread overcame them because of this.

"By our word," said Ciabhán, "if we were on land, we would defend ourselves well in battle and conflict." They remained in that great peril until they saw a lone warrior approaching them on a dark-grey horse with a golden bridle. Nine waves were below the horse and he rode on top of the tenth, yet not a stitch of his clothing or his chest was wet.

The warrior asked them what reward they would give to the one who rescued them from that great peril.

"Is the reward you ask within our power to give?" they asked.

"It is indeed," said the warrior. "It is that you yourselves enter the service and friendship of the one who rescues you." They agreed to this and placed their hands in the warrior's hand.

Then the warrior took the three of them out of the boat and onto the horse. The boat floated along the side of the horse until they reached a harbor and landing place in the Land of Promise <note>Tír tharrngaire</note>. They dismounted there and came to the Lake of the Dwarfs and the city of Manannán. A banqueting hall had been prepared for them, and the four warriors were served and attended to after their arrival. Their horns, cups, and goblets were raised. Beautiful, blue-browed youths stood with fair, decorated buffalo horns. They played sweet-stringed tympans || and fresh, melodic nine-stringed harps until the entire house was filled with a symphony of music.

# In the Colloquy

Then there arose long-snouted, long-heeled, thin-ankled, red-bald, and sharp-featured churls who used to perform feats and games in the house of Manannán. This was the feat they would perform: they would take nine pointed javelins and cast them to the ridge-pole and the shoulder of the hostel while standing on one leg and using one hand, and then catch them again in the same manner. The reason they did this was to shame the noble, well-born classes who came from distant, neighboring lands. That night, they performed the feat just as they had done before. One came toward curly-haired Ciabhán and placed the nine javelins in his hand, for Ciabhán had the finest form, bearing, and reputation of all the Tuatha Dé Danann and the sons of Míl who were in Manannán’s house. Ciabhán rose and performed the feat in the presence of Manannán and the nobles of the Land of Promise as if it were the only thing he had ever studied. He then placed the javelins in the hand of Eolus, son of the king of Greece, who performed the feat with agile precision. He then passed the javelins to Lodán, son of the king of India, who performed it in the same way.

Now, Manannán had a chief poet in the Land of Promise named Libhra, the chief physician. He had three daughters: Clíodhna, Aife, and Etáin of the fair hair. These three were the treasures of purity and virginity of the Tuatha Dé Danann, and they feared nothing could kill them except for the "death-wound of chastity" <note>This likely refers to the loss of their virginity or the breaking of their vows of maidenhood</note>. All three fell in love at the same time with those three warriors and they decided to elope with them on the very next fair day. They came to the harbor to meet those three young heroes. Lodán, son of the king of India, and Eolus, son of the king of Greece, went in one coracle, while Ciabhán, son of Eochaid Imderg, and Clíodhna went in another. From there, they sailed forward to the Strand of Téite, daughter of Ragamnach, in the south of Ireland. It was called the Strand of Téite because Téite the Bright, daughter of Ragamnach, went there to play in the waves with three times fifty maidens, and they were all drowned there; from that comes the name "Téite’s Strand."

As for Ciabhán, son of Eochaid Imderg, he took harbor and landed on that same strand. He went to hunt and fowl in the territory nearest to him, and the wave came in from the sea toward Clíodhna || and she was drowned there. Because of her, it is called Clíodhna’s Wave. The household of Manannán’s house came after her—namely Ildathach and his two sons—because they had fallen in love with the maiden, and they were drowned on that same strand. As Cáilte said:

> Fair-headed Clíodhna, lasting is the calamity,
> Upon the shore her death occurred;
> A cause for her mother to be dead
> Is the event from which the ancient name came.

"Not at all," said Cáilte, "but at the festive time of Samhain she used to come here to speak with her druids and her poets, to learn what good or evil would befall her that year. She used to arrive there in her nine chariots: nine chariots in front of her, nine chariots behind her, and nine chariots on each of her two sides." "Why did she do that?" asked Patrick. "So that the dust and spray of the road and the foam from the horses' mouths would not reach her, and so they would not soil her fresh, clean garments." "That is a reason for happiness," said Patrick.

Then the entire host rose up to the Wood of the Steeds, which is called Elphin; and this is why it was called the Wood of the Steeds: when the provincial kings of Ireland were drinking at Cruachan, it was there their steeds and horses were kept in captured paddocks.

"You speak untruthfully," she said, "considering the separation that was forced upon us." "That is not strange," said Cáilte, "for we are not of the same generation or the same time. She is of the Tuatha Dé Danann, and they are unfading and their lifespan is eternal; but I am of the Sons of Míl, and they are short-lived and subject to decay." "Give the woman her answer, Cáilte," said Patrick. "I will indeed," said Cáilte.

And he went forward to a lovely mound to the northwest of Cruachan, and he placed his left elbow against the mound and reached past it. After Patrick had performed his hours, his office, and his mass, Cáilte was brought to him, and Patrick asked him: "Why was this glen below called the Glen of the Hag?"

"One day Fionn and the Fianna were here," Cáilte said, "and we saw a distorted, crane-legged, jet-black witch of a hag approaching us. She challenged us to a race, and a common wager was made by the Fianna for it; the agreement that was bound there was that whoever was left behind would have their head struck off. Three of us from the Fianna ran against her: Oisín, Diarmaid ua Duibne, and myself. We ran to the great ford which is called Áth Mogha at this time. It is from her that the glen has been named from then until now."

After that, they went over into the settlement, and it was blessed by them. A legion of angels was above it after it was blessed, and they remained there after that for a month and a fortnight.

Another day, while they were in that place, they saw a lone young warrior approaching them, and his appearance and dress were excellent. "Who are you, young man?" asked Patrick.

I won seven games against the youths, and during the final game I won, two women wearing green cloaks reached me. They were the daughters of Bodb Derg, son of the Dagda, named Slad and Mumain. I came running from the hostel until I reached you, O holy Patrick. Let me be under your protection, so that their strength or their power will not prevail over you."

He placed nine foster-sisters with her and then told everyone she was dead. The King's horses were caught and his chariot was harnessed, and he came..."

# In the Colloquy

Cáilte and Coscrach of the Hundreds approached the fortress where Saint Patrick was. Coscrach placed his head in Patrick's lap, and his seven sons and seven daughters did the same and bowed to him. For two benefits had come to him that night: Patrick for the benefit of his soul, and Cáilte for the protection of his crops—that is, by killing the stag that had been plundering them. They were drinking and making merry that night. The next morning, the entire host arrived, and Saint Patrick went out onto the field of the fortress.

Then Coscrach of the Hundreds asked Cáilte: "Why was this very strong stone pillar called the Stone of the Weapons?"

"That is the stone," said Cáilte, "against which the <term>Fianna</term> used to sharpen their weapons on the day of <term>Samhain</term> every year. And on that stone was the best symbol of peace and authority that ever existed in Ireland or Scotland during the reigns of Conn, Art, Cormac, and Cairbre Lifechair: a ridged ring of red gold which contained eightscore ounces of red gold. There was a hole through this pillar, and the ring passed through that hole. Such was the excellence of the rule of those kings that no one dared to take it away. And such was the excellence of the druids' knowledge and the kings' authority that no one dared to move it. Those kings passed away until the time of Cairbre Lifechair, son of Cormac. Cairbre fell in the Battle of Gabra, and we, the last of the Fianna who remained, came to this ford," said Cáilte. "And I turned the pillar over and put the half that was above facing downwards, so that it is as you see it now."

"If we could see the hole and the token, we would believe that," said the host.

"Grant me a moment," said Cáilte, "so that I may raise the half <column-break/> that is down until it is up again. For the Gael is an impatient thing." And from that comes the saying: *The Gael is an impatient thing.* All of them together rose toward the stone, as many as they were, but they could not move it at all. Cáilte then came and put his two arms around it and lifted it from the ground. And there it was, with its gold ring through the lower hole, so that everyone saw it.

Cáilte went to the ring and divided it in two. He gave half to Patrick and the other half to the people of the town where they were. Thus <term>Cluain Fhalach</term> <note>Meadow of the Ring</note> has been the name of that place from then until now, and the Stone of the Weapons is the name of that stone. And Cáilte spoke the verse:

->Many a spear that causes damage, and the sword of a fair warrior:<-
->were sharpened by us against the stone, here, O Coscrach, every day.<-

"Success and a blessing to you, Cáilte," said Patrick. "It is a good history you have told us."

Then his horses were caught and his chariot was harnessed for him...

Coscrach of the Hundreds set out and came to speak with the King of Leinster, Eochaid Red-side, at the broad ridge of Laegaire, son of Ugaine, in the east, to tell them the news of Cáilte. "Scáithderc, daughter of Cumall, was drowned in it while she was looking at the marrow-redness of Loch Lurgan," Cáilte replied. "It was from her that the brimming, cold-pooled lake of Lurgan arose, and it spread from the 'crooked apple tree' at the head of Slieve Bloom—which is called Sliab Bladma son of Edlecar at this time—until it reached this place. It was spreading over the entire province. It was then that Fionn performed the most mighty and choice feat that anyone ever performed before or since: he brought the 'sucker' from the land of India, and the druids from the land of Germany, and the female warriors from the lands of the Saxons and the French, and they sucked up that brimming, cold-pooled lake."

"That first Fianna of Fionn was illustrious," said the King of Leinster. "Every man of them was no worse than any man of ours, except that they did not live in the same era or time as you." And that was the entertainment...

"Fionn and I rose up then," said Cáilte, "for I was a match for a good man that day, and he fell by me from the exhaustion of combat. And they went forward from there to the great fort of Magh Fea, to the fortress of the King of Leinster. It was then that a fire caught in the roof-beam of the house. Everyone was looking at the fire at once, and the musician was about to let the *timpán* fall from his hand to protect it. His servant said to him: "Do not let this hinder you from your art or your music; let me see to the house." The servant had a stone in the lining of his shirt, and he made a great cast with it, so that it carried the fire and the roof-beam out past the high fences of the townland, so that "Árd Féice" <note>Height of the Roof-beam</note> is the name of the place from then until now. "A blessing on your throwing, my son," said Patrick, "and a blessing on sharing, and a blessing on victory." Everyone in the house said, "We have never seen a musician's servant with better strength, throwing, or generosity than that lad." They remained there until the next day.

The hosts and Saint Patrick rose and went to the Hill of the Kings, which is called Maistiu, and Patrick sat there. As for the King of Leinster, a hunt and a chase were arranged by him in the place called "Árd na Macraide" <note>Height of the Youths</note> at this time—and "Árd Scol" is its other name now—and as far as the Fort of the Great Queen, which is called Maistiu. None of Patrick's people were with him at that hunt except for the musician and his servant. No one of the King of Leinster’s people achieved the first kill of a pig or a deer before the musician and his servant; and no hunt more fruitful than that one has been made since the Fianna departed.

Then Patrick rose and delivered a teaching and a sermon to everyone. The province of Leinster gave a third of their children and a third of their wealth to Saint Patrick; so that "Hill of the Tithe" has been the name of the hill from then until now, and "Plain of the Third" the name of the plain, and "Height of the Preaching" the name of the height where Patrick delivered the sermon.

### The Colloquy.

"You shall get it," said Patrick. Then the host and the multitude of the fortress rose up and they made their pact and friendship with the youth, so that there was a host of one thousand by the time of rising the next morning.

All the host went forward and Patrick along with them, and Cáilte went in the chariot that the King of Leinster gave him. They came forward to the Hill of the Halting of the Fianna <note>*Árd Fostada na Féinne*</note>, out across the River Sláine, and Cáilte dismounted from the chariot there and a hunt was arranged by them. "Well, Cáilte," said the King of Leinster, "why was this hill called the Hill of the Halting of the Fianna?" "I remember," said Cáilte, "though the event from which it is named is not a recent one:—"

"One day Fionn mac Cumaill and the three battalions of the Fianna came to this ford, and while we were sitting there," said Cáilte, "we saw a solitary maiden on the standing stone above the ford over there. She was wearing satin and a green cloak, with a gold brooch in the cloak and a gold diadem as a sign of a queen upon her head, and she said: 'Let one warrior of yours, O Fianna of Ireland, come to speak with me.' Then Sciath-brec son of Dathchán went to speak with her. 'Who do you want?' he asked. 'Fionn mac Cumaill,' she said. Fionn went to the ford to speak with the maiden: 'Who are you, maiden?' asked Fionn, 'and what do you want?' 'I am Dairenn, daughter of Bodb Derg son of the Dagda,' she said, 'and I have come to sleep with you in exchange for a bride-gift and a dowry.' 'What bride-gift?' asked Fionn. 'That I be your only wife for a year,' said the maiden, 'and have half of your bed forever after.' 'I do not give that to any woman in the world,' said Fionn, 'and I will not give it to you either.'"

"Then the maiden took a cup of white silver from her bosom, and it was full of delicious mead, and she put it into Fionn's hand. 'What is this, maiden?' asked Fionn. 'Delicious, intoxicating mead,' she said. Now, it was a <term>geis</term> <note>a mystical prohibition or obligation</note> for Fionn to refuse a feast, so he took the cup and drank from it. After drinking the draught, he was thrown into a drunken confusion; he turned his face toward the Fianna, and every evil, every blemish, and every battle-sorrow he knew about each man among them, he threw it in their faces because of the intoxication the maiden had put upon him."

"Then the nobles of the Fianna of Ireland rose up and left the place to him—that is, each of them went <insert>to go toward</insert> his own estate and his land—and no one was left on that hill <insert>said Cáilte</insert> except for me and Fionn. Then I rose up <insert>after</insert> the Fianna and said: 'O men, do not <insert>leave your lord</insert> and your master because of the ruin a strange fairy woman has brought upon him.' Twelve times I gathered them and brought them together on this hill. And when the end of the day and the beginning of the night came, the poison left Fionn's tongue, and the last time I halted them, his senses returned."

I looked around me until I saw a great, bright fairy mound with many goblets, horns, and cups. I stayed for a time at the door of the fairy mound looking at it, and I considered how I should proceed: whether to enter the mound to ask for news of it, or whether I should go to Fionn and his few remaining warriors. The counsel I decided upon was to go inside the mound. I sat in a crystal chair in the center of the mound and looked at the house around me. I saw twenty-eight young warriors in one half of the house, with a beautiful woman at each man's shoulder. There were six gentle, yellow-haired maidens in the other half of the house, wearing soft-textured gowns up to the points of their shoulders. A gentle, yellow-haired maiden sat in a chair on the floor of the mound with a harp in her hand, playing and performing constantly. Every time she sang a poem, a horn was given to her so that she might drink from it. She would then return the horn to the hand of the man who had given it to her, and they were all making merry around her.

"Let me perform your humble service <note>Umhal-fhosaig: the traditional ritual of washing a guest's feet.</note>, my soul, Cáilte," said the maiden. "I will not have it at all," I said, "for there is one of better rank than myself with me, namely Fionn mac Cumhaill, and he would like to have a night’s lodging in this mound tonight." # In Agallamh.

"It has been thirty years until tomorrow since the kingship of the Tuatha Dé Danann was given to Bodb Derg, son of the Dagda, at the dewy, bright-shining Brug. # The Colloquy.

We were in a sorry state after that last battle, for the bitterness and the overwhelming violence of the combat lay heavy upon Oscar and Diarmaid. Hoops of white hazel were used to hold their clothing off them as they lay in their bed of blood. The four of us warriors who remained healthy went out onto the green, and Oisín said: "This is a wretched journey we have made to the fairy mound of Midir’s son, only to leave my son and my companion in such a state." "Woe to him," said Mac Lugach, "who would face the Fianna after leaving Oscar and Diarmaid behind; for there were never two better men maintaining the deeds of the Fianna." "Whoever returns to them," said Fionn, "it will not be I." 

Then Donn, son of Midir, came to us. "Tell me, friend Donn," said Fionn, "do you know of anything that could heal those men?" "I know of nothing," said Donn, "except for a single physician who belongs to the Tuatha Dé Danann. Unless their spinal marrow has been severed, help and healing can be had from him within nine days, so that they would be smooth and whole again." "How could we get him?" asked Fionn, "for the people he serves are not our friends." "At early dawn," said Donn, "he comes out from the mound to gather healing herbs while the morning dew is still upon them." # The Colloquy.

I heard the conversation of my two sons and Fionn's two sons, and their dialogue was sad to me. 'There,' said Donn, 'are my two kinsmen; look and see if they are fit for nursing or if they are curable.' After that, a messenger came from Cormac son of Art, King of Ireland, to the Fianna at Allen, because of the absence of their lord and master Fionn son of Cumhall, asking them to go with Cormac to drink at the Feast of Tara. And the Fianna of Ireland arrived in full—men and women, lads, young warriors, and entertainers—at the Mound of the Druids on the green of Tara.

"I will not oppose Fionn regarding the high-captaincy," said Goll, "until he has been missing for three years from everyone, and until no man of the men of Ireland has any hope of him returning."

We took counsel to bring those three heads with us and return, but we abandoned that plan and turned back toward the ships on the shore. We killed four hundred of their young warriors in our first clash of battle. Then the three battalions poured upon us and we were fighting them for the duration of the fair day continually. When they saw their strong men falling, they fled to their ships and their swift boats, and we came away wounded and blood-stained.

Despite that, he drank it. And he vomited an emission with the variety of every color in it. "What is that, O maiden?" asked Cáilte. "The mixture of every run, every great strength, and every feat of skill you performed against every hill, mound, and rock. And the blood color that is upon its surface is the blood-sickness of your own body and flesh, and that is what is nearest to health." Then the maiden gave him a small cup of new milk, and he drank it. He was weak and infirm after that vomiting for three days and three nights.

"It seems to me, my soul, Cáilte," said the maiden, "that you have found relief and help." "I have indeed," said Cáilte, "except for the amount of trouble in my head..."

They were buried here under the earth so that they are under these three standing stones, and it is from them that the stones are named. Etáin, Aife, and Aillbe were their names.

"O Cáilte, my soul," said Cas Corach, "it is time for me to depart now, and may the blessing of every foster-son be upon you." "The blessing of every foster-father who ever had a foster-son be upon you," said Cáilte, "for you are the most skilled in your art that I have ever seen." Then [the King of Ireland, namely] Diarmait son of Cerball said: "The office of Chief Poet of Ireland <column-break/> shall be yours from me as long as I am in the kingship."

It was at that time and season that three groups of nine—the remnant of the Fianna who were with Cáilte—came to the hill on the western side of Tara. They took notice and realized that they were without their vigor, their presence, and their full agility; having neither prosperity nor any attention paid to them, no one would converse with them. They put their faces to the ground on the hill and died there, and they were buried under the earth of that hill. Thus, "The Hill of the Thrice-Nine" is the name of the hill after them.

"That is truly sad," said Oisín. "That is all that remained of the great and noble people that Fionn son of Cumall and we once had." The elders were weary and wretched that day because of those three groups of nine, since of the three battalions of the Fianna, none remained but Oisín and Cáilte and those men. All the men of Ireland remained silent, with not one man speaking to another, so greatly were they moved by the sorrow the elders showed after the loss of their Fianna and their true companions. And Oisín said:—

> Is there anyone here who would know, though he be weak or lowly:
> the place where Fionn’s cup was left alone in a winding glen?

"There was never a day," said Cáilte, "when I was not eager to speak with you, O Oisín, except for today." And Cáilte said:—

> There is one here who would know where Fionn turned sunwise;
> the place where it lies in the green glen is hidden by nothing but a magical wood.

Oisín said: "The dwarf's grave in Tara was no more of a wonder, even if all the men of Ireland came to see it, than our being recognized by Mael-muiri son of Dubán, the steward of Tara, and by Cuarnait, daughter of Becán the cattle-lord, his wife."

If all the diseases of the world afflicted a person, if he but laid his hand on them, they would be cured. And if the men of Ireland were in the midst of battle and combat, he would make peace between them. There was a stone here in Tara," Oisín continued, "and it was upon that stone that his bed was made. The nature of his bed was a marvel," said Oisín; "the largest man among the men of Ireland would find it a perfect fit, and the smallest infant that could be found would also find it a perfect fit. That, and the **Lia Fáil** <note>The Stone of Destiny</note> that was in Tara, were the two great wonders of Tara."

"What wonders were in the **Lia Fáil**?" asked Diarmait mac Cerbaill. "Anyone against whom there was even a rumor of a charge among the men of Ireland," Oisín said, "would be brought to that flagstone. If he were innocent, it would turn white and red for him when he was placed upon the **Lia Fáil**. But if he were guilty, a black spot would appear in a prominent place on him. And when the King of Ireland stepped upon it, the flagstone would scream beneath him so that the main waves of Ireland would answer it: the Wave of Clíodhna, the Wave of the North, and the Wave of Rudraige. When a provincial king stepped upon it, the stone would roar beneath him. When a barren woman walked upon it, a dew of black blood would break through it. ## The Death of Eochaid son of Mairid.

A good king took the sovereignty of Munster: Mairid son of Caireid. He had two excellent sons, Eochaid and Rib. Eibliu, daughter of Guaire from the *Brug Maic ind Óc* <note>Newgrange</note>, was Mairid's wife. She set her heart on his son, Eochaid. It is from this Eibliu that the mountain range Slieve Eilim <note>Sliab nEiblinne</note> is named. She continued to solicit the lad for a long time. Finally, she laid a solemn obligation upon him to elope with her. She said:

# The Death of Eochaid

Moreover, Rib said to his [brother] that he should take this woman with him, or else he would be under reproach; and he himself would go into the land with him. Then Eochaid took Eiblenn with him in flight, and Rib came with them. Their number was ten hundred men. It was thus they came, with their clothing and their flocks with them. Their druids told them that it was not destined for them to take an inheritance in one single place. Therefore, they separated at Belach Dá Liac. Rib went westward to the land of the games of Midir and the Mac Óc (that is, Mag Finn).

Midir came to them with a harnessed horse with a pack-saddle upon it, after he had killed their own horses before him. They put all their wealth upon it until he brought them to Mag nArbthen—that is, the place where Loch Rí is today. The nag lay down there with them and its urine flowed until it became a well. Consequently, that water came over them afterward and drowned them all, and that is Loch Rí.

Furthermore, Eochaid went until he reached the Brug Maic ind Óc. A large man came to them and ordered them out of the land, but they did not obey him. Then the man killed all their horses in that night. The same man came the next day and said to them: "I will kill all your people tonight," he said, "unless you leave the land you are on."

"You have already done much evil to us," said Eochaid, "by killing all our horses. Even if we wished to go, we cannot go without horses." Oengus gave them a large horse and they put all their property upon it. And he told them not to unharness the horse and not to let it rest, so that it would not urinate, lest it be the cause of death for them.

After that, they traveled on a Sunday in the middle month of autumn until they reached Liathmuine in Ulster. They all went to the horse and took all their property from it at once, and not one of them turned the horse's head back the way it came. Then the horse urinated there until it became a well. After that, Eochaid built a house around the well and a lid over it, and one woman was there to tend it. After that, Eochaid contested the half-kingship of Ulster against Muiredach mac Fiachach Finnamnais.

Once, however, the woman did not close the well, and the lake of the thicket rose over Liathmuine, and Eochaid was drowned there with his children, except for Líban and Conaing and Curnán the fool. It is from that Conaing that the Dál mBuain and Dál Sailne descended. Now Curnán was prophesying to them that the lake would come over them, so that it was then he said:

> **C** ome, come! Seize your blades! Shape your boats! The thicket shall come over Liathmuine with its half-stone. Airiu and Conaing shall be drowned in that broad pool; it shall swim east and west, here and there, over every sea.

That was true for him. For Líban was three hundred years throughout the sea, and her lapdog was in the shape of an otter following her wherever she went, never separating from her at all. And it was she herself who told of her wanderings.

It details the migration of Eochaid and Rib, the neglect that led to the flooding of their lands, and the survival of Líban as a mermaid.</summary>

It was this event that most scattered the Ulstermen throughout Ireland: the eruption of Loch Neagh over the land. The name Muirgein (meaning "sea-birth") was given to Líban after her baptism. Half of her was a salmon and the other half was a human. It is of her the historian sang these verses:

Líban and Airiu were the two daughters of Eochaid the Fair, son of Mairid. Airiu, the wife of Curnán, was drowned there; and Curnán also died of grief for her. *From this, Curnán's Cairn is named*; that was the finding of Curnán there.

Líban remained for a full year in her bower beneath the lake, with her lap-dog with her, and God protected her from the waters of Loch Neagh. One day she said: "O Lord," she said, "happy is the one who might be in the form of the salmon, so that they might be swimming through the sea with them." After that, she was transformed into the shape of a salmon, and her lap-dog was transformed into the shape of an otter, so that it followed her through the waters and the seas wherever she went in every direction. She remained in that state from the time of Eochaid son of Mairid until the time of Comgall of Bangor.

Comgall sent Beoán son of Innele from the house of Dabeoc to Rome to speak with Gregory regarding order and rule. However, while Beoán's boat-crew were rowing upon the sea, they heard the singing of angels beneath the boat. Beoán asked: "From what does this singing come?" "I am doing it," said Líban. "Who are you?" asked Beoán. "I am Líban, daughter of Eochaid son of Mairid," she said. "What caused you to be like this?" he asked. "I have been three hundred years under the sea," she said. "And I have come || to tell you my story, and that I am coming to you in the west at the estuary of Ollorba. Let me be met by you and the saints of Dál nAraidi on this day in a year's time. Tell this to Comgall and to the other saints." "I will not tell it," said Beoán, "unless my reward is given to me." "What reward do you ask?" she said. "To have your burial with me in my own monastery." "You shall have that then," she said. Beoán came from the east after that and told Comgall and the other clerics the news of the mermaid.

### The Death of Eochaid
<page-num>237</page-num>

<meta>41 a]</meta>

<margin>41 a]</margin> The year passed in that way, and the nets were prepared, and she was caught in the net of Fergus of Míliuc. She was brought to land after that, and her description and form were a wonder. A multitude came to see her while she was in the boat with water around her.

A chieftain of the Uí Conaing was there among the others, wearing a purple cloak. She was constantly staring at him. The young warrior asked her: "Is it because of the cloak," he said, "that your attention is on it? You shall have it." "No," she said, "I am not looking at it for that reason at all, but because of a purple cloak that Eochaid wore the day he was drowned. Grace be upon you then," she said, "and upon your successor in your place in exchange for that, and may it never be necessary to ask for your successor's seat in any assembly where he may be."

A great, ugly, black warrior came and killed her lap-dog. She left as a legacy for him and for his tribe that their prowess would be in their <term>notraigib</term> <note>Likely referring to a physical deformity or trait in the heels or shins.</note> and that their wrongs would not be avenged by them until they fasted against her. Then the warrior bowed to her.

There was then a dispute concerning her. Comgall said that she belonged to him because she was caught in his land. Fergus said that she was his because she was caught in his net. Beoán then said that she was his because she had promised herself to him. All those saints fasted then so that a judgment might be delivered between them regarding their dispute.

An angel said to a certain man there: "Two wild stags will come tomorrow," he said, "from Cairn Airenn. Place the chariot upon them," he said, "and let them carry her to whatever place they will." The stags came the next day as the angel had promised, and they carried her to the house of Dabeoc. The clerics then gave her a choice: to be baptized and go to heaven immediately at that hour, or to remain for the same length of time [she had already lived] and go to heaven after a long life. The choice she made was to die then. Comgall baptized her, and the name he gave her was Muirgein, that is, "birth of the sea," or Muirgeilt, that is, "wanderer of the sea." Another name for her was Fuinche.

Then wonders and miracles were performed through her there, and she is held with honor and reverence like every holy virgin, as God granted to her from heaven.

# The Death of Fergus
<page-num>238</page-num>
<header>The Death of Fergus.</header>
<meta>[30 b : 1]</meta>

*[The adventure of the king of the region of the Luchra and leprechauns to Emain, and the cause of the death of Fergus mac Léite, King of Ulster, as follows]*

A righteous, illustrious, and just-judging king took the sovereignty and supremacy over the prosperous clans of Rudraige: namely, Fergus mac Léite, son of Rudraige. These were his heroes and battle-warriors: Ergenn and Amergin the Iurtunach, Conna the Yellow son of Iliach, and Dubán son of Lugaid.

A great feast was prepared by that king in Emain Macha until it was ready for enjoyment and fully prepared. At that same hour and time, a feast was held by the king of the region of the Luchra and leprechauns: namely, Iubdán son of Abdán. These were the names of the battle-warriors who were with Iubdán: Conán son of Ruiched, Gerrchú son of Gared, Rigbec son of Robic, Luiccín son of Luicced, Glúnán son of Gabarn, Febal son of Feornín, Cinnbec son of Gnumán, Brigbec son of Buán, Bran son of Luán, and Mether son of Mintán.

The champion of the region of the Luchra and leprechauns was brought to them: Glómhar son of Glass, son of Glomraide. His champion’s feat was to knock down a thistle with a single blow; yet it took the strength of twelve of their men to knock that man down. The king's deputy was brought to them, Bec son of Bec, as well as the king’s <term>ollam</term> <note>A high-ranking poet or scholar.</note> and man of verse, Eisirt son of Bec, son of Buaidgen, along with the other nobles of the region of the Luchra and leprechauns.

That drinking-hall of theirs was arranged according to arts and entitlements. Iubdán was brought to the side of the drinking-hall with his wife, Bébo, at his shoulder, and his <term>ollam</term> at his other shoulder. Bec son of Bec was brought to the other royal side facing Iubdán, with the noble chieftains around him. The king's champion, Glómar son of Glass, son of Glomraide, was placed at the door-post of the house. The <term>cinnbecca</term> <note>Small lids or stoppers.</note> were then struck off their vats; those vats were brown, the color of red yew. The cup-bearers rose to serve and the carvers to divide the portions, and old, sleepy, delicious ale was poured for the hosts until they were all intoxicated and merry on both sides.

Then their high king and head of counsel, Iubdán, rose up with the speckled drinking horn. Bec son of Bec rose from the royal side opposite...

Iubdán was being honored, and he was very affable. He asked, "Have you ever seen a king who was better than I?" 

"We have not," they said. 

"Have you ever seen a strong man better than my strong man?" 

"We have not," they said. 

"Have you ever seen a champion or a battle-warrior better than those who are in this house tonight?" 

"By our word," they said, "we have not." 

"I give my word on it," said Iubdán, "that it would be difficult to take hostages or captives by force out of this house tonight because of the excellence of its champions and battle-warriors, the number of its houses and its strong men, and the multitude of its fierce, strong, and brave royal heirs."

Eisirt, the king's <term>ollam</term>, laughed upon hearing that. Iubdán asked him, "Why did you laugh, Eisirt?" 

"I know of a single province of Ireland," said the <term>ollam</term>, "and one man of them could take hostages and captives from the four battalions of the Tuatha Luchra that you have here."

"Let the <term>ollam</term> be seized," said Iubdán, "so that his boastful words may be punished." And it was done so. 

"That arrest will be bad for you, Iubdán," said Eisirt. "For you yourself will spend five years in captivity in Emain Macha to pay for this seizure, and you will not leave until you leave behind the best of your treasures and wealth. And because of this arrest, Cobthach the Curly, son of the King of Munster, and Eochaid son of Néd, son of the King of Leinster, will fall. I myself will go to the house of Fergus mac Léite, and I will be in the drinking horn swimming on the rim, and I will nearly be drowned there." And he said:

> A great feast tonight in Emain, bad for women, bad for men;
> though the hosts are cheerful from it, it will be sorrowful, gloomy, and dark.
> I will go to Emain from here, to the house of Fergus mac Léite;
> when everyone is drinking, I will be in the horn swimming on the rim.
> It is through this that Cobthach the Curly will fall, the son of the great, fierce King of Munster;
> and Eochaid son of Néd <unclear>connim</unclear>, though he is the high king over the Leinstermen.
> You will be a captive for a year, kept by rough servants;
> because of the seizing of Eisirt thereafter, because of that feast.

"That arrest you have made of me is bad, O high king," said Eisirt. "Give me a respite of three days and three nights so that I may go to Emain Macha, to the house of Fergus mac Léite. And if I find a distinctive token by which you will recognize that I speak the truth, I will bring it back with me. And if I do not bring it, do with me whatever you please." 

Then Eisirt was released. He arose and put on a shirt of smooth, bright, soft satin against his white skin, and a white-pleated, gilded tunic over it on the outside, and a very beautiful, long, soft, fringed purple cloak of the purple dye of the land of the Fair ones, with its border of speckled white gold. # The Tragic Death of Fergus

...wrapped in a satin hooded cloak. He came forward by the shortest route and through every known path, and his journey is not recounted until he reached Emain Macha. He shook his poet's wand at the gate of the town. The doorkeeper heard that sound and came out, and he saw a small, lively, and eternally beautiful man. The fine, sleek green grass of the lawn reached to his knee and to the thick of his thigh. Wonder seized the doorkeeper upon seeing him, <column-break/> and the doorkeeper went inside and told Fergus and the host.

They said: "Is he smaller than Aed?" (That Aed was the <term>ollam</term> of Ulster and a dwarf, and he used to sit on the palms of the big men.) "By my word," said the doorkeeper, "he would fit on Aed's palm." The host rushed out all at once to see him, for everyone longed to see him and speak with him. A crowd of men and women pressed in from every side. 

Eisirt said: "O great people, do not let your foul, short breaths reach me. Instead, let that man who is smallest among you come to me; for though he is small to you, he would be great in the land where I live." Then Aed the poet took him on his palm into the great house. Fergus asked for news of who he was. "I am Eisirt, son of Beg, son of Buaidgen," he said; "the <term>ollam</term>, poet, and sage of the Tuatha Luchra, and a <term>lupracán</term>."

Then the hosts were consuming the feast, and the cup-bearer came with the drinking horn to Fergus. "Give it to the little man," said Fergus. 

"I will not eat your food and I will not drink your ale," said Eisirt. 

"By our word," said Fergus, "since you are a trifling and ridiculous man, it is only right to put you into the horn so that it would be easy for you to drink the ale from all sides of you." Hearing this, the cup-bearer closed his hand around him and tossed him into the horn, so that he was swimming on the surface of the drink. 

"By my conscience," said Eisirt, "O <term>ollam</term>s of Ulster, you would need to gain much news and knowledge from me, even though you allow me to be drowned." 

He was then taken out and cleaned with beautiful cloths of speckled satin and excellent silken shirts. Fergus asked him: "What is the impurity you mentioned earlier as to why you would not consume our food?" 

"I will tell you the thing," said Eisirt, "unless your anger turns against me." 

"It shall not," said Fergus, "and tell me every prohibition." 

And Eisirt spoke the poem:

> O Fergus, do not be angered by the sharp words of a poet;
> restrain your harsh, fiercely strong voice; do not rise against me without cause.
> O little man <note>The word 'hairide' is obscure here.</note>, it is your fire that is lacking;
> or do you go in weakness upon the liquid <unclear>inethach</unclear>?

After that poem, the Ulstermen provided for him with an abundance of every good thing, so that every heap of every kind was as high as a tall man among them. "We give our word," they said, "that even if we gave you our wives and our cattle, we would not take a single thing back from you; and what we have given, we will not take back." "O <term>ollams</term> and poets of Ulster," said Eisirt, "divide that, and let two-thirds of it be yours, and give the other third to the messengers and the jesters of Ulster." Eisirt remained in Emain for three days and three nights, and he took his leave of Fergus and the nobles of Ulster. "I will go with you," said Aed—that is, the <term>ollam</term> of Ulster and its man of poetry. He used to be in the lap or the bosom of every great warrior among them, yet he was like a giant compared to Eisirt, and Eisirt used to stand on Aed's palm.

# The Death of Fergus

"It is not I who will ask you to go with me," said Eisirt, "for even if a good thing were done for you, you would say it was promised to you if I asked you to accompany me; but if it were done for you without a promise, you would be grateful."

Those two poets traveled forward from Emain Macha, and Aedh's stride was the larger of the two. "You walk poorly, Eisirt," said Aedh. Then Eisirt made a burst of speed so that he was an arrow-shot's distance ahead of Aedh. "The right way lies between those two points," said Aedh. "By our word," said Eisirt, "that is what I have heard you call 'the right way' ever since I have been with you."

They went on until they reached the Shore of the Champions in Ulster <note>Ulaid</note>. "What shall we do now?" asked Aedh. "Cross the sea over its depths," said Eisirt. "I shall never achieve that," said Aedh. "It is a wonder that I should reach it and you should not," said Eisirt. And Aedh composed a poem, and Eisirt answered him:

> O noble Eisirt, what use shall I make
> of the great sea?
> The wind carries me down
> to the relentless wave;
> if I go up, I shall find death.
> The horse of fair Iubdán
> will come for you;
> mount upon it
> across the clear great sea.
> A good horse, it is no lie,
> a treasure held by a king;
> it is equally beautiful
> between sea and land.
> A yellow, sleek horse,
> it will carry you;
> stay upon it without fear
> and go to its feast.

They were not there long before they saw the "fluttering one" coming toward them over the very crests of the waves. "Woe to its appearance and its gloom!" said Aedh. "What do you see?" asked Eisirt. "A red-maned beast of the field," said Aedh. "It is not that," said Eisirt, "but the horse of Iubdán coming for you."

And this is how it was: it had two fierce, clear-shining, glorious eyes in its head, and a beautiful, pure crimson mane, and four green legs beneath it, and a long, naturally curled tail, and a golden, highly-crafted luster upon it, with a gold-ridged bridle. Eisirt mounted its back. "Come up, Aedh," said Eisirt. "O poet," said Aedh, "it does not even have the capacity of your own small boat." "Do not complain about it, Aedh," said Eisirt, "for though the weight of wisdom is in you, it will carry us both."

They both went upon it over the crests of the waves, over the heroic surface of the sea, and over the depths of the ocean until they reached Magh Faithlinn without sorrow or drowning. The people of Luchra <note>Tuatha Luchra</note> were at an assembly waiting for them. "Eisirt is coming to us," they said, "and a giant <note>literally a "fomóir"</note> along with him." Then Iubdán came to meet Eisirt and gave him a kiss. "O poet," he said, "why have you brought that giant to us to kill us?" "He is no giant," said Eisirt, "but the poet of Ulster."

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Iubdán’s captivity at the court of King Fergus in Emain Macha. Having previously discussed the nature of trees and his own palace, Iubdán now demonstrates his prophetic and insightful nature through a series of observations about the human condition.</meta>

# The Death of Fergus

He remained in the settlement in that manner under noble custody; and it was a delight of mind and spirit for the Ulstermen to be watching him and listening to his words.

One day, Iubdán went to the women’s quarters while they were washing, bathing, and smoothly combing their hair. Iubdán laughed at this. "Why did you laugh, Iubdán?" asked Fergus. "The dressing is far from the wound," said Iubdán. "What is meant by that?" asked Fergus. "Women wash and tend to their heads for the sake of their bottoms," said Iubdán, "for the wound is below and the washing and bathing—that is, the washing and beautifying of the heads—is above."

Another time, Iubdán went to the house of one of the king's mercenaries, who had new shoes and was putting them on. He was complaining about the thinness of the soles of his shoes and grumbling about them. Iubdán laughed at this. "Why did you laugh, Iubdán?" asked Fergus. "A cause for laughter to me," said Iubdán, "is that man complaining about the thinness of his shoes, yet he does not complain about his life. For though those shoes are thin, he will never wear them out." And what Iubdán said was true, for that man and another man of Fergus's household encountered one another and killed each other <column-break/> before nightfall.

Another day, a man of the household was picking bits of straw from his wife's clothing, and Iubdán laughed. "Why did you laugh, Iubdán?" asked Fergus. "Good is the reason for my laughter," said Iubdán. "That man who picks the straw from his wife's clothing—he should rather be killed, for those clothes were under her until now while another man was on top of her."

Another day, the household members were discussing everything they intended to do, but they did not say "if God wills it." Iubdán laughed at them and composed this poem:

> Man speaks; God tells;
> everything is a gathering of workers to them; leave it as God knows.
> The High King of the elements; everything He has promised would be right;
> the King of kings knows all that I ask of you, O Fergus.
> As brief as a glance of an eye is the life of every person, though it be harsh;
> even a king's son does not know if he speaks the truth.

In any case, Iubdán remained in Emain in that manner until the <term>Tuatha Luchra</term> <note>The tiny people or leprechauns</note> came in seven equally large battalions to seek him at the green of Emain. None of them exceeded another in height or in size. Fergus and the nobles of Ulster came out to speak with them, and they said to Fergus: "Give us our king to ransom him," they said, "and we will give a good price for him." "What is that price?" asked Fergus.

# The Death of Fergus

"We will give," said they, "this great plain of Emain under a crop of wheat every year, without the need for seed or plowing." "I will not give up Iubdán," said Fergus. "We will commit a raid upon you tonight," they said. "What is that raid?" asked Fergus. "We will let the calves of Ulster to their mothers, so that not even enough milk for a single infant, neither thick nor thin milk, will be found in the province of Ulster in the morning." "That is what you shall have," said Fergus, "but it shall not be Iubdán." And they committed that raid that night. They came in the morning to the green of Emain and were asking for Iubdán, saying they would restore everything they had destroyed. But Fergus said he would not give him up.

"We will perform another vengeance tonight," they said. "What vengeance is that?" asked Fergus. "We will defecate in the waterfalls and in the river-mouths of the province." "That is a small raid," said Fergus. From that comes the proverb: "defecating in a well." "You shall not get Iubdán for that," said Fergus. And they did so, and they came the third day to Emain and asked for Iubdán. "I will not give him up," said Fergus. "We will perform another vengeance," they said. "What vengeance is that?" asked Fergus. "We will burn the kilns and the mills of the province tonight." "You shall not get Iubdán."

They went on their way and did as they had promised, and they came the fourth day to Emain and asked for Iubdán. "I will not give him up," said Fergus. "We will perform a vengeance upon you." "What vengeance is that?" asked Fergus. "We will cut the heads off the ears of corn in the province tonight." "Iubdán shall not be had for that," said Fergus. And they did that, and they came the fifth day to Emain and were asking for Iubdán. "I will not give him up," said Fergus. "We will perform another vengeance upon you." "What vengeance is that?" asked Fergus. "We will shave the hair of your women and your men so that they will be under shame and disgrace forever." "By my word," said Fergus, "if you do that, I will kill Iubdán."

"That is not the right thing to do," said Iubdán. "Instead, let me go out myself to speak with them, and to tell them to depart and to repair what they have destroyed." And he was let out to them. When they saw him coming toward them, they gave great shouts of laughter aloud, for they were certain that he had been allowed to leave with them.

"O comrades," said Iubdán, "depart, for I am not allowed to go with you. Repair what you have destroyed and do not destroy anything more, for if you do, I will be killed." They departed gloomily and sorrowfully, and one of them composed the poem as they went:

> A raid from us upon you tonight, O Fergus of many strongholds:
> We will strike the heads from your ears of corn; your tables will be none the better for it.
> We burned your kilns because of it, and we destroyed your mills;
> We let your calves go precisely to their cows all at once.
> We will cut the hair of your men and the hair of your daughters;
> It will be no beauty to your inheritance; that will be the end of our raiding.

Fergus then took his choice of those treasures of Iubdán, and the choice he made was Iubdán’s shoes. After that, Iubdán took his leave of Fergus and of all the nobles of <term>Ulster</term>; he left a blessing with them and received a blessing from them, and the Ulstermen were sorrowful after he left. The story is not told further for now.

As for Fergus, however, this is why he chose the shoes as his prize: one day he and a youth were walking by the sea near <term>Loch Rudraige</term>, and they went into the lake to bathe. The monster that lived in the lake noticed them—that is, the <term>sinech</term> <note>a water-serpent or monster</note> of <term>Loch Rudraige</term>. She shook herself until the whole lake became a fierce and terrible storm, and she rose up like a standing, long, radiant arch, as large as a rainbow in the sky. They saw her coming toward them, and they swam from the lake toward the shore. She swam after them strongly and swiftly, so that the two waves around her sides were like the violent red surge of a flood. Fergus let his youth go before him toward the land. The breath of the monster struck Fergus so that it made a distorted, squint-eyed creature of him, twisting his face from his mouth to the hollow of his neck. He himself did not know he was in that state, and no one dared to ask him what had caused it, nor did anyone dare to bring a mirror into the same house as him.

Nevertheless, the youth told his own wife about it, and the wife told the Queen, Fergus’s wife. It happened during a dispute over a bath between the King and the Queen that the King gave her a blow with his fist and broke a tooth in her head. Anger seized the Queen and she said: "It would be more fitting for you," she said, "to take your revenge on the <term>sinech</term> of <term>Loch Rudraige</term>, who twisted your mouth to the hollow of your neck, than to perform bloodless deeds <note>The text uses "báinghn," suggesting unheroic or cowardly acts</note> against women." A mirror was then brought to Fergus; he looked at himself and said: "What the woman said is true," he said, "and it is the monster that has dealt this to me." For that reason, Fergus had chosen the shoes above all of Iubdán’s treasures.

The whole province of <term>Ulster</term> was then gathered by Fergus with their ships and galleys at <term>Loch Rudraige</term>, and they put their ships upon the lake. When they reached the middle of the lake, the monster rose up and shook herself fiercely and violently, so that she made fragments of all the ships. Every ship was like the smashed branches of withered trees under the feet of a team of horses, so that they were all drowned before they reached the shore. Fergus said to the Ulstermen: "Wait

"Here," he said, "and sit all of you so that you may see what course I and the beast take against each other."

Then Fergus put Iubdán’s shoes on and leaped into the lake like a radiant, tireless arch toward the beast. When the beast heard the noise of the royal warrior, she bared her teeth like a hound on a scent, and her eyes flashed like two blazing royal candles. She quickly and roughly readied her sharp claws, and she arched her neck into a great curve, and fiercely tightened her lips, and flattened her shaggy ears hideously, and a horrible, fierce grimace came over her. Woe to any person in the world destined to face that beast in combat, for she was a giant-headed, flat-toothed monster. Such was that strong, hardy, and violent monster: crested, large-headed, flat-toothed, maned, ugly, rough-haired, wide-mouthed, harsh, and deep-eyed. She had three times fifty hard, broad legs on each side of her, and three times fifty back-hooked claws on every single foot; she had a combative, thick body, large, hideous shaggy ears, and monstrous, sharp teeth. Her knees were blacker than coal or the back of a beetle. She was three times fifty feet high when she stretched herself; she was rounder than an apple when she contracted, and she was as large as a high, noble, gorse-rough mountain <gloss>sic</gloss>. The King saw the beast and attacked her readily and suddenly, and he performed this <term>rosgad</term> <note>an archaic, rhythmic Irish verse</note> there:

> Evil has come to me as an omen; the province of Ulster of great fame. A great monster easily wounded; Loch Rudraige she raced through. Sighs before the spoil of habitual anger; a battle-combat he boasts of. From his golden brilliance; the equipment of horses in an unequal struggle. The strength of lords established; ships... they shall be without a king before great battles. Of Iubdán I beseech, while slaughtering the monster; control the form of mutual anger. The world-huge beast shall fall, by my armor and my great blows; it is long since evil came to me.

After that, they rose up in the middle of the lake and shook it so violently that the blue-edged salmon were leaping over the banks of the lake. Indeed, they found no resting place in the lake, because the sand of the white beach was stirred up to the surface. At one moment the lake was whiter than milk; at another, the entire lake was a crimson foam of blood. Then the beast rose up out of the lake like a great royal oak, fleeing from Fergus. But the royal warrior attacked her with equal strength, power, and hardness, dealing quick and massive death-blows until she fell by his hand. He cut her into small pieces with the sword that was in his hand—the *Caladcholg* <note>meaning "hard-blade," the name of his sword</note>, the best sword that was in Ireland at that time—and he brought the heart of the beast with him to the shore.

His soul then separated from his body. His grave was dug, his Ogham name was written, and his funeral games were performed. And it is from the breast-beatings <note>hulltaib; a folk etymology for the name of the province</note> that the Ulstermen performed while lamenting him that they are called Ulstermen.

So those are the adventures of the people of the <term>Luchra</term> <note>the tiny people, or leprechauns</note> and the death of Fergus up to this point.

## The Birth of Cormac, Grandson of Conn, follows here.

Art, son of Conn of the Hundred Battles, went to fight the Battle of Mag Mucrama against Mac Con. He traveled with the great armies of the men of Ireland westward across the Shannon. He stayed as a guest the night before the battle in the house of Olc Acha the smith. There were ill omens and grim words among them that night. Olc Acha told Art that it was neither fitting nor safe for him to give battle to Mac Con or to Eogan, son of Ailill Ólum, and he harbored ill will toward Art because Lugaid owed him a debt. "How many children do you leave behind?" the smith asked Art. "I do not know," Art replied, "except for one son only." "That is far too few," said the smith. "Sleep with my daughter tonight, O Art, for it is prophesied for me that a great and noble lineage shall be born from me." This was true; great was the nobility—that is, Cormac, son of Art, son of Conn of the Hundred Battles.

The king then slept with Etáin, daughter of Olc Acha, that night, and it was then that Cormac was conceived. Art told her she would bear a son who would be king over Ireland. He then revealed to her every hidden treasure for the boy's benefit, and he told her that he himself would be killed the following day. He then took his leave of her and said: "Take your son with you to be fostered by his friend among the Connachta—namely, Lugna Fertrí in Corann." The king was later killed in the battle, just as he had predicted.

Etáin was indeed pregnant, and she intended to go to the house of Lugna Fertrí so that she might give birth to the child she carried in her womb. She set out in her chariot, accompanied by a single woman, to find Lugna in Corann. When she reached that land, her labor pains came upon her; she stepped down from her chariot and gave birth to a son. Her handmaid went and cut brushwood to place under her, which is why that place in Corann is called Fidnacha <note>Derived from the Irish *fidnach*, meaning brushwood</note>. A great thunderous crash echoed through the air at the birth of the boy. Hearing the noise, Lugna said:

> A crash, a thunder, the birth of a king; an increase of prosperity, the destruction of falsehood for the child of grace.
> A quickening of sense, the kindling of truth, the silencing of all other speech; corn and milk shall come
> from Art’s journey to the house of Olc, and from the birth of his great son; heaven foretells joy
> and gladness, for the great prince and the son who has arrived shall be sociable and well-spoken;
> heaven celebrates him with this mighty sound.

"It is true," said Lugna. "This is the son of the true prince, Cormac son of Art..."

# The Birth of Cormac

"...is born now. Let us go in search of him," he said, "for to me was entrusted his protection until he should be of age to inherit."

Etáin, however, fell asleep after the labor, and she ordered the handmaid to guard the boy until they were ready to travel. The handmaid also fell asleep. A wolf reached them and carried the boy away to the place where her cubs were, to the stone cave at the head of Cráibech by Achall, in what is now known as Cormac's Mound <note>Síd Chormaic</note>. The woman woke up afterward and gave a cry of woe because she could not find the boy. Lugna then came to her and asked why they were grieving. The young woman told him everything: that she had come to seek him specifically because the boy had been entrusted to him for fostering. Lugna then took the woman to his house and declared that whoever could find information or a trace of the boy would be granted whatever they desired.

One day, Grec son of Arodh was searching the land when he happened upon the cave. He saw the cubs playing at the mouth of the cave with a small boy among them, moving on his hands. "It is true," he said. He then went to Lugna and bound him to a promise of a reward if he found the king’s son. Lugna agreed to this. For this reason, the land where the <term>Grecraige</term> <note>A population group in ancient Ireland located in modern County Sligo.</note> are settled was given to Grec as the price for finding Cormac. Afterward, Lugna and Grec went to the cave and took the boy and the cubs from it. It was then that Lugna sang this, prophesying for him:

->Welcome, Conn’s successor, victorious, true in knowledge, of truth in his judgment regarding urgent matters. He shall be famous for wisdom; he shall be sober; he shall be satisfied; he shall be a warrior. He shall be generous; he shall be a well-mannered nobleman; he shall be swift in his great deeds. He shall be a subduer of the proud for the sake of the hosts who follow him. He shall be a true prophet of fair feats against all champions if there should be a loss of their most mighty lords. He will allow an exile when he is absent for a period of nine months. He will fulfill the <unclear>caipthiug</unclear> with the color of the points of the war-goddesses. He will cut down hosts with his <unclear>luaignib</unclear>. He will set right the crooked law over the lands of Banba <note>A poetic name for Ireland.</note>. There shall be an assembly of the men of Ireland where his great judgments shall be consulted in this island until the end of the world. Banba shall put away her sudden sorrow at the inheritance of the established ruler. He shall be king of Tara three times. He shall die among the spirits after spending forty years in the kingship over the city of <unclear>croainn</unclear>. To whom it shall be said: "Welcome, successor of Conn's Tara."<-

The boy was afterward reared by Lugna, and no one dared to provoke his anger because of his father’s enemies. The boy was a delight to many eyes: in his form and his dress, his harmony and symmetry, his speech and his joy, his beauty and dignity, his vigor and strength and spirit. The name given to him by Lugna was <term>Corpmac</term> <note>A play on the name Cormac, suggesting "Chariot-son" or "Body-son."</note>, in the state that Art had left him.

# The Birth of Cormac

Once, while he was playing, he struck one of the men. The man was enraged: he struck the boy back, saying it was unknown what tribe or family he belonged to, except that he was a foundling without a father. Cormac went then in deep sorrow to the place where Lugna was and told him of his grievance. "That is not true," said Lugna. "You are the son of the true ruler—the son of Art son of Conn of the Hundred Battles—and it is prophesied that you shall take up your father's steering-oar. For there shall be neither grain, nor milk, nor mast <note>Nuts from forest trees used as animal feed.</note>, nor sea-produce, nor fair weather in its proper season as long as you are away from the lordship of Tara." "Let us go then," said Cormac, "so that we may seek our rightful knowledge in our father’s house at Tara." "Let us go indeed," said Lugna.

They went then—Lugna and Cormac with his hounds—accompanied by the "True-Backs" <note>firchúl</note>, a troop of soldiers who had been in Corann from the time of Eochaid Aireman until then; for it was they who killed Eochaid Aireman because of a heavy tax imposed upon them. They are the "True-Backs of Bregia" today; they are the ones who went as his escort.

They proceeded until they reached Tara. They were welcomed there, and Cormac was received as a foster-son. At that time, there was a female landowner in Tara named Bennaidh. Her sheep strayed and ate the queen's woad <note>glaisín; a plant used for blue dye.</note>. The case was brought before Lugaid [mac Con]. He judged that the sheep should be forfeited to the queen in payment for the woad. "No," said Cormac, "the shearing of the sheep is enough for the eating of the woad, for both will grow again." "That is the true judgment!" everyone cried. "It is the son of the true ruler who gave that judgment." Half of the house where the false judgment was given collapsed down the slope. It shall remain so forever; that is the "Crooked Mounds of Tara" <note>Claenfherta Temrach</note>.

However, the reign of Mac Con was not good. The men of Ireland expelled him afterward and gave the kingship to Cormac. The world was full of every good thing after that, as long as Cormac lived. Cormac kept his hounds afterward, and that was the reason for the great respect Cormac had for hounds—because of his upbringing by them.

Tara was rebuilt by him as it had never been before, including houses, ramparts, and other structures, as well as warrior-halls, sunny chambers, and underground dwellings. Ireland was prosperous during that king's time. The waters of the rivers could not flow easily because of the abundance of fish. The woods could not be easily traversed because of the abundance of mast. The plains were not easy to travel because of the abundance of honey bestowed from heaven through the righteousness of his sovereignty. The abundance of wild game would have fed and satisfied his people even if they had not harvested any crops.

Cormac reigned in Tara after that, and he constructed the most excellent building ever made in Tara. He was never separated from the kingship, though he was attacked by the men of Ulster, until he died in...

### [*The Adventure of Laegaire Son of Crimthann to the Plain of Delight*]

The men of Connacht were once gathered at a meeting by a certain lake on the Plain of Ai. Crimthann Cas was the king of Connacht at that time. They remained at the meeting that night. They rose early the next morning and saw a man coming toward them through the mist. He wore a five-folded purple cloak and held two five-pointed spears in his hand. He had a shield with a gold boss and a gold-hilted sword at his belt, and his golden-yellow hair fell over his back.

"Welcome the man who comes toward you," said Laegaire the Radiant, son of Crimthann; he was the most noble youth in Connacht. "Welcome to the warrior whom we do not recognize," said Laegaire. "I am grateful," the man replied. "Why have you come?" asked Laegaire. "To seek help," he said. "Where are you from?" asked Loegaire. "I am of the people of the fairy mounds," he replied. "Fiachna son of Retach is my name. My wife was taken from me; Eochaid son of Sal took her. I killed him in a battle, but then she went to his nephew, Goll son of Dolb, the king of the fortress of the Plain of Delight <note>Magh Mell, the Irish Otherworld.</note>. I have fought seven battles against him, and I have lost them all. A battle has been declared against us today, and I have come to seek help. I will give a share of silver and a share of gold to every man who is willing to come with me." With that, he turned away from them.

"It is a shame for you," said Loegaire, "not to help that man." Fifty warriors followed after him. The stranger went before them down into the lake, and they followed him. They saw the fortress ahead of them and the two armies face to face. He went before them until he reached his fortress.

Fiachna son of Retach saw the two battle-hosts there. "Well then," said Loegaire, "I will encounter that leader over there with fifty warriors." "I will oppose you," said Goll son of Dulb.

They struck at each other with their two groups of fifty. Loegaire escaped alive with his fifty after the fall of Goll and his fifty warriors around him. The battle broke out before them after that, until a great slaughter was made.

"Where is the woman?" asked Loegaire. "She is in the fortress of Mag Mell <note>The Plain of Delight.</note>," said Fiachna, "and the army is around her." "Stay here until I and my fifty warriors reach her," said Loegaire. Loegaire then went to the fortress of Mag Mell. They were then in the process of capturing the fortress. "This is of little use," said Loegaire; "your king has fallen and your nobles have fallen. Let the woman come out, and safety shall be granted to you in exchange." That was done. It was then said as she came out: "the sigh of the daughter of Eochaid the Mute."

Loegaire went after that and put his hand into Fiachna’s hand. Loegaire was wedded that night to Der Gréine <note>Sun’s Tear.</note>, the daughter of Fiachna; and fifty women were given to his fifty warriors, and they stayed with them until the end of a year. "Let us go to seek news of our land," said Loegaire. "If you return again," said Fiachna, "take horses with you and do not dismount from them."

This was done. They traveled until they reached the assembly. The men of Connacht were there, mourning the aforementioned band at the end of the year, when the warriors arrived above them. The Connachtmen leaped up to welcome them. "Do not come near," said Loegaire; "we have come only to bid you farewell." "Do not leave me!" said Crimthann. "The kingship of Connacht shall be yours; its gold and its silver, its horses and its bridles, and its beautiful women shall be at your command—only do not leave me."

After that, Loegaire turned away from them into the fairy mound again, so that he remains in joint-kingship of the mound with Fiachna son of Retach, with the daughter of Fiachna at his side; and he has not come out from there since.

### [*The Pursuit of the Difficult Servant and his Horse*]

A noble and illustrious king took sovereignty and high-lordship over Ireland once: Cormac son of Art, son of [Conn] of the Hundred Battles. Ireland was prosperous, orderly, happy, peaceful, and rich in wealth during the time of that strong king. It was no wonder it was so, for that Cormac was a landowner in hospitality, a poet in poetry, and a king in kingship.
