# In Gilla decair. [134, 135]

Fionn mac Cumhaill, son of Trenmór, grandson of Baoiscne, was in high command over the Fianna of Ireland during the time of that mighty king, namely Cormac the High King and king of the provinces, and the royal leader of the Fianna. Fionn was considered one of the seven kings counted in Ireland at that time.

The wages and rewards of Fionn and the Fianna were great at that time: a townland in every territory and a quarter-land in every townland; a hound puppy or a dog in every house from Samhain <note>November 1st</note> to Beltane <note>May 1st</note>, and many other benefits not mentioned here. And though those benefits were great, the hardships and difficulties that fell upon Fionn and the Fianna of Ireland because of them were much greater—such as the restraining and expelling of foreigners, pirates, thieves, and outlaws from Ireland <column-break/> along with every other evil. Thus, the Fianna faced much hardship and anxiety while defending Ireland, as is shown here.

One day, when Fionn and the Fianna of Ireland were in broad, great Almhain <note>The Hill of Allen</note> in Leinster, drinking at an intoxicating and merry feast of Samhain, the nobles and great lords of the Fianna of Ireland were with him. Fionn asked them if it was time for them to go hunting and searching for game. For it was the custom of Fionn and the Fianna of Ireland to spend the year in this way: from Beltane to Samhain in hunting and venery, and from Samhain to Beltane keeping a fixed and general watch over the men of Ireland.

However, it was decided after that to go and hold that great hunt of theirs. The place they went to perform it was throughout the two assembly-rich provinces of Munster. They then moved by the shortest paths from Almhain until they reached the territory of the Ui Builc, to the center of Fir Cell, to the river Brosna of Slieve Bloom, to the twelve mountains of Evlinn, to Cnamhchoill of the son of Raighne, and to Drom Collchoille which is called Aine Cliach at this time.

The hunt was spread out and driven by Fionn and the Fianna of Ireland around the borders of the forest called Fermoy <note>Fir Maighe</note> today, and through dark, hidden places and rugged lands, and through fair, beautiful, and smooth territories, and through the high mountains of Desmond which are called <column-break/> Luachair Dheaghaidh today; around the beautiful mountain of Crot, and the smooth, lovely hills of Sliabh Muice, and the gentle coastal lands of the green-streamed Suir, and the grassy, truly green plains of Femen, and the high, rough, and uneven Desi of Ethne, and from there to the blue-wooded pass of Gowran.

However, there was neither wood, nor plain, nor great mountain in the two provinces of Munster where there was not a leader of nine men hunting and following the Fianna way...

It was then that Fionn sat upon his hunting mound, and a group of noble warriors remained in his company: Oisín son of Fionn; Oscar son of Oisín; Goll mac Mórna; Art of the Mighty Blows son of Mórna; Sciath Brec son of Dathchaoin, who was Fionn’s shield-bearer; the three Mutes from the Burren, who were the three sons of the smith of Beirre; Caoilte son of Rónán; Diarmait of the Bright Teeth, descendant of Duibne; Liathán the Swift from Luachair Dhegaid; Conán [the Bald] son of Mórna, the man of insults and foul speech of the Fianna; and Fionn [the Fair] son of Bresal. Furthermore, Fionn and the Fianna of Ireland thought the voice and baying of the hounds, the swift shouts of the youths, the noise of the strong men, and the whistling and true shouting of the Fianna in the forests and wilderness around them were sweet music.

It was then that Fionn asked that group who were with him which of them would go to watch and guard the hill. Fionn Bán son of Bresal, of the house of Baoiscne, answered the royal leader of the Fianna and said that he himself would go there. Then Fionn Bán laid a noble warrior's quick hand upon his broad weapons and proceeded to the height of the hill. He began looking out from it on every side of him—east, west, south, and north. He had not been there long when he saw, coming directly from the east, a manly but truly hideous Fomorian <note>A supernatural giant from Irish mythology</note>, a diabolical and misshapen creature, a gloomy and unsightly servant.

He was like this: he had a solid, black, ugly, dark shield on the arch of his back, and a broad-grooved, clean-striking sword on his jet-black left thigh. He had two charmed, broad-bladed spears at his shoulder that had not been raised for a long time in battle or conflict. He wore a broken, threadbare cloak over his gear and clothing, and every limb of him was blacker than a smith’s coal that has been quenched in cold, icy water. He had a gloomy, unsightly, skin-and-bone horse with a thin, gray, clumsy hindquarter and weak legs; a rough iron halter was on it, and he was dragging it behind him. It was a great wonder that he did not pull its head from its body or its neck with every tug he gave the rough iron halter while trying to force it to travel and move. And a greater wonder still was that the horse did not pull the long, thick arms of the big man out <column-break/> of his chest with every stop and delay she made while pulling backward. Every heavy, forceful, and strong blow the man struck was like the noise of a mighty wave.

After that poem, they saw the large man approaching them, and though he was a short distance from them, it took a long time to arrive because of the poorness of his pace and movement. He greeted Fionn when he came before him, bowed his head, bent his knee, and gave a sign of humility to Fionn. Fionn raised his hand above him and gave him leave to speak and address him. Fionn asked for news: "Of what noble or ignoble blood of the great world are you?" asked Fionn.

He said he did not know which of those he was, except for one thing: that he was a Fomorian who was wandering among the just-judging kings of Christendom seeking hire and wages in exchange for himself, and he had heard that Fionn never refused any man hire. "I never have, indeed," said Fionn, "and I will not refuse you either. What causes you to be without a servant, big man?" asked Fionn.

"There is good reason," said the large man, "for there is nothing in the world more difficult to me than having a servant. For the meal of three hundred men serves as my food and sustenance until the end of a day; I find that little enough for myself, and I would think it too much to have a servant around it."

"If so, what is the name you bear?" asked Fionn. "I am called the Gilla Decair <note>The Difficult Servant</note>," he said. "Why was 'the Difficult Servant' given to you as a name?" asked Fionn. "There is good reason," said the large man, "for there is nothing in the world I find more difficult than doing anything || for the benefit of my master or anyone I am with. O Conán son of Mórna," said the large man, "which is greater: the wages of a rider in the Fianna or the wages of a foot-soldier?"

When Taise of the Fair Side was brought back to him, the King || of Greece took counsel to have no more of his people killed by Fionn, and he proceeded onward to the territories of Greece.

Fionn trembled the next morning at the discovery that Taise of the Fair Side had been taken, and he was gloomy and dejected after the King’s daughter. "O Fionn," said the King of Sorcha, "do not let gloom or dejection be upon you for the loss of the maiden; for I will go with a full host with you to the territories of Greece, and we shall bring the daughter of the King of Greece back with us, whether by will or by force." After that poem, a day of assembly and high council was held by Fionn and the king of Sorcha. They saw the smooth-speckled, <column-break/> polished banners and the ensigns of soft silk, and the hard grey battle-swords upon the shoulders of the heroes and battle-champions. There were dense, very large forests of long, sturdy spears above their heads, and bright-toothed Diarmait ó Duibne was at the head of that truly great troop. Fionn recognized him and sent Fergus of the Fair-Mouth to him to ask what kind of craft that was, or what company he was in, or if he had received news of his people. Diarmait said that he was the Wizard of Valour, and that he had revealed through his powerful magical art that it was Abartach mac Allchaid who took those fifteen men from Fionn to the Land of Promise. This was the plan made by Fionn, since the grandson of Duibne had overtaken Goll and Oscar: to send them to the borders of Greece for the king’s daughter, and to send Fergus with them to boast of their deeds and triumphs; while he himself and the rest of his people would go to the Land of Promise, and whichever of them arrived there first should wait for the others.

Then a spacious and very large ship was prepared for Fionn and his people, and no account is given of them until they were in the Land of Promise. They saw the assembly and high council where Abartach <column-break/> mac Allchaid was. Fionn sent a message to him, demanding his people or that he give him battle. The plan Abartach decided upon was to grant Fionn the return of his people and to give Fionn his own judgment as compensation for the insult and for his great journey. Fionn brought them home to his own camp, and the best feast Fionn ever received was given to him there. Fionn remained in the Land of Promise until Goll and Oscar should reach him.

# The Gilla Decair

They turned their faces to the sea and the shores of the speckled-green ocean, and to the angry, slanting, gloomy, cold-wet peaks of the sea. They set out strongly, laboriously, and swiftly until they were listening to the cry of the seals and the mermaids, and to the wonderful monsters of the abyss, until they took harbor and port in the territories of fair-clean Greece. They hauled their ship ashore in a place where no wave could strike it or shatter it, nor any rock break it. They saw from afar the city of Athens in Greece. After going ashore, they found the shepherds of the court and the cattle of the territory. They asked news of the shepherds: what was the name of the city they saw, or what <column-break/> territory was it in, or who was the ruler over it? The shepherds asked them if they had been born in remote, unknown glens, since they did not know the name of that city; and they told them that it was the city of Athens in Greece, and that there was no city in the world with more strong-handed warriors, heroes, champions, and great throngs for valor and feats of arms than it.

"What shall we do now?" Oscar asked Goll.

"What should we do," said Goll, "but go into the city and take Fair-sided Taise with us, whether by her will or by force?"

"We shall not do that," said Fergus of the Fair-Mouth. "Put a four-stranded braid in your hair and say that you are sharp, word-perfect <term>poets</term> <note>Irish: *fileda*</note> traveling among the crowned, right-judging kings of Christendom."

"What shall we do," said Goll, "if a craft is requested of us?"

"I will perform the craft on your behalf," said Fergus of the Fair-Mouth.

They acted accordingly and proceeded toward the fortress, and they struck a blow of a rod against the lintel of the city. The doorkeeper said that the king was not at home, as he had gone to hunt, and that no one was inside but Fair-sided Taise and her attending handmaid, and that no one should come <column-break/> into her presence until the king came home.

The king arrived, and a great and wonderful hunt was held by him. The hounds were red-headed, the heroes were red-handed, and the king's servants and rough household were heavy-headed after that heavy-yielding hunt. They greeted the king, and the king asked news of them and brought them inside to the city of Athens. Fair-sided Taise recognized them, but she did not speak to them. When the time for sleep and slumber came, Fair-sided Taise requested that those unknown artists be allowed to come to her to tell stories. They went into a single room and revealed their identities to each other, and Fergus asked her by what arrangement she would escape to Fionn.

# The Gilla Decair

Again, she said that the king would go to the same hunt on the morrow and that she herself would escape with Goll and Oscar to the ship from which they had come. The king went to the hunt, and Fair-sided Taise escaped with Goll and Oscar until they reached the Land of Promise. And when Fionn saw those five at a distance from him, he recognized them and said that the people he saw were dear to him—namely Goll and Oscar <column-break/>, Fergus of the Fair-Mouth, Fair-sided Taise, and her accompanying maidservant.

When all his people reached Fionn, Abartach son of Allchaid told Fionn to pass his own judgment for the insult and for his great journey. Fionn said that he would set the wages he had promised to Abartach and the judgment against one another. "That is of no use to me," said Abartach, "as long as a man of insults and ill-speaking of the Fianna, such as Conán mac Morna, is not given his own judgment." "By the stars of heaven as a bond upon me," said Conán, "I would not be at peace unless I received that." Abartach promised that to Conán, and the judgment Conán passed on Abartach was that he should bring the fourteen best women in the Land of Promise with him, along with his own wife. And he was to put his own wife on the tail of the horse of the Gilla Decair, just as Liagán the Swift from Luachair Dhegaid had been, and those other fourteen women of his people were to ride upon it until they reached West Corca Dhuibne.

And let it be known to you that it was not gold or silver that Conán took as his judgment, but as we have said: namely, to take the <column-break/> fourteen best women in the Land of Promise along with Abartach’s wife. And Abartach's wife was to be put on the tail of the horse as Liagán the Swift had been, and the other fourteen women were to be put riding as he and the rest of his people had been, until they reached Cat’s Head Causeway in West Corca Dhuibne.

"There are your people, O Fionn," said Abartach. Fionn looked on every side of him, and he saw Abartach neither below nor above. And Fionn took Fair-sided Taise with him to great, broad Almha of Leinster, and they celebrated the wedding of that pair.

So ends the pursuit and adventure of the Gilla Decair from beginning to end.

O’Donnell’s Kern. [64; 64 b]

## *[The Adventure of the Narrow-Striped Kern, or O’Donnell’s Kern, according to some]*

One day while O’Donnell—namely Black Hugh, son of Red Hugh, son of Niall Garbh, son of Turlough of the Wine—was at Ballyshannon, partaking in a banquet and a feast with the nobles and great lords of his land and territory gathered around him. They were served and attended to with the newest of every food and the oldest of every drink besides. And when everyone in general was cheerful, satisfied, and high-spirited, a <term>gallowglass</term> <note>A heavy-armed mercenary soldier</note> of O’Donnell’s people spoke and said: "By God’s protection," he said, "from here to the wall of the house of the King of the Greeks, there is no house better than this house, nor is there a group of twenty-two more melodious than the twenty-two who are in this house—such as Red-bald Conán O’Rafferty, Diarmaid O’Gilligan, Cormac O’Keerigan, Tadhg O’Crooghan, and other people who are not numbered here."

During that conversation, they saw the <term>cetharnach</term> <note>A kern, or light-armed foot-soldier</note> known as the Narrow-striped Kern approaching them, with the water splashing in his shoes, the tips of his two ears showing through his old mantle, half of his naked sword sticking out behind his backside, and three soft, fire-hardened spears of holly in his <column-break/> right hand. "May God bless you, O’Donnell," he said. "May God bless you," said O’Donnell. "From what side have you come, unknown youth?" he asked. "In Dunmonaidh, in the town of the King of Scotland, I slept last night," said the kern. "I am one day in Islay, one day in Kintyre, one day in Man, one day in Rathlin, and another day on the white cairn of the watch on Sliabh Fuait. I am a wandering, pleasant, traveling man, and I am with you now, O’Donnell," he said. "Call the doorkeeper to me," said O’Donnell. The doorkeeper came forward. "Was it you who let this man in?" asked O’Donnell. "It was not I," said the doorkeeper, "and I have never seen him before now." "I will sit, or I will not sit," said the kern, "for I do nothing at all except as I please." In this way, the kern set the gallowglasses to hacking at one another with the backs of their axes, both horsemen and gallowglasses, until they were all lying in a bloody mass. At that time, there was a good man of the Leinstermen named Mac Eochaid, a master of poetry, whose leg had been broken for eighteen weeks. I spend one day in Islay, one day in Kintyre, one day in the Isle of Man, one day in Rathlin, <column-break/> and another day on the white cairn of the watch on Sliabh Fuait; for I am a wandering, lowly, eccentric person."

"Will you give up the churlishness and the greed on my advice?" asked Cathal O’Céin.
"I will indeed," said Mac Eochaid.
Cathal O’Céin took out a healing herb and rubbed it on Mac Eochaid’s leg. "Rise up, Mac Eochaid, so we may see if you can run."
Mac Eochaid stood up and made a dash out across the edge of the plain, with everyone following him in amazement; he left the twelve doctors behind by the speed of his running.

"I have performed your cure, Mac Eochaid," said the Kern. "And if you practice churlishness or greed from now on, I will come to you and break that leg I healed; and not only that leg, but the leg..."

# O’Donnell’s Kern

"I will not [be churlish]," said Mac Eochaid, "and I have a beautiful daughter, and I would give her to you, along with three hundred cows and three hundred horses <column-break/> and three hundred sheep and three hundred grey pigs. And I myself will be a good father-in-law to you."
"That is well," said Cathal O’Céin. "Whether she is fair or whether she is ugly, I will have her."

Mac Eochaid ordered a great feast to be prepared and celebrated for Cathal O’Céin. And when the feast was ready and the ale was fit for drinking, Cathal O’Céin rose up; and a red-maned hare on a March day was no swifter than Cathal as he went over the brow of the hill that faces the town. The servant came to Mac Eochaid and this is what he said: "That physician you had from the Ulstermen, called Cathal O’Céin—the red-maned creature called the hare is no swifter than he as he goes over the brow of yonder hill." Then Mac Eochaid composed the verse as follows:¹

> The physician from Ulster is beloved, as the Ulstermen themselves are beloved;
> The son of the father from the northern height—it is no misfortune for him who found Cathal O’Céin.

Cathal O’Céin set off and did not pause or rest until he reached Sligo. And that was the very time and hour that O’Connor was going to avenge the Connacht hag’s little basket upon the Munster hag. As he was traveling, he saw <column-break/> the slender-brindled Kern approaching him.
"God bless you, O'Connor," said the Kern.
"God bless you," said O'Connor. "And where have you been just now?" he asked.
"Last night I was in the Lagan of Leinster in the house of Mac Eochaid. And I was the night before that twelve thousand [paces] from Limerick at Cnoc Áine in the house of John, son of the Earl of Desmond. I was the night before that in the house of O’Donnell in Ballyshannon, and in Dunmonadh, in the town of the King of Scotland, the night before that. I was born in Aileach of the Kings. I spend one day in Islay and one day in Kintyre; one day in the Isle of Man and one day in Rathlin, and another day on the white cairn of the watch on Sliabh Fuait; for I am a lowly, wandering, eccentric person."
"What is your name?" asked O’Connor.
"Gilla Dé is my name," he said. "What has brought you from home?"

### O’Donnell’s Kern

"Gilla Dé," said O'Connor, "I am going to battle against the Munstermen."
"If you would hire me, I would go with you," said Gilla Dé.
"By my word," said a kern of O'Connor's people, "not only will we not hire you, but we would not accept any payment or gift to have the likes of you with us."
"I would not go with you," said Gilla Dé, "but with O'Connor; and perhaps <column-break/> it would be no worse for O'Connor if I were with him."
"What is your wage, Gilla Dé?" asked O'Connor.
"I ask only that no unfairness be shown to me," he said, "as long as I am with you."
"You shall have that," said O'Connor.

They moved forward across the Shannon westward, and all the men of Connacht together, and they skirmished for three days in a row among the Munstermen, plundering them and carrying away everything that could be moved. They gathered their cows, horses, and flocks into one place. They found three brindled cows and the hornless bull of the Munster hag, and O'Connor gave them to the Connacht hag to avenge her little basket. They were not long driving the prey when they saw a band of warriors from the two provinces of Munster in pursuit of their herd. Then the Gilla Dé came before O'Connor and gave him his choice: to drive the prey or to check the pursuit. O'Connor said that he preferred to check the pursuit. The Gilla Dé turned back toward the pursuit with a bow and twenty-four arrows; and he did not let off a single shot that did not fell nine times nine <note>nine groups of nine, or eighty-one</note> of the Munstermen, so that no one remained within bowshot of him. And if <column-break/> all the men of Connacht had gone around just twenty of those cows, they could not have kept them a bowshot's distance away.

Then O'Connor sent word to Gilla Dé and told him to drive the prey. Gilla Dé answered suddenly and went around the prey with the swiftness of a swallow; he gathered them and drove them all at a great run until they were far out of the sight of the men of Munster. When the Munstermen saw the Gilla Dé turning his back to them, they hurried after the men of Connacht and were killing them without mercy, so that it was necessary for the Gilla Dé to turn back to the pursuit again.

In this way, he was running between the pursuit and the prey until they crossed the Shannon from the west, and from there to Sligo and to O'Connor's fortress. O'Connor went inside before the others. A drink was placed in his hand, and he did not think of the Gilla Dé until he had drunk it. The Gilla Dé came before O'Connor and said that he was taking his leave of him; and O'Connor did not like that and

# O’Donnell’s Kern

The kern placed three grains of oats on his palm and said that he would blow the middle grain away with a puff of breath and leave the two outer grains there. "Let that be done by you," said O'Kelly. The kern put the tips of two fingers on the two grains furthest apart and blew the middle grain from his palm. "There is a trick for you, Tadhg O'Kelly," said the kern. "By my conscience, it is not a bad trick," said O'Kelly. "May no good from God come to the man who did it," said a kern of O'Kelly's people, "for if you gave me half of those five marks, I would do that trick myself." "Perform that trick in the same way," said the slender-striped kern, "and I will give you half of those five marks." The warrior put three grains in the middle of his palm and put the tips of two fingers on the two outer grains and gave a puff to the middle grain, so that the tips of his two <column-break/> fingers went through the flat of his palm and out the back of his hand. "Ob, ob, man," said the slender-striped trickster, "that trick you performed is clumsy, and it is not how I did it myself. But nevertheless, since you have lost the money, I will heal you." The trickster rubbed a healing herb on the hand so that it was healed immediately.

"Tadhg O'Kelly," said the trickster, "if you would give me five more marks, I would perform another trick for you." "What trick is that?" asked Tadhg. "I would wag one ear on one side of my head while the other ear stayed still," said the trickster. "Do that for us," said O'Kelly. The trickster put his hand up, took hold of one ear, and wagged it on one side of his head. "By my word, truly, that is a good trick," said Tadhg O'Kelly. "May you have no good fortune," said O'Kelly's kern, "and were it not for my bad luck, I would do that trick myself." "Since the other trick bested you," said the slender-striped kern, "do that trick now." The warrior put his hand up and wagged his ear on one side of his head so that the ear came off the side of his head in his hand. "This is an unlucky kern you have, Tadhg," said the trickster, "for that is not how I perform the trick. But nevertheless, I will heal him, and if you would give me five more marks, I would perform another trick for you." <column-break/> "I will give them," said Tadhg.

A feast was being held in the house of the King of Leinster at that time, and || they saw the narrow-striped kern coming toward them, with water whistling in his old shoes and the point of his sword naked behind him. "God bless you," said the kern. "God bless you," said the King of Leinster, "and from where have you come to us?" asked the king. "From the house of Tadhg O’Kelly I have come just now; and I was in the house of O’Connor in Sligo the night before that. In <term>Aileach</term> of the kings I was born. I am one day in Islay, one day in Kintyre, one day in the Isle of Man, one day in Rathlin, and another day on the white cairn of the watch on Sliabh Fuait. I am a wandering, wretched, silly person," said the kern. "What is your name?" asked the King of Leinster. "The Difficult Lad is my name," he said.

There were sixteen men playing stringed instruments in the King of Leinster’s house at that time. "I give my word," said the Difficult Lad, "since I myself heard the noise of the hammers in the bottom of hell, I have never heard music as bad as yours," he said. "You greasy rogue," said the man who was the strongest of the musicians, "it is a bad thing that you should be the one to say that to us." "Truly I say to you," said the Difficult Lad, "though it is hard to surpass those other fifteen men in bad music, it is you who take the prize for bitterness over them all." The musician raised his sword and struck¹ the || Difficult Lad on the top of his head, and it seemed to him that he made two clean halves of his head. But it so happened that the place where the blow struck was on his own head, so that he made two halves of it. And as many of the musicians as could reach him, each one of them struck him with the full of his hand, but the blow fell upon each of themselves in the end.

Then the King of Leinster ordered some of his own foster-brothers to take that evil man with them and hang him. They seized him and hanged him, as they thought. But when they returned to the king's presence, they found the Difficult Lad there before them inside. "Are you not the one we left hanging on the gallows?" they asked. "Look there," said the kern. They looked, and the foster-brother who was dearest to the King of Leinster was found hanging.

## Here is the journey of Iron-Waist (Caol an Iarainn), son of the King of Thessaly, to Ireland, and how unfortunately his journey turned out for him.

A day of fair and high assembly was held by Fionn mac Cumaill, son of Cumall, son of Art, son of Trénmór of the Ui Bhaoiscne, with the seven battalions of the Fenians and the seven battalions of the regular Fenians at the Hill of Howth <note>Beinn Edair</note>, son of Edgaoth. They cast an eye over the sea and the great ocean until they saw a capacious and very vast ship under full sail on the sea from the east, coming directly toward them, equipped for war and strife. And it was not long for them until they saw a single great, soldierly, active, and brave warrior rising on the shafts of his spears and the poles of his lances until he took the breadth of his two soles on the bright-sandy shore. He wore a polished and very beautiful breastplate, with strong, unbreakable armor around him; a brown-beautiful shield was above his shoulder; a hard-iron helmet upon his head; a wide-grooved, straight-pointed sword on his left side; his two thick-shafted, dark-red, sharp spears in his two fists; a beautiful scarlet cloak about his shoulders, and a brooch of burnt gold in his broad chest.

He came before Fionn and the Fenians in that equipment and order. And Fionn spoke and said: "Who are you, O warrior of the noble or ignoble blood of the world? Or from which of the four quarters did you come to us?" Caol an Iarainn is

---

and he was a man of craft and magic over every person until it finally happened that he departed from us, leaving us with nothing but his account, just as every magician and every man of craft who was ever there has departed; and so it is with the Fenians and every group that has come since then and that will come forever, and we after them. Written by Próinsias O Maoildúin from Bridge Street on the twentieth day of the last month of autumn, 1740.

"...warrior is my name: the son of the King of Thessaly <note>Tesáille</note>. As much of the world as I have traveled since I left my own country until now, I have not left an island or isle without placing it under the high-tribute of my sword and my own hand. And it is my desire to take the high-tribute and sovereignty of Ireland <note>hEireann</note> with me this time."

"We have never heard of a hero," said Conán, "nor have we seen a warrior who could not find a man to overcome him in Ireland."

"Your speech is nothing but the talk of a fool and an idiot to me, O Conán," said Caol (Iron-Waist). "For if all of the Fenians who have died within the last seven years were added to those who still live, I would bring a drop of death and a short life upon them all in a single day. However, I will make a simpler deal with you: if you find among yourselves even a single hero who can best me in running, fighting, or wrestling, I will cause no further trouble or distress to you or anyone else, but will return back to my own country again."

"If that is the case," said Fionn, "the traveling messenger we have, namely Caoilte mac Rónáin, is not at home at this time; if he were, he would have to race against you. And if you are a warrior," he said, "who will stay with the Fenians or make friendship and a covenant with them until I go for Caoilte to Tara <note>Temair</note> of the Kings—and if he is not found there, he will surely be found at Keshcorran <note>Céis Chorainn</note> of the Fenians—then let us do that."

"Let it be done so," said Caol.

Then Fionn set out on the path, and he had not gone far when he came upon a rugged, dark wood and a very deep, muddy road running right through the center of that great forest. He had not gone far into it when he encountered a devilish, ill-shaped creature, a senseless monster, and a wild giant <column-break/> with a sallow body and thick bones, wearing a long, grey coat that reached down to the calves of his legs. Each of his legs was like the mast of a very large ship, supporting the irregular body of the big man; and each of the two shoes on the giant's clawed, crooked-nailed feet was like the side of a wide-bellied boat. There was a layer of yellow mud as wide as a pewter dish <note>méise pétair</note> on the hem of the grey coat the big man wore; and with every step he took, that muddy hem would strike the calves of his legs so loudly that the sound could be heard a full mile away. Every time he lifted a foot, a barrel-full of mire would splash up against his buttocks and his sallow body. Fionn stood watching the big man for a long time, for he had never seen his like before; he continued along the path until the man spoke...

# The Churl in the Grey Coat.

...and he said: "What kind of journey or wandering has happened to you, O Fionn son of Cumall?" he asked, "all alone and in solitude, without a single man of the Fenians of Ireland <note>Fianna Eireann</note> with you?"

"It is," said Fionn, "because of the greatness of my confusion and my trouble that I have no time to tell you that; and even if I did, there would be no benefit in it for me."

"Unless you tell me," said the big man, "you shall be under its sorrow and its loss forever."

"Well then," said Fionn, "if I must tell you that, let it be known to you that it is Iron-Waist <note>Caol an Iarainn</note>, the son of the King of Thessaly <note>Tesáille</note>, who came into Beinn Edair <note>the Hill of Howth</note> in the middle of the day today, demanding the high-tribute and high-sovereignty of Ireland, unless he finds a single hero who will win a victory over him in running, fighting, or wrestling."

"What do you intend to do?" asked the big man, "for I know him well, and there is nothing that warrior said that he cannot fulfill; and he would bring slaughter upon our men and warriors and the Fenians entirely."

"It is my intention," said Fionn, "to go for Caoilte at Tara <note>Temair</note> of the Kings; and if I do not find him there, I will certainly find him in Keshcorran <note>Céis Chorainn</note> of the Fenians, so that he might win a racing bet from that warrior."

"Well then," said the big man, "you are a man without kingship if Caoilte son of Rónán is your support."

"I do not know then what I should do," said Fionn.

"I know that," said the big man: "if you would accept me, by my oaths, I would win a racing bet from that warrior."

"I think," said Fionn, "that you will have all you can do to carry your coat and your big shoes even half a mile of land in a day, without going to race against that warrior."

"By my truth, if I do not win it from him, no man of the men of Ireland will," said the big man.

"Let it be so," said Fionn, "but what is your name?"

"The Churl in the Grey Coat <note>Bodach in chóta lachtna</note> is my name," he said.

Then Fionn and the Churl in the Grey Coat turned back, and their journey or their travels are not recounted until they reached Beinn Edair.

Then those two good warriors set out: namely Caol an Iarainn <note>Iron-Waist</note>, son of the King of Thessaly <note>Tesáille</note>, and the Churl in the Grey Coat. "Let it be so," said the Churl, "but if I manage to build a house or a hut, anyone who would not give their help toward building it shall be kept far away from it."

Then the Churl went into the rugged, dark wood that was nearest to him; and he did not stop nor rest much until he had bound together twenty-four pairs of great timbers, and he brought them with him—along with their share of forest rafters and fresh rushes from the mountain in that load—and he set up a long, spacious house under roof and shelter. After that, he set a massive, huge fire of fresh wood and withered brush from the forest on the floor of that lodging, and he spoke a second time to Caol: "If you are a man who will come with me to hunt at all in these woods." "I do not know," said Caol, "and even if I did, it is not with the likes of you I would go hunting."

He went against the herd, and the strongest boar he saw he separated from the herd, and he followed it through every path and every secret place until he overcame it with the strength of his running and exertion. Then Caol set out on the way, and he was not without great fear concerning the indifference he saw the Churl showing him. But when the Churl had slept his fill, he stood up, washed his face and his hands, put food on the table for himself, sat down comfortably and calmly, and ate half the boar and half the bread, and drank a barrel of wine down into his body afterward.

Then the Churl stood up and placed the bones of the pig properly in the hem of his grey coat. He moved forward with the speed of a swallow or a doe <note>ferbóige</note>, or like a blast of the red wind of March passing over the brow of a hill or a rough-topped rock, until he caught up with Caol an Iarainn. # The Churl in the Grey Coat.

...as if he would become a true madman of the glen, until he had covered thirty miles of his way on that stretch. Then Caol moved on, and the Churl turned back until he found the corners of his coat, just as Caol had said. He sat down and pulled out his needle and thread and sewed them back into their proper place again. Then the Churl turned back. Caol had not gone far when the Churl caught up with him and said to him: "Oh Caol," he said, "you ought to put on a better pace than you have shown yet, if you wish to take the high-tribute of Ireland with you as you have already said. For I shall not be turning back again from now on."

Then the Churl moved with the speed of a swallow or a fawn, or like a blast of the fierce March wind, traveling over the brow of a hill or a rough-peaked rock as if he would become a true madman of the glen. Such was the powerful, rushing pace of the Churl that he reached the brow of a hill that was within five miles of the Peak of Howth <note>Beinn Edair</note>, son of Edgaoth. Then the Churl stooped down and began eating blackberries from the brambles until he had made a juice-filled sack of himself. Furthermore, the Churl took off his grey coat and pulled out his needle and sewed his coat until he had made a long, wide, and very deep bag of it. The Churl filled his coat to the brim with the blackberries and rubbed a great many of them onto his skin until he was as black as a blacksmith’s coal. The Churl lifted that load of blackberries onto his shoulder and moved forward stoutly and <column-break/> swiftly toward the Peak of Howth.

Fionn and the Fianna in general were full of great fear that Caol an Iarainn was in the lead. For they had all put their trust in the Churl of the Grey Coat, though they had no knowledge at all of who he was. # The Churl in the Grey Coat.

...Caol was arriving at the mouth of the road with [what he thought was] the dead Churl on his shoulder. Fionn promised a suit of arms and armor to whoever would bring us better news than that. A second messenger went out and recognized that it was the Churl who was actually there. All the Fianna of Ireland gathered very joyfully around the Churl and asked him for news. "I have good news for you," he said. "But my hunger is so great that I cannot spread the word until I eat my fill of parched meal and blackberries mixed together. I brought the blackberries myself, so you must give me my fill of parched meal." Then a large cloak was spread on the peak under the Churl with a heap of parched meal in its exact center. The Churl poured his sack of berries throughout the meal and stooped to eat heartily.

They had not been there long when they saw Caol at the entrance of the road, his hand on the hilt of his sword and his two eyes glowing red in his head, ready to fall upon the Fianna to slaughter and hack them to pieces. Upon seeing Caol in that state, the Churl picked up a fistful of the meal and berries and gave a powerful throw at Caol, which knocked his head a good distance from his body. The Churl ran to where the head was and gave a second throw, sending it back toward the body so that it was fixed as firmly as ever. However, it was fixed so that his face was on his back and the back of his head was on his chest. The Churl ran to where Caol was, struck his chest and body quickly to the ground, and bound him hard, painfully, and indissolubly. He said: "Oh Caol," he said, "wasn't it a poor opinion you held, to say that the high-tribute and sovereignty of Ireland would be yours this time? But let it not be said by the Fianna of Ireland that they would deal a stroke of death or a short life to a lone hero when he had no one but himself for defense. If you are a man who will pledge the sun and moon as surety to send the tribute of Thessaly <note>Tesáille</note> every year of your life to Fionn and the Fianna of Ireland, you shall keep your soul in the condition you are in now."

Caol pledged the sun and moon to fulfill this every year of his life. Then the Churl took Caol by the hand and led him to his ship and sat him down in it. After that, the Churl gave a kick to the stern of the ship and sent it seven leagues out to sea with that single kick.

That is how the journey turned out for Caol of the Iron, son of the King of Thessaly: to be sent home in the manner of a fool and a madman, and...

### [The Healing of the leg of Cian, son of Maelmuaid, son of Brian, below]

One day, the stewards of Brian Boru, son of Cennétig, went to collect his rent and tribute in West Munster, and they arrived at the house of O'Cronagan of the Cauldron. O'Cronagan himself was not at home; O'Cronagan was a warrior of Cian, son of Maelmuaid.

And O'Cronagan's wife asked who they were. "The stewards of the King of Ireland," they said. "Who is the King of Ireland?" asked O'Cronagan's wife. "Brian son of Cennétig," they said, "and we are here collecting rent and tribute." "We never gave rent to anyone before, and we will not give it to him." The stewards then departed for Kincora, where Brian and the nobles of the <term>Dál gCais</term> were. Brian was giving a great feast to the men of Ireland, and the stewards told of the dishonor that the wife of O'Cronagan of the Cauldron had given them. "And I know how that shall be dealt with," said Brian; "I will go before the men of Ireland disperse from me to avenge my dishonor upon O'Cronagan." "That is appropriate," said all the nobles of the <term>Dál gCais</term>. They proceeded to the cauldron of O'Cronagan and burned the <term>triucha cét</term> nearest to it; and O'Cronagan was not at home.

And after that, O'Cronagan's wife followed them and found Brian and the nobles of the <term>Dál gCais</term> at the rear of the plundered herds. She greeted them, and Brian answered her. And she said: "O Brian, it is wrong for you to carry out these raids against us, for we never gave rent to any man before; for the lord who is over us never took rent from us." "Who is that?" asked Brian. "Cian son of Maelmuaid, and he is a warrior of yours."

"If so," she said, "grant a request to me, O Brian." "I will grant it," said Brian. "If so," she said, "give me my little hounds and my sheep." They traveled on until they reached Slieve Luachra. There, O'Cronagan saw a hound coming toward him that was half white and the other half green. He caught it and immediately put a chain upon it. But O'Cronagan said he preferred what he had already received over all the wealth of Ireland.

He proceeded on to Slieve Luachra. A hare started up, and O'Cronagan set the hound after the hare, and the hound pursued it. O'Cronagan sat down, and his people said they would leave and would not wait for him. O'Cronagan had been there only a short time when he saw the hare coming toward him with the beagle and the hound after it. There was only a short distance between the hound, the beagle, and the hare. The hare leaped into O'Cronagan’s lap and said, "I seek protection, O O'Cronagan." Then the hare was transformed into a beautiful young woman. "You shall have it," said O'Cronagan. The young woman said she would grant O'Cronagan any request he liked, and the girl said, "Come with me tonight." They went into a beautiful <term>sídbrug</term> <note>fairy dwelling</note>, and an aged couple was inside waiting for them. They consumed food and drink, and a couch and a high bed were prepared for O'Cronagan. He told the young woman to go before him into the bed, and said that this was the only favor he would ask of her. She said that though she was reluctant, she would fulfill it. And the aged couple said that the time seemed long to them, and they did not know but that this good fortune belonged to Brian.

And after that, O'Cronagan and the young woman arose the next morning and they traveled forward to O'Cronagan’s enclosure. And as they were going to the town, they met a young warrior who told O'Cronagan that his wife had died. And after that <column-break/> O'Cronagan saw halls and great houses in his town, and he wondered at that. And he had that woman with him until the end of three years. O'Cronagan was prospering again, so much so that he had a great cavalry and many people. And it was said that there was no fault upon him except for one fault. His wife asked him what that one fault was, and he said it was not giving a feast to the King of Ireland. She said that it was not necessary, for Brian had heard of his reputation and his fame. But he said he would not refrain from giving it to him.

So he prepared a feast for Brian, and he went himself to Kincora and brought Brian and the nobles of the men of Ireland with him to the enclosure. They were in the town for three days with excellent service and attendance. Brian and Murchad, son of Brian, gave her—that is, O'Cronagan's wife—their soul's love. But that was little compared to the love that Cian, son of Maelmuaid, gave to her. Brian arose at the end of four days to depart, and O'Cronagan said that he was sorry Brian was leaving that night. His wife said it was no harm to let them depart, as they would not find a better feast in Ireland than a feast of three days and nights. O'Cronagan said he would not let Brian go that day, so they stayed in the town that night.

Cian said that he himself would do the serving that night. O'Cronagan sat down, and Cian and O'Cronagan's wife were there. Cian said to O'Cronagan’s wife that he had given her very great love and that he desired to be with her. She said that she would never be with him. Then Cian rose and struck her down, and she screamed, and she was turned into a great brood-mare. She rushed toward the door, and Cian caught her by a hind leg. She raised the other leg and struck Cian on his leg and broke it, and then she went on her way.

And the hosts arose the next morning to return to their homes, and Cian went to Innis Céin. He was a year in the sickness of his leg, so that physicians could not knit it nor take any of the poison out of it. And on the day at the end of a year, when Cian's people had gone to mass, a youth came in and sat beside Cian. Cian asked him where he had been at mass. "I was in the city of Rheims of the kings in France," he said. "That is a great wonder you speak," said Cian. "I saw <column-break/> a wonder greater than that," said the youth. "What is it?"

<header>The Hostel of Keshcorran. [75 b; 76]</header>

### [The Hostel of Keshcorran, as follows]

A hunt, a chase, and a warrior’s slaughter were organized by Fionn mac Cumaill, son of Cumhall, son of Art, son of Trenmór, of the Ui Bhaeiscne, with the beautiful <term>Fianna</term> of the Gaels, throughout the fair territories of Corann, the lovely lands of Luighne, the territories of Bréifne, the strong and mysterious glens of Dallán, the fruitful regions of Cairbre, the sturdy forests of Conchobar, and the smooth, vast plains of Conaille.

It was then that Fionn mac Cumaill sat upon his hunting mound atop the high Kesh of Corann. No one remained with Fionn at that time except for his two hounds, namely Bran and Sceolaing, and Conan Maol mac Morna. Fionn found it pleasant at that time to watch and listen to the voices of the hounds, the clear and spirited calls of the young men, the movements of the vigorous heroes, the clamor of the strong men, and the whistling of the <term>Fianna</term> throughout the wild forests of the land. The hunting shouts they released were heard in the neighboring territories, so that deer were driven from the wilds, hares from the hilltops, foxes to wandering, badgers from their dens, and birds into flight. Every fierce and truly venomous hound was released from its leash around the hill at that time.

However, the lord who was in charge of Keshcorran at that time was Conarán mac Imideil, a chief of the <term>Tuatha Dé Danann</term>. When he heard the wandering noise of the hounds, he told his three ugly daughters—who were full of sorcery—to go and take revenge for the hunt upon Fionn, the royal leader. The daughters went to the entrance of the cave on the hill and sat down together. They placed three magical, spell-bound iron hanks upon three crooked poles of holly and were winding them counter-clockwise at the cave's entrance. They had not been there long in that state when Fionn and Conan arrived at the edge of the cave and saw the three extremely hideous hags sitting at that work at the cave's entrance. They had three very rough, disheveled heads of hair, and six dripping, coal-red eyes; they had three black, misshapen mouths, and very sharp teeth...

<summary>Fionn mac Cumaill leads the Fianna on a massive hunt through the territories of Corann, eventually resting atop Keshcorran with Conan and his hounds. In response to the disturbance, the Tuatha Dé Danann chief Conarán sends his three sorcerous daughters to use magic hanks of yarn to entrap the hunters.</summary>
<keywords>Fionn mac Cumaill, Fianna, Keshcorran, Conarán mac Imideil, Tuatha Dé Danann, Irish mythology, hunting, sorcery, Conan Maol</keywords>

--- Page 317 ---
<meta>This page continues the narrative of "The Hostel of Keshcorran," describing the monstrous appearance of the daughters of Conarán and their capture of Fionn and the Fianna.</meta>

<page-num>307</page-num>
<header>76 b; 77; 77 b] The Hostel of Keshcorran.</header>

Truly venomous and crooked were the jaws in the mouth of each of those wicked women; their three bony necks supported their heads upon those warrior-hags. They had six very long arms, and every truly hideous and fierce nail upon each of their fingers was like the thick-based, narrow-tipped horn of a buffalo. Six crooked, hairy, slender-toed feet were beneath them, and they held three hard and sharp distaffs in their hands.

Fionn and Conan went through the iron rings to look at the hags, and the tremor of death came upon them so that they lost their strength immediately. They were bound firmly and inextricably by those brave hags. Two others of the <term>Fianna</term> came, along with the sons of Nemhnann, and they went through the iron rings to where Fionn and Conan were. They too lost their vigor and were bound in hard fetters by the same hags. Afterwards, the hags carried the heroes inside into the cave.

It was not long after that until Oscar and Mac Lugach arrived on the scene, along with the nobles and great chiefs of the <term>Clann Baiscne</term>. The <term>Clann Morna</term> also arrived, and upon seeing the iron rings, not even the strength of a woman in labor remained in any one of them. The <term>Clann Chorcráin</term> arrived, and when they saw the iron rings, their valor and heroism failed them in the same way. <column-break/> Nevertheless, the <term>Clann Smóil</term> and all the <term>Fianna</term>, both low and high-born, were bound; the hags took them away as fettered and tightly-bound captives into dark, mysterious pits and obscure, gloomy passages.

Indeed, there was much howling of hounds at the entrance of the cave, seeking their lords and masters after their journey and travel. There were many wounded and bone-slashed deer, wild boars that had been killed, torn badgers, and red-maned hares of the plain that had been slaughtered on the side of the hill after the binding of the party that had been carrying them until then.

Then those great, warlike, and fiercely brave women came to the place where the <term>Fianna</term> were bound, carrying three hard, broad-grooved swords in their hands. They looked out on every side to see if they could find any man or traveler of the <term>Fianna</term> of Ireland, so that they might bring death and final destruction to them. Since they found no one, they intended to go into the hostel to slaughter and mangle the <term>Fianna</term> without mercy.

They were not long there when they saw a single, great, warlike, and fiercely brave warrior, white-toothed and well-skilled, coming toward them. And that was...

The vigorous, full-furious lion, the madness of battle, and the shining torch on the day of strife: Goll the high-spirited, son of Morna, son of Cormac, son of Maghtan, son of Garad Black-knee, son of Aed of the Poems, son of Aed of Ceann Claire, son of Conall, son of Sadhbh, son of Cet, son of Magach, son of Cairbre, King of Connacht. 

And when those three dark, dismal, and foul-shaped women saw him, they quickly approached him and fought a terrifying, sharp, and hateful struggle against one another. However, the hero was truly and immensely enraged, and he dealt deadly, lasting blows and fierce strokes upon those furious and truly hideous wild women. He raised his wide-grooved, straight-bladed sword and gave an ever-powerful blow to the phantoms before him—namely, Caemóg the hard-fighting and Cuillenn Red-head—so that he made equal and large pieces of them with that single stroke. 

And that was one of the three greatest blows ever struck in Ireland: the blow Fergus mac Rosa struck in the great Cattle Raid of Cooley, where he cut off the three peaks of Meath with one stroke; the blow of Conall <column-break/> Cernach to Cet mac Magach; and this blow by Goll mac Morna, with which he killed Caemóg and Cuillenn Red-head, the two daughters of Conarán son of Imidel.

Then the eldest of Conarán's children, Iaran daughter of Conarán, threw her arms around Goll from behind his back while he was beheading the other two. Goll turned against her in spite of her efforts and locked his two long, reaching arms around her. They fought a brave, strong-handed, and fierce wrestling match with one another for a time. Then Goll gave a single heroic and brave twist to the hag, which threw her down to the ground and the very earth. He bound her firmly and inextricably with a shield-strap. Then he bared his sword to slaughter and carve the hag, but she said: 

"O hero who was never wounded and O strongman who was never timid in battle or combat, I place my body and my soul under the protection of your valor and your prowess. It would be better for you to have Fionn and the <term>Fianna</term> restored to you in their entirety, without bleeding or wounding to any one of them; and I swear by the gods I worship that I will fulfill what I say."

Then the royal warrior released the hag, and they went afterward to the hill where <column-break/> the <term>Fianna</term> were bound and hard-fettered, with Fionn among them. Goll said: "Let Fergus of the Fair Lips and the men of art of the <term>Fianna</term> be released first."

Fionn, Oisín, the twenty-nine sons of Morna, and the Fianna in general were released from that point forward. The hag released them in that manner. The Fianna rose up suddenly out of the cave after that and sat on the side of the hill. Fergus "Fair-lips," the poet of the Fianna, looked at Goll and began to praise him for the deed he had performed.

It was not long for them like that until they saw approaching them a gloomy, ill-shaped creature and an irrational monster: namely, a lumpy, hard-veined, wrinkled old hag. On every hair of the rough, grey-blue eyebrows she had was the fury of a small apple or a large sloe. She had dripping eyes burning in her head; a large, dark, wide, grey nose above the edge of her black, gloomy, ill-shaped string-mouth; and a hideous, rough set of chewing teeth in her gaping throat. She had thin, hard-veined hands with long, predatory, and truly venomous nails. She wore strong, unbreakable armor, a wide-grooved, straight-bladed sword at her thigh, and a large heroic shield high on her back. <column-break/>

She came before Fionn in that manner and bound him under <term>geasa</term> to give her a sufficient amount of single combat. Fionn said to Oisín, "Rise up, my son," he said, "and stop that monstrous hag for us." "I cannot," said Oisín, "after the evil and humiliation I have already received from the other hags." This was Iarnán, daughter of Conarán, coming to avenge her sisters. And so Oisín, Oscar, Conán, mac Lughach, Diarmait ó Duibhne, Caeilte mac Rónáin, Cairell, and the other nobles of the Fianna refused to fight the hag. Fionn then said he would go to fight her himself. At that, Goll mac Morna said: "Fionn," he said, "it is not fitting for you to fight a hag; I will go to fight her, for it is then that a friend is proven when the need is greatest."

Then Goll rose up quickly and readily to meet the hag. He fought a spirited, high-minded, heroic, and proud combat—a fierce and frantic struggle where neither of them showed fear or weakness toward the other. Finally, Goll put his hand into the grip of his shield and drew out his venomous blade. He gave her a direct shot, without slant or deviation, so that it went through <insert>the boss of</insert> her shield <column-break/> and through the hag's heart to the other side. Thus the hag fell dead on that spot.

### [This is the foundation of the Battle of Mucrama and the cause of the death of Lugaid Mac Con]

Ailill Ólom, son of Mug Nuadat, of the seed of Eber son of Míl of Spain, was the king of Munster. Sadb, daughter of Conn of the Hundred Battles, was his wife. She had three sons: Eogan son of Ailill, Cian son of Ailill, and Cormac son of Ailill; from whom are descended the Eoganacht, the Cianacht, and the Dál Cais. Lugaid Mac Con of the Corcu Loígde was also a foster-son to Ailill and Sadb. He was reared on the same knee and the same breast as Eogan son of Ailill.

Then Ailill went on Samhain night to tend his horses at Áine Cliach. A bed was prepared for him on the hill. The hill was stripped bare that night, and it was not known who had stripped it. It happened to him twice in that way, and it was a wonder to him. He sent messengers to Ferches son of Commán the poet, who was in the borders of Leinster; he was a seer and a warrior. He came to speak with Ailill. They both went on Samhain night to the hill. Ailill stayed on the hill, and Ferches was outside it. Sleep then fell upon Ailill as he listened to the grazing of the cattle. They came out of the <term>síd</term> <note>a fairy mound or supernatural dwelling</note>, and Eogabal son of Durgabal, king of the <term>síd</term>, was after them, with Áine daughter of Eogabal, and she had a bronze <term>timpán</term> <note>a stringed instrument</note> in her hand, playing it before him. Ferches rose up and struck him. Eogabal ran before him into the <term>síd</term>. Ferches pierced him with a great spear so that his back broke through it just as he reached Ailill. He encountered the girl there. While he was in that position, the woman bit his ear so that she left neither flesh nor skin on it, and it never grew back on him from that hour on. Thus, Ailill <term>Ólom</term> <note>"Bare-ear"</note> has been his name ever since. "You have been evil to me," said Áine, "outraging me and killing my father. They rose after that. "Give us a judgment, Ailill." "Of little use," said Ailill. "What did you say when the man was found?" "I said," said Lugaid, "the music is mine." "I said," said Eogan, "the musician is mine." "It is true," said Ailill, "the man belongs to Eogan." 

"It is a bad judgment," said Lugaid. "It is the truth for me," said Ailill. "It is not true," said Lugaid; "truth is not customary on your lips." "May it not happen as you say," said the druid; "you are a wretched doomed man. I will go in your place," said the druid, "with your diadem on my head and your dress around me, so that everyone will say it is you who comes there."

Lugaid then came with the exiles and with that great, heavy host to avenge his grievances upon the men of Ireland. He was not a dutiful son who brought them. They then plundered Ireland so that a great many people submitted to him; and they encountered no conflict until they reached **Mag Mucrama** in the territory of the Óic Bethra, north of Aidne, and north of Áth Cliath.

**Mag Mucrama**, then, was so called because magical pigs came out of the Cave of Cruachain—that is the gate of hell in Ireland. From it also came the three-headed creature <note>teillén tréchenn</note> that devastated Ireland, until Amergin, the father of Conall Cernach, killed it in single combat before all the men of Ulster. From it also came a flock of blood-red birds that withered everything in Ireland that their breath touched, until the Ulstermen killed them with slingshots. It was from there, afterward, that these pigs came. Wherever they passed over, for seven years no corn, grass, or leaf would grow. In whatever place people tried to count them, they would not stay there, but would move into another territory if their number was being reckoned. They could not be counted correctly: "There are three of them there," one man would say; "There are more than seven," another would say; "There are nine there," said another; "Eleven pigs," "Thirteen pigs." Their counting failed in that manner. Furthermore, they could not be wounded; for if they were shot at, they would not appear.

Once, however, Medb of Cruachain and Ailill went to count them—that is, on the plain of Mag Mucrama. They were then counted by them. Medb was in her chariot. One of the pigs leaped over the chariot. "That pig is one too many, Medb," everyone said. "It will not be this one," said Medb, grabbing the pig's leg. The skin stripped off its head, so that she was left with the skin in her hand along with the leg, and it is not known where they went from that hour. From that event comes the name **Mag Mucrama** <note>The Plain of the Counting of Pigs</note>.

Mac Con was then permitted to plunder Ireland until he reached Mag Mucrama in eastern Connacht. "It is time," said Art son of Conn, "for the men to do battle." "It is time indeed," said Eogan son of Ailill. Eogan then went the day before that to Díl mac hú Chreca of the Osraige, who was at Druim Díl; he was a druid and he was blind. "Come with me," said Eogan, "to test the men and to chant against them." "Good," said he, "I will go with you." "Speak, father," said his daughter. She was an unmarried woman, Moncha daughter of Díl. The daughter served as his charioteer. When they reached Mag Cliach, the druid recognized by Eogan’s speech that he was doomed. "Well, Eogan," said the druid, "did you leave any offspring?" "None at all," said Eogan. "Well then, daughter," said Díl, "sleep with Eogan to see if there might be a kingship of Munster from me forever."

A bed is prepared for the couple. It was a good child who was conceived there, namely Fiacha Muillethan son of Eogan.

Fiacha also had a nickname, which was *Fer Dá Liach* (The Man of Two Sorrows). For on the day he was conceived, his father was killed the following morning; and on the day he was born, his mother died. Each of those events was a sorrow, and for that reason he is called the Man of Two Sorrows. As for the name Fiacha Muillethan (Fiacha Broad-crown), it was given to him because labor pains seized Moncha, daughter of Díl, at Áth Nemthenn on the Suir. "It is a pity that you are not delivered tomorrow morning," said her father <note>the druid Díl</note>, "for if the child were born then, his descendants would rule over Ireland forever." "It is true indeed," she said, "and unless he comes through my sides, he shall not come by any other way." She went away from them into the water. She sat upon a stone that was in the middle of the ford. "Support me," she said. She remained in that position until the hour of tierce the next morning. "It is time now," said her father. The waters subsided from her. Her lips perished <note>she died</note>. The infant’s head had flattened against the stone, so that he was called Fiacha Muillethan. He is the ancestor of all the Eoganachta.

Art mac Cuinn then went westward across the Shannon, with a great host of the men of Ireland around him. Olc Acha, a smith of Connacht, gave him hospitality the night before the battle. These were his thoughts: "Heavy is this ox-herd that Mac Con has brought against you. Fierce will be the bellowing of these oxen of Britain and Scotland against you. They have no intention of fleeing, for it is a long flight for some of them back to the Alps <note>Sliab Elpa, likely meaning the highlands or distant mountains</note>. Evil is the cause of the man with whom you go to battle. Lugaid has a claim against him this time. How many children have you left behind, Art?" he asked. "One son," said Art. "That is too few indeed," said he. "Sleep with my daughter (her name was Achtan) tonight, Art. It is prophesied to me that great dignity shall spring from me." That was true; the dignity was great, namely Cormac son of Art, son of Conn. He slept with her that night. It was then that Cormac was conceived. He told her she would bear a son and that son would be King of Ireland. Then he told her of every hidden treasure for that son’s benefit. He said he would be killed the next day, and he took leave of her, telling her to take her son to be fostered by his friend among the Connachtmen. Then he went to the battle the next morning.

Lugaid’s plans, however, were ready. Half of his warrior-band went into the ground for him; that is, a pit was made from the first sod and hurdles were placed over them. A spear would be broken at the socket, with its point sticking through the hurdle—a place where there was the fresh earth of the men of Ireland. Furthermore, the leg of the Gael was bound to the leg of the Scotsman so that the Gaels should not flee. There were two Britons for every Gael. Then the two battle-arrays were set on each of the two sides. The kings who were in the vanguard of the battle were Lugaid Mac Con and—

Lugaid Lága and Béinne Brit were in the vanguard of one of the two armies. Art son of Conn, Eogan son of Ailill, and Corbchacht son of Ailill were in the vanguard of the other army. Lugaid then challenged Eogan to single combat. Eogan said he would not go against him on that occasion, because Lugaid's deeds against him had been evil. Lugaid then said that Eogan should not be a fool at that time, even if he should fall; for Lugaid would rather the dogs of the men of Ireland eat him than stay outside his own land any longer.

The air above them, meanwhile, was black with demons waiting for the wretched souls to drag them down to hell. Only two angels were there; they remained above Art wherever he moved through the host, because of the true nature of a righteous ruler.

Then each of the two armies attacked the other. The assault they launched on both sides was fierce. Terrifying were the sights there: white clouds of chalk and lime rose toward the heavens from the shields and bucklers as they were struck by the edges of swords and the points of spears and arrows, after being skillfully parried by the warriors. There was the clashing and shattering of bucklers under the blows of blades and stones, the whirring of flying weapons, and the gushing and spilling of blood and gore from the limbs of the enemies and through the sides of the soldiers. The two Lugaids <note>Lugaid Mac Con and Lugaid Lága</note> moved through the battle like bears among a litter of pigs, attacking every man in turn; each had a crested helmet on his head, an iron hauberk around him, and a great sword in his hand.

They fell upon the hosts and struck down hundreds of them. In the same manner, Eogan son of Ailill and Corbchacht son of Ailill fought on the other side. This combat where the men of Ireland and Scotland met was fierce and manly; the men almost trod on each other's feet as they exchanged blows. When they were face to face, a man might be wounded from the ground through both heels so that he was knocked over. The men of Scotland rose up against them from the ground and closed around them. Then Art son of Conn and the men of Ireland were defeated and slaughtered.

The rout broke toward Áth Cliath <note>Áth Cliath Medraige</note> in the territory of Óic Bethra. Their burial place is north of the ford: namely, the seven sons of Ailill Ólum. There is also the turlough <note>a seasonal lake</note> of Art, the place where Lugaid Lága, son of Moga Nuadat, took his <note>Béinne's</note> head off upon the stone that is in the turlough. For when Béinne Brit was cutting off the head of Eogan son of Ailill, Lugaid Lága reached him. Then he spoke, for a pang of kinship seized him; Béinne struck Eogan from the two shoulders up. "A low blow Béinne strikes! A high blow Béinne strikes!"

"My fury breaks its bounds!" cried Béinne Brit as he struck. With that, Lugaid Lága dealt a blow to Béinne across his neck, so that his head fell upon the breast of Eogan. Mac Con caught him then. "That is a wicked way to treat a comrade, Lugaid," he said. "It is all the same to you," said Lugaid; "I will give you the head of the King of Ireland now in its place." He went back against the retreating host toward the north until he met Art, and he killed him and struck off his head. From this comes the name of Art’s Turlough <note>Turloch Airt</note> in the territory of Óic Bethra.

Afterward, Lugaid Mac Con took the kingship of Ireland by force and remained at Tara for seven full years. He took Cormac son of Art into his lap to be fostered.

Ailill Ólom, however, was still alive, and this was his lament:
->Withered today is my fold; neither sons nor grandsons watch over it; it is my faultless testament, I give it in love to Mac Con.<-

This was Mac Con’s lament for his jester:
->No laughter has escaped since Dadera left, because of the smallness of your place, after the little jester of Dáirine.<-

This was the lament of Sadb, daughter of Conn of the Hundred Battles:
->Woe to me and woe to my fame, since the man of fury was found in his chariot; for this reason Art son of Conn fell, along with the seven sons of my Ólom.<-
->Woe to me and woe to my fame, since the man of fury was found in his chariot; it caused unfair odds for Art, while lying beside Corbchacht.<-

Once, the sheep belonging to the queen ate the woad-crop <note><term>glaisín</term></note> belonging to Lugaid. The matter was brought before Mac Con for judgment. "I declare," said Mac Con, "that the sheep are forfeit for it." Cormac was then a small boy sitting on a couch beside him. "No," he said, "the shearing of the sheep would be more just as payment for the 'shearing' of the woad, for the woad will grow again and the wool will grow upon the sheep." "That is the true judgment!" everyone cried. "It is the son of the true ruler who has given it." At that moment, half of the house fell down the cliff—the half where the false judgment was delivered. It shall remain that way forever, and is known as the Crooked Mound of Tara <note><term>Clóenfherta Temrach</term></note>. Of this it was sung:
->Heroic Lugaid gave a false judgment in a mist, as I see; it remains for him from then until forever: the mound is crooked on this side.<-

He remained in the kingship at Tara for a year after that, but no grass grew through the earth, no leaves upon the trees, nor grain in the corn. Therefore, the men of Ireland expelled him from his kingship because he was an unlawful ruler. He then went westward with a great company to his own territory. However, Lugaid Lága did not go with him. "Since I turned against my brother for your sake and committed kin-slaying," he said, "I will not return again. I will give myself in atonement to the son of the king I killed." Three times Mac Con recognized Cormac and turned back toward him; then he bid him farewell. He went westward to Ailill, to be cared for by him...

Lugaid went toward him. Sadb put her two hands around his neck. "Do not go, my boy," she said, "the man you go to is wicked; he is not forgiving." "Welcome indeed," said Ailill; "come to me then, that we may embrace, so that you may make a father of me and I may make a son of you, for I have no sons left to care for me." Then he put cheek to cheek with him, but he struck him with a poisonous tooth <note><term>fiacail fidba</term></note> that was in his head, into his cheek. "You have it now!" he said, "and you shall lament it for a while." Lugaid went out from him then. It was then he met Sadb. "Alas!" she said, looking at him:—

> This is the thrust by which a king falls; a poisonous tooth has wounded him;
> his form has lost its beauty; grievous was that farewell.

->This was true.<-

Afterward, Ferches son of Commán came to Ailill. "Woe, Ferches!" said Ailill. "Go after Lugaid for me." Before the end of three days, half of Lugaid's head had rotted. Ferches went after him. He reached his territory then. He put his back against a pillar-stone among the host. They did not see Ferches. "Do not let him near Lugaid!" The men formed a shield-wall between them. He cast at him across the host, so that it struck him in his forehead and reached the pillar-stone from behind, so that he died without a soul. Ferches, however, fled before the host into the waterfall, so that he threw wood-shavings from his spear to them upon the water. From this comes the name *Es Ferchis* <note>Ferches's Waterfall</note>. It was of this that Sadb, daughter of Conn, said:—

> Woe to me because of it, woe today, since the man of the venomous spear was found;
> it is what shall bring me to my grave: the cast of Ferches at Mac Con.

It was then Ailill said:—

> Thirty years until now, I have been a feeble old man;
> until I was awakened from my gloom by the cast of the son of Commán the poet.

After that, Ailill held the kingship of Munster for seven years. That was the Battle of Mag Mucrama, in which Art son of Conn and the seven sons of Ailill fell, along with the noblemen of Ireland around them, of which it was said:—

> The morning of Mag Mucrama, in which many kings fell;
> it was a tragedy for Art son of Conn; in that way he died upon the path.

Others say, however, that Lugaid Mac Con was thirty years in the kingship of Ireland, as it is said:—

> Mac Con took the land of Banba <note>Ireland</note>, every side as far as the bright-colored sea;
> thirty glorious years he was in the kingship of Ireland.

### [The Battle of Crinna, the story follows below]

There was a famous king over Ireland, namely [Cormac] grandson of Conn. There was a king over the Ulstermen at that time, namely Fergus Black-tooth. Fergus had two brothers: Fergus Long-hair and Fergus Fire-under-Bregia. Cormac's house was in Tara at that time, and every high king in Ireland had a house there for the purpose of holding the Festival of Tara <note><term>Féis Temrach</term></note>: that is, a fortnight before Samhain, Samhain day itself, and a fortnight afterward. The reason they used to gather every Samhain was because the mast and fruit were then at their ripest for them. The Festival of Tara was held because the laws the men of Ireland made there, no one dared to violate until they met again at the end of a year; and whoever violated them was declared an outlaw by the men of Ireland.

The Ulstermen came then to attend the Festival of Tara, bringing a great gathering with them. They sent messengers ahead of them to inspect their own house and to view Tara. This is how they found their house: without thatch or shelter, having been dismantled and used as a paddock for the cattle and dogs of the royal town. The messengers returned and said that the house was not fit to enter, and they reported that Cormac was in Tara with only a few people. The Ulstermen then entered into a single council to decide what they should do. The plan they made was to prepare for battle and to go against Cormac. They then sent word to Cormac to come and meet them, with preparations for battle between them. Cormac, however, did not have enough men for a battle, so what he did was avoid them. He went westward from Tara, and his officers <note><term>aes grada</term></note> came to him. He asked them what counsel they would give and from where he should seek an army. Then said Cesarnn, Cormac’s poet:—

> O Cormac, unless you love a victorious battle, seek from Munster a strong, proud warrior-lord who will take the horror of enmity from you. Do not consume the inheritance of a house for yourself, though the plain of the kingdom you reach be noble; so that the prosperity of Conn may not be a reckoning without a pure inheritance.

Cormac said then that if the advice Cairpre gave was the same as what Cesarnn had given, he would follow it. Then Coirpre said:—

> Gentle, my dear Cormac || . . . for you on an expedition . . . if you are wise . . . it is promised it will be a deed . . . about my brother who was bound . . . the will of the tribe. Since he is the grandson . . . of an heir; he was not weak in attack; let there not be a fearful, impatient one; he was not a watcher, a tearful complainer; he did not die of a stone for his bride-price . . . until you bring the battle-soldier from Munster with you.

<summary>Cormac mac Airt avoids a direct conflict with the Ulstermen after they find their hostel in Tara desecrated and declare war. On the advice of his poet Cesarnn and his son Cairpre, Cormac decides to seek military aid from Munster.</summary>
