Tadg, indeed, the son of Cian, son of Ailill Ólum, is the one who fights the Battle of Crinna, and it is prophesied that he will fight it. His father was the son of Conn’s daughter. Go south to Tadg and give him everything he asks of you in return for coming with you to fight the battle.

Cormac then went to the house of Ailill Ólum and was greatly welcomed there. "It is for this reason, indeed, that we have come," said Cormac, "to seek your welcome." "You shall have that," they said—namely Cormac Cas son of Ailill Ólum, Fiacha Muillethan son of Eoghan, and Ailill himself. For they were the heirs of Ailill at that time: Cormac and Fiacha Muillethan. And it was between them that he divided his land, because he himself was not able to manage its administration; that is, every other wood to Cormac and the other wood to Fiacha, of the land from one ford-hurdle to the other. And Tadg son of Cian was the heir-apparent between them.

They then held a council among themselves—namely Ailill, Cormac Cas, and Fiacha Muillethan—and this is what they decided: to give guidance to Cormac to the place where he would find Lugaid Lága, so that he might go with him northwards to fight the battle. They went after that to the place where Lugaid Lága was. He was then in Etharlach, where they found him bathing while he was unarmed. They then made three circuits around him, and Cormac approached him and bared his sword over his head and said to him, "Death over you, O Lugaid." "Death from me in exchange for my death," said Lugaid. "Your head off you, O Lugaid," said Cormac. "A head from me instead of my head," said Lugaid. "I will not accept that," said Cormac, "unless it is the head of a king in battle." "That thing shall be given," said Lugaid. <column-break/> "I will not accept it," said Cormac, "unless it were the head of Fergus <note>Fergus Black-tooth</note> king of Ulster." "<note>You shall have that,</note> said Lugaid. <note>Give your</note> word on it," said Cormac. "<note>I give it,</note>" he said. Lugaid then raised <note>his head</note> after that and said, "Your instruction was not good for you; that is the counsel of an old counselor. Although its beginning was bad for us, its end will be bad as well." After that, Cormac went to Tadg, and Tadg gave him a great welcome. Then Cormac said to Tadg, "O grandson of Sadb, daughter of Conn of the Hundred Battles, come to remove our oppression from us, for it is prophesied for you to remove it from us." "I will not go, indeed," said Tadg, "to fight the Battle of Crinna, for it is not required of me; it is not my land that is occupied there, and it is not my hearth that is farmed." Then Cormac said, "Consider which of us it would be more fitting to defend this territory of Conn. You are the grandson of Sadb, Conn's daughter, O Tadg. And if I should regain my land, there would be given to you as much as your chariot could travel around."

"...from the hour the battle is won until nightfall, and for your kindred forever, and your wages besides. "I will not take that task in hand," said Tadg, "and I will not go to battle against the Ulstermen." Then Cormac said:—

->The Farewell of Conn's Health (and so on).<-

Tadg then came with Cormac, and a great welcome was made for him. Tadg fell into a heavy sleep, and visions and a prophecy of what was before him were shown to him. Cormac stayed awake, listening to him, and Tadg said:—

> Great valor, great heat, great wisdom. Many journeys of unequal combat; folly is encountered. Many sharp enmities... many doomed ones will be driven there in great sorrow. Many bodies will be spoiled; hosts will be shaken when the hard sword deals its string-strokes (and so on).

After singing that lay, Tadg woke up and passed || his hand over his face and said: "It is time for us to set out to join the battle." "It is time indeed," said Cormac, and he sang this lay:—

> These visions, oh, these visions, that Tadg sees before the Battle of Crinna: many will lie under sharp blades, and blood will cover the sides of young men.
> Woe to the Ulstermen, oh, woe to the Ulstermen, to fight against me at this time; we have brought a bright-ranked army from broad, populous Munster.
> The heroes, oh, the heroes, I brought with me from Munster: women will be in lamentation because of them, and the Ulstermen will have a broken state.
> Prostrate bodies, oh, prostrate bodies, will be in Crinna without friends; this is what was heard tonight, and the paths will be red.
> The Battle of Crinna, oh, the Battle of Crinna, where Tadg will set fifty youths; Cesarnn and Cairbre have named them from the man who voiced his visions on high.

They came after that to Crinna, and Tadg said to Cormac: "Come and arrange the hosts for battle, for I have come with only a few from my country—namely, fifty warriors, thirty kings, Lugaid Lága, and myself." "I will not give you an army to fight the battle," said Cormac, "but give me the rights to my own territory and land, and I myself will provide the battle. Or else, fight the battle with the number you have brought, and take your land as was promised to you forever." 

Tadg then arranged his people for battle. He placed his youths in the front of the battle, his young warriors in the middle of the battle, and his old men in the rear. For that was the custom in Ireland until then: the old men in the front, the young warriors in the middle, and the youths in the rear. The men of Ireland did this so that everyone would exhaust their own lifespan. Therefore, Tadg put his youths in the front of the battle so that fear would not seize them upon seeing the old men being mangled in their presence.

### The Battle of Crinna.

The Ulstermen then formed a battle-array. They placed their old men in the front, their young warriors in the middle, and their attendants at the rear. Then Cormac came to Lugaid Lága: "A word from every prince and every righteous man," he said. "I want the head of a king in battle from you as the <term>eric</term> <note>blood-fine or compensation</note> for my father's head whom you killed at the Battle of Mucraime; and let it be the head of Fergus Black-tooth, King of Ulster." || "That shall be given to you," said Lugaid.

It was then that the armies rose up to attack one another. The Ulstermen made such a frantic leap that the earth trembled under the feet of the heroes, and their foreign and frenzied horses broke out in fury and madness at the shimmering of the sharp, blood-red, gilded spear-points, at the clashing of the blood-brown battle-shields, at the din of the white-bladed, thick spears, and at the rattling of the strong, shining mail-coats. Then the old men of Ulster and the youths of Munster fell together in mutual slaughter.

Lugaid then went through the battle to Fergus and vented his wrath upon the hosts until he reached him. He was greatly mangled by Fergus, but he seized the head of Fergus and struck it off. He went with the head to the place where Cormac was and said to him: "Here, O Cormac, is the head of a king in battle as I promised you: the head of Fergus Black-tooth." "A blessing on your valor and your prowess, Lugaid," said Cormac, "but I do not value the king's head more than the head of his brother." "Is that what has happened?" asked Lugaid. "It is indeed," said Cormac. Immediately, the Ulstermen gave the kingship to Fergus Long-hair and placed the king's helmet upon his head; he was proclaimed king by the Ulstermen, and they fought the battle on his behalf.

"Well then, Lugaid," said Cormac, "as for what you promised me—that I would receive the head of a king in battle from you—it is clear to you now that this is not the head of the king, for we still see the king with his helmet upon his head." "It is evident then," said Lugaid; "put dry tow into my wounds to see if I might be able to do anything to that Fergus." Cormac's charioteer came to him and put the tow into his wounds with the butt of his own spear; and Lugaid went through the host in that manner.

Then it happened that Tadg and Fergus Long-hair and their warriors encountered each other. Lugaid went past them through the battle to seek Fergus and to strike off his head as he had promised ||; and the warriors from the east and the west fell together in mutual slaughter, while Tadg was still standing. Fergus went to the place where his brother had been killed, and Lugaid followed him. They fought until Lugaid took his head from him on the same stone where he had taken his brother's head, and his helmet fell from his head onto the stone.

And Lugaid brought the head and his spoils with him to Cormac and said to him: "A king's head in battle for you, O Cormac!" "The triumph of your honor and your soul to you, O Lugaid," said Cormac. "But we do not value this king's head more than the head you gave us before." "Why so? Is it not the king's head?" "It is not, indeed," said Cormac. "It is true," said Lugaid. "It is true," said Cormac.

"Look now, O lad," said Lugaid, "how the armies meet, or is Tadg still standing?" "He is indeed," said the lad. "What do they do now?" he asked. "The grey-haired heroes from the west," said the lad, "are attacking the attendants to the east." "Give me a little broth in my wounds so that I may unleash my death-roar upon the Ulstermen along with the grey-haired men of Munster."

A king's proclamation was made by the Ulstermen for Fergus Fire-under-Brega, and the king's helmet was placed upon him. The attendants of Ulster went around him to join the battle. On the other side, the grey-haired men of Munster went around Tadg and Lugaid to join the battle, and a fierce battle was fought between them. The attendants of Ulster were defeated, and Fergus Fire-under-Brega was killed. Lugaid took his head from him on the same stone as before and brought it with him to Cormac.

However, what Cormac did was to put Deilenn the druid in his place as king, for he was seized with fear of Lugaid. Deilenn, moreover, said that he would not go until the freedom of his kindred was granted to him as far as the borders of Brega. "That shall be given to you," said Cormac. Then Deilenn went into the royal position and placed the king's helmet upon his head. Lugaid then came toward Cormac with the head of the last Fergus in his hand. He threw the head at Cormac, but it killed Deilenn—who was in the guise of Cormac. || And his stone was set there, so that from it comes the name Deilenn’s Mound.

Cormac then came to Lugaid and said to him: "It was not well done to me, O Lugaid, to kill my druid." "It was not he I wished to kill," said Lugaid, "but yourself." It was then the poet said:

> On the same stone at Ráith Cró, the three Ferguses were slain;
> Cormac spoke of it then; their poems did not hide it.

Then Lugaid heard a great shout from the north. "What shout do I hear now, O lad?" asked Lugaid. "The shout of the men of Munster following the rout," said the lad. Then he heard a heavy shout against them from the east. "What shout is this from the east, O lad?" asked Lugaid. "The shout of the Ulstermen turning back to the battle," said the lad. Then Cormac said:

> Arise, O Lugaid, do not be weak; go against Eochaid Gunnat;
> and attack, as you are wont, against the chief from Munster.
> Eochaid Gunnat is a hero's deed; it is no work for a soft youth;
> I fear for Tadg who loved me, the tall man being mangled.

"It is true," said Lugaid. "It is Eochaid Gunnat who has now entered the battle, and there is no man to meet him unless I go to him. And what little life remains in me shall be spent against him," said Lugaid. He rose up after that and went to where the others were fighting the battle, and a fight took place between them. And when they had finished using all their weapons, neither man would do anything but tear out the other’s entrails with his hand; so that from this comes the name *Áth an Inathair* (Ford of the Entrails) to the northeast of Crinna.

The Ulstermen were defeated after that. Uninformed people say that Eochaid Gunnat was killed by Lugaid in that battle, but that is not true. Seven battles were won that day against the Ulstermen: the battle of Crinna, the battle of Ráth Cró, the battle of Airceitros, the battle of Conachad, the battle of Sithbiu, the battle of Áth an Inathair, and the battle of Druim Fuait.

After that, the Ulstermen gave the kingship to Ernemach and fought a battle on his behalf at Sithbiu. They were defeated, and Ernemach was killed there. They went then to Airceitros and fought a battle there, and they were defeated after their king was killed there. They went from there to Conachad, and likewise to Druim Fuait, and they were not pursued further than that.

Tadg then came to Cormac after the battle was won. "Give me that which was promised to me—that is, whatever my chariot should encircle until evening after the battle is over." "That shall be given to you," said Cormac. Cormac’s chariot and his charioteer, Maeldóit, were given to guide him on the path he should take. And Cormac said to Maeldóit: "O lad," he said, "whenever Tadg is in a faint <note>Tadg was drifting in and out of consciousness due to his severe battle wounds.</note>, turn the front of the chariot eastward." "What reward shall be given to me for that?" asked the lad. "Freedom for your children and your kindred forever," said Cormac, "and do not let Tadg include Tailltiu or Temair in his circuit." "That shall be done," said the lad. Tadg then went to encircle his land. And this is what the lad would do: whenever Tadg was in a faint, the lad would turn the heads of the horses and the chariot eastward again. However, when Tadg would wake, the lad would turn the horses' heads westward. They reached the River Liffey in that manner, and it was evening for them. "Well, O lad," said Tadg, "what river is this?" "The Liffey indeed," said the lad. "Did we include Temair and Taillte in our circuit, O lad?" he asked. "We did not," said the lad. "Did we include either of them?"

### The Adventure of the Sons of Eochaid Muigmedóin.

There was a famous and noble king over Ireland, namely Eochaid Muigmedóin. He had five sons: Brian, Ailill, Fiachra, Fergus, and Niall. Moingfionn, daughter of Fidach, was the mother of Brian, Fiachra, Fergus, and Ailill. Cairenn of the Dark-Curly-Hair, daughter of Saxall the Mute, king of the Saxons, was the mother of Niall. The queen [Moingfionn] felt hatred for Niall because the king had fathered him with Cairenn against her wishes. Furthermore, the hardship Cairenn suffered from the queen was great. The extent of the hardship was such that she was forced to carry the water of Tara herself, and every servant-woman was set against her. And when she was pregnant with Niall, she was forced to do all that work so that the child might die in her womb.

The time for her delivery arrived, yet despite that, she did not cease her labor. After that, she bore a son on the green of Tara while she was alone with her carrying-load. She did not dare to take the boy up from the ground to herself, but left him in that place for the birds of prey. No man of Ireland dared to take him away for fear of Moingfionn, for the fear of her was great upon everyone. Tórna the Poet came then to the middle of the green and saw—

# The Adventure of the Sons of Eochaid.

He found the infant alone and the wild beasts attacking him. Tórna then took the boy into his lap and revealed everything that would happen afterward, saying:

> Welcome, little guest! He shall be Niall of the Nine Hostages. He shall be known before the era of lords. Plains shall be magnified. Hostages shall be subdued. Battles shall be fought. Long-sided of Tara. Master of fortresses of the plain of Femen. Restrainer of the plain of Maenmag. Respected and battle-heavy. Ancient hero of the Liffey. White-kneed of Codal. Twenty-seven years ruler of Ireland. And from him shall be the royal lineage forever. For the beginning was good, and the ending [was] Forgal of the Rough Hair, until he died in the late afternoon of a Saturday over the Ictian Sea <note>The English Channel.</note> after being wounded by Eochaid son of Enna Ceinnselach.

Tórna took the boy with him after that and fostered him. Neither Tórna nor his foster-son came to Tara after that until the boy was of age for the kingship. Then he and Niall came to Tara. There they came upon Cairenn as she was bringing water to Tara. Niall said to her then, "Leave the labor alone," he said. "I do not dare," she said, "because of the queen." "My mother shall not be in service," he said, "while I am a son of the king of Ireland." He brought her with him then to Tara and put purple clothing upon her.

The queen became angry, and she thought that was a bad thing. The word of the men of Ireland then was that Niall would be king after his father. Therefore, Moingfionn said to Eochaid, "Pass judgment between your sons," she said, "as to which of them shall receive your inheritance." "I will not judge," he said, "but Sithchenn the druid shall." They were sent then to Sithchenn at the smithy that was in Tara. He was a wonderful prophet. After that, the smith burned the workshop over them. Niall came out, carrying the anvil and its block with him. "Niall is supreme," said the druid, "and he shall be a solid anvil forever." Brian came and brought the hammers with him. "Brian for your fighters," said the druid. Fiachra came with the vessel of ale and the bellows with him. "Your beauty and your art with Fiachra," said the druid. Ailill came and the chest in which they were [the weapons] with him. "Ailill for your vengeance," said the druid. Fergus came with a bundle of dry brushwood and a yew branch within it. "Fergus the Withered," said the druid. That was true, for the seed of Fergus is not good except for one, namely Cairech Dergan of the clan of Bairinn. Thus, there is a yew stick in a bundle of dry brushwood. To testify to that, the historian sang:

> Five sons of Eochaid: Niall is the anvil, great Brian is the sledgehammer for striking truly; Ailill is the chest of spears against a tribe, Fiachra is the [bellows/beauty?], Fergus is withered. To Fiachra belongs the drinking of ale, to Ailill the spears of battle; to Brian belongs the going into the fight, to Niall the assembly of the host.

This was a heavy matter for Moingfionn. She said to her sons, "Fight," she said, "you four sons, until Niall comes to separate you."

...and he kills him. They fight afterward. "It is better for me to separate them," said Niall. "No," said Tórna. The sons of Moingfionn were at peace then, and from that comes the proverb.

Moingfionn then said she would not abide by that judgment. They were sent to the same Sithchenn to seek weapons. They went afterward to the smith, and he made weapons for them. He placed the most excellent weapon among them into Niall's hand and delivered the other weapons to the other sons. "Go now to hunt," said the smith, "and test your weapons."

The sons went afterward and hunted. They went astray after that for a long time, as darkness closed in on every side around them. When they stopped wandering, they kindled a fire for themselves; they roasted some of the game and ate until they were satisfied. They were in great thirst and parched after that from the cooked meat. "Let one of us go to seek water," they said. "I will go," said Fergus. The lad went to seek water until he came upon a well, and he found an old woman guarding the well.

The hag was such that every joint and every limb of her, from top to bottom, was as black as coal. The gray, bristly mane that grew through the crown of her head was like the tail of a wild horse. She could cut a green oak branch with the stroke of the sickle-shaped green tooth that was in her head reaching to her ear. She had black, smoky eyes and a crooked, prominent nose. Her midsection was sinewy, speckled, and diseased. She had twisted, bowed shins with bony ankles and wide, shovel-like feet; she was big-kneed and green-nailed. Truly, the appearance of the hag was horrible.

"Is it so?" said the lad. "It is so indeed," said she. "Are you guarding the well?" <column-break/> asked the lad. "Yes," she said. "Do you permit me to take some of the water with me?" he asked. "I permit it," she said, "provided that I get one kiss on the cheek from you." "No," said he. "Then no water shall be taken from me," said she. "I give my word," he said, "that I would sooner die of thirst than give you a kiss." Then the lad went to where his brothers were and told them he had found no water.

Oilill went to seek water and came to the same well. He refused to kiss the hag and returned without water, and he did not admit to finding the well.

Brian, the eldest of the sons, went after that to seek water and came upon the same well. He refused to kiss the old woman and returned without water.

Fiachra went and found the well and the hag, and he asked for water. "I will give it," she said, "if you give me a kiss for it." He gave the kiss.

Niall went to seek water and happened upon the same well. "Give me water, woman," he said. "I will give it," she said, "if you give me a kiss." "I will lie with you as well as give you a kiss." For it is not obtained without battle and without conflicts, but at last, it is beautiful and fair for anyone. However, do not give the water to your brothers until they grant you favors: namely, that they grant you their seniority and that you may raise your weapon a hand's breadth above their weapons." "It shall be done so," said the youth.

The lad then took his leave of her and brought water to his brothers. He did not give it to them until they gave him every condition he asked of them, just as the maiden had instructed him. He bound them then never to go against him or his descendants forever.

### The Death of Crimthann son of Fidach and the three sons of Eochaid Mugmedón—namely Brian, Ailill, and Fiachra.

A noble and venerable king once held the kingship of Ireland: Eochaid Mugmedón, son of Muiredach Tírech. He had a worthy wife named Mongfind, daughter of Fidach. She bore four sons to Eochaid: Brian and Fiachra, Ailill and Fergus were their names. Their mother saw a vision concerning them. The vision was of them going into the forms of four dogs: Brian in the form of a lion, Fiachra in the form of a greyhound, Ailill in the form of a harrier, and Fergus in the form of a mutt. They were then struggling and contending among themselves. The greyhound overcame the lion at first, but then the lion grew stronger than the other three, and they submitted to him finally and obediently without him harming them. Mongfind tells the vision to Sithchenn the druid. "It is true," said the druid: "it shall be..."

# Aided Crimthainn.
<meta>263 β]</meta>

Brian will be a bold-handed, fierce-striking lion, and his seed after him; they will be a venomous battle in the anger of all, and they will be firm in enduring the attacks of everyone upon them. Fiachra after him will be a hook and an enclosure. He will strive against Brian, and Brian will strive against him; there will be battles and conflicts between them, and the kingship will be shared from time to time between their clans. However, the seed of Brian will ultimately prevail over the clans of the other sons, so that the supremacy will belong to them alone. Ailill, moreover, will be a hunting hound, seeking and defending the youthful territories of his brothers. As for Fergus, his descendants will be nothing but a badger of commoners, and his lineage will scarcely even be known.

Eochaid died afterward. Then there was a great dispute over Eochaid's inheritance among his five sons—namely, Niall alone on one side and the four sons of Mongfind on the other. Indeed, Mongfind achieved nothing because she did not otherwise obtain the kingship for her son Brian—for he was her favorite among her children. She urged the men of Ireland through persuasion and through the art of druidry—for she was skilled in every art of druidry and sorcery—to give the kingship to his brothers, so that she might send Brian across the sea to learn military arts and so that he would later be a famous warrior to contest the kingship.

Brian then went across the sea and learned wisdom from Senoll son of Onga in the north of Scotland <note>Alba</note> until he was proficient in every art of weaponry and prowess. After completing his education at the end of seven years, Brian returned from the east. Brian was a brown-haired, sturdy, bull-like man with strong limbs, the strength of nine men, and equal dexterity in both hands.

Crimthann was still in the kingship of Ireland. It was a grief to Mongfind that Brian was not king. Crimthann then went on a royal circuit in Scotland. For this is how the king of Tara used to go on his royal circuit: first in Tara, then in the province of the Gailian <note>Leinster</note>, and from there to the two provinces of Munster, to the province of Olnécmacht <note>Connacht</note> in the old way, from there to the province of Ulster, and finally to Scotland. Then the sons of Mongfind took power and control over Crimthann's lands. He came from the east afterward, having heard that, and he gathered armies and hosts with him in Connacht to expel his sister's sons from his kingdom. He marched until he took camp at the river Moy in Connacht. A plan was then devised by Mongfind: she decided to offer a feast to her brothers at Inis Dornghlais on the Moy in the territory of the Uí Amalgaid. She invited her brother there as if to make peace with her sons, but her purpose was to serve him poison so that the kingship would go to Brian.

# Aided Crimthainn.

Then Mongfind came to her brother's house and made a treacherous peace between them and her children. She brought her brother with her to the feast. When the serving of the feast was finished, Mongfind put a cup of poison into her brother's hand. "I will not drink," said Crimthann, "unless you drink first." Mongfind drank a draft, and then Crimthann drank. Mongfind died then, specifically on the eve of Samhain <note>aidche samna</note>. That is the death of Mongfind the sorceress <note>bansídaide</note>. For that reason, the common people call the festival of Samhain the "Festival of Mongfind," for she was powerful and a sorceress while she was in the flesh. That is why women and the common people address their petitions to her on the eve of Samhain.

Crimthann then came from the north to visit his native territory—that is, the men of Munster—until he reached the mountain of "The Seat of the King" <note>Sliab Suide in Ríg</note>, and he died there. Because of that, it is called the Grave of Crimthann <note>Fert Crimthainn</note>. Fidach, his father, his mother, and his foster-mother went to the place where Crimthann died. They displayed a wretched mourning there, and the three of them died in that place. Concerning this, the historian <note>senchaid</note> sang this:

**F**rom what does the little grave <note>fertán</note> of Crimthann come? Let the elders declare the history: the son of Fidach, who was a man of secrets, in the hill of the chief fortress.
**G**reat and clear was the kingship Crimthann took, both near and far: over the land of Banba with its fames; it was the cause of great sickness.
**O**f evil intent was Mongfind, with her reasons, that the kingship should be with her brother: she preferred that the kingship of every land and the high kingship should belong to her own son.
**L**oving was Mongfind toward her child, the very handsome Brian son of Eochaid: it was for him that she desired, through treachery, the kingship of all Ireland.
**D**one was a great feast by her, by Mongfind among the great hosts: so that a draft of death was poured out for the son of Fidach of the truly great deeds.
**I**t was from this that Mongfind put the drink into the hand of Crimthann son of Fidach: Crimthann did not drink the ale until Mongfind drank it.
**I**ndeed, Mongfind drank the proper cup, and Crimthann drank after her: though the man was killed by the ale, because of that, Mongfind died as well.
**I**mmediately after that, Crimthann came from the north across the territory of red-sworded Connacht: that was the length of his delay there, and Crimthann died at the little grave.
**A**fterward came the king’s mother, in sorrow and in anxiety: her commoners built with great effort this fortress around the little grave.
**A**fterward Fidach came from the south, the senior fosterer of our poets: when he reached the mound in grief, he died there at the little grave.
**A**nd though the Mound of Ferchar <note>carn Ferchair</note> is the place which is upon this mound where I am: if you were to see other versions, its name is more truly the Grave of Crimthann.
**A**fterward came the king’s foster-mother, and her anxiety was no less: and there is nothing but a mound alone from that mound unto the little grave.

That treachery she practiced against her brother did not profit Mongfind, nor did choosing death for herself so that Brian would be king after her; for it was Niall of the Nine Hostages <note>Niall náigiallach</note> who took the kingship of Ireland after Crim-

...thann. However, it was Brian who was the smiter of battle at his side, taking hostages and tribute for him from every land.

Brian then took the kingship of the province of Connacht. Fiachra, moreover, took the land from Carn Feradaig to Mag Mucrama. There was contention and great envy between Brian and Fiachra because of this, so that war grew between them. The battle of Damchluain was fought between them, and victory was declared against Nathí and against his father. Nathí escaped from there, but Fiachra was captured and sent to Tara into the hands of his brother Niall. Because of this, a great high-war grew between Nathí and Brian again. At that time, Brian's camp was at Damchluain in Uí Briuin Seola, near Conmaicne Cuile. Nathí, with the clans of Fiachra, was in Aidhne against Brian.

His druid, namely Drithliu the druid, was brought to Brian, and Brian asked him how the conclusion of his war with Nathí would be. The druid said that Nathí would be the victor, and that he would take the kingship as far as the Alps <note>Sliab nEalpa</note>. Brian's children were brought to him, and he blessed them; he said to them that Eichen, his eldest, would be king over them after him. Brian had twenty-four sons, of whom the poet said:

> Brian, son of Eochaid Mugmedón, his children are good without weakness;
> A bright-faced company that was not small or insignificant, she had the four sons of Fiachra.
> Dái Galach, the generous and excellent, his offspring went into fame;
> Better is the one ordained son than the twenty-four sons.

Then he blessed the youngest, Dái Galach, greatly, and prophesied for him that the kingship would descend from him. Nathí came with weapons of battle to attack Brian at the place where he was with only a few in his camp, and a fierce struggle was fought between them. Brian was then defeated in the battle of Damchluain, and Brian was pursued from the battle to the hills of Domnall <note>Tulcha Domnaill</note>. Crimthann son of Enna Cennselach killed him, and Enna Emalach, the son of Brian, killed Crimthann immediately. Brian was buried in that place. Long afterward, Beoed of Ros Cam <note>Beoed Roiss Chaim</note> came and took Brian's remains with him to Ros Cam, and he buried them in Ros Cam; so that is why Brian’s burial place <note>otharlige</note> is there today. Drithliu the druid was also killed on the bank of Fionnloch, and from him the assembly of Drithliu <note>Aenach nDrithliud</note> is named. Concerning these things, the historian sang:

> Brian took a spirited kingship over the northern half <note>Leth Cuinn</note> of fair, triumphant Conn;
> The honor of the northern half was good, since the descendant of Olum did not survive.
> At the end of five victorious years, he won the battle of Damchluain;
> The battle was broken against Nathí and against Fiachra, son of Eochaid.
> Fiachra was captured in the fight and taken southeast to Tara;
> Until the King of Ireland decided his fate—to be brought to his brother.

# The Death of Crimthann

From that grew, without deception, the war
Between Brian and the children of Fiachra;
From that was struck, as I have heard,
Against Brian the noble battle of Damchluain.
Good was the pair that fell there,
The king who was the heir of Ireland;
Through the treachery of the men around the glen,
From that comes the Fair of Drithliu.
Brian of Badna, who brought forth challenges,
The son of Eochaid son of Muiredach;
A warrior of the Leinstermen, I have heard,
Slew him in the battle of Damchluain.
From that story—the better for it—
Fiachra went into the kingship;
And he was the smiter of battle alone,
Regarding the taking of the kingship.

Niall of the Nine Hostages then released Fiachra from his fetters and gave him the kingship of Connacht; and after that, he was the smiter of battle at Niall's hand while collecting hostages for Tara. Fiachra and the son of Amalgaid, son of Fiachra himself, were taken as hostages into Niall’s hand, so that it was while in hostage-ship at Tara that Fiachra son of Nathí died; from him descend the Uí Fiachrach of Cúil Fabair in Meath.

The sons of Eochaid, namely Fiachra and Ailill, then went to collect tribute and hostages in Munster with a great host and a vast company. They proceeded forward to Caenraige of the Uí Cairpre. Then the men of Munster gathered against them around Eochaid son of Crimthann the Great, son of Fidach, and around Maige Mescorach, with weapons of battle against Fiachra. Truly, he who was encountered there was a good man, namely Fiachra; he was a warrior in valor, a regulator of battle and territory in wisdom, and kingly in form. He was a long, fair-haired warrior, such that the tips of his hair touched his shoulder-blades; for this reason, he is called Fiachra of the Thread-like Hair. Then the men of Munster gave him battle at Caenraige, and Maide Mescorach wounded Fiachra severely in the battle. Fiachra then saw the battle turn against the men of Munster and the Erna through the strength of the fighting, and a great slaughter was inflicted upon them. Fiachra then brought fifty hostages from Munster with him and took their full tribute, and he went forward afterward to travel to Tara.

When he reached Forrach in Uí Meic Uais in Meath, Fiachra died of his wounds there. His grave was dug, his burial mound was raised, his funeral games were celebrated, and his name was written in Ogham. The hostages who were brought from the south were buried alive around Fiachra’s grave, so that it might be a perpetual shame for Munster and a trophy over them. This is what every man said while they were being put alive into the earth: "It is upon their chests <note>for uch</note> that these mounds are made," said everyone. "Forrach" shall be its name, said the druid. To testify to these deeds, the historian sang:

The sons of Eochaid, high is their fame,
Including Niall, the collector of tribute;
Including Fergus of the showers of spear-points,
Including the three sons of Mongfind.
Good was Fiachra of fierce valor,
Whose son was the stubborn Nathí;
And Brian over the front of Ireland,
And Ailill the valiant.

# The Death of Crimthann

Three fierce ones of great fury used to kill for the territory of Crimthann;
he took his territory while he was in the east, on a high-king's tour in Scotland.
Ailill and Brian, a fierce flame, and Fiachra the fair with long hair;
they divided Banba <note>a poetic name for Ireland</note> of strong abundance into three equal portions.
Curly-haired Crimthann came toward them with pride, truth, and success;
and he imprisoned every warrior with him on the bushy island of Dornghlas.
The mother of Eochaid’s sons came—the mighty Moingfionn of great judgments;
she requested a firm alliance from the fiery king of Dairine.
From the edge of the island she brought a drink of bitterness;
the grandson of Daire <note>Crimthann</note> fell by it, from a heavy, piercing poisoned draft.
Great was the deed she performed through her strength, against Daire’s brother through her pride;
that was the cause of the burial mound in truth: the hard battle of the warriors of Caenraige.
A spear for Fiachra, a chosen man; Maide Mescorach broke;
it was the strength that promised a wound to the host of Drum Eogabuil.
A salmon of a red flame... the face of the grandson of Muiredach Tírech;
he was not weary though he was doomed; he brought a great hostage-taking from Munster.
The sons of the men who fought the battle against Fiachra at the <unclear>tirath</unclear>;
there are fifty of them, hand to hand, around Fiachra’s grave in the mound.
Four of the seed of fair Breogan filled the whole of Ireland:
Eber and Lugaid, who was not weak, and Eremon the noble son.

The men of Munster came thereafter from the west after hearing of Fiachra’s death. Ailill was captured by Eochaid son of Crimthann, son of Fidach, the King of Ireland. The men of Munster resented this, for they thought the sons of the woman who killed their lord would encounter them; for that man used to carry his raids into foreign territories, he sought the hostages of everyone, and he brought the lands of Ireland and Scotland under the sovereign rule of Munster. A <term>guin galann</term> <note>a ritualized revenge-killing</note> was then performed upon Ailill, and in that manner he died. There was a great war between them for a long time after that, the cause of which was the contest for the land on which they are today. These are the causes of the war between the Connachtmen and the men of Munster thereafter, and of every conflict that arose between them; concerning which the historian said:

The three sons of Eochaid of the pleasant deeds: Fiachra, Brian, and Ailill;
Fiachra fell after a struggle in valor, from the wounding of Maide Mescorach.
At Dun Daire of the vats yonder, Brian of the famous deeds was wounded;
Ailill found—no fair cry—a poisoned drink at the hands of high Eochaid.
Those are the deaths of the three: proud, noble, and of high power;
a high deed of the combats east and west; there was no superior force for those three.

Lugaid Mend, son of Aengus Tírech, son of Ferchorp, was the one who first seized the territory of Thomond by force; and because of that, it is called the "rough sword-land of Lugaid Red-hand." For these are the two territories which the men of Munster contested by force: namely, the territory of Ossory as <term>éraic</term> <note>blood-money or compensation</note> for Ederscel whom the Leinstermen killed, and the territory of Thomond as <term>éraic</term> for Crimthann son of Fidach. However, they are not entitled to those by right.

It establishes these events as the historical basis for long-standing territorial conflicts between the provinces of Munster and Connacht.</summary>

### The Little Brawl of Almhain

A great, joyfully intoxicated feast was convened by Fionn mac Cumaill, son of Trenmór, grandson of Baiscne, in broad and great Almhain of Leinster. When the feast was ready and fit for consumption, the nobles and great aristocrats of the Fianna came to partake in it. Those who were the most noble and honored among them facing Fionn were: merry, deed-performing Goll mac Morna; truly wise and truly fierce Oisín, son of Fionn; heroic Oscar, son of Oisín; the dexterous son of Lugaid; bright-faced Diarmait, grandson of Duibne; Caeilte, son of Rónán; the powerful clans of Duibdhíorma; the clans of Smól; the tribe of Dub dá boirenn; Goll Gulban; the swift-footed Corr and his sons, namely Conn, Donn, Aedh, and Anacán; great-deeded Iobhar, son of brave and victorious Crimthann; and two sons of the king of Leinster (who were both foster-sons of Fionn); and victorious Coirell, grandson of Conbron. Two sons of the king of Scotland came to the feast, and fierce groups of the sons of kings and great nobles of the world accompanied them.

Furthermore, all the Fianna of Ireland came there, and Fionn sat in the warrior’s seat of honor <insert>in the center</insert> of the hostel. Merry Goll mac Morna sat in the other warrior’s seat of honor, and the nobles of their own people sat around each of them. Everyone else sat from then on according to their nobility and their patrimony in their own certain, appropriate places, as was customary for them in every place and time before then.

Then the stewards rose up very formidable for the service and attendance of the hostel. They took up jewel-encrusted horns with pure-beautiful glass pearls and with shapely, shining craftsmanship on every gleaming, fully-embellished, and very beautiful vessel among them. Strong, intoxicating drinks of smooth, very sweet ales were poured...

...those good heroes; and spirit arose in their attendants, vigor and courage in their soldiers, gentleness and modesty in their women, and knowledge and prophecy in their poets.

Then a herald rose up quite nimbly and shook a harsh iron chain to restrain the servants and rabble, and he shook a long chain of old silver to restrain the nobles and great aristocrats of the Fianna and the men of art as well. Everyone listened in silent stillness <column-break/> and Fergus Finnbeoil (the "Fair-mouthed")—that is, the poet of Fionn and the Fianna—rose and performed songs, poems, and fine verses of Fionn’s ancestors and forebears in the presence of Fionn mac Cumhaill. Fionn, Oisín, Oscar, and the son of Lugaid paid the loud-voiced poet with the best of every kind of wealth and goods. Afterward, he went before Goll mac Mórna and recounted stories of the hostels, destructions, cattle-raids, and courtships of his ancestors and forebears, so that the sons of Mórna were joyful and high-spirited from those arts.

Then Goll said, "Where is my own messenger?"

"I am here, O royal leader of the Fianna," she said.

"Have you brought my hand-tribute from the Vikings to me?" he asked.

"I have certainly brought it," she replied. Having said that, she rose quickly and nimbly and cast down a mass of beautiful, refined gold upon the floor of the hostel in front of Goll—it was as large as a great hog or the burden of a strong, brave warrior. She undid the covering that protected that tribute and spread the noble, beautiful treasures on the floor in front of the hostel. Goll then paid Fergus as was his custom; indeed, there was no wise, sharp-worded poet, nor any generous man of art, nor any sweet-stringed harper <column-break/> nor any skilled, eloquent historian—nor any person of art from either Ireland or Scotland who was in the hostel of Almhain that night—to whom Goll did not give a gift of gold, silver, or various riches.

Then Fionn spoke and said, "O Goll," he said, "how long have you had that tribute from the Vikings, while my own tribute is also upon them? That warrior is Ciarán mac Lathairne; he is a hard-fighting champion, and he has a household of ten hundred fully brave warriors of his own."

"Your father waged war and strife against me, and the King of Ireland, with his provincial kings, went against me along with Cumhall. I was forced to leave Ireland to them, and I went forward to Britain. I conquered that territory, killed the king himself, and slaughtered his people. And Cumhall drove me out from there. I went from there to the land of the Fair Vikings, and the King of the Fair Vikings fell by my hand, along with his household. And <column-break/> Cumhall drove me out from there. I came from there to Scotland, and the King of Scotland fell by my hand. And Cumhall drove me out from there. I came from there to Saxony, and the King of the Saxons fell by my hand, along with his household. And Cumhall drove me out from there. 

Then I came to the Battle of Cnucha, and your father fell by my hand there. And that was the time," said Goll, "that I obtained that tribute from the Vikings. I rescued you yourself after going to the fortress of the King of the Vikings, along with your fifteen men. The wife of the King of the Vikings had fallen in love with you, and you had been held captive in an underground dungeon for a year, with a day appointed for them to put you and your people to death. By your hand, O Fionn, I went to the fortress of the King of the Vikings and I killed the king himself—namely, Eogan Mór. I slaughtered his people, took their gold and silver from them, and I left a king over the Vikings—namely, Tine the Mighty, son of Trioscall—and I bound the Vikings to pay a tribute to me. There it is," said Goll. 

"And O Fionn," he said, "you do not have a tribute of might from them, but rather you hold the <term>ríghféinnidecht</term> <note>royal leadership of the Fianna</note> and the <term>maerchoiméta</term> <note>office of steward</note> over them. Then Fionn answered angrily <column-break/> and truly heroically, saying, "O Goll, you have admitted in that story that you came from the city of Bergen to Cnucha and that you killed my father there. It is bold of you to tell me that," said Fionn.

# **Bruiden na hAlmaine**

Then Faelán, son of Fionn, rose up with his three hundred brothers along with him, and he went strongly and most bravely into the combat, and all the sons of Morna were driven from their positions by him.

Then the most brave lion rose up—the proud and high-spirited soldier, the fierce and raging dragon, the excellent bear, the gift-bestowing champion, the pillar of battle, and the hard-fighting column of war: namely, the jovial, deed-performing, red-cheeked, and pure-spirited Goll mac Morna. He put his armor of battle and combat about him: a beautiful, splendid breastplate around his neck, his fine, honorable, white-bordered tunic <note>A 'cotún' or gambeson</note> against his fair skin, his sharp-pointed, very strong, well-striking sword in his dark-nailed fist, and his great, soldierly, bossed shield on his left hand. He went boldly, ragingly, and uncontrollably through the hall; he left neither a heavy-flaming taper nor a shining, full-lighted lantern in the great hall unextinguished, nor did he leave a table without shattering it into small, scattered fragments.

Then Fionn sounded his battle-shout—his "echo of the woods"—loudly, and he commanded the Fianna of Ireland to overwhelm and kill the sons of Morna without mercy.

Then the Fianna of Ireland formed close, strong, and unbreakable ranks of their shields around them; Fionn went to the head of those champions, and they began bone-cutting one another without mercy. Then a boiling rage seized Goll, and he made himself a strong, protective shield for his people's sake. Then the strong bands and the noble lords were fierce; the soldiers were swift; the warriors were numerous; and the battle-champions were wounded <column-break/> by the powerful, unfriendly, and venomous battle those true warriors waged against one another. There was much blood dripping in streams from the sides of the noble clans, and there were deep, incurable wounds upon that destructive and fierce company. It would have been a terrible place for a weak or infirm person, or for a gentle, slender-fingered woman, or for an aged, ancient senior to be in the small hall of Almhain that night, listening to the sighs of the young and the old, the low-born and the noble, as they grew faint and weak from being struck and mangled. And they continued in that manner from the beginning of the night until the rising of the sun the next morning, without showing any mercy to one another.

Then the prophetic and sharp-tongued poet rose up—the generous and gifted man, Fergus Finnbheoil—along with the other men of art among the Fianna.

along with him. And they performed their poems, their fine songs, and their compositions of high praise for those warriors for the purpose of restraining and calming them.

After that, they ceased their slaughtering and their wounding at the music of the poets. They dropped their weapons to the ground, and the poets took up the arms and took charge of the reconciliation between them. Fionn said that he would not make peace with the clans of Morna until he received the judgment of the King of Ireland; and of Aillbhe, daughter of Cormac mac Airt, son of Conn of the Hundred Battles; and of Cairbre Lifechair, the heir to the throne of Ireland; and the judgment of Fithal and Flaithrí; and that the final word of the judgment should rest with Fionntan mac Bóchna. Goll said that he would grant him that. Both sides then placed themselves under the guarantee of the poets, upon their lives, to maintain that peace. They fixed a specific day—that is, a fortnight from that day—on the green of Tara.

The losses of the Fianna were examined then, and the loss to Fionn's people was eleven hundred men and women. Many a prosperous and very noble queen, many a beautiful and many-formed lady, many a gentle and sweet-spoken maiden, and many a full-brave and valiant hero had fallen there. Many a nose was wounded, many an eye disfigured, many an ear mutilated, many a leg bone-cut, many a hand severed, many a body mangled, and many a side pierced among those of Fionn mac Cumhaill's people who remained alive at that time.

As for the affairs of Goll and his good people—the clans of Morna—only eleven men and fifty women were missing from them. It was not by killing that the women died, but they died of terror and of fear. Everyone of them who was curable was sent to be healed, and very deep, wide-turfed graves were made for the number of those who were killed on each side.

After that, the great house of Almhain was cleaned, and each one of them sat according to his nobility and his patrimony. They remained for fourteen days in that order, and at the end of that period and time, they went to Tara. Cormac and Cairbre, Aillbhe and Fithal, Flaithrí and Fionntan mac Bóchna sat in the place of judgment. Fionn went to begin telling his story first, but Goll said: "O Fionn," said he, "it is not to you we should give the telling of the stories that are between us, for you would make truth of the lie and a lie of the truth against me. Let us both give the telling of our story to Fergus, and let him swear by the gods to do justice between us."

After that, the Fianna were called together and the judgment was announced to them, and peace was made between them in that manner. So far, that is the Little Hall of Almhain.

### [**The Adventure of Tadhg son of Cian follows here**]

Once when Tadhg, son of Cian, son of Ailill Olum, was on a visit as a royal heir in West Munster, his own brothers were with him: namely, Airnelach and Eogan. Their total number was one hundred and fifty warriors. That was the hour and time that Cathmann, son of Tabarn, arrived; that man was the king of the very beautiful land of Fresen—that is a land which lies opposite...

Southeast of Spain, that Cathmann came with a fleet of nine very large ships from the lands of Frisia for the purpose of cruising and searching the sea, until they were scouting the land—namely, western Munster—until they found the land vulnerable around Beara <note>Beire</note> primarily. The fleet came ashore, and the land was plundered and ravaged by them. The people of the territory did not notice them until they had closed in for the taking of people and the taking of cattle. All of Tadhg’s people were captured there, though he himself escaped from them by force through his prowess and valor. Captured there also were Líban, daughter of Conchobar of the Red Eyebrows and wife of Tadhg mac Céin, and her two brothers, namely Airnelach and Eogan. They were taken in forms of bondage and seizure in the hands of robbers and at the mercy of foreigners until they reached Spain and the lands of Frisia. Cathmann took Tadhg's wife for his own bed and attendance, and he put her two brothers into slavery and hardship: Eogan was forced to carry people generally across a narrow stretch of water that was in that country, and Airnelach was cutting firewood and making fires for the host. They were given nothing to sustain them but barley seed and jet-black clay water.

The affairs of Tadhg are told here now. Great sorrow and dejection came upon him because his brothers-in-law, his wife, and his people had been taken from him by foreigners. However, forty warriors of his people escaped without being slaughtered by the foreigners; they had killed man for man and brought one of the foreigners with them as a prisoner. He told them news of the land from which they had come to them. The counsel that Tadhg decided upon then was to firmly construct a fair, strong <term>curach</term> of twenty-five thwarts, upon which went forty ox-hides of hard, bark-tanned brown leather. He then ordered everything that was necessary for the equipment of his <term>curach</term> <column-break/> [of fore-masts] of great size, and [fully-skilled pilots, and wide-bladed oars], and [very firm, well-placed thwarts] fitted into their places, [so that] that <term>curach</term> [was] well-proportioned and compact.

They [strongly nailed and] then earnestly [launched] the <term>curach</term> upon [the sea; some] of the veterans were in the vessel to attend to the powerful, towering, heavy-green waves, and the rising of the salmon-kingly, red-maned sea to a great height, and the very rough currents of the spring tide. They filled their <term>curach</term> with foods and provisions, so that even if they were at sea for a year’s duration, the warriors would have their sustenance of drink and food and fine clothing. And when the young men were ready, Tadhg said: "O men," he said, "bring your <term>curach</term> upon the sea."

->Put your curach out upon the high, stormy sea;
Upon the rough currents, a joy to me, upon the home of the white seagulls.

They then put out their fair, swift-running <term>curach</term> into the vast and infinite abyss, and across the tide of the strong, heavy, and immense flood, so that they saw neither land nor ground before them or behind them, but only the surface of the vast abyss. And they heard around them then the singing of many unknown birds, and the heavy roar of the mighty ocean, and the shimmering, white-bellied salmon leaping all around the <term>curach</term>, and the very large, thick-brown porpoises following them so that they split the radiant oar-track in their pursuit, and the great sea-monsters following them. It was a spectacle for the warriors to be contemplating and <unclear>gazing at them with wonder</unclear> because of the extraordinariness of their appearance, their order, and their variety, for they were not used to seeing many vast, natural beasts or great sea-monsters until then.

They were thus rowing upon the sea for a period of twenty days and twenty nights, and then they saw in the distance a wondrous, beautiful-sided, choice land. They rowed straight toward it until they reached it; they all went ashore and hauled up their <term>curach</term> there. They kindled fires, and their warrior-provisions were brought to them, and the heroes consumed them vigorously. They made beds for themselves upon the beautiful, green grass, and they fell into their slumbers from then until the bright hour of rising on the following morning.

Tadhg rose early the next morning and went to traverse and search the land, and to make a circuit to see if there was any dwelling of people or animals on that island. Tadhg arose then and put his battle-dress about him, and thirty warriors of his people rose along with him in their armor. They went forward and searched the island, and they found no dwelling of people at all there, except for flocks of sheep. Their size was beyond description, for they were no smaller than huge horses, and the whole island was full of their wool. And they found...

...a vast and incomparable flock of huge rams was there, and there was one ram there that surpassed them all. It had nine horns upon it, and it made a violent charge at the brave men. Tadhg's people turned fiercely against it, and a fight was waged between them; the ram broke five of their shields in that skirmish. Then Tadhg drew the <term>gái doimghabála</term> <note>Literally a "spear of avoidance," likely a specialized javelin or throwing spear</note> and gave a fearsome cast at the ram so that he killed it. It was the burden of twenty-nine men to carry it, and they took it with them to the <term>curach</term>. They prepared and cooked it quickly so that it was edible food for the warriors. They gathered much of the wool because of its beauty, its strangeness, and its greatness, and they put it in the <term>curach</term>. They were three nights on the island, and a ram each night satisfied the good men. They found very large human bones there, and they did not know what death had taken them—whether it was people who had killed them, or a plague <column-break/> or pestilence that had destroyed them, or whether it was the rams that had killed them.

After that, they left that island and rowed on. They found two strange islands in the direction they went, with many wondrous blackbirds in them. Some of them were the size of eagles or cranes, and they were purple with green heads, and they had blue and bright purple eggs. Some of the men ate some of those eggs, and a covering of feathers grew immediately upon everyone who ate them; however, when they bathed in water, those feathers would fall off them immediately. The foreigner who was with them was the one who gave them that knowledge, for he had been on a voyage on the sea another time along the path they were traveling.

They rowed on after that for a period of six weeks, and they found neither land nor ground during that time, until the foreigner said: "We are," said he, "astray on the sea, and we have been carried into the deep ocean of the world's end, the vast abyss." A harsh-voiced wind rose after that, and a great roar came into the sea so that it rose in lifting hills and very large, impassable mountains. Great fear seized the people of Tadhg mac Céin at encountering the storms and the tempests—that is, something they were not used to enduring or encountering until then. Tadhg began then urging and inciting his people, and he told them to attend to the sea manfully, and he said:

> Arise, O youths of Munster, O remnant of the high heroes;
> defend all your lives beneath the waves of the heavy flood.
> Their fame remains for a time after them; it is fitting for you to relate it;
> to everyone who is in danger, enjoin courage upon them.
> Often many who are in danger escape—great is the effort;
> and another person goes to their death, even if a hundred were guarding them.

After that, they proceeded through the forest nearest to them and found an apple orchard with fair, purple-topped apples, beautiful leafy oaks, and hazels laden with clusters of yellow nuts. They traveled forward after that to a great, smooth, flowery plain under honey-dew. "I am knowledgeable to tell it," said the maiden. And they spoke the poem:

> **I**t is well you have spoken, O woman, O daughter of bright and lovely Gothniad: it seems a long time to us since you were in Ireland.

They made for the fortress fiercely and reached it without being noticed, for there was no guarding of the doors at that time. They struck against the wall of the hostel with a great crash and gave sudden, startling shouts around the building, and they set fires and torches against its sides.

When Illann the Victorious saw those deeds and losses, his anger rose, and his spirit surged when he saw his people being killed and destroyed. The combat was equally strong, for the champions fell together in the struggle. When Tadhg and Eochaid Airmderg saw those deeds and saw their own original people being endangered, they threw themselves upon the hosts and inflicted great slaughter and losses upon them, so that two hundred champions fell by the warriors in <column-break/> that confusion. And the foreigners did not wait for the youths in that place, so that an opportunity for the hostel was found by that onslaught, until Tadhg with his Irishmen reached the chamber of the fortified king where he was. Eochaid and Airnelach followed the foreigners and began destroying and swiftly killing them as long as they remained to strike at the youths. When the veterans returned, they found Tadhg and Cathmann striking each other in the very center of the hostel. Cathmann inflicted thirty heavy wounds upon Tadhg in that struggle, and Tadhg gave him the "upper ground"—that is, he separated the heir of the body from the torso, namely the head. And he triumphed with the head and the victory over Cathmann after that.

Now when the queen, namely Líban daughter of Conchobar Abratruad, heard those shouts and deeds, she came toward her husband without delay or hesitation, and she began to rejoice and exult.

## *The Beginning of the Bóroma.*

A High King took rule over Ireland, namely Tuathal the Legitimate, son of Fiacha of the White Blood, son of Fergus of the Fair Fortune. It was that Tuathal who took Ireland by force. It was by him that Ellim mac Conrach was killed in the battle of Aichill beside Tara. He won twenty-five battles against the Ulstermen, another twenty-five against the Leinstermen, thirty-five against the men of Munster, and twenty-five against the Connachtmen. This was in revenge for the killing of his father and his grandfather, whom the vassal-tribes <note>aithechtuatha</note> of Ireland had killed; for it was against the vassal-tribes of Ireland that Tuathal the Legitimate won all these battles. 

He settled at Tara afterward, and the Feast of Tara was held by him. The men of Ireland came to him—men, women, boys, and girls—and they gave oaths by all the elements that they would not contest the kingship of Ireland against him or against his descendants forever. These are the kings of the provinces who were at that feast: Fergus Febail, King of Ulster; Eogan son of Ailill Erann, King of Conroi’s province; Eogan son of Daire, King of Eochaid mac Luchta’s province; Conrach mac Deirg, King of Connacht; and Eocho mac Echach Doimlén over the Leinstermen.

Tuathal also had two beloved daughters named Fithir and Dáirine. Eocho mac Echach Doimlén, King of Leinster, married the elder daughter, Fithir; for it was not the custom at that time in Ireland for a younger sister to be married before an elder one. Eocho then took his wife with him to Ráth Imil in Leinster. She was, moreover, a dear foster-child of the King of Conn-

...except that daughter of Tuathal. The Leinstermen, however, said to him: "The daughter you left behind is better." Because of that, he went north again to Tara and said to Tuathal: "The daughter I took with me is dead," he said, "and I would like to take your other daughter." Tuathal said: "If I had fifty daughters," he said, "they would be given to you until you had a wife from among them." 

The other daughter, Dáirine, was given to him then; she was a foster-child of the King of Ulster. He took her with him to the border fort <note>Ráith Imil</note> where the other daughter was waiting for him. When Fithir saw Dáirine, she died of shame instantly. When Dáirine saw the death of her sister, she died of grief. The funeral washing of the two daughters was performed then, so that everyone said: "This is a rough washing <note>garb-thanach</note>." It is for this reason that the place is called Garbthanach.

Then the truth of that story reached Tuathal at Tara. Afterward, word was sent from Tuathal to the King of Connacht—the foster-father of Fithir—and to the King of Ulster—the foster-father of Dáirine. They gathered their armies and went to where Tuathal the Legitimate was. When they had met in one place, Tuathal said: "Great," he said, "is the crime the King of Leinster has committed, for my two daughters to have died through his trickery." This is what he was saying as he composed a poem:

> Fithir and Dáirine, two daughters of Tuathal the Towering:
> Fithir died of shame; Dáirine died of grief.
> Great are the injustices; I say it was destined:
> Heavy are the fates that bring them to the meeting with death.
> From one pregnancy they were born, the two daughters of Tuathal of the Herds:
> Strong are the fates that at another time bring death.
> Beautiful, modest Fithir, daughter of the High King of Tara:
> Her match was a worthy one—the man the King of the Barrow <note>the Berba</note> gave her.
> If Dáirine has fallen among the King of Leinster's many people:
> I declare it is no small thing; from me comes her vengeance.
> Since my daughters have fallen, I say to you—it is no secret:
> It shall be avenged on the Leinstermen, on the heroes of the Liffey <note>alLife</note>.

Then the Connachtmen said they would accept nothing from the Leinstermen except war. The Ulstermen said the same thing. The King of Ireland, however, said: "It is not pleasing to me," he said, "to bring war to the Leinstermen; and yet, even so, if it is your counsel, let everyone go toward them." Their total number was twelve thousand. The province of Connacht went before them across Gualu to Naas and established a camp there. The armies of Tara also rose up around the King of Ireland, crossing through Graifrenn, Buaidgein, the Rige, and Mag Nuadat to Naas, and they established a camp there.

The Ulstermen also rose up across Esa, Odba, Fithairt, and Faendruim to Lethduma, and they established a camp there.

However, the Leinstermen gathered in their assembly and fought a battle against the Ulstermen, where Fergus Febail, King of Ulster, fell, along with all the Borbraige of Ulster as well.

Then all the armies rose up and burned Naas and Ailinn, Maistin and Ráirinn, and they destroyed the fortress of Bresal. That fortress was made of seasoned wood by Bresal Brathairchenn, the High King of the world. The Leinstermen advanced to meet them, nine thousand being the total number of the Leinstermen. They fought a battle at the boundary fort <note>Ráith Imil</note>, which is called the *Garbthanach* <note>Rough Washing</note> today. A fierce and cruel battle was fought between them until the Leinstermen were defeated, for they were not granted a fair fight. Thus, Eocho mac Echach Doimlén, King of Leinster, was killed in that battle, along with twenty other kings. 

From the beginning of autumn until the beginning of winter, the people of the Half of Conn <note>Leth Cuinn, the northern half of Ireland</note> were plundering Leinster, until the Leinstermen finally made peace with Tuathal—that is, by paying the blood-fine <note>éraic</note> for his daughters to him. He then left the kingship of Leinster to Erc mac Echach Doimlén. This, however, was the blood-fine: three times fifty hundred <note>15,000</note> cows, three times fifty hundred pigs, three times fifty hundred cloaks, three times fifty hundred silver chains, three times fifty hundred wethers, and three times fifty hundred bronze cauldrons. There was also a great bronze cauldron into which twelve pigs and twelve oxen would fit, for the house of Tara itself. Furthermore, there were thirty red-eared white cows with calves of the same color, with bronze halters, bronze yokes, and bronze bells upon them. Of this it was sung:

> Tuathal the Legitimate, possessor of the land, they used to come to Tuathal at his house:
> He subdued ten hundred battles; he plundered the five fields of Uisnech.

> Older are their sons than their fingers; they were whiter than the clouds of heaven.

> Two daughters had Tuathal the Legitimate; the two were an evil cause of strife.

> From Eocho mac Echach of Ailinn; "The Tiller" was his hereditary name.
>

> Until her husband broke his word to her, under the fruit of the mountain of curly Collan.

> She remains in the south on the plain of Mugna; her hair was yellower than fragrant forest-fruit.

**T**he flesh-fork for the steam of the food, it is what is fitting for a high king: 
the cauldron to boil the portions <note>nom: possibly 'raw pieces' or 'nine portions'</note>, Christ ordained the fellowship. 
**T**he shield against the breast of the battle, against the tyrant: 
the sword to overcome the hosts; have it, O son of Eochaid. 
**C**onlaed, Bridget’s smith, I will not hide it, it is he who made the flesh-fork:

**I** am Maedóc the balancer; you are Brandub, King of Leinster: 
I am at prayer and protection; you are rising against a grievance.

Maedóc then bid farewell to Brandub and spoke these few words:—

**M**y triple-pronged, high-lifting flesh-fork was brought by me to fierce Brandub. My sturdy red-handled cauldron was given by me to the high-victorious son of Eochaid. A hundred flitches of bacon would fit there at a single stroke of the fork.

Maedóc departed after that. Then Brandub put a slave’s clothing about him and called Aengus son of Airmedach, King of Uí Failge, to him and said to him: "Let us go," said he, "and put that cauldron on the fire and fill it with pigs and cattle." Then the cauldron was lifted by them onto the fire and was filled with boars and cattle. A great, blazing fire was kindled around it until it boiled.

It was then that the son of the King of Ireland said: "Where," said he, "is Brandub's wife?" A messenger was sent for the queen. It was there that Lóichine Lonn the Fierce, grandson of Lonán and superior <term>airchinnech</term> of Cill Rannairech, met him. He struck his head off after Cumascach had identified himself to him. He took the head to the place where Brandub was and showed him the head. It is because of that deed that freedom <note>from taxes or tribute</note> was granted to Cill Rannairech.

At that time, Bishop Aedán came to them—the Bishop of Glendalough. He was the brother <note>literally "son of the mother"</note> of Aed mac Ainmeirech. Laighde, King of Osairge <note>Ossory</note>: what good did he do for Aed above the other kings? "Not difficult," said Coluim Cille. "He gave silver oxen, so that no cleric ever left him with a refusal. He never shamed a cleric, and he never harassed a church or a sanctuary, and he gave much to the Lord. As for Ailill Banda, this is how he found the Lord's mercy: in the battle of Cúil Chonaire, which he fought against the descendants of Fiachra, they were prevailing against him in that battle, so that he said to his chariot-driver: "Look behind us for us, and find out if the slaughter is great and if the people doing the killing are near us." The driver looked behind him and this is what he said: "The slaughter being done to your people is unbearable," he said. || "It is not their own fault that falls upon them," he said, "but the fault of my pride and my injustice. Turn the chariot around for us to face them," he said, "for if I am killed eventually, it will be a salvation for many." The chariot was turned afterwards to face the enemy, and that Ailill performed intense repentance then and fell by his enemies. "That man also found the Lord's mercy," said Coluim Cille.

Feradach the Fair, son of Duach, however, the King of Osairge, was a greedy and conscienceless man. Even if he heard of only a single scruple of gold or silver held by a person in his land, he would take it by force for himself and put it into the ornamentation of drinking horns, chests, swords, and fiddles. Afterwards, an unbearable sickness seized him. His treasures were gathered to him until they were in his own bed with him. His enemies (that is, the descendants of Connla) came afterwards to attack his house; his sons also came to him to carry the treasures away with them. "You shall not carry them away, my sons," he said, "for since I have tormented many for those treasures, it is my will for the sake of God that I myself am tormented here regarding them, and that they be taken by my own will by my enemies from me, so that the Lord does not torment me in the afterlife." His sons went away from him then, and he himself began intense repentance and died at the hands of his enemies, and he found the Lord's mercy.

"And I myself then," said Aed, "shall I find the Lord's mercy?" "You shall not find it at all," said Coluim Cille. "O cleric," he said then, "obtain from the Lord for me that my defeat not be carried out by the Leinstermen." "That is difficult for me," said Coluim Cille, "for my mother is of them, and the Leinstermen came to me at Durrow and they began a fast against me so that I might give them a sister's son's gift, and what they requested of me was that no foreign king should take a victory over them; and..."

<summary>Coluim Cille describes how the kings Laighde, Ailill Banda, and Feradach the Fair achieved salvation through generosity or final repentance. However, he refuses to grant King Aed salvation and notes his conflicting loyalty to the Leinstermen, who have secured a promise of protection from him.</summary>

That was the very cowl that Aed asked of his servant at that hour. However, the servant said: "We left that cowl at Ailech," he said. Aed then said: "It is more likely then," he said, "that I will be left tonight with the Leinstermen."

As for Brandub here: he had his horses and his oxen gagged, and he arranged his battle ranks. He went forward in the darkness of the night until the Airgialla <note>Oriel</note> heard the noise and the din of the great host, the neighing of the horses, and the lowing of the oxen under the wagons. The Airgialla rose up, and whatever hand a man reached out, he found a beef or a pig beneath his hand. || "It is true for them," said the King of the Airgialla; "let them pass you by. Let us go then," said the Airgialla, "lest our share of that division be forgotten." The Airgialla went on to their camp huts.

The Leinstermen proceeded to the Hill of the Candle in the middle of the camp and took the cauldron off the candle. "What light is that we see?" asked the king. "It is not difficult," said the leper <note>referring to the disguised Rón Cerr</note>; "the food has arrived." The leper rose up and struck off his wooden leg, and his hand reached for his sword. The bindings were taken off the oxen, and the horses were let loose among the quarters of the men of Ireland so that they went into the wagon-camp and broke the huts and tents of the men of Ireland.

The Leinstermen rose out of their baskets like a flood-tide from the cliffs, with the hilts of their swords in their hands, the hollows of their shields ready, and in their coats of mail. "Who is this?" asked the Cenél Conaill and Cenél Eogain. "The people displaying the food," said the leper. "Indeed!" said everyone; "there are many of them." And the Conall and Eogan clans rose up, and even they were like hands in a nest of serpents. A fold of spears and shields was made by them around the King of Ireland, and he was placed on his horse, and they took him to the Pass of the Shields <note>Bernaid na Sciath</note>; the shields of the men of Ireland were left at the front of that pass.

After that, Rón Cerr made a rush toward the King, seized his leg, and dragged him toward him off his horse, and he struck off his head upon the stone of the breaking of bones. He took the portions out of the bag and put the head into it. He went forward, carrying it under his arm, across the slopes of the mountain and stayed there until morning. Afterward, they levied the Boroma: namely, Colmán Rímid and Aed Uairidnach, Maelcoba, Suibne Menn, Domnall mac Aeda, Cellach, and Conall Cael (the two sons of Maelcoba), Bláthmac, and Diarmait. The Conall and Eogan <note>the northern dynasties</note> came, as did the Airgialla, the men of Brega, and Meath to the slope of Mná Fine. The Leinstermen came against them. The King of Leinster at that time was Faelán mac Colmáin, and they fought a battle. Sechnasach was defeated, and a slaughter was inflicted on the Northern Half. The Boroma remained with the Leinstermen.

Cennfaelad mac Crunnmáil ruled for four years until he fell by the hand of Finnachta. Then Finnachta Fledach <note>the Festive</note> mac Dúnchada took the kingship of Ireland for twenty years. He took the Boroma twice without opposition. The third time he came to levy it, the Leinstermen rose against him. A great gathering of the Northern Half was made by him at the site of Muireadach on the border of Leinster and Meath. Word of this reached Bran mac Conaill. He gathered the Leinstermen, both warriors and clerics, at Ailenn. However, Moling did not come with them, so they sent for Moling. Moling was then at Ros Bruic, which is now called Tech Moling <note>St. Mullins</note>; for since Moling came from Sruthair Guaire, he had found no place to dwell until he reached Ros Bruic. Concerning this, Moling sang:

> To this place I have made my tryst; it is here I shall perform my hours:
> I will not depart from this dwelling until the day of judgment comes.
> Here shall be my inheritance, my house above the flood:
> My sleep is not much, while under your protection, O Son of Mary.

"What has brought you now, O Finnachta," said Adamnán, "since you did not come when the first messengers were sent?"

"That is not hard to answer," said Finnachta. "You threatened me," said Finnachta, "stating that none of my descendants would hold the kingship of Ireland, and no man of my name would ever rule. I am content with that. As for the other thing you promised me—shortness of life—I consider that a light matter, for Molling has promised me heaven. But the third thing you promised me—that I should not find the Lord’s mercy—I could not endure hearing that without coming to answer your call."

God arranged it so, because He did not allow Adamnán to deprive Finnachta of what Molling had promised him in exchange for remitting the Boroma tribute.

"Is it true that you have remitted the Boroma tribute until Monday?" asked Adamnán.

"It is true," said the king.

"You have been deceived by that," said Adamnán, "for when the cleric said 'Monday,' he meant the Monday of the Day of Judgment. If it is not collected today, it will never be collected until eternity."

Now, Adamnán and Finnachta had been friends since the time when Finnachta was a prince and Adamnán was a young student.

It was then that Adamnán composed these verses:

> **A**nd today, who binds the drinking cups, the withered, grey, toothless king?
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The deal he granted to Molling—it is a cause for regret for the king; he will not recover it.
> **D**id I possess Finnachta’s power—Finnachta, the lord of Tara—
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I would never have granted it until Doomsday; I would not have done what he has done.
> **C**very king who does not remit his tribute, his fame lasts long;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Woe to him who made the grant he made; for him who is weak, it is a cause for shame.
> **D**eparted is your wisdom, and folly has taken its place;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Woe to the king who remitted the tribute, O heavenly Jesus of heaven.
> **S**uccessful is everyone who thrives; woe to him who follows the grey-haired;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Long is this deal if it stays so; it would be better if the debts were paid.
> **I**f I were a king who reddens blood, I would strike down my enemies;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I would raise my fortresses; my battles would be many.
> **M**any would be my battles; my judgments would not be false;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;My dealings would be honest; my tribes would be full.
> **M**y standards would be visible; my strongholds would be strong;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Whatever might happen regarding this deal, I would not yield it to the Leinstermen.
