I pray a prayer to God that death or ill-fortune might not reach him;
> so that Molling may escape today, let him not fall by point or edge.
The son of Faillén, a man over walls, he will not be turned back;
> he knows the secrets of the Son of God, and the Son of God knows his secrets.
Three fifties of psalms <note>150 psalms, the full Psalter</note> every day is what he recites for God;

After that, the men of Ireland rose up after Molling. And it was then that Molling was marking out the site of a mill in Fornocht when they saw Finnachta with the men of Ireland coming toward them. When Molling saw them, he then said:

> O my powerful Lord, who created every king under heaven;
> O King who knows every secret...
> Finnachta, O Finnachta, his royal beds have come to an end;
> my curse and the curse of the Heavenly King be upon the King of Tara, upon Finnachta.
> Finnachta, O Finnachta, his royal beds have come to an end;

> from Tuathal the Acceptable of the generations, until the reign of Finnachta.
> It is I who took the Boroma for the Leinstermen with endurance;
> from the Uí Néill without harsh strength, O my powerful Lord.

Molling proceeded forward across the ford and rang his bell and startled the cattle of Leinster so that every cow of them reached its shelter and its stronghold. The Half of Conn <note>The northern half of Ireland, led by the Uí Néill</note> made a warlike circle around them. Then Molling said:

> Let the rocks be like brown oaks, let the waves be like gray pools;
> let the bell-towers be over the churches, let it not be a fleeting vision.

Molling went forward westward until he reached the place where Molling's Cross is. He sat there and made this verse:

> Let us sit here, a seat of joy; let us rise for victorious battles.
> Whoever is under the protection of Colum, his body will not be among the wolf-packs.
> My curse upon Finnachta, and the curse of the King of Heaven;
> Finnachta has turned against me, may his kin not be exalted.
> O Brigid of Kildare, O son of Tál <note>Saint Connlaed</note> of Kilcullen;
> and O Son of Mary, every seat I sit in is yours.

It was after that that Molling said: "Help will be needed here at this time." This was revealed to Mothairén, who was in the assembly of the King of Leinster. "It is a hardship," he said to Molling at this time, "and if it please the Lord, we would like to cast a mist over them." There was given...

# Boroma.

A mist came over them, and they did not know who brought it or how it was given. It seemed to them that they saw their enemies. They went forward to the Ford of Laegaire, the place where Labraid Loingsech was born. It was there that Molling said: "Who is in that settlement over there where we hear the bell?" Then Colmnait the nun said to him: "Alas, indeed, O cleric! It seems to me that fear has confused you. That is the church of Usaille <note>St. Auxilius</note>," said the nun. Molling said: "What is that great peaked and many-gabled dwelling we see in the corner of the sanctuary?" "That is Kildare," said the nun. Then it was that Molling made this intercession:—

> O Brigid, bless our path, let no harm befall us on our journey;
> O nun of the full Liffey, may we reach our home safely from you.

> whether our journey be long or short, may your spirit be with us.
> O Brigid, clear my road, O swift young nun over there;
> come to our aid a hundred times, so that our path to you may be prosperous.
> A famous word, oh, a famous word; O Christ, come to my protection;
> O Brigid, spread your white cloak over my head to protect me.
> O son of Tál, oh, son of Tál, O noble, ordained cleric;
> O Brigid || of the track of the Liffey, let no sons of evil come to meet us.
> O Máel Ruain, oh, Máel Ruain; O Michael, pure archangel;
> let us not be weak but strong, so that our help from you may be prompt.
> A strong prayer, oh, a strong prayer; let Mochua of Clondalkin be with me;
> if Usaille is in his church, let him come to meet us with a sweet bell.
> My King is alive, oh, my King is alive; the Son of the living God lives and shall live;
> on every road in this world, let him prevent the army of enemies from reaching us.
> God's strength with us, oh, God's strength with us, so that our spirit be not captured;
> O holy Kevin, if you are in your glen, lift your head at Molling's request.
> Living Comgán, oh, living Comgán, to protect me in every fight;
> Molaise with hundreds of saints, and Airnín along with them.
> A vessel of gold, oh, a vessel of gold, Aed son of Eogan of Clonmore;
> many kings are around his grave; may they be numerous in coming to our rescue.

> the man is of the world's nobles, welcome is that man's help.

> O Crón, daughter of Sétna, bless the path of my way.
> O Tacán, noble pilgrim, who is in the land of the Uí Chrimthannáin;
> let no enemies come to meet us, let them not be surrounding us.

[*The Minor Annals here: as they are from the taking of the kingship by Suibne Menn onwards until the death of Conghal Cinn Maghair; that is, from the year of Christ 615 to the year 710.*]

A.D. 615 . . . One day, then, when Suibne Menn was a young man in his own house, he was saying to his wife: "I wonder," he said, "at how little the <term>Cenél nEogain</term> have taken lordship over everyone now."
The woman said [through] a kind of mockery: "What is it to you," she said, "not to show hardiness and go before them to make war on everyone and to win victory often?"
"It shall be so," he said.

He came out after that, armed, on the following morning, and he met a young warrior of the people of the land who was armed. And he fought with him until the warrior submitted to the point of a spear for him. And in that way, he gathered an army by force, and Suibne took the kingship of Ireland.

It was before that time that there was a war between the two Fiachnas: that is, Fiachna son of Demán and Fiachna son of Baetán. This was the mother of that Fiachna...

<meta>This page continues the "Mionannala" (Minor Annals), recounting legends surrounding Fiachna mac Baetáin and his son, the famous Mongán.</meta>

She said, when she was brought to the father, as she saw a wolf going among the sheep and killing them: "I would like," she said, "to bear a son from you and me who would put that restraint <note>The word *aradhain* means a rein or restraint, suggesting the son would subjugate the father's people.</note> upon your kin." "That son shall not come into the world," said the father. Nevertheless, she later gave birth to Fiachna, and he was given over to fosterage.

He came one time to the house of his father and mother, but his father did not love him because of his harshness and because he possessed his mother’s nature. His mother then took him into a separate chamber, and he and his foster-father were served there. Afterward, the boy went out to the other youths with his leftover meat on a spit in his hand, and he came toward the royal house where his father was. When the father saw him coming, he unleashed a fierce dog he had and set it upon his son. At that same moment, a hawk came at him to take the meat. He, however, dealt with both the dog and the hawk: he struck with the spit and its meat into the dog's throat until it reached the dog's heart, and he caught the hawk with his other hand. When his mother saw the dog on one side of her son and the hawk on the other, she was startled; and so great was her shock that she never conceived in her womb from then on.

Regarding the very great war between the two aforementioned Fiachnas, it was Fiachna mac Baetáin who was always victorious. Not only did he triumph over Fiachna mac Demáin, but he triumphed over all the kings who faced him. The famous Mongán was a son of that Fiachna mac Baetáin; though historians say he was the son of Manannán and that he could take many shapes, that is not to be believed—rather, Mongán was a man of great knowledge, and his intellect was sharp, wise, and clever.

One day, Mongán came along the shore with his mother and large companies of people. The mother saw a beautiful stone with many colors on the beach; she picked up the stone and showed it to her son. "That stone you see, mother," the son said, "it is by it I shall be killed." The mother was greatly startled to hear this and ground the stone entirely into dust. The son said: "That labor is in vain, mother; for even if you turn it to ashes and bury it under the earth, it is by it your son will be killed." After that, the mother went in a ship, carrying the ashes of the stone in the middle of a head-cloth, until she was the distance of a sight into the sea and could see neither land nor ground; then she cast the cloth and the ashes into the sea.

625. Many years after that, a great fleet from the Britons came and plundered the lands near them until Mongán came with armies alongside him and defeated them. They were forced back into their ships. However, one of them took a stone from the beach and threw it, and it struck Mongán in the head so that he fell. And that stone was the very same stone that had been cast up by the waves onto the shore, having been formed from those ashes that were in the cloth. The stone was then recognized, and Mongán died from that wound in the eleventh year of Suibne Menn. Before he died, Mongán placed the stone in his mother's hand, and his mother recognized it. Furthermore, the man who killed him and all his ship’s crew were in his power, yet Mongán did not allow a single one of them to be killed but let them go. Nevertheless, although the fleet was large, not one of them reached home across the sea to the east without being killed or drowned, except for one man alone.

As he was dying, Mongán said to his mother: "I shall be alive exactly one year from now in my tomb; open the tomb then." However, the mother was deceived, for she did not take the <term>bissex</term> <note>a leap year</note> into account; for that year was a leap year, and she did not come on the correct day. On the day she did come, however, she found warmth in her son's body, and hot sweat through his side, and blood dripping from his nostrils, and he was attempting to rise (*if it be true*). He lived for a year and an addition after his father.

626. Now Fiachna mac Demáin, having been frequently defeated by Fiachna mac Baetáin, questioned many people. Specifically, he questioned a young kinsman of his who was a student of Comgall as to what caused him to be so frequently defeated and humiliated by Fiachna mac Baetáin. The student of Comgall answered him: "Do you know," he said, "which of you is more favored by the <term>érnaidhte</term> <note>prayers</note> that Comgall says? That is, whether he prays more fervently for his father's kindred than for our party, even though we have devotedly accepted him?" "That is true," said the king, "and he shall not be allowed to continue that for long."

The king came immediately with a large army to find Comgall, and he asked Comgall: "For which of us do you pray most to the Lord, O cleric?" "I pray for you both," said Comgall, "that is, for my father's kindred and for the kindred that has devotedly accepted me." "For which of us, then," said the king, "do you give the greater devotion of your heart in your prayers?" "To my father's kindred," said Comgall. "Pity, pity is that, O holy man," he said; "many of our nobles have been killed and captured because of that. I myself, indeed," he said, "would be better..."

"...that I should be dead rather than suffer the frequent shames that have been brought upon me. If it pleases you, take pity on me and my shamed kindred quickly, or else we will become your enemies." Comgall said: "Do you seek prosperity in this world here, or the kingdom of heaven hereafter?" The king said: "I seek victory," he said, "over my enemies, and to see their wealth and spoils in my possession; and to kill the king who has frequently defeated me until now, so that it may be music at feasts to tell of his shame and death from the mouths of bards."

Comgall was saddened by that news, and he called Fiachna son of Baetán to him and said: "What choice do you make?" he asked. "To take victory as you have before and have heaven taken from you, or to be killed in battle by the son of Demán and be in the kingdom of heaven forever?" "I prefer," said Fiachna son of Baetán, "to have a short life here and be in the kingdom of heaven forever." Comgall thanked God for that. Now, Fiachna son of Baetán's jester <note>druṫ</note> was listening to that conversation with his ear against the house. He later asked Comgall that he might die at the same time as his lord in the battle, so that as he was in his lord's company here in the world, he might be with him in the kingdom of heaven. Comgall said: "God will make it so; and just as you are here praising your lord, you will be honorably listening to the sweet music of the people of heaven praising the Son of Mary."

The two Fiachnas then gathered their full strength from every side for the battle. However, the Fiachna who had been victorious until then was overcome in this battle, and the Fiachna who had been defeated there was the one who won. Thus, Fiachna son of Baetán, King of Ulster <note>Ulaid</note>, was killed by Fiachna son of Demán. But Fiachna son of Demán's life was not long after that, for he gathered a great assembly in Ulster and was killed through the snares of his enemies. It is told, moreover, that a man of the mounds <note>fer síde</note> used to converse with that Fiachna son of Demán, but that man of the mounds was actually a demon. Fiachna asked his demon, when the enemies came near him: "What is the rank of this army and my own rank?" said Fiachna. The demon said: "Which of the two dirty sods you see," said the demon, "do you choose to fall upon? For on one of them you shall find death as your destiny has ordained." From this comes the famous proverb: "As his demon ordained for Fiachna." Fiachna son of Demán was then killed in that manner.

Fiacha, king of Ulster, at the end of fourteen years (was killed by Conghal Claen son of Scannlán, and not by Maelcoba son of Fiachna).

Domnall son of Aed son of Ainmire also took the kingship of Ireland after Suibne. His stories and his travels are told regarding the Battle of Magh Rath [636 AD]. In the eighth year of Domnall's reign, the Battle of Magh Rath was fought.

643. Conall and Cellach, the two sons of Maelcoba, took the kingship of Ireland after that. Diarmait and Blathmac, the two sons of Aed Sláine, took Ireland after them. It was in their time that Scandlán Mór, king of Osraige, expelled the Corca Laigde completely from the territory of Osraige.

649. It was in the time of these kings that Raigellach son of Fuatach, king of Connacht, was killed; that is, *in the sixth year*. Raigellach was very lustful and deceitful. He had a nephew whom he wished to kill, but he could not catch him until he made himself wretched through fasting. For he ate no food except sheep's tallow <note>suet</note> and said he was sick. But indeed, the sickness he had was great: envy <note>jealousy</note>. Envy is the greatest pain in this world, for it is what causes one brother to kill another.

Raigellach became thin because of this envy and lack of food, so that death was very near to him. He sent messengers to his kinsman to come speak with him as if he were at the point of death. The kinsman, however, did not go immediately when he was called, for he recognized the deceits of his elder kinsman. He waited to gather a host around him. He entered the house where Raigellach was with his naked swords under his cloak among his host, and they were all around their lord.

Raigellach, though he had a large host of his own, did not trust in them but in his own deceits. And he said: "Alas, alas! Great is the wickedness and the misery I am in, when my kinsman—the one I desire to take the kingship after me and whom I love more than all others—does not trust me, but keeps a host to guard him. As I thank God that you are of my own kin and are worthy to take my kingdom after me, yet it is a great malice for you to bring a host to guard against me, when I am on the brink of death, departing from my body and my flesh." When the young kinsman heard those words, his heart moved greatly for him, and he shed great showers of tears.

He came the next day with fewer men to check on him. He came the third day with...

...Raigellach's people sprang upon him [the kinsman] then and killed him. Raigellach then rose as if he were in good health; however, he was not whole at all after the killing of his kinsman, and he began feasting cheerfully and joyfully.

Mairenn, Raigellach's wife, asked her druid (since he was a foreknower of the future): "Is it a great prosperity," she said, "that Raigellach is in, now that all his enemies have fallen by him and he is in great prosperity?" She asked this because she knew that Raigellach would meet his death from some enemy, though she did not know who. The prophet answered and said: "The king who killed all his kinsmen shall be opposed by his own children, though he does not expect it; and you yourself, moreover, shall be opposed in your prosperity soon, and it will be the fruit of your womb that will come against you." Then Raigellach told her that she should have the children killed secretly as soon as they were born, so that this trouble would not come to them through their children.

It was not long after that until Mairenn bore a daughter, and she told a swineherd to take her away and kill her. When the swineherd saw the face of the infant, his heart went out to her, and he put her back into the same bag and brought her to the door of a pious woman who lived nearby, and he left her there on a cross beside the church. The pious widow came out at early morning and found the bag on the arm of the cross and looked at what was in it. When she saw the little infant inside, she loved her immediately and raised her in a holy manner <column-break/>. And there was no one in all Ireland more beautiful than she was. The fame of her beauty reached the ears of Raigellach, and Raigellach sent messengers to the girl's foster-mother to request the girl from her, but the foster-mother did not give her to him. She was taken to him by force afterwards from the sanctuary where she was. And when the king saw her, he loved her greatly and kept his own daughter sinfully. Mairenn then began to loathe that deed and to make it known. She fled to Diarmait Ruanaid, king of Ireland, across the Shannon, swimming to Ailech Muirinne; and it is from this Muirinn that the hill <note>fort or height</note> took its name.

The fame of this evil spread throughout Ireland. It was a grief to the saints of Ireland. Féichín of Fore came to Raigellach to rebuke him, and many saints came along with him so that he might be separated from her, but he did not yield to them at all. They fasted against him. For such was the greatness of the love he gave her that if her chariot were ahead, she would have to turn her face back toward him. If his chariot...

643. The saints prayed that he might find death before May-day, and that it might be at the hands of wicked men, by wretched weapons, and in a filthy pit; and it all happened in that way. On the eve of May-day, moreover, it happened that a wild stag was wounded, and it ran toward the island where Raigellach was, while he was guarding the island. When he saw the wild stag coming toward him, he took his spear and gave it a blow that went through the stag from one side to the other. The stag went swimming away from him. He went in a boat after the stag. The stag went a long distance from the lake until it came to some churls who were cutting turf; they killed the stag and divided it between them. The king came to them and made a great threat against them for dividing the wild stag among themselves, and he told them to give up the meat of the stag. However, what the churls decided was to kill King Raigellach before they would give him the meat by force; and they fulfilled that indeed. They struck him in the head with the spades that were in their hands until they left him without a soul, just as the saints had promised. Then Guaire sent Cuimín Fota, son of Fiachna, the <term>successor</term> <note>comarba</note> of Brendan, to meet Diarmait to request a truce of twenty-four hours from him, so that he would not come westward across the Shannon. It was then, moreover, that Diarmait met Cuimín on the hurdle-weir at the side of the Shannon, and Cuimín spoke his message to him. Diarmait answered him cheerfully and joyously, and said: "The request is not great; and if you had asked for something even greater, you would have received it."

"If that is so, then," said Cuimín, "turn back as far as the opposite bank."

"I give my word indeed, O head of wisdom and piety of Ireland," said Diarmait, "that I will not go back until I obtain either peace or battle."

"Come then," said Cuimín, "to the other bank."

"I swear to God," said Diarmait, "that if you had met me even further to the east, I would not have come to violate your honor during the time of the truce you requested."

The two of them were there until morning, the king and the cleric. Then Cuimín said to him: "It is a wonder to me, O king, your victories in battles and contests, considering the small number and the ugliness of this host I see with you; for though this host is numerous, the host that is against you is far more numerous. It is also more beautiful and much more noble."

"Do you not know, O cleric," said Diarmait, "that it is not by numbers or by appearance that a battle is won, but as it pleases God? And furthermore, as you say our host is unshapely: it is not beautiful forms that win a battle, but hard hearts. And this is not only among men, but also among other living creatures. For even the single wolf kills and drives away a large flock of sheep; and not only that, but he drives away herds of cattle and kills many of them. The hawk, also, and the falcon drive away birds though they are larger and more beautiful than themselves."

"O king," said Cuimín, "what is the reason you said that a battle is won as it pleases God?"

"Why indeed, O cleric? Is it not true that he who has the truth defeats the man of lies or of injustice? For Christ, as you have said, was few in number against the devil and the Jews; and yet, nevertheless, it was He who was brave, because the truth was with Him. It is enough for me, then, the host I have against the men of Connacht, for it is they who are in the wrong."

Then the men of Connacht, led by Guaire, and Diarmait Ruanaid with his host met, and a hard, fierce, and savage battle was fought between them. However, the battle was broken against Guaire, and a slaughter of the men of Connacht and the men of Munster was made there, including the two Cuans <note>Cuan mac Amalgado and Cuan mac Conaill</note> who had come with the reinforcements. While Guaire was in that position, Diarmait said: "We shall find out," said he, "whether it is for God’s sake or for mere vanity that Guaire performs this great <term>inneinech</term> <note>Hospitality or generosity.</note>." He ordered a jester of his people and a wretched, poor leper to ask something of Guaire. "Nothing for me," said the leper. Guaire gave his gold pin to him, for he had no other wealth. The poor man left. A man of Diarmait's people followed the poor man and took the pin from him and gave it to Diarmait. The poor man came again to Guaire, complaining, and told him that the pin had been taken from him. Guaire's heart went out to him and he gave his belt with gold to the poor man, and the poor man left. A man of Diarmait's people followed him and took the belt from him and gave it to Diarmait. The poor man came again to Guaire, while Guaire was lying on his back with the point of Diarmait's sword between his teeth. And when he saw the poor man so weary, a great stream of tears broke over his cheeks. Diarmait asked him: "Is it because of the misery of being under my power that you weep?" "I give my word," said Guaire, "it is not for that, but for the misery of that poor man." It was then that Diarmait said: "Rise up," said he, "and you shall not be under my power. For you are under the authority of a King who is better than I: under the authority of the King of Heaven."

Guaire then went to the Fair of Tailtiu with a large bag of silver to distribute to the men of Ireland. However, Diarmait commanded the men of Ireland that neither the wretched nor the strong should dare to ask anything of Guaire at the fair. Guaire then sat at Diarmait's hand, beside the King of Ireland at the fair. He remained like that for two days. On the third day, Guaire said to Diarmait: "Bring a bishop to me," he said, "so that I may make my confession to him and be tonsured." "Why is that?" asked Diarmait. "Death is near me," said Guaire. "How do you know that?" asked Diarmait. "It is not difficult," said Guaire: "the men of Ireland are in one place, and not one wretched person among them asks me for anything." "Everyone shall no longer be forbidden from asking of you," said Diarmait; "here is a bag of silver from me to you." "No," said Guaire, "I have enough silver myself."

Guaire then stood up and gave to everyone with both his hands. They say that one of his arms was longer than the other from that time on, from stretching it out toward the poor. And Diarmait placed his head in Guaire's lap, and all the men of Ireland took counsel from Guaire with one accord from then on.

The generosity of Guaire was very great in the eyes of the Connachta, and they thought it too much that he should bestow cattle throughout the land. They were telling Cáimín of Inis Cealtra to stop that giving. Cáimín said: "I will not stop him. However, I pray to the Lord that someone of his seed may come who will collect from the men of Ireland abroad as much as he gives away." And that was fulfilled, for Mac Lonán received for his poetry from the men of Ireland nothing less than what Guaire gave away.

This Guaire was one day in the church of Inis Cealtra along with Cuimín Fota and Cáimín. That was a great church which was built by Cáimín after Colum <note>Likely referring to Saint Colum Cille or another contemporary saint of that name.</note>. "What would you like to have this church full of, O Guaire?" asked Cuimín Fota. "It is not difficult," said Guaire: "I would like to have it full of gold and silver, not to store it up, but to bestow it for my soul's sake upon the poor and the needy of the Lord." "And you, Cuimín," said Guaire, "what would you like it to be full of?" "I would like," said Cuimín, "to have it full of books, and for them to come to the hands of students so that they might instruct the human race." "And you, Cáimín," they said, "what would you like it to be full of?"

"...[earth] full for you." "It is not difficult," said Cáimín. "I would like a great deal of hardship and disease upon my body, so that not one bone of mine would stay joined to another in the earth."

God made it so. God gave Guaire a long and prosperous life, and Cuimín was a master of wisdom and instruction. However, there was no success in Cuimín's teaching ever since Mochúta of Lismore cursed him because of his instruction of his own people in Mochúta’s presence while they were in the harvest-group, so that they were witnesses. Mochúta said: "Though the labor of Cuimín's instruction is great, let it be no more than a hornless, dun cow in a paddock that gives no milk through the world’s instruction." As for Cáimín, a great fire of inflammation seized him, and not one of his bones stayed joined to another in the earth.

Aena mac ú Laigse, the successor of Ciarán, was the spiritual advisor to Guaire. A widow's son was seized by Guaire of Aidne in his orchard. The widow came to Aena to complain of that trouble to him. "I have nothing else for you," said Aena, "except to recite this verse for him." The old woman went before Guaire and recited the verse to him:—

> O Guaire, do you contemplate the turning green after the fading?
> You shall sit all alone without anyone in the soil of the church of the son of Duach.
> My little smooth one, I reflect and indeed I wash purely:
> Everyone who has come to his aid has not gone without relief from misery.

"It is my only son who is my misery," she said. "You shall have that then," said Guaire, "and I shall take vengeance for this upon Aena." And that was true. A laborer of the community of Clonmacnoise killed Aena’s horse while chasing it out of his field. The laborer was caught by Aena until a hundred cows were pledged for the laborer as payment for the horse. The laborer then came to Guaire to beg for help. "Recite this verse to Aena," said Guaire. The laborer went before Aena and recited the verse:

> To the son of Laigse it was a great lie: one head for a hundred cows.
> Does the great go for the small? Is the little priest a mockery?

"It is a mockery indeed," said Aena; "I will ask nothing of you but one cow." There were many such exchanges between Aena and Guaire.

665. These kings then died: Blathmac and Diarmait, in the tenth year of their reign. Blathmac died of the <term>buidechair</term> <note>the Yellow Plague</note> in Caladh Truim in Buaighnib. Diarmait died in the same place, and he was stretched against a cross while standing. As he saw the men of Leinster coming toward him to kill him, his soul left him.

671. Sechnasach son of Blathmac took the kingship of Ireland after him, and Dubhdúin of the Cairbre killed Sechnasach through treachery.

675. Cennfaela, son of Crunnmael, son of Blathmac, followed him for four years until he was killed in battle by Finnachta, son of Dunchad, son of Aed Sláine, at Aircheltra. Finnachta the Festive, son of Dunchad, took the kingship after that for twenty years until he fell by the hands of Congalach and Aed, son of Dluthaig, at Grellach Dolluid.

Now, this Finnachta was poor in wealth at first. He had a wife || and a house, but he had no property except for one ox and one cow. Once, the king of the Fir Rois happened to go astray and wander near Finnachta’s hut. There had never been a night worse than that one, with storms, snow, and darkness. The house that the king, his wife, and his followers wished to reach was beyond their power to find because of the intensity of the darkness and the storm. Their plan was to stay under the trunks of trees. Finnachta heard that conversation, for his hut was not far from them. He came to meet them on the path and said it would be better for them to come to his poor house than to travel through the dark night and the great storm. The king and his followers said: "What you say is right; we are glad it was said to us." They then came with him to his house, and the size of the house was greater than its riches. Finnachta then struck a blow to the head of his ox and another blow to the head of his cow. The king’s own followers prepared the food quickly and hastily on spits and in a cauldron, and they ate until they were satisfied. They slept after that until morning came.

In the morning, the king of the Fir Rois said to his own wife: "Wife," he said, "I do not know if this house was poor before now, but it is poorer now since his only cow was killed for us." "That is true," said the wife, "and it is right for me to enrich him according to my own judgment. And however much you give to the man, I shall give the same amount to the woman." "It is well spoken," said the lord of the Fir Rois.

The king of the Fir Rois then gave a very large herd of cows, many pigs || and many sheep, along with their herdsmen, to Finnachta. His wife gave the same number of cows, pigs, and sheep to Finnachta’s wife. They also gave them fine clothing, excellent horses, strong steeds, and everything else they needed in the world.

It was not long after that when Finnachta came with a large troop of horsemen to his sister’s house, having been invited by her and receiving hospitality from her. As they were riding on their journey, it was then they met Adamnan—

...Adamnán was a student walking along that same road with a vessel full of milk on his back. It was not long after that when Finnachta and his friend, the king of the Fir Rois, went to his father's brother, Cennfaelad, to ask him for land. And when that half is loyal to you, arrange a meeting with the other half and kill their nobles and their fighting champions. And not only will you have the kingship of Meath...

...but the kingship of Tara shall still be yours if you wish. Finnachta then took that advice and afterwards declared war against his father's brother, namely Cennfaelad. When Cennfaelad's wife heard that, she was rebuking her husband regarding the stewardship he had granted to Finnachta. It was then the woman spoke this verse:

> The warriors of the western land have closed around Finnachta;
> His power was greatly diminished; his kingship was ended around Cennfaelad.

675. A battle was then bravely fought between Finnachta and Cennfaelad, and Cennfaelad was killed there along with many others. Finnachta then took the high-kingship of Ireland for a period of twenty years.

It was this Finnachta who remitted the <term>Borama</term> <note>A heavy cattle-tribute</note> to Molling after it had been levied by forty kings before him, from the time of Tuathal Techtmar down to Finnachta. Molling then came on behalf of all the Leinstermen to ask for the remission of the Borama for "a day and a night." In Finnachta’s view, it was only for one day and one night, but for Molling it meant forever. Finnachta then granted that respite. Molling went out and said: "You have granted a respite from it forever." Finnachta then understood that Molling had deceived him, and he said to his people: "Go quickly after the holy man and tell him that I did not give him a respite except for one day and night; for it seems to me," he said, "the holy man has deceived me, since there is nothing in the whole world but day and night." When Molling knew that they would come after him, he ran quickly and hastily until he reached his house, and the king's people did not catch him at all. Others say that Molling brought a poem with him to the king, and it is true that this is the poem:

> Finnachta over the Uí Néill, like the sun upon the shore:
> He is the bark above the wave, he is the wave upon the shore.
> He is the battle upon the land, so that kings do not dare to attack him:
> He is the king of royal Tara, he is the lord to whom all needs come.
> He is the flood-tide of deeds against valor, he is the wave out and in:
> He is the king of northern Tara, he is the firm lord before the battle.
> He is the heart of Conn’s enclosure, the tree of Tara, strong upon strong:
> It is Finnachta who is not weak, he is the fair vine-tree of the garden.
> I have heard from the elders here, praise is better than any other way:
> Generous Finnachta does not know that wealth does not last long.
> Wealth passes into the possession of everyone among the seed of Adam in a short time:
> Every person under the noble heaven is in danger, as their life passes from them in turn.
> Coirpre and Cormac and Art, and Conn before the royal bed of heaven:
> Though they held strong Tara, I believe Finnachta is better.

The Borama was then remitted to Molling in that manner; and although Finnachta was sorry for it, he was not able to levy it again from the Leinstermen.

Others say, however, that it was for the sake of heaven that Finnachta remitted the <term>Borama</term> <note>A heavy cattle-tribute</note>, *and this is truer*. For Adamnán came immediately to seek Finnachta after Molling had left, and he sent a cleric of his people to Finnachta so that he might come to speak with him. At that time, Finnachta was playing <term>fidchell</term> <note>An ancient Irish board game often compared to chess</note>. "Come to speak with Adamnán," said the cleric. "I will not go," said Finnachta, "until this game is finished." The cleric went back to where Adamnán was and told him Finnachta's answer. "Go to him," said Adamnán, "and tell him that I will recite fifty psalms in that time; and there is a psalm in those fifty, and I will ask the Lord in that psalm that neither his son nor his grandson, nor any man of his name, shall ever hold the kingship of Ireland." Finnachta, however, paid no heed to that, but played his <term>fidchell</term> until he won the game. "Come to speak with Adamnán," said the cleric. "I will not go," said Finnachta, "until this game is finished." The cleric told Adamnán. "Tell him," said Adamnán, "I will recite another fifty here; and there is a psalm in those fifty, and I will ask the Lord in that psalm for a shortness of life for him." The cleric told this to Finnachta. Finnachta paid it no mind but played his game until he had finished it on the board. "Come to speak with Adamnán," said the cleric. "I will not go," said Finnachta, "until this game is finished." The cleric came to Adamnán and told him Finnachta's answer. "Go," said Adamnán, toward Finnachta, "and tell him I will recite the third fifty; and there is a psalm in those fifty, and I will ask the Lord that he should not obtain the kingdom of heaven." The cleric told this to Finnachta. When Finnachta heard that, he threw the <term>fidchell</term> away quickly and came to where Adamnán was. "What has brought you now," said Adamnán, "and why did you not come at the first message?" "This is the reason," said Finnachta: "the threats you made against me—that is, that no son or grandson of mine, nor a man of my name, should take the kingship of Ireland, and that I should have a shortness of life—those were light to me. Molling promised me heaven. But you have now promised that I should not find the Lord’s mercy. That is why I have come, for I cannot endure that." || "Is it true," said Adamnán, "that you remitted the <term>Borama</term> for a day and a night to Molling?" "It is true," said Finnachta. "You have been deceived," said Adamnán, "for that is the same as remitting it forever." And thus he was rebuking him, and he sang:—

> Today, though the withered-grey, toothless king binds up his hair:
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The cattle he remitted to Molling, it is right the king shall not get them.
> If I were Finnachta, [and if I were] the lord of Tara:
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I would never have given them until Doom, and I would not have done what he did.

695. Finnachta then bowed his head into the lap of Adamnán and performed penance in the presence of Adamnán. However, Adamnán did not grant him that which Molling had promised him for remitting the <term>Borama</term> <note>The heavy cattle-tribute formerly paid by the Leinstermen</note>—namely, the kingdom of heaven. While Finnachta and his son Bresal were in their tent, his kinsmen came to attack them—namely, Aed son of Dluthach and Congalach—without being noticed in the tent. They killed Finnachta and his son and took their heads off them upon the pole. Loingsech son of Aengus took the kingship of Ireland after Finnachta for eight years.

697. The death of Molling occurred in the first year of Loingsech's reign. In the same year, the <term>Cáin Adamnáin</term> <note>The Law of Adamnán, also known as the Law of the Innocents, which protected women, children, and clerics during war</note> was established throughout Ireland.

699. In the fourth year of his reign, three shields were seen fighting from the east to the west like the waves of the sea, head to head: a bright white shield, a fire-colored shield, and a blood-colored shield. It was understood from this that the evils which came afterward—namely, the death of almost all the cattle of Ireland; and truly that was not in Ireland alone, but in all of Europe.

700. In the following year—that is, in the fifth year of Loingsech's reign—the majority of the people of Ireland died, and there was a great famine so that people ate things that are not lawful to mention.

702. In the seventh year of Loingsech's reign, it happened between Irgalach

Irgalach, son of Conaing, and Adamnán were at odds because Irgalach had violated Adamnán's protection by killing Niall, his own brother, while he was under Adamnán's safeguard. What Adamnán used to do was fast every night and stay awake without sleep, standing in cold waters to shorten Irgalach's life. However, that champion, Irgalach, used to ask Adamnán: "What will you do tonight, O cleric?" Adamnán did not wish to tell a lie, so he would tell him that he would be fasting without sleep in cold water until morning. Then Irgalach would do the same, in order to save himself from Adamnán's curse. Nevertheless, Adamnán deceived him; for Adamnán said to a cleric of his people: "Stay tonight in my place and wear my clothes. If Irgalach comes to ask you what you will do tonight, tell him that you will be feasting and sleeping, so that he may do the same; for it is easier for a man of Adamnán’s people to tell a lie than for Adamnán himself."

Then Irgalach came to find that cleric, thinking it was Adamnán who was there. He asked him: "What will you do tonight, O cleric?" said Irgalach. "Feasting and sleeping," said the cleric. Irgalach then feasted and slept that night. Adamnán, however, performed a fast and a vigil, staying in the river until morning.

While Irgalach was sleeping, he saw Adamnán in a vision, standing in the water up to his neck. Irgalach started violently out of his sleep because of this and told his wife. Now, the woman was humble and lowly before the Lord and before Adamnán, for she was pregnant and feared her child would be destroyed through Adamnán’s curse; she often used to beg Adamnán not to curse her offspring. Then Irgalach rose early the next morning and met Adamnán face to face, and Adamnán said to him: "O cursed son," said he, "and the most cruel and evil person God ever made, know that it is a short time until you shall be separated from your kingdom, and you shall go to hell." When Irgalach’s wife heard that, she came to Adamnán and lay at his feet, saying: "Do not curse the child that is in my womb." Adamnán said: "The child in your womb shall certainly be a king," he said, "but his eye shall be broken now through the curse of his father." and so it happened. The boy was born immediately, and he was half-blind.

703. In the eighth year of the reign of the aforementioned Loingsech, a great hosting was made by him into Connacht to plunder and raid it. Loingsech's poets were satirizing the king of Connacht, namely Cellach son of Ragallach. They were saying that it was not fitting for a palsied <note>shaking from age or illness</note> old king like Cellach to rise up or contend against the King of Ireland, and that if he did so, he would be defeated.

However, it did not happen that way, but quite the opposite. For when Cellach, King of Connacht, saw his country and land being destroyed and plundered, he called to him the two Dúnchads—namely, Dúnchad Muirisce and the other Dúnchad—and he decided then that they should hold the kingship of Connacht after him. He himself, however, had bathed and had oils and many herbs applied to his royal body. He placed one of the two aforementioned men—the two Dúnchads—at his right side and the other at his left, and he drew up the Connachtmen around him for the battle. Then Cellach himself leaped far and nimbly out of his chariot; everyone heard the cracking of the old man's bones as he leaped from his chariot. Then he spoke with a loud voice as he leaped boastfully toward the battalions: "O men of Connacht," he said, "defend and keep your own freedom, for the people against you are no more noble or vigorous than you are, and they have done no more good than you up to this day." And thus he spoke, with his voice trembling and his eyes flashing.

Then the Connachtmen took notice of this, and that palsied king led them against the King of Ireland. He triumphed over them afterward; Loingsech, King of Ireland, was killed there, along with a great slaughter of his people around him, including his three sons and the two sons of Colgu.

<meta>This page continues the historical accounts within the Minor Annals, following the death of Cellach of Loch Cimme and the reign of Fógartach son of Niall, focusing now on the conflict between Congal and the Leinstermen.</meta>

While in his country, the plan he [the King of Leinster] made was to send messengers to him with much wealth to give to Congal in exchange for obtaining peace from him. When Congal heard that—namely, that the messengers of the King of Leinster were on the road coming toward him—he prepared a deceitful trap involving himself, his brother, and his army. For it is the custom of kings, even if they have the strength of an army to overpower their enemies, to devise and arrange deceits and signs by which their enemies are defeated; for they do not care whether they overpower their enemy through strength or through deceit. 

Just as Congal practiced deceit here: he told the nobles of his army to leave the camp by sunrise the next morning and not to be present in the camp at all when the messengers of Leinster arrived. Instead, vassals and ill-favored people were to be in their places, and they were to be poorly dressed throughout the camp. He himself was also poorly dressed. He sent his own horse-boy onto the road to meet the messengers <column-break/> and said to the boy: "Belittle me as much as you can; insult me and say I am not myself because of misery and wretchedness, so that the Leinstermen will neglect us and think nothing of us." And the boy came and did as Congal told him.

As for Congal himself, when he heard the messengers were coming, he put wretched clothing on and sat among the vassals as if they were his high-ranking nobles. A little hen with a broken leg was brought to him, and he was very busily occupied with binding the hen's leg. When the messengers saw that—namely, the wretchedness of the king’s situation and the ugliness of the army—this is what they said among themselves: "We will not think anything of this king or his army; if we were to give him our wealth or our gifts, it would not be fitting for us at all." The messengers were taken to speak with Congal in a dirty house, and a pig with its hair still on was given to them for food. They went on the next day toward Leinster and Faeláin and told their news; they said that Congal and his army were nothing, that he was no king, and that neither hostages nor lordship should be given to them.

As for Congal: after the messengers left, his nobles were gathered to him and they held their counsel. The plan they made was to go against the Leinstermen and to burn, fire, and kill them. They did so: they burned and plundered all the Plain of Leinster and committed a red slaughter of people. Nevertheless, the king [Faeláin] did not pay them any attention, for he did not take notice of them at all but treated them as nothing. This was for two reasons: because of the reports of the messengers, and because of the victory he had previously gained over Fógartach on the feast day of Saint Martin.

Consequently, when Congal later plunders Leinster, King Faeláin ignores the threat until it is too late, blinded by the false reports and his own previous military success.</summary>

However, there was a certain warrior, fierce and full of life, of the Leinstermen at that time; Cuan Fithise was his name. He used to kill many of Congal's people every day and wound many more; he would escape safely from all of Leth Cuinn <note>The Northern half of Ireland</note> without a wound or a spear-thrust because of the swiftness of his horse. For however many good horses were sent after him, they could not overtake him.

One day, Congal came to speak with Cuan Fithise with a valley between them, and Congal said to him: "What causes you to inflict such persecution upon my army?"

Cuan said: "That is a question of conscience," said Cuan, "for you know indeed that the persecution you inflict upon my people is hard." Cuan said that it was because of the great persecution Congal was doing to his fatherland that he was persecuting him. "And if everyone were like me toward you, your journey into Leinster would not be a good one."

"That is indeed true," said Congal, "and you are not boasting in saying it, for your deeds are as your words are. Why then should we not make a friendship, you and I?" said Congal, "and that would be a profitable friendship for your fatherland. But I would make friendship with you in this way: if you would sell that horse <note>The text uses "tech," likely a scribal error for "each" (horse)</note> to me for twice its value."

"Do not say that at all, O king," said Cuan; "I give my word that this horse shall never be at the disposal of anyone of Leth Cuinn to persecute Leinster as long as I am alive."

"By your conscience then, Cuan," said Congal, "what is the breed of that horse, and from where did she get that great speed that is in her?"

"By my conscience," said Cuan, "it was a mare of no great quality in my own castle that bore her, and it was there she was reared and nurtured on my land."

They parted upon that, namely the king and Cuan. And the king called his own best horsemen to him and said to them: "Follow Cuan today," he said, "to the gate of his own castle, and it will not be difficult for you to catch..."

...on that horse with its rider, between its pasture and the horses among which it was reared. And Congal's cavalry did as he told them. They followed Cuan until they reached the place where the horse used to graze every day and the place where it was born. And there was no horse faster than it until then. There was a great noise and shaking of the earth from the horses of Leth Cuinn <note>The Northern half of Ireland</note> following it. Their tracks remained in the stones and in the earth for a long time because of the speed of the run, so that there was a trail of sparks of fire in the air behind them. In any case, Cuan Fithise was overtaken there. Fair play was not granted to him by the men; instead, he was given a warrior's death, and he was killed and beheaded, and a shout of triumph was raised over him. They came back with victory and triumph, bringing Cuan's head and his horse with them to the camp of King Congal. All the hosts gave a shout of triumph over the head of Cuan Fithise. *Whence Congal sang:*—

->O the delights of this occasion, after the plundering of the Liffey;<-
->beautiful is the sound of his vigil, over the head of Cuan Fithise.<-

As for the Leinstermen, they gathered both warriors and clerics in one place. Their spirits were not good because of the destruction of their land and the killing of Cuan. They were saying that it would not be easy for them to give battle to Congal because of his own hardiness and the great number of his troops. Therefore, they said that the freedom of his children and his kindred would be granted by the kings of Leinster forever to the warrior who would kill Congal, and that heaven would be granted to him by the clerics.

Now a warrior of the Leinstermen undertook, in exchange for heaven from the clerics and freedom for his kindred from the kings, to go to Congal's camp to kill Congal. He came in this way: with two very large spears in his hand as if he were going to sell them. When he reached the thick of the host, a man of them asked him: "O youth," said he, "do you wish to sell one of those spears?" "I do," said he, "as the king shall value either of them." They went forward through the groups and through the doorkeepers to the place where the king was. The warrior struck a blow with one of the very large spears into the king's chest. But that was in vain; for the king's cunning was such that he had a board of hard yew <note>clár cruaidiubair</note> as broad as his chest, reaching up to his chin. It was there the spear struck, passing through his satin tunic and hitting the board. And the Leinster warrior said while dealing the blow to the king: "O king," said he, "value this spear for me!" The king said, after the thrust was made: "See for yourself," said he, "if it is better than the board that is between me and it."

The king's bodyguards rose up to kill the warrior. But the king said: "Sit down, and do not kill him at all." But he asked—

<summary>Congal's forces overtake and kill the swift warrior Cuan Fithise, after which a Leinster assassin attempts to kill Congal with a spear but is thwarted by the king's hidden wooden breastplate.</summary>

[Congal] asked of him: "What reward," he said, "did the Leinstermen promise you for coming to kill me?"

"They promised me, indeed," he said, "heaven from their clerics, and their kings promised freedom for my kindred forever."

"You shall be my bodyguard," said the king, "and it will be necessary for the Leinstermen to give those rewards to you."

And it happened that the king was at that time at the foot of an oak tree; there was much snow there, and ripe acorns <note>mes</note> were upon it at that time. And while the Leinster warrior was at the scene, a group of the soldiers were seized with envy concerning the duty that had been given to him. A man of Congal’s people said: "It is better for me," he said, "to test that loyal bodyguard of the King of Ireland. I will throw this apple at the king's head, and if the apple should hit the king's head past him, it is no less likely that a stone or a tree would hit his head." He then threw the apple at the king's head. However, that Leinster bodyguard parried it so that he split the apple in two with his sword, and he gave a blow to the man who threw it in his head so that he killed him. The king returned to his house after the victory of triumph and after avenging his grandfather upon the Leinstermen.

† 710. Congal then died at the end of seven years from a plague.
*et cetera.*

## [The Sequel of the Sinful Daughter of the Greeks]

There was a wonderful king of the Greeks in a fortress once. It was always a custom for the kings in the east to be drinking and consuming food while the queens stayed at home. News came to the king: "Honor and rank to you, O king! A daughter was born to you last night."

"May it be a prosperous omen," said the king; "a blessing on the womb that bore her."

"Honor to you, O king," said a young lord there; "a son was born to me last night."

"Give the daughter to him then," said the king. It was always a custom for them that a boy born on the same night as a girl should be betrothed to each other. Even if one of them should die immediately, the one who survived was to be kept pure always, without intercourse with any other person. So the king's daughter was betrothed to the son of the young lord. The daughter was then reared diligently in reading, wisdom, and art, so that it was her whom her father would consult and take counsel from. She lived in a separate apartment, and no one dared to enter it except those who were serving her. It was she then who used to distribute <column-break/> the last serving every night so that it might be like communion and a consecrated thing.

<summary>King Congal takes his intended assassin as a bodyguard after promising to fulfill the rewards the Leinstermen offered; the page then begins a new legend about a Greek princess betrothed at birth to a nobleman's son.</summary>
<keywords>Congal, Leinstermen, bodyguard, King of Greece, betrothal, Greek legend, Irish annals, 710 AD</keywords>

<header>The Daughter of the King of the Greeks.</header>

Whatever might happen from one hour to the next, she would go in her soft slippers <note>original: *maelassaib*</note> to take the drink <note>original: *innescra*</note> and pour it into the drinking horns, and she would turn back out again after that. She loved a handsome youth <note>original: *gilla*</note> who was in the household. He was once sent with the maidens into the house; he did not leave the house until he and the princess became lovers. Once, the youth slept with the princess in the chamber. The king came to the door. "Open up," said the king. The princess rose and threw the quilt <note>original: *colcaid*</note> over the youth. The king came in and sat down upon the quilt. She sat down beside him and they remained in conversation until the evening hour. The king went out. The man who was under the quilt was dead <note>having been smothered by the weight of the king</note>. This was a source of great distress to the maidens.

Then a great churl <note>original: *bachlach* — a term often used for a rough or low-born man</note> came to the door of the maidens' house. They called to him and gave him food: "Carry that carcass <note>original: *faistin*</note> away from us, and you shall have your reward." It was bound up then. "Throw it away over the cliff." "It will be better if I go with you," she said. She went with him. "Throw it away over the cliff." While the churl was sitting down, she put her two hands against both of them <note>the churl and the corpse</note> and pushed them into the glen. "His secret will be kept the better for it," she said.

"Well then," said the young lord, "it is time for the princess to be given to this son of mine." "Let her be given then," said the king, "here is a young and beautiful girl of good lineage and good learning." He came to sleep with her. "What shall I do?" she said, "my crime will be known and I will be burned at once. Help me," she said to her companion <note>a handmaid or confidante</note>, "sleep with the man in my place. If he asks for you later, let me take your place." "But I have been given to a man already," said the companion. "We will find a way around that too." They were brought into a house for him—a dark house so that they could not see each other until the next morning.

He was let in to them. "Welcome to you," she said, "come to your young queen; may good and luck be to you and to sons and daughters." She went aside until the couple <note>original: *lánamain*</note> had united. When the youth slept, she said: "Let me into that place now." "No," said her companion, "not until everyone sees the man who has come to me." "Fine," she said. They slept. She went out, found a candle, and put it under the thatch <note>original: *dúpla*</note> of the house so that the house caught fire.

The youth rose to save the house. "Water from the vat!" <note>original: *diaenai*</note> she said to the handmaid <note>original: *inailt*</note>. The handmaid went to the vat. She followed behind her. While the handmaid was leaning over the water, the princess grabbed her two feet and thrust her head under the water until she killed her. She did not let her up. Before the princess returned, the youth had saved the house. "Where is my handmaid?" she asked. "Alas if she has been drowned!" They saw her dead. She began to keen <note>cry out in mourning</note> over her. "Do not mind it," said the youth. She slept with him after that, and went with him to his own country.

Her father died after that, and another high-king <note>original: *airdrí*</note> took the land. Her husband also died. Great was the dignity of the king who took power there, and great was her own dignity. She called upon the king to give her a gift. She came to the king...

<meta>This page continues the story of the daughter of the King of the Greeks, following her arrival at the king's fortress and the beginning of her interactions with the court.</meta>

<page-num>415</page-num>
<header>The Daughter of the King of the Greeks.</header>
<sig>280 a]</sig>

The king gave her a great welcome, and she was at the feast along with him. "Do you have a confessor <note>anmchara</note> here?" she asked. "I have indeed," said the king: "a wonderful man." "He shall be my confessor," she said. She went then to make her confession. Everyone else was sent out. She gave her confession without concealment. When the priest <note>fer gráid</note> heard of the mortal sins she had committed and saw her very beautiful form, he began to entreat her. "No," she said; "whatever folly was done then, perhaps we have not yet done penance for it, and we shall not add further to it." The cleric did not persist in the confession. She took her leave of the king. The king went after that to speak with the confessor. He told the king the woman’s confession. "That is bad," said the king. The woman was called back to the king. "Well, woman," he said, "did you give your confession?" "Yes," she said. "Did the cleric entreat you?" "I will not be the one to say," she replied. "That is bad," said the king. "Go away, O cleric," he said, "to a place where I shall not hear mention of you."

The woman was taken by him, and an oak house was built for her at the meeting of three roads, with no way out except through small windows. She was left there. Pious people used to give her small morsels of food through them. She was seven years in that condition until she became a thin and wretched skeleton. It was told to the king that she was still alive. The house was opened for her so that she was taken into his arms and cared for until she was the most beautiful woman that ever lived. "Choose a king now," said the king, "so that you may go to him, and I will be under your spiritual guidance." "I have given myself to a King," she said, "namely to the Lord. No king to whom I might go could be better. I will not change from Him as long as I live. Let a hermitage <note>dísert</note> and a church be built for me by you." That was done. The hermitage was filled with cows, oxen, horses, gold, and silver. "Come to your building now," said the king. "Let a cleric go before me into it, namely a confessor," she said. "Who is that?" asked the king. "My own confessor," she said, "who shamed me." He was a saint then because of the penance he had performed. He came to her. They were both in the hermitage then until they went to heaven, and great miracles <note>ferta</note> were performed through them. The city that was built around them is the best city the Greeks have. That, then, was the end of the story of the sinful daughter of the Greeks.

->. The End .<-

<page-num>416 [274 a</page-num>
<header>Ambacuc.</header>

### [*These are some of the wonders of the Fair of Tailtiu*]

The Fair of Tailtiu was held by Diarmait mac Cerbaill. Ciarán mac intsaeir, his confessor <note>anmchara</note>, was at the fair along with him. Games were played and the races <note>graifni</note> of the fair were run. A woman came to find her husband at the fair and began accusing her husband of being with another woman. The man was denying that deed. "I will take his oath under the hand of Ciarán," said the woman. The man gave his oath under Ciarán’s hand that he was not guilty of the deed his own wife accused him of, but it was a lie on his part. Then a cancerous tumor <note>cnoc aillsi</note> grew on his neck where the cleric’s hand had been, and his head fell off him so that he was walking through the fair in the presence of the men of Ireland without a head, so that the name of God and of Ciarán was magnified by that miracle.

The headless man was taken by Ciarán to Clonmacnoise <note>Cluain</note> after that to be cared for as long as God should determine his life. He lived for seven years among the monks after Ciarán's death. A woman was brought to him once and he united with her, and the woman was impregnated by him and bore a son; so that he is the ancestor of the Sogain in Meath, *as others say*. However, after he had intercourse with the woman, he died immediately. He was buried by the clerics at the eastern end of Comgall’s ridge, at the place where the cross of Comgall stands today. The flagstone and grave of Ambacuc are there in memory of the story for everyone; that is one of the wonders of the Fair of Tailtiu.

This is another wonder also among the wonders of the same fair: the sight of three ships sailing in the air above them while the men of Ireland, along with Domnall mac Murchada, were holding the fair.

->. *The End* .<-
